details.point: He failed to earn marquis title despite many campaigns; astrologer attributed it to killing 800 surrendered Qiang.

details.point: In final campaign under Wei Qing, he was assigned a circuitous route, lost his way, and committed suicide rather than face trial.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Li Gan was killed by Huo Qubing; grandson Li Ling surrendered to Huns after battle, leading to family's decline.
details.label: included

details.point: Hu Sengyou was a champion from Nanyang, served Wei, returned to Liang in Datong 2nd year, and was sent to guard Xiangcheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiangcheng was captured and Hu Sengyou fell to Wei again.
details.label: included

details.point: In Zhongdatong 1st year, Hu Sengyou returned to Liang and became prefect of Nantianshui and Tianmen counties.
details.label: included

details.point: Hu Sengyou was not good at poetry but tried to compose at banquets, often ridiculed.
details.label: included

details.point: During Hou Jing's rebellion, Hu Sengyou was imprisoned for remonstrating against killing barbarian chiefs.
details.label: included

details.point: In Dashi 2nd year, Hu Sengyou was released to aid Wang Sengbian, made Marquis of Xinshi County.
details.label: included

details.point: Hu Sengyou told his son to open red and white gates for luck, vowing not to return unless victorious.
details.label: included

details.point: Hu Sengyou defeated and captured Ren Yue at Chisha Pavilion, causing Hou Jing to flee.
details.label: included

details.point: Hu Sengyou was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry and Kaifu Yitong Third Division in Chengsheng 2nd year.
details.label: included

details.point: Hu Sengyou died at 63 from a stray arrow while defending against Western Wei; his death led to panic and city capture.
details.label: included

details.point: Xu Wensheng, courtesy name Daomao, from Pengcheng, led his father's troops to surrender to Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: Xu Wensheng became governor of Ningzhou, reformed barbarian customs through virtue and power.
details.label: included

details.point: In Taiqing 2nd year, Xu Wensheng led 10,000 troops to rescue the country, appointed to command eastern campaign.
details.label: included

details.point: Xu Wensheng faced Ren Yue at Wuchang, later joined by other generals under his command.
details.label: included

details.point: Xu Wensheng refused to attack Hou Jing despite generals' advice, secretly communicated with Hou Jing due to gratitude.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xu Wensheng's army was defeated after Yingzhou was captured; he fled to Jingzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Xu Wensheng was punished for corruption, imprisoned, and died in prison.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Chan, from Duling, was the seventh son of Du Huaibao, known for courage.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Chan followed Wang Sengbian to conquer Hou Jing, fought at Baling and Shitou, defeated Hou Jing.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Chan died of illness after suppressing rebellions; Shizu mourned and granted posthumous honors.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Kuai was a dog butcher from Peixian who later hid with Emperor Gaozu.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Kuai helped Xiao He and Cao Shen bring back Liu Bang to lead the uprising.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Kuai served as a Sheren and won many battles, earning titles from Peigong.
details.label: included

details.point: At the Hongmen Banquet, Fan Kuai broke into Xiang Yu's camp and rebuked him, saving Liu Bang's life.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Kuai was granted the title of Marquis of Wuyang after Liu Bang became emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Kuai married Empress Lü's sister Lü Xu, making him close to the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Kuai once broke into the palace to admonish the ill Emperor Gaozu, comparing him to Zhao Gao.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Kuai was falsely accused of colluding with the Lü clan and was arrested, but later released by Empress Lü.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fan Kuai died in the sixth year of Emperor Xiaohui and was posthumously named Marquis Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shang gathered followers during Chen Sheng's uprising and surrendered to Peigong with 4,000 men.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shang was granted the title of Marquis of Quzhou for his military achievements.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Shang's son Li Ji deceived Lü Lu, allowing Zhou Bo to seize the Northern Army and eliminate the Lü clan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiahou Ying was a county official in Peixian who became friends with Gaozu and later served as his charioteer.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiahou Ying rescued Emperor Xiaohui and Princess Lu Yuan during the retreat from Pengcheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiahou Ying was granted the title of Marquis of Ruyin and served as a servant to Gaozu and later emperors.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Guan Ying was a silk merchant who became a cavalry commander and fought many battles for Liu Bang.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Ying led cavalry to pursue and kill Xiang Yu at Gaixia.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Guan Ying helped suppress the Lü clan and supported Emperor Wen's ascension.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fu Kuan served as a cavalry officer under Peigong and was granted the title of Marquis of Yangling.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Jie followed Gaozu as Zhongjuan, fought in many battles, and was granted the title of Marquis of Jianwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian and Ban Gu compiled biographies of Sima Xiangru, highlighting his literary fame.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Gu also wrote biographies of Jia Yi, Zou Yang, Mei Cheng, and Lu Wenru because of their literary works.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fan Ye's Book of the Later Han includes a 'Biography of Literary Figures' with detailed accounts.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu of Liang valued literary talent, rewarding good poems with gold and silk.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Yue, Jiang Yan, and Ren Fang were renowned for their literary talent.
details.label: included

details.point: Dao Hang (Dao Mao) was a talented writer from Pengcheng, known for his intelligence and literary skill.
details.label: included

details.point: Dao Hang served as a prince's tutor and was favored by Emperor Gaozu.
details.label: included

details.point: Qiu Chi, from Wuxing, was a skilled writer who authored important documents for Emperor Gaozu.
details.label: included

details.point: Qiu Chi wrote a letter that persuaded Chen Bozhi to surrender during the Northern Expedition.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bao, from Pengcheng, was a filial son and talented writer, serving in various official posts.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bao was known for his upright character and criticism of friends' faults.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Jun, from Chen County, was a diligent scholar who copied books daily and wrote 'Guan Zhen'.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Yuling, from Nanyang, was a knowledgeable official who handled Xiao Zilong's funeral.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Jianwu, Yu Yuling's brother, was a poet and official, serving under Emperor Taizong.
details.label: included

details.point: The prince criticized contemporary literary trends for being weak and imitative.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Zhao annotated Fan Ye's Book of the Later Han, producing 180 volumes of commentary.
details.label: included

details.point: He Xun, from Donghai, was a poet praised by Fan Yun and Shen Yue, known for his refined style.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhong Rong wrote 'Poetry Criticism', evaluating five-character poems from ancient to modern times.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhong Rong's preface discusses the origins and development of five-character poetry.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Xingsi, from Chen County, was a scholar and writer, composing inscriptions and poems for Emperor Gaozu.
details.label: included

details.point: Xie Bei was born in Yangxia, Chen County, with courtesy name Jingchong.
details.label: included

details.point: His grandfather Hongwei was Taichang Qing in the Song Dynasty; his father Xie Zhuang was a doctor named Youguanglu.
details.label: included

details.point: Xie Bei was intelligent as a child and could write articles at age ten.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jingwen of Langye praised Xie Bei as a child prodigy.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaowu of Song also called him a child prodigy after he composed 'Praise to the Dongjing'.
details.label: included

details.point: Xie Bei initially served as Fujun Fa Cao Xing and joined the army, then resigned as Prince Sheren due to his father's death.
details.label: included

details.point: He later served as Zhongshulang and General Yuan Can of the Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Can compared Xie Bei to Xie Lingyun.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xie Bei was impeached for bribery while serving as internal history of Linchuan, but Yuan Can shelved the case.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Qi Gao appointed Xie Bei as chief historian and he became one of the 'four friends of the emperor'.
details.label: included

details.point: Xie Bei refused to take off the jade seal during the abdication to Qi, saying 'Qi himself should have an attendant'.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Wu of Qi wanted to kill Xie Bei, but Emperor Gao said killing him would enhance his reputation, so he was dismissed and stayed home.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yongming first year, Xie Bei was recalled as Tongzhi Sanqi Changshi, then served as servant and Guozi doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yongming fifth year, he became champion general and prefect of Yixing, where he delegated tasks to subordinates.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Longchang period, he refused to serve as master of King Xin'an and became general of conquering captives and governor of Wuxing.
details.label: not_included

details.point: When Emperor Ming sought succession, Xie Bei avoided involvement and advised his brother Xie Man to drink wine and avoid personnel disputes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In Jianwu fourth year, Xie Bei refused appointments as Shizhong and Zhongshuling, and built a house in the county.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Ming issued an edict praising Xie Bei and granting him gifts, allowing him to stay in place.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In Yongyuan second and third years, Xie Bei refused further appointments, and later was forced by rebel forces but did not comply.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Emperor Gaozu of Liang ascended, Xie Bei was recruited as Shizhong, Situ, and Shangshu Ling, but he declined due to foot illness and eventually accepted after repeated urging.
details.label: included

details.point: Wan Shijun, originally named Shi Fen, was from Zhao and moved to Wen County after Tongguo fell.
details.label: included

details.point: At age 15, he served Gaozu as a minor official and was appointed Zhongjuan after Gaozu took his sister as a concubine.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to Taizhong doctor under Emperor Xiaowen and later became Prince Taifu.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Emperor Jing, he became Jiuqing and then prime minister of a princedom.
details.label: included

details.point: His four sons all reached rank of 2000 shi, and he was named Lord Wan Shi due to total salary of 10,000 dan.
details.label: included

details.point: In his old age, he retired but still showed extreme respect: dismounting at palace gates, bowing to imperial carriages.
details.label: included

details.point: He disciplined descendants by not eating; they would apologize and correct mistakes.
details.label: included

details.point: He treated imperial gifts with utmost reverence, as if before the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: His family was famous for filial piety, even surpassing Qilu literati.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianyuan 2nd year, Empress Dowager favored Wan Shijun's family over Confucians, appointing his sons Shi Jian and Shi Qing.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Jian, while visiting, secretly washed his father's clothes without his knowledge.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Jian was cautious in court: spoke freely alone but appeared inarticulate in public.
details.label: included

details.point: When Shi Qing came home drunk and didn't dismount, Wan Shijun stopped eating until Shi Qing apologized.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wan Shijun died in Yuanshuo 5th year; Shi Jian mourned deeply and died over a year later.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Jian was meticulous, e.g., counting dots in the character 'ma' and counting carriage horses.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Qing governed Qi well without punishment, earning a stone temple.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shi Qing became prince's tutor, then imperial censor, and finally prime minister in Yuanding 5th year.
details.label: included

details.point: As prime minister, he was obedient and handled affairs respectfully but offered no advice on current affairs.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yuanfeng 4th year, due to refugee crisis, he was forced to retire after offering resignation.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shi Qing died three years later; his son Shi De inherited but was dismissed for lawbreaking, ending the fief.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhao Chongguo was from Shangbang in Longxi and later moved to Jincheng Lingju.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to a guard of the feather forest due to his skill in horseback riding and archery.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Wu's reign, Zhao Chongguo broke through a Xiongnu siege, suffering over 20 injuries, and was promoted to Zhonglang and General of Chariots and Cavalry.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Emperor Zhao, he quelled a rebellion in Wudu and was promoted to Zhonglang General.
details.label: included

details.point: He captured Xiongnu King Xiqi and was promoted to post-general.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Chongguo and Huo Guang supported Emperor Xuan and were named Yingpinghou.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Benshi period, he led a campaign against the Xiongnu and was appointed Hou General and Shaofu.
details.label: included

details.point: He led 40,000 cavalry to garrison the border after a Xiongnu threat, causing Shanyu to retreat.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Chongguo impeached Yiqu Anguo for disrespect after Anguo mishandled Qiang affairs.
details.label: included

details.point: He warned that the Qiang tribes were forming alliances and recommended preparations.
details.label: included

details.point: After Anguo killed Qiang leaders and provoked a rebellion, Zhao Chongguo was appointed to lead the campaign despite being over 70.
details.label: included

details.point: He arrived at Jincheng, crossed the Yellow River cautiously, and avoided engaging enemy cavalry.
details.label: included

details.point: He used a strategy of kindness and power to recruit Han and Kai tribes, disrupting enemy plans.
details.label: included

details.point: He opposed Xin Wuxian's plan for a winter attack, arguing it was impractical and risky.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan initially favored Xin Wuxian's plan but later accepted Zhao Chongguo's strategy after his detailed rebuttal.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Chongguo defeated Xianling Qiang, capturing many livestock and vehicles, and spared villages to win over Han and Kai tribes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He proposed a farming garrison plan to reduce costs and wait for the enemy to collapse, listing twelve advantages.
details.label: included

details.point: The emperor approved the farming plan after initial debate, and Zhao Chongguo's strategy led to the surrender of over 31,000 Qiang people.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Chongguo died at age 86 and was given the title Zhuanghou; his portrait was placed in Weiyang Palace.
details.label: included

details.point: Xin Wuxian and his son Xin Qingji were also notable generals, but the Xin family later declined due to political purges.
details.label: included

details.point: Sages used xuanji to simulate the North Star and observed celestial movements to determine the calendar and agricultural seasons.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Yan distinguished eight seasons; Xuanyuan established three principles and appointed Xihe, Chang Yi, and others for astronomical duties.
details.label: included

details.point: Rong Cheng synthesized earlier methods, established the five elements, and wrote 'Adjusting the Calendar'.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties, calendars differed; the 'Biography' notes Mars visibility in different months.
details.label: included

details.point: With the Zhou decline, astronomical duties were neglected; Qin adopted the water virtue and used October as the first month.
details.label: included

details.point: Han initially followed Qin calendar; Emperor Wu ordered Sima Qian to create the 'Han Calendar' using Xia Zheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xin created 'Santong Li' but Ban Gu included it erroneously; later 'Four Point Calendar' was used from Yongping period.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Hong developed the 'Qian Xiang Calendar' with 589 as rule and 145 as dou points, improving accuracy.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Xuan annotated Liu Hong's calendar; during Huangchu, Han Yi created 'Huang Chu Li' with different parameters.
details.label: included

details.point: Debates over calendars led to testing solar eclipses; Liu Hong's predictions were more accurate than Han Yi's.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Five solar and lunar eclipses tested: Qian Xiang had four correct, Huang Chu had one correct.
details.label: included

details.point: Planetary appearances tested: Qian Xiang was closer to sky seven times, Huang Chu five times.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Wei formulated 'Jingchu Calendar' in Jingchu period; after emperor's death, Xia Zheng was reinstated.
details.label: included

details.point: Shu Han used 'Four Point Calendar'; Wu used 'Qian Xiang Calendar' until its fall.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin adopted 'Jingchu Calendar' as 'Taishi Li' but later replaced planetary calculations with Qian Xiang method.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Hong's calendar technique became the model for later calendars; his method is detailed with parameters.
details.label: included

details.point: The Qian Xiang Calendar includes calculations for solar terms, leap months, lunar phases, and eclipses.
details.label: included

details.point: The calendar provides methods for planetary positions, including Jupiter, Mars, Saturn, Venus, and Mercury.
details.label: included

details.point: Detailed steps for calculating planetary conjunctions, visibility, and retrograde motion are given.
details.label: included

details.point: The text concludes with specific numerical parameters and procedures for the Qian Xiang Calendar.
details.label: included

details.point: King Ping of Chu restored Cai with Cai Jinghou's youngest son Lu as Pinghou.

details.point: Liu Xun was born in Jie County, Hedong, and his father Shilong was Sikong in the Qi Dynasty.

details.point: Liu Xun served as Sangonglang, Prince Zhongsheren, and friend of Prince Xiang of Badong.

details.point: Liu Xun followed Zixiang to Jingzhou but returned to Beijing claiming illness, avoiding disaster.

details.point: Liu Chen was granted title of Prefecture Lingbo with 700 households for founding merit.

details.point: Kuang Heng was praised for his expertise in the Book of Songs.

details.point: Kuang Heng was appointed as Taichang's storyteller and later Pingyuan County Literature.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Wangzhi and Liang Qiuhe questioned Kuang Heng, who answered profoundly.

details.point: King Zhuang of Chu asked about the Nine Tripods, was rebuked by Wang Sunman.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhuang restored Chen state after conquering it.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhuang besieged Song for five months, withdrew due to Hua Yuan's plea.
details.label: included

details.point: King Gong of Chu was defeated at Yanling, shot in the eye.
details.label: included

details.point: King Ling of Chu built Zhanghua Terrace, asked for Zhou tripod.
details.label: included

details.point: King Ling died of starvation after his brothers usurped throne.
details.label: included

details.point: King Ping of Chu killed Wu She and his son, leading to Wu Zixu's revenge.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Zikai was the eldest son of Emperor Yi of Yin and half-brother of King Zhou.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhou ruled darkly, ignoring state affairs and indulging in licentiousness.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Zikai repeatedly advised King Zhou but was ignored.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Zikai consulted the Grand Master and Junior Master about whether to die or leave.
details.label: included

details.point: The Grand Master advised Wei Zikai to leave, so he left the Yin Dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: Jizi, a relative of King Zhou, lamented when King Zhou made ivory chopsticks, foreseeing luxury.
details.label: included

details.point: Jizi remonstrated with King Zhou but was ignored; he pretended to be mad and became a slave.
details.label: included

details.point: Prince Bigan, a relative of King Zhou, remonstrated bluntly and was killed by King Zhou, who dug out his heart.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wu of Zhou defeated the Yin Dynasty; Wei Zikai surrendered with ritual objects and was restored to his title.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wu visited Jizi and asked about the great laws; Jizi explained the Nine Great Laws (Hongfan).
details.label: included

details.point: The Nine Great Laws include Five Elements, Five Matters, Eight Political Rules, Five Epochs, Imperial Principles, Three Virtues, Divination, Various Signs, Five Blessings and Six Extremes.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wu granted Jizi the state of Korea and no longer treated him as a subject.
details.label: included

details.point: After King Wu's death, Zhou Gongdan acted as regent; Guan Shu and Cai Shu rebelled with Wu Geng.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Gong killed Wu Geng and Guan Shu, exiled Cai Shu, and enfeoffed Wei Zikai in Song to continue Yin sacrifices.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Zikai was benevolent and capable; the people of Yin loved him.
details.label: included

details.point: After Wei Zikai's death, his brother Wei Zhong succeeded; the Song ruling line continued.
details.label: included

details.point: Song Xuan Gong passed the throne to his brother Mu Gong instead of his son; later Mu Gong's son returned the throne to Xuan Gong's son.
details.label: included

details.point: Song Xianggong sought hegemony but was defeated by Chu at the Battle of Hongshui due to his insistence on chivalry.
details.label: included

details.point: Song Jinggong refused to transfer a celestial disaster to his ministers, people, or harvest, showing virtue.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Song Jun Yan (King Yan of Song) was tyrannical, called 'Jie Song', and was killed by Qi, Wei, and Chu, ending the Song state.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Hu of Chen was a descendant of Emperor Shun of Yu.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wu of Zhou enfeoffed Guiman, a descendant of Shun, in Chen to continue Shun's sacrifices.
details.label: included

details.point: The Chen ruling house traced its lineage through multiple dukes: Hu, Shen, Xiang, Xiao, Shen, You, Li, Wu, Yi, Ping, Wen, Huan, Li, Zhuang, Xuan, Mu, Gong, Ling, Cheng, Ai, Hui, Huai, and Min.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 20th year of Duke You, King Li of Zhou fled to Zhi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In the 7th year of Duke Ping, King You of Zhou was killed by Quan Rong, and the Zhou capital moved east to Luoyi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Duke Li of Chen was killed by his brothers Yue, Lin, and Chujiu with the help of Cai people.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Duke Xuan of Chen killed his crown prince Yu Kou to favor his son Ji.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Wan (Jing Zhong), fearing harm, fled to Qi and became an official under Duke Huan of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: A divination predicted that Chen Wan's descendants would prosper in Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 37th year of Duke Xuan, Yuan Taotu was arrested by Duke Huan of Qi for deceit.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Linggong, Kong Ning, and Yi Xingfu committed adultery with Xia Ji; Xia Zhengshu killed Linggong.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhuang of Chu initially annexed Chen but restored it after Shen Shushi's advice.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Ai of Chen was forced to hang himself after his brother Zhao killed the crown prince and made Liu the ruler.
details.label: included

details.point: King Ling of Chu destroyed Chen in 479 BC, but King Ping of Chu later restored Chen under Duke Hui.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Huai of Chen was detained and died in Wu after refusing Wu's summons.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 24th year of Duke Min, King Hui of Chu destroyed Chen, ending the state.
details.label: included

details.point: The descendants of Shun were enfeoffed in Chen; the descendants of Yu were enfeoffed in Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi was destroyed by Chu 34 years after Chen's fall.
details.label: included

details.point: The descendants of Shun (Chen) eventually took over Qi through Tian Chang.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian praised Shun's virtue for allowing his descendants to enjoy sacrifices for generations.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu was from Pixian County, Shu County, and learned to sing poems with Yang Fuzhong in Chengdu at age 14-15.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He Wu studied the Book of Changes, became a doctor through marksmanship test, and was promoted to county magistrate of E County.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu's brother He Xian was insulted by tax collector Qiu Shang; He Wu reported to prefect and recruited Qiu Shang as soldier.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu became governor of Yangzhou and handled cases of officials with salary of 2000 dan, including Dai Sheng.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu treated Dai Sheng's son fairly in a theft case, earning Dai Sheng's respect.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu served as governor for five years, then became Prime Minister Sizhi, later prefect of Qinghe.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu was promoted to Sili Xiaowei, Jing Zhaoyin, then demoted to internal history of Chu due to recommendation fraud.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu became imperial censor, then Da Sikong, and was granted title of Marquis of Fanxiang.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu recommended scholars like Gong Sheng, Tang Lin, and others, but hated cliques and cross-examined officials.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu and Fang Jin proposed changing internal history to lieutenant, which was approved.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu was dismissed by Emperor Ai for unfilial conduct and returned to fief.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu was later recruited as imperial censor, then former general.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu and Gongsun Lu recommended each other as Da Sima, but Empress Dowager appointed Wang Mang.
details.label: included

details.point: He Wu was dismissed and later committed suicide after being framed in Lu Kuan affair.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jia was from Huling, passed Ming Jing exam, became doctor, then magistrate of Nanling and Changling.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jia was summoned to Propaganda Office, promoted to Taizhong doctor, then governor of Jiujiang and Henan.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jia became Da Honglu, Jing Zhaoyin, imperial censor, and finally prime minister in 3rd year of Jianping.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jia advised Emperor Ai to select talented officials and forgive minor faults, recommending Gongsun Guang, Manchang, etc.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jia opposed granting titles to Dong Xian and others without proper discussion, citing loss of public trust.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jia was imprisoned and died after refusing to commit suicide; his son later granted title of Xinfu Marquis.
details.label: included

details.point: In the fourth year of Huangchu, the moon violated Antares, interpreted as the emperor's dislike.
details.label: included

details.point: In June of the same year, Venus appeared during the day, heralding war, death, rebellion, and change of monarchs.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Quan accepted Wei's title but later raised troops to resist.
details.label: included

details.point: In the fifth year of Huangchu, Venus appeared during the day again, and Jupiter retrograde in Taiwei Yuan for 149 days.
details.label: included

details.point: Divination said five stars entering Taiwei Yuan for over 30 days meant great trouble for the monarch.
details.label: included

details.point: In the seventh year of Huangchu, Emperor Wen died, Emperor Ming ascended, and granted amnesty.
details.label: included

details.point: In the sixth year, Mars entered Taiweiyuan and violated the right law enforcement star.
details.label: included

details.point: Divination said moon and five stars clashing with law enforcement stars meant trouble for ministers.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In the seventh year, several high officials died, including Cao Hong, Xiahou Shang, and Emperor Ming.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Ming asked Huang Quan about orthodoxy; Huang Quan cited celestial phenomena.
details.label: included

details.point: In the fifth year of Taihe, Mars invaded the house, divination said generals would be in trouble.
details.label: included

details.point: General Zhang He was killed by Zhuge Liang in July of that year.
details.label: included

details.point: In the sixth year, Venus appeared in the Southern Dipper during the day, indicating war in Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Quan sent Zhang Mi; Gongsun Wenyi killed Zhang Mi and captured his army.
details.label: included

details.point: In the third year of Qinglong, the moon violated Yugui, divination said many diseases and trouble for ministers.
details.label: included

details.point: In the fourth year, Venus appeared during the day for over 30 days, indicating war in Qin and Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuge Liang and Sun Quan attacked Wei; Emperor Ming marched east.
details.label: included

details.point: In the third year, a fire broke out in Chonghua Hall.
details.label: included

details.point: Saturn and Venus clashed with Jingsu Iron Star, indicating war and ministers killed.
details.label: included

details.point: In the first year of Jingchu, Saturn entered Jingsu, divination said respected person in trouble and floods.
details.label: included

details.point: An Si Yan Queen Yan Ji was born in Xingyang, Henan.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Ji was selected to join Ye Ting in the first year of Yuan Dynasty and became a noble person.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In the second year of Yuan Dynasty, she was established as queen.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Yan poisoned Li family, who gave birth to Prince Liu Bao.
details.label: included

details.point: In the third year of Yuan Dynasty, Yan Chang, Queen Yan's father, was appointed as Shizhong of Changshui and granted title of Marquis of Northern Yichun.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In the first year of Yanguang, Yan Xian was granted title of Marquis of Changshe with 13,500 households.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Queen Yan, with Jiang Jing and Fan Feng, slandered Crown Prince Liu Bao and deposed him as King Jiyin.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor An died in Ye County in the fourth year of Yanguang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Queen Yan and her brothers lied about Emperor An's illness and rushed back to Beijing.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Yan was respected as Empress Dowager and Yan Xian became chariot and cavalry general.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Dowager Yan welcomed Liu Yi, Marquis of Beixiang, as emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Xian and others purged Geng Bao and his associates.
details.label: included

details.point: After Beixiang Hou died, Sun Cheng and others conspired to establish King Jiyin as Emperor Shun.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Xian, Yan Jing, Yan Yan and their accomplices were executed; Empress Dowager Yan moved to palace and died the following year.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Shun's mother Li was posthumously named Empress Gongmin.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Shunlie Liang was the daughter of Liang Shang.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Nv was elected to Yeting at age 13 in the third year of Yongjian.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Shun regarded Liang Nv as a noble person and she declined special favor.
details.label: included

details.point: In the first year of Yangjia, Liang Nv was established as queen.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Emperor Shun died, Empress Liang became Empress Dowager and governed during Emperor Chong and Emperor Zhi's reigns.
details.label: included

details.point: Yi says: After heaven and earth, there are all things; after all things, there are men and women; after men and women, there are couples.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Morality between husband and wife is supreme.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Zhou etiquette system includes emperor establishing concubines: three wives, nine concubines, twenty-seven wives, eighty-one royal wives.
details.label: included

details.point: In early Yi Dynasty, titles followed Qin: empress dowager, empress, beauty, beloved, eighth son, seventh son.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu was frugal, ate poor food, wore simple clothes, and kept concubine numbers low.
details.label: included

details.point: Taizong and Shidan did not increase concubine numbers.
details.label: included

details.point: The queen's biological mother was Mrs. Xiao, Saitong's cousin.
details.label: included

details.point: The queen became Saitong's concubine and gave birth to King Lu Deng of Xuanwu, Lu Ti of King Zhao of Yongyang, and Zhidan.
details.label: included

details.point: The queen saw flowers growing in Changpu, picked and swallowed them, and Gaozu was born that month.
details.label: included

details.point: The queen died in the seventh year of Taishi and was buried in Dongcheng Mountain.
details.label: included

details.point: In the first year of Tianjian, she was honored as Queen with title Mi.
details.label: included

details.point: Her father Mu Zhi was a sixth-generation grandson of Zhang Hua, served as General Ningyuan and Governor of Jiaosha.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Mu Zhi died of illness before being appointed governor of Manye.
details.label: included

details.point: Gaozu posthumously gave Mu Zhi title of Guanglu Doctor and gold medal.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Xiao Yan, Emperor Wu of Liang, was named Hui, from Jinxiang, Gaoping.
details.label: included

details.point: At birth, a red light shone in the room; wizard performed exorcism by water.
details.label: not_included

details.point: She was smart, good at official script, liked histories and biographies, proficient in women's work.
details.label: not_included

details.point: She refused marriage proposals from Song deposed emperor and Anlu King Xiao Mian.
details.label: included

details.point: She married Gaozu and gave birth to three princesses.
details.label: not_included

details.point: She died in Xiangyang in first year of Yongyuan, buried in Dongchengshan.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Mian, son of general Hong Ce, was recognized as extraordinary by his grandfather Liu Zhongde.
details.label: included

details.point: At age 10, he showed emotional reactions to army victories and defeats.
details.label: included

details.point: His father Hong Ce was killed by demon thieves in 502; Zhang Mian mourned excessively.
details.label: included

details.point: He inherited the title of Marquis of Taoyang County after mourning.
details.label: included

details.point: At 18, he became governor of Huainan; his decisions were praised.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Prince Sheren and other posts, known for literary talent.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recommended for a palace vacancy due to literary merit.
details.label: included

details.point: As prefect of Wuling, he gave his salary to his mother, living frugally.
details.label: included

details.point: As internal history of Yuzhang, he governed with favor, inspiring honesty.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Yushi Zhongcheng, known for uprightness; Emperor Gaozu had his portrait painted.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at 42; Emperor Gaozu mourned deeply; Prince Zhaoming wrote a eulogy.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Mian collected over 10,000 volumes and wrote 'Hou Han Ji' and 'Jin Chao'.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Zan, Zhang Mian's brother, married Princess Fuyang at 11.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Zan was eager to learn, reading his brother's collection day and night.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Secretary Lang and refused promotion to read all books in the pavilion.
details.label: included

details.point: As Minister of Personnel, he promoted the upright and resisted pressure from the powerful.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He wrote 'Ode to the Southern Expedition' while traveling to his post.
details.label: included

details.point: As governor of Xiangzhou, he implemented reforms, leading to peace and increased households.
details.label: included

details.point: During Hou Jing's rebellion, he sowed discord between Xiao Yi and Xiao Yu, contributing to Liang's chaos.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Wan, another brother, served as Yushi Zhongcheng, known for fearlessness; he suppressed a rebellion in Yuzhang.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaoling, Liu Hong, was the great-great-grandson of Emperor Suzong.
details.label: included

details.point: He became emperor at age 12 after Emperor Huan died without children.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Dou and Dou Wu sent for Liu Hong to be emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: In 168, Dou Wu was appointed general, and Liu Hong entered Luoyang and became emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Fan was appointed Taifu, and together with Dou Wu and Hu Guang, he participated in government.
details.label: included

details.point: In 168, Duan Jiong attacked the Xianling Qiang.
details.label: included

details.point: In 168, a solar eclipse occurred, and officials were ordered to submit criticisms.
details.label: included

details.point: In 169, eunuch Cao Jie falsely claimed an imperial order to kill Chen Fan, Dou Wu, and others.
details.label: included

details.point: The Empress Dowager was moved to Nangong.
details.label: included

details.point: In 169, party members were arrested and imprisoned, with many killed or exiled.
details.label: included

details.point: In 170, the Eastern Qiang were pacified by Duan Jiong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 172, Empress Dowager Dou died.
details.label: included

details.point: In 175, the Five Classics were carved on stone tablets and set up at the Imperial Academy.
details.label: included

details.point: In 178, the Hongdumen School was established.
details.label: included

details.point: In 178, the West Residence began selling official positions.
details.label: included

details.point: In 184, Zhang Jiao led the Yellow Turban Rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: In 184, a general amnesty was granted to party members except Zhang Jiao.
details.label: included

details.point: In 189, Emperor Xiaoling died at age 34.
details.label: included

details.point: Prince Bian became emperor, with Empress Dowager He regent.
details.label: included

details.point: In 189, Dong Zhuo deposed Emperor Bian as Prince of Hongnong.
details.label: included

details.point: Yelang is the largest among the rulers of Nanyi.
details.label: included

details.point: People in these countries wear cone-shaped buns, cultivate fields, and have towns.
details.label: included

details.point: Lun and Kunming have braided hair, move with livestock, and have no fixed residence or ruler.
details.label: included

details.point: King Chu Wei sent Zhuang Qiao to capture areas west of Bajun and Qianzhong.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuang Qiao became king in Yunnan after Qin blocked his return.
details.label: included

details.point: During Qin, the area was captured and officials appointed; after Qin fell, Han abandoned the area.
details.label: included

details.point: Tang Meng proposed using Yelang's troops to attack Nanyue via the Zangke River.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu agreed, and Tang Meng established Jianwei County in Yelang.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Xiangru established counties in Xiyi, but road-building difficulties led to suspension.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Qian reported Shu goods in Daxia, prompting searches for a route to Shendu.
details.label: included

details.point: Dian king and Yelang marquis asked which was larger, Han or their own state.
details.label: included

details.point: Qielan rebelled and killed Han envoys; Han suppressed and established Zangke County.
details.label: included

details.point: Yelang marquis submitted and was made King of Yelang.
details.label: included

details.point: Han established counties in Qiongdu, Zhadu, Ranmang, and Baima areas.
details.label: included

details.point: Dian king initially refused to submit; after military pressure, Dian became Yizhou County.
details.label: included

details.point: Yelang and Dian were the only southwestern barbarian leaders to receive royal seals.
details.label: included

details.point: Later rebellions in Yizhou were suppressed with heavy casualties.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Li killed Yelang king Wang Xing for disobedience.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang demoted Gouding king; rebellions followed, causing great expense and loss.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Tuo established Nanyue kingdom; after initial conflict, submitted to Han under Emperor Wen.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang served as Lu Lu's retainer during Empress Lu's period.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang criticized Zhou Bo as a 'hero' not a 'state minister' for his pride.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang defended Zhou Bo when he was accused of treason, leading to their friendship.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang advised reducing the fief of Liu Chang, King of Huainan, but was ignored.
details.label: included

details.point: After Liu Chang rebelled and died in exile, Yuan Ang consoled Emperor Wen by citing his three virtues.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang humiliated eunuch Zhao Tan, causing him to be removed from the emperor's carriage.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang stopped Emperor Wen from galloping down Baling slope, citing safety.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang corrected seating order between Empress and Consort Shen, citing propriety.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang served as prime minister of Wu, following his nephew's advice to avoid conflict.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang confronted Prime Minister Shen Tujia for arrogance, leading to reconciliation.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang and Chao Cuo were enemies; Chao Cuo investigated Yuan Ang's acceptance of Wu's money.
details.label: included

details.point: During Wu-Chu rebellion, Yuan Ang advised Emperor Jing to kill Chao Cuo to pacify rebels.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang was sent to Wu as envoy; Wu king tried to kill him, but a former subordinate helped him escape.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang retired but was assassinated by Liang king's agents for opposing his succession.
details.label: included

details.point: Chao Cuo studied Shangshu under Fu Sheng and became a favored advisor to Crown Prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Chao Cuo wrote on military affairs, comparing Han and Xiongnu strengths, and advocated frontier colonization.
details.label: included

details.point: Chao Cuo proposed building fortified settlements and recruiting criminals and volunteers to defend borders.
details.label: included

details.point: Chao Cuo's policies on reducing feudal territories caused resentment among princes.
details.label: included

details.point: Chao Cuo was executed after Wu-Chu rebellion, despite his father's warnings.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Gong defended Chao Cuo posthumously, saying his death served the rebels' interests.

details.point: Legend advocates governing with etiquette to foster integrity and correct mistakes.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu's era is considered inferior to the Fuxi clan's era in terms of governance.
details.label: included

details.point: Prison sentences are looked down upon; benevolent policies are prioritized to eliminate disasters.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius emphasized eliminating lawsuits entirely.

details.point: Zhou Dynasty collected weapons, nurtured people, and imitated Yao and Yu's benevolence.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin Wen invented torture for three tribes; Qin Shihuang added beating and threatening.

details.point: Liu Bang made a three-chapter agreement to appease people; Emperor Wen ruled with punishment, bringing happiness.

details.point: Human life is most important; killing is easy but survival is hard.

details.point: Emperor Shizu adopted ancient criminal law and unified laws, making people comfortable.

details.point: Jin Dynasty moved south; for 102 years, they yearned for old laws.

details.point: Three Emperors and Five Emperors used image punishments; people knew prohibitions.

details.point: Shun ordered Gao Tao to punish according to crime; five punishments executed in wilderness, city, and court.

details.point: Zhou Dynasty used three types of criminal laws and five listening methods to understand people.

details.point: Sima Fa stated that armies are raised to conquer unjust people; those who disturb order are punished.

details.point: Wu Huanghu ordered new laws because previous laws were suspicious.

details.point: Emperor Guangwu paid attention to litigation and personally adjudicated suspicious matters.

details.point: Emperor Wen reduced corporal punishment and excepted criminal law of sitting; world reached peace.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Wu mobilized troops; people were exhausted; cunning officials played with law.

details.point: Liu Fei, King Hui of Qi, was the eldest son of Emperor Gaozu.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu granted Liu Fei the title of King of Qi with seventy cities.
details.label: included

details.point: In the second year of Emperor Xiaohui, King Qi visited the capital and was treated as a brother by the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Lu was angered and wanted to kill King Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: King Qi donated Chengyang County to Princess Lu Yuan to appease Empress Dowager Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: King Hui died in the sixth year of Emperor Hui; his son Liu Xiang succeeded as King Ai.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Xiaohui's death, Empress Dowager Lu took control and enfeoffed Lu family members as kings.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Lu divided Qi's Jinan County to King Lu and later Langxie County to Liu Ze.
