details.point: Cao Shen was born in Peixian County and served as warden under Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: He followed Liu Bang (Duke of Pei) as Zhongjuan.
details.label: included

details.point: He led attacks on Huling, Fangyu, and defeated Qin forces.
details.label: included

details.point: He captured Xuexian and defeated the Sishui Governor's army.
details.label: included

details.point: He recaptured Fangyu and Fengyi after they rebelled to Wei.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was granted the title of Seventh Doctor by Duke Pei.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He defeated Qin Sima Yi and captured Shanzhiyi, Hufu, and Qi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He attacked west of Xiayi and fought Zhang Han's army.
details.label: included

details.point: He was first to climb the tower at Yuan Qi and Kang Fu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He rescued Dong'a, captured Chen, and pursued to Puyang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He killed Li You and captured a Qin commander at Yongqiu.
details.label: included

details.point: After Xiang Liang's death, Pei Gong became governor of Dang; Cao Shen became Jiancheng Lord.
details.label: partially_included

details.point: He defeated Dongjun's army and Wang Li's army.
details.label: included

details.point: He defeated Zhao Bi and Yang Xiong, captured Sima and Yushi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He captured Wuguan and Yaoguan, then defeated Qin at Lantian, reaching Xianyang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Xiang Yu made Liu Bang King of Han, Cao Shen became Marquis of Jiancheng.
details.label: included

details.point: He pacified the Three Qins, capturing Xiabian, Gudao, Yong, and Xi.
details.label: included

details.point: He defeated Zhang Ping, Zhao Bi, and Nei Shibao, and captured Xianyang (renamed Xincheng).
details.label: not_included

details.point: He served as acting Left Prime Minister, defeated Wei, captured King Bao of Wei and 52 cities.
details.label: included

details.point: He followed Han Xin to defeat Zhao, Qi, and Long Qie, pacifying over 70 counties in Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor An, named Dezong, was the eldest son of Emperor Xiaowu.
details.label: included

details.point: In 396, Emperor Xiaowu died and Dezong became emperor, changing the reign title to Long'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Gong and Yu Kai raised troops against Wang Guobao and Wang Xu, who were killed to appease them.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun En rebelled in 399, capturing Kuaiji and killing officials.
details.label: included

details.point: Huan Xuan rebelled in 402, defeated the imperial army, and took control of the capital.
details.label: included

details.point: In 403, Huan Xuan usurped the throne, forcing Emperor An to abdicate.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yu raised troops in 404, defeated Huan Xuan, and restored Emperor An.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor An was restored in 405, and Liu Yu became the dominant power.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yu led campaigns against Murong Chao (409-410) and Yao Hong (416-417), expanding Jin territory.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor An was intellectually disabled, unable to speak or care for himself.
details.label: included

details.point: In 418, Liu Yu had Emperor An strangled to fulfill a prophecy of two emperors after Ming.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gong, named Dewen, was Emperor An's half-brother and succeeded him.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gong was initially Prince of Langxie and held high offices under Huan Xuan.
details.label: included

details.point: After Huan Xuan's defeat, Emperor Gong was restored as Prince of Langxie.
details.label: included

details.point: In 420, Liu Yu forced Emperor Gong to abdicate, ending the Jin dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gong was made Prince of Lingling and later killed by Liu Yu's agents in 421.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gong was known for his filial piety and devotion to Buddhism.
details.label: included

details.point: The Jin dynasty lasted 104 years from its founding to the abdication.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor An's reign was marked by rebellions and the rise of Liu Yu.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gong accepted abdication calmly, writing the edict on red paper.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan of Han believed fair administration and lawsuits define a good governor.
details.label: included

details.point: Local governors are called officials close to the people, responsible for moral education and customs.
details.label: included

details.point: At the end of Qi Dynasty, government was chaotic with harsh taxes and corvée.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu of Liang, understanding people's suffering, exempted heavy taxes and allowed recuperation.
details.label: included

details.point: Gaozu personally handled affairs, sent envoys to inspect customs, and set up lung stones for complaints.
details.label: included

details.point: In Tianjian 1st year, taxes on minors were removed; Gaozu wore washed clothes and promoted frugality.
details.label: included

details.point: Gaozu selected honest local governors, personally summoned and encouraged benevolent policies.
details.label: included

details.point: Gaozu promoted capable magistrates to larger counties and governors; examples: Qiu Zhongfu and He Yuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Mi, a filial son, served in various posts, was honest and poor, refused gifts, died in poverty.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Zhen punished bullies, was trusted by Xiao Ziliang, built roads efficiently, and planted trees.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Zhen persuaded Chen Bozhi to surrender to Gaozu, later served as Yuyao magistrate, punished corrupt families.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Zhen was killed by robbers, likely by Xiao Yingda; his son sued but Xiao died.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Shuzeng, a scholar, served as governor of Yongjia, refused gifts, left with simple luggage.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Qiu Zhongfu, a former thief, became Shanyin magistrate with outstanding achievements, later served in various posts.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Qian served as magistrate of several counties, was honest, frugal, and lived to 92.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Qu served as governor of Yongyang and Xin'an, was honest, used salary to pay taxes for people.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fu Qu resented being surpassed by He Yuan, feigned illness, was impeached but pardoned by Gaozu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He Yuan, a former rebel, served as Wuchang prefect, bought cold water, was frugal and strict.
details.label: included

details.point: He Yuan was promoted to Xuancheng governor, built roads, used salary for poor people's taxes.
details.label: included

details.point: Yao Cha commented that Liang Dynasty's benevolent policies led to honest customs, no cruel officials needed.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun, courtesy name Yanlong, was born in Wuyin, Nanxiang, and was a sixth-generation descendant of Jiewang, the Pingbei general of the Jin Dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: At age eight, Fan Yun met Yin Yan, governor of Yuzhou, and impressed him by composing a poem instantly.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun studied with his relative Yuan Zhao, who predicted he would become a talented person.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun was captured by Shen Youzhi's rebel forces but remained calm and was released.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun served as chief administrator under Prince Jingling of Qi and was highly valued.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun correctly interpreted the omen of a white crow for Emperor Gao of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: As internal history of Lingling, Fan Yun governed with integrity, reducing government burdens.
details.label: included

details.point: As internal history of Shixing, Fan Yun pacified the region by removing surveillance posts and using kindness.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun was imprisoned due to a false accusation but was pardoned by amnesty.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun served as Huangmen Shilang under Liang Gaozu and assisted in strategizing.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun and Wang Mao remonstrated with Liang Gaozu about his affair with Yu, leading to her dismissal.
details.label: included

details.point: After Liang Gaozu's ascension, Fan Yun was made Marquis of Xiaocheng County with 1,000 households.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun was praised by Liang Gaozu as a brother and honored by princes Xiao Hong and Xiao Hui.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun was known for his integrity, supporting his widowed sister-in-law and helping the poor.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun advised Prince Wenhui of Qi to understand farming hardships.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun died in the second year of Tianjian at age 53; Liang Gaozu mourned deeply.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun was posthumously given the title Wen, and his collected works comprised 30 volumes.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Yue, courtesy name Xiuwen, was born in Wukang, Wuxing; his father was Shen Yilong.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Yue was a key advisor to Liang Gaozu, urging him to accept the throne and drafting the abdication edict.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Yue served as Shangshu Ling and other high offices, but was criticized for not recommending talents.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jiao was the younger half-brother of Emperor Gaozu and was made King of Chu in the sixth year of Gaozu's reign.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu resented his sister-in-law for pretending to have no soup, so he did not initially enfeoff her son, but later granted him the title of Marquis of Genjie.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jiao died in the 23rd year of his reign, succeeded by his son Liu Ying (King Yi).
details.label: included

details.point: King Yi died in the fourth year of his reign, succeeded by his son Liu Wu (King Wu).
details.label: not_included

details.point: Twenty years into King Wu's reign, he committed a crime during Empress Dowager Bo's mourning period and lost Donghai County.
details.label: included

details.point: The next spring, King Wu conspired with the King of Wu to rebel, killing his prime minister Zhang Shang and Grand Tutor Zhao Yiwu.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wu of Chu joined the King of Wu in attacking Liang, capturing Jibi, but was defeated by Zhou Yafu at Changyi.
details.label: included

details.point: The Han army cut off Wu and Chu's food supplies; King Wu of Chu committed suicide, and the rebellion was suppressed.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaojing initially wanted to continue the Chu line, but Empress Dowager Dou opposed continuing Wu's line.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Li, then Zongzheng, was made King of Chu (King Wen) to continue Liu Jiao's ancestral temple.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wen died after three years, succeeded by his son Liu Dao (King An).
details.label: not_included

details.point: King An died after 22 years, succeeded by his son Liu Zhu (King Xiang).
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Xiang died after 14 years, succeeded by his son Liu Chun.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In the second year of Dijie, eunuchs accused Liu Chun of rebellion; he committed suicide, and Chu was abolished as Pengcheng County.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Sui, King of Zhao, was a son of Gaozu, posthumously named You (King You).
details.label: included

details.point: After Empress Gao's death, ministers executed Lu Lu and made King You's son King of Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: In the second year of Emperor Xiaowen, Liu Sui's younger brother Piqiang was made King of Hejian (King Wen).
details.label: included

details.point: King Wen of Hejian died after 13 years, succeeded by his son Ai Wang Fu, who died without heirs, and Hejian was abolished.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Xiaojing's reign, Chao Cuo deprived Zhao of Changshan County; King Zhao conspired with Wu and Chu to rebel.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhao killed his prime minister Jiande and internal history Wang Han, but was besieged by Li Ji and Luan Bu; Handan fell, and King Zhao committed suicide, ending his line.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Chui was from Wu County, Wu County, and was the sixth-generation grandson of Lu Wan, Taiwei of Jin.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Chui studied diligently, built a thatched house, and could recite texts after one reading.
details.label: included

details.point: He silently copied missing volumes of Han Shu from memory without error.
details.label: included

details.point: At 17, he was elected as a scholar of the state.
details.label: included

details.point: He served in various official positions under Liang, including Yi Cao and Fa Cao.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Chui was friends with Ren Fang and wrote 'Perception of Ji Fu' for him.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was highly regarded by Emperor Gaozu for his literary talent, receiving silk rewards.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He held many high offices, including Zhongshu Shilang, Huangmen Shilang, and Taichang Qing.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lu Chui died at age 57; his collected works had 20 volumes.
details.label: included

details.point: Dao Qia was from Pengcheng, known for talent and moral character.
details.label: included

details.point: Xie Tiao praised Dao Qia as having both civil and military talents.
details.label: included

details.point: Dao Qia refused official posts and lived in seclusion for years.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Fang admired Dao Qia, calling him unparalleled in the world.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Dao Qia served as crown prince's sacrificer and later as Zhongcheng, known for strong uprightness.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at age 51; posthumously given title of Shizhong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shan Bin was from Pingyuan, learned in scriptures and rituals from age 13.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Doctor of Five Classics and later as governor of Northern Yanzhou.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shan Bin secretly released grain to help people during famine and did not defend himself when blamed.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at age 85; posthumously given Shizhong and General Xinwei.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yin Jun was from Chen County, married to Princess Yongxing, and served in various posts including Huangmen Shilang and Neishi of Linchuan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Wu's name was Sima Yan, courtesy name Anshi, eldest son of Emperor Wen of Jin.
details.label: included

details.point: He was granted the title of Tinghou of Beiping during the Jiaping period of Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: He welcomed Changdao Xianggong to the throne and was made Xinchang Xianghou of Jin.
details.label: included

details.point: He was established as heir apparent of Jin State and appointed General of Fujun.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen initially intended to pass the throne to Sima You, but He Zeng and others insisted on Sima Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: In 265, Sima Yan became crown prince of Jin, then inherited the titles of Prime Minister and King of Jin after Emperor Wen's death.
details.label: included

details.point: He relaxed punishments, pardoned sinners, and reduced corvee labor.
details.label: included

details.point: In November 265, he set up the Fourth Guard Army.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He ordered officials to recommend talents based on six standards.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Wei emperor abdicated, and Sima Yan became emperor in December 265, establishing the Jin Dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: He granted the former Wei emperor the title of King Chenliu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He posthumously honored his ancestors as emperors and enfeoffed many imperial relatives as kings.
details.label: included

details.point: He promoted frugality, removed pearls and jade from the palace, and rewarded officials.
details.label: included

details.point: He established the crown prince Sima Zhong in 267.
details.label: included

details.point: He implemented a system of local officials touring counties every three years.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He launched a large-scale campaign against Wu in 279, leading to Wu's surrender in 280.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Hao surrendered, and Jin unified China; Wu's territories were incorporated.
details.label: included

details.point: He granted Sun Hao the title of Marquis of Guiming.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In his later years, he neglected state affairs, indulged in banquets, and favored the queen's family.
details.label: included

details.point: He died in 290 at age 55, buried in Junyang Mausoleum; his reign saw initial prosperity but later decline.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Dynasty inherited Warring States turmoil, leading to arrogant and cunning people.
details.label: included

details.point: Officials acted arbitrarily, killing traitors first and then reporting.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Wenshu was known as 'tiger-crowned official', Yan Yannian as 'butcher'.
details.label: included

details.point: Since Zhongxing, laws tightened, but eunuchs and relatives harmed the world.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Xuan killed Gongsun Dan's son for murdering a passerby to ward off disaster.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Xuan arrested and killed over 30 of Gongsun Dan's clan for armed protest.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Xuan was imprisoned but recited poems without worry; Guangwu pardoned him.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Xuan became magistrate of Luoyang, killed Princess Huyang's slave for murder.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Xuan refused to apologize to princess, Guangwu called him 'stiff-necked magistrate'.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Dong Xuan died poor, with only barley and a broken cart; Guangwu honored him.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fan Ye sent dry food to Guangwu when poor; later became prefect of Tianshui.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fan Ye ruled Tianshui harshly; people sang 'rather see tiger's cave than enter Tianshui temple'.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Zhang killed Zhao Gang at a banquet, then attacked his fortress.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Zhang led troops to rescue prefect Chu Xing, killed rebel Xia Changsi.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Jin killed dozens of powerful criminals in Tang; later hid pardons to execute first.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Jin arrested Ting Yu for murder, exposed his deception; nobles feared him.
details.label: included

details.point: Huang Chang reunited with his wife after 20 years; she was captured by thieves.
details.label: included

details.point: Huang Chang executed Mrs. Peng for watching him from a high building.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Qiu killed Wang Fu and his son by torture, displayed corpse with 'thief Wang Fu'.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Qiu was executed after plotting against eunuchs; Wang Ji killed over 10,000 in five years.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Mu (Sima Dan) became emperor at age 2 with Empress Dowager regent.
details.label: included

details.point: In 345, Huan Wen appointed Anxi General, governor of six provinces.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 347, Huan Wen conquered Shu; Li Shi surrendered.
details.label: included

details.point: In 349, Shi Jilong died; his sons fought for power.
details.label: included

details.point: In 350, Ran Min killed Shi Jian, founded Wei.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 351, Fu Jian proclaimed himself king of Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: In 352, Ran Min killed by Murong Jun; Murong Jun founded Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: In 354, Huan Wen's northern expedition defeated at Bailuyuan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 356, Huan Wen defeated Yao Xiang; captured Luoyang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 357, Fu Jian killed Fu Sheng, became king of Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: In 361, Emperor Mu died at 19; succeeded by Emperor Ai (Sima Pi).
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Ai took elixirs, became ill; Empress Dowager regent again.
details.label: included

details.point: In 365, Murong Ke captured Luoyang; Shen Jin died.
details.label: included

details.point: In 366, Sima Xun rebelled, claimed King of Chengdu; later killed.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 369, Huan Wen's northern expedition reached Fangtou, then retreated.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 370, Fu Jian conquered Yan; Murong Wei captured.
details.label: included

details.point: In 371, Huan Wen deposed Emperor Fei (Sima Yi) as Duke of Haixi.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Fei was accused of impotence and having illegitimate sons.
details.label: included

details.point: Deposed emperor lived in Wu, avoided politics, died at 45.
details.label: included

details.point: Huan Wen's deposition increased his power; emperor's compliance saved his life.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yuan Faseng was a relative of the Wei family and a descendant of Emperor Daowu of Northern Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as an official in Northern Wei, including Guanglu doctor and Xuzhou governor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In the fifth year of the ordinary era, he occupied Pengcheng and proclaimed himself emperor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He later submitted to the Liang Dynasty and was appointed Shizhong and Sikong.
details.label: included

details.point: He was favored by Emperor Gaozu of Liang and given a house, female musicians, and gold and silk.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He died at age 83, holding titles including Taiwei.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Yuan Jinglong was granted titles and served as governor of Guangzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Yuan Jingzhong responded to Hou Jing's rebellion and hanged himself after being abandoned by his troops.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuanshu, a close relative of Northern Wei, served as an official in Wei and later submitted to Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuanshu was captured and died angrily in Northern Wei at age 48.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Yuanda, a branch of Wei, submitted to Liang and was granted titles; died at 57.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Shennian, from Qi, was fond of Confucianism and served as an official in Northern Wei and Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Shennian demolished a temple to stop superstition; died at 75.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hua, from Wudu, was forced into adultery by Empress Dowager Hu and surrendered to Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hua surrendered to Hou Jing during the rebellion and died in enemy territory.
details.label: included

details.point: Yangkan, from Taishan, was a brave general who shot Mo Zhe Niansheng's brother.
details.label: included

details.point: Yangkan led troops to return to Liang, killing a Wei envoy; arrived with over 10,000 soldiers.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yangkan defended the capital against Hou Jing, refusing to surrender and shooting at his captured son.
details.label: included

details.point: Yangkan died of illness at 54 during the siege; his son Yang Min killed Hou Jing.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang Yaren, from Taishan, led troops to aid the court during Hou Jing's rebellion and was killed fleeing.
details.label: included

details.point: Kang Shu was the half-brother of King Wu of Zhou and was granted the state of Wei after the rebellion of Wu Geng and Guan Shu and Cai Shu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Gongdan wrote 'Kang Gao', 'Jiu Gao', and 'Zi Cai' to instruct Kang Shu on governance.
details.label: included

details.point: Kang Shu governed Wei well, and the people were happy.
details.label: included

details.point: After Kang Shu's death, his descendants ruled Wei for many generations.
details.label: included

details.point: Qing Hou bribed King Yi of Zhou to have the ruler of Wei titled marquis.
details.label: included

details.point: During Li Hou's reign, the 'Republican Administration' occurred when King Li of Zhou fled.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Gong reorganized Kang Shu's government and helped King Ping of Zhou, earning the title of duke.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Zhuang of Wei married a daughter of Qi, but she was childless; he later made Wan his heir.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Xu killed Duke Huan and usurped the throne, but was killed by Shi Que.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Xuan of Wei took his son's bride and later killed his son Ji and Ji's brother Shou.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Hui of Wei fled after being attacked by the left and right sons, but was restored by Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Yi of Wei loved cranes and was killed by the Zhai people.
details.label: included

details.point: The people of Wei made Dai Gong and then Wen Gong rulers; Wen Gong reduced taxes and won the people's hearts.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Cheng of Wei fled to Chu after conflict with Jin, but was later restored.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Xian of Wei was driven out by Sun Wenzi after offending him, but later restored by Jin.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Duke Linggong's son Kuai Kui tried to kill Nan Zi and fled; after Linggong's death, Zhe became duke.
details.label: included

details.point: Kuai Kui later returned and became Duke Zhuang of Wei with the help of Kong Kui.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Zhuang fled after conflict with Rongzhou, and Wei had several short-lived rulers.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei was demoted to a marquisate and later to a lordship, eventually losing territory to Qin.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The state of Wei ended when the Second Emperor of Qin deposed Lord Jiao, making him a commoner.
details.label: included

details.point: The Wei family descended from Bi Gonggao, a descendant of the Zhou royal family.
details.label: included

details.point: Bi Wan, a descendant, served Duke Xian of Jin and was granted Wei, becoming a high official.
details.label: included

details.point: Bi Wan's descendants adopted Wei as their surname.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Wuzi followed Chong'er (Duke Wen of Jin) into exile and later became a high official.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Jiang served Duke Ao of Jin, killed Yang Qian's servants, and later made peace with Rong and Di.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xianzi served Duke Zhao of Jin and later took charge of state affairs.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Chi, Wei Huanzi, and others fought against the Fan, Zhonghang, and Zhibo families.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Wenhou (Wei Si) was the first ruler of Wei as a state.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Wenhou respected Confucian scholars and wise men, earning praise from the princes.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Wenhou appointed Wei Chengzi as prime minister over Zhai Huang based on Li Ke's advice.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Wuhou succeeded Wenhou and fought against Zhao and Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: King Hui of Wei succeeded Wuhou after a succession struggle.
details.label: included

details.point: King Hui suffered defeats by Qi, Zhao, and Qin, and moved the capital to Daliang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Hui recruited scholars like Mencius, who advised him to focus on benevolence and righteousness.
details.label: included

details.point: King Xiang succeeded Hui and faced Qin attacks, ceding land to Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhao of Wei faced Qin invasions and lost territory, including the cession of 400 li.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Anli of Wei faced Qin attacks and sought help from Qin, but later considered attacking Han.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lord Xinling Wuji advised King Anli against allying with Qin and later rescued Zhao by stealing the army.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Jingmin succeeded Anli and lost 20 cities to Qin, which established the East Commandery.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei was finally destroyed when Qin flooded Daliang and captured King Wei Jia.
details.label: included

details.point: Cai Yong, courtesy name Bo Zhe, was from Chenliu Yuxian.
details.label: included

details.point: His sixth-generation ancestor Cai Xun refused to serve Wang Mang and fled into the mountains.
details.label: included

details.point: Cai Yong was filial, tending to his ill mother for three years without undressing.
details.label: included

details.point: He lived with his uncle and brothers, with the family undivided for three generations.
details.label: included

details.point: He was erudite, studied under Hu Guang, and excelled in literature, mathematics, astronomy, and music.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Huan's reign, he feigned illness to avoid serving the eunuchs.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote 'Explanation' to encourage himself, inspired by Dongfang Shuo and others.
details.label: included

details.point: In 175 AD, he led a petition to correct the Six Classics, and Emperor Ling approved.
details.label: included

details.point: He personally wrote the classics on stone steles, erected outside the Taixue gate.
details.label: included

details.point: He submitted a memorial criticizing the three-mutual prohibition and urging its abolition.
details.label: included

details.point: He submitted a secret memorial listing seven measures to address disasters and maladministration.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The memorial was leaked by Cao Jie, leading to enmity from eunuchs.
details.label: included

details.point: He was falsely accused and imprisoned, sentenced to death, but reduced to exile in Shuofang.
details.label: included

details.point: Assassins sent by Yang Qiu were moved by his righteousness and did not kill him.
details.label: included

details.point: He was pardoned after nine months but fled to Wu for twelve years due to further threats.
details.label: included

details.point: In Wu, he made the 'Jiaowei Qin' from a burnt tung tree.
details.label: included

details.point: He demonstrated his musical perception by detecting murderous intent in a neighbor's music.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Dong Zhuo forced him into service; he was promoted rapidly and became Marquis of Gaoyang.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised Dong Zhuo against taking the title 'Shangfu' and on earthquake omens.
details.label: included

details.point: After Dong Zhuo's death, he sighed and was executed by Wang Yun despite pleas for his life.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Suzong Xiaozhang, named Huodan, was the fifth son of Xianzong.
details.label: included

details.point: He became emperor on the sixth day of August in the eighteenth year of Yongping at age 19.
details.label: included

details.point: He issued a general amnesty and granted titles and grain to the people.
details.label: included

details.point: He appointed Zhao Xi as Taifu and Mou Rong as Taiwei.
details.label: included

details.point: A solar eclipse occurred on the 30th day of the 11th month, leading to avoidance of the main hall and suspension of court.
details.label: included

details.point: He praised Emperor Xiaoming's virtues and ordered sacrifices according to his wishes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In the first year of Jianchu, he ordered aid for the poor and encouraged agriculture.
details.label: included

details.point: He defeated the Che Division and appointed Duan Peng as Wuji School Lieutenant.
details.label: included

details.point: Wuling and Lizhong barbarians rebelled.
details.label: included

details.point: He ordered recommendations of virtuous and upright persons.
details.label: included

details.point: He granted Shanglin Garden land to the poor.
details.label: included

details.point: A comet appeared in Tianshixing.
details.label: included

details.point: Yongchang Ailao Yi rebelled and was suppressed.
details.label: included

details.point: Fuling King Liu Yan rebelled and was demoted.
details.label: included

details.point: He criticized extravagance and ordered correction of illegal behavior.
details.label: included

details.point: He ordered the return of families displaced by rebellions.
details.label: included

details.point: The Shaodang Qiang rebelled and were defeated by Ma Fang.
details.label: included

details.point: He established the noble Dou family as queen.
details.label: included

details.point: He ordered the construction of river canals to be stopped.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Fang was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry.
details.label: included

details.point: The Rites of Zhou describes the emperor's harem hierarchy: queen, three wives, nine concubines, twenty-seven wives, and eighty-one female concubines.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Guo Shengtong was from Zhending, daughter of Guo Chang and Lord Guo, married Guangwu in 24 CE, became queen in 26 CE, deposed in 41 CE, died in 52 CE.
details.label: included

details.point: Guangwu deposed Queen Guo due to her resentment and declining favor, made her Queen Mother of Zhongshan, later of Pei.
details.label: included

details.point: Guangwu favored the Guo family, ennobled Guo Kuang as Marquis of Yang'an, known as 'Golden Cave'.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Yin Lihua was from Nanyang, married Guangwu in 23 CE, became noble, then queen in 41 CE after Guo's deposition.
details.label: included

details.point: Yin Lihua was known for her virtue and humility, refused the queen position initially because Guo had a son.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Ming honored Yin as empress dowager, she died in 64 CE, buried with Guangwu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Ma (Mingde) was daughter of Ma Yuan, entered crown prince's palace at 13, became queen in 60 CE.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Ma raised Emperor Zhang as her own, was known for frugality and virtue, refused to ennoble her brothers.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Ma issued edicts against ennobling relatives, citing historical warnings.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dou (Zhangde) was from Fufeng, became queen in 78 CE, favored, had no children, slandered Song and Liang nobles.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou caused deposition of Crown Prince Liu Qing and death of Liang nobles, later her family conspired and was executed.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Yin (Hedi) was great-niece of Yin Lihua, became queen in 96 CE, deposed for witchcraft in 102 CE, died.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Deng Sui (Hedi) was granddaughter of Deng Yu, entered palace in 95 CE, became queen in 102 CE.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Sui was known for her intelligence, virtue, and humility, served as regent after Hedi's death.
details.label: included

details.point: As regent, Empress Dowager Deng reduced palace expenses, abolished superstitions, and promoted education.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Sui handled state affairs during disasters, maintained peace, and was praised for her governance.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Deng died in 121 CE, after 20 years of regency, buried with Hedi.
details.label: included

details.point: Historians criticized Deng for not returning power to Emperor An, but noted her good intentions.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The text traces the evolution of the concubine system from Zhou to Han, highlighting the dangers of female regents and favoritism.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Sheng and Wu Guang were leaders of the Daze Township uprising.
details.label: included

details.point: They were among 900 conscripts delayed by rain, facing execution for missing the deadline.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Sheng argued that fleeing and rebelling both lead to death, so rebellion is better.
details.label: included

details.point: They decided to use the names of Prince Fusu and General Xiang Yan to gain support.
details.label: included

details.point: They used omens: a fish with a silk book saying 'King Chen Sheng' and a fox cry 'Great Chu will rise, King Chen Sheng'.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Guang provoked the escorting officers, leading to their killing by Chen Sheng and Wu Guang.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Sheng declared, 'Are princes, generals and ministers born noble?' to inspire the troops.
details.label: included

details.point: They proclaimed the uprising in the name of Fusu and Xiang Yan, calling it 'Great Chu'.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Sheng appointed himself general and Wu Guang as captain.
details.label: included

details.point: They captured Daze Township, Qi, Feng, Kuzhe, Qiao, and Chen County, growing their army.
details.label: included

details.point: At Chen County, Chen Sheng proclaimed himself king, naming his state 'Zhang Chu'.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Guang was sent to attack Xingyang but failed to capture it.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Sheng sent Zhou Wen west to attack Qin; Zhou Wen was defeated by Zhang Han and committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Chen proclaimed himself King of Zhao; Chen Sheng initially angry but later confirmed him.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Guang proclaimed himself King of Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan proclaimed himself King of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Ningling Jun Jiu was made King of Wei by Chen Sheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Guang was killed by his own generals under Tian Zang, who then led troops against Qin and died.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Sheng was betrayed and killed by his charioteer Zhuang Jia in December.
details.label: included

details.point: After Chen Sheng's death, his general Lu Chen killed Zhuang Jia and reoccupied Chen County.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Taizong gave birth to Prince Xiao Daqi, Xiao Dalian; Chen Shurong gave birth to Xiao Daxin; Mrs. Zuo gave birth to Xiao Dalin, Xiao Dachun; Mrs. Xie gave birth to Xiao Daya; Mrs. Zhang gave birth to Xiao Dazhuang; Bao Zhaohua gave birth to Xiao Dajun; Mrs. Fan gave birth to Xiao Dawei; Chu Xiuhua gave birth to Xiao Daqiu; Mrs. Chen gave birth to Xiao Daxin; Mrs. Zhu gave birth to Xiao Dazhi.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Daxin, King of Xunyang, was granted title of Dangyang Gong in 4th year of Zhongdatong, with 1,500 households.
details.label: included

details.point: In 1st year of Datong, Xiao Daxin became governor of Yingzhou at age 13; Taizong advised him to delegate affairs.
details.label: included

details.point: In 7th year of Datong, Xiao Daxin was recalled as servant and stone garrison.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 1st year of Taiqing, Xiao Daxin became General Yunhui and governor of Jiangzhou.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 2nd year of Taiqing, Hou Jing invaded; Xiao Daxin raised 10,000 troops to rescue the capital.
details.label: included

details.point: In 3rd year of Taiqing, capital fell; Xiao Daxin received title of General of Pingnan from Xiao Shao.
details.label: included

details.point: In 1st year of Dashi, Xiao Daxin was named King of Xunyang with 2,000 households.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Daxin trusted Zhuang Tie, who later rebelled; Xiao Daxin sent Wei Yue to attack Zhuang Tie, who surrendered.
details.label: included

details.point: King Poyang Xiao Fan sent Hou Ti to rescue Zhuang Tie, causing rift between Xiao Daxin and Xiao Fan.
details.label: included

details.point: Hou Jing's general Ren Yue attacked; Xiao Daxin's Sima Weizhi was defeated. Xiao Daxin hesitated to flee, persuaded by mother Chen Shurong to stay.
details.label: included

details.point: In autumn of 2nd year of Dashi, Xiao Daxin was killed at age 25.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Dalin, King of Nanhai, was granted Duke of Ningguo in 2nd year of Datong with 1,500 households.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Dalin was known for filial piety after mother's death at age 11; excelled in studies and became Minister of Zhongshu.
details.label: included

details.point: During Hou Jing rebellion, Xiao Dalin was stationed at Xinting, then Duanmen; collected over 1,000 cattle to reward soldiers.
details.label: included

details.point: In 1st year of Dabao, Xiao Dalin was named Prince of Nanhai with 2,000 households; later became governor of Yangzhou and Wu County.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Dalin refused to join Zhang Biao's rebel army; in autumn of 2nd year of Dashi, he was killed in Wujun at age 25.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Dalian, King of Nanjun, was granted Duke of Lincheng in 2nd year of Datong with 1,500 households.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Dalian was talented in writing, music, and painting; accompanied Gaozu on a visit and impressed him with riding skills.
details.label: included

details.point: In 1st year of Taiqing, Xiao Dalian led 40,000 troops to rescue capital; after fall, returned to Yangzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Dynasty promoted Confucianism, with Taixue having over 10,000 students.
details.label: included

details.point: At the end of Han, political turmoil led to decline of Confucianism.
details.label: included

details.point: After Zhengshi period of Wei, Taoist Xuanyuan Nihility theory gained favor, reducing Confucian study.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin Dynasty moved to Jiangzuo, too busy to run schools.
details.label: included

details.point: Song and Qi dynasties had sporadic Chinese studies, but schools were abandoned for many years.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu of Liang issued edicts to search for scholars and rectify rituals, laws, calendar, and measures.
details.label: included

details.point: In Tianjian 4th year, Emperor Gaozu ordered establishment of Five Classics doctors and schools.
details.label: included

details.point: Pingyuan Mingshanbin, Wu Jun Lu Lian, Wu Xing Shen Jun, Jianping Yan Zhizhi, Kuaiji Hechang were appointed as replacement doctors.
details.label: included

details.point: Hundreds of students in academy, with salaries provided by court.
details.label: included

details.point: In Tianjian 7th year, Emperor Gaozu ordered crown princes, princes, and nobles to study in schools.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu personally visited schools to pay tribute to saints and encourage students.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Manrong was a scholar proficient in Laozi and Book of Changes, taught students, and wrote annotations.
details.label: included

details.point: He Tongzhi was an expert in Three Rites, served as official, and determined ritual standards.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Zhen wrote 'Theory on the Destruction of Gods' arguing spirit perishes with body, debated Buddhism.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Zhizhi was a scholar of Zhuangzi, Laozi, and Five Classics, taught hundreds of students.
details.label: included

details.point: He Yuan was a scholar of Three Rites, wrote 'Five Classics Meanings' for crown prince.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Sima Yun debated mourning rites for loving mother, leading to new regulations.
details.label: included

details.point: Bian Hua was a scholar of Five Classics and music rhythm, taught at academy.
details.label: included

details.point: Cui Lingen was a scholar of Three Rites and Three Legends, taught hundreds of students.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Jun was a scholar of Zhou Guan, taught hundreds of students, and helped compile 'Liang Guan'.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Jue, ancestor of Han, was a descendant of Han Wuzi.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Jue tried to stop Tu'anjia from killing Zhao Shuo.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Jue agreed to Zhao Shuo to preserve the Zhao family line.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Jue feigned illness during the massacre of the Zhao family.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Jue knew about Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu hiding Zhao Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Jue led 800 chariots to defeat Qi in the 11th year of Jin Jinggong.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Jue became first of six ministers, titled Xianzi.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Jue persuaded Jinggong to restore Zhao Wu's title.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xuanzi moved to Zhouyi.
details.label: included

details.point: Jizha of Wu predicted Han, Wei, Zhao would divide Jin.
details.label: included

details.point: Han, Zhao, Wei divided Qi and Yangyu counties.
details.label: included

details.point: Han, Zhao, Wei defeated Fan and Zhonghang families.
details.label: included

details.point: Han, Zhao, Wei defeated Zhibo and divided his territory.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han, Zhao, Wei were recognized as vassal states in 6th year of Han Jinghou.
details.label: included

details.point: Han destroyed Zheng and moved capital to Xinzheng in 2nd year of Han Aihou.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shen Buhai served as prime minister under Han Zhaohou, stabilizing the state.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han Zhaohou built a high gate during drought, which Qu Yijiu criticized.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han Xuanhui followed Gongzhong's advice to ally with Qin against Chu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chu's false promise of aid led Han to break with Qin, resulting in Qin attacks.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han eventually perished when Qin captured King Han and established Yingchuan Commandery.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan (Sima Yi) was from Xiaojingli, Wen County, Henan, with the surname Sima.
details.label: included

details.point: His ancestors were descendants of Chongli, the son of Emperor Gaoyang, serving as Xia Guan Zhurong.
details.label: included

details.point: During King Xuan of Zhou, Cheng Baixiu's father was given the surname Sima for conquering Xu Fang.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Yi was the second son of Sima Fang.
details.label: included

details.point: He was known for extraordinary integrity, intelligence, and devotion to Confucianism.
details.label: included

details.point: At the end of Han, he was recommended for office but initially declined due to declining Wei fortunes.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Cao summoned him as a literary advisor, and he took office after threats of imprisonment.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised Cao Cao to attack Shu after capturing Zhang Lu, but Cao Cao refused.
details.label: included

details.point: He served under Cao Pi, becoming a trusted advisor and one of the 'Four Friends' with Chen Qun, Wu Zhi, and Zhu Shuo.
details.label: included

details.point: He proposed agricultural policies to cultivate land and accumulate grain, which Cao Cao adopted.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised against moving the capital during Guan Yu's siege, suggesting Sun Quan be used to attack Guan Yu's rear.
details.label: included

details.point: After Cao Cao's death, he managed the funeral and maintained order.
details.label: included

details.point: He defeated Meng Da's rebellion in Xincheng, capturing the city in 16 days.
details.label: included

details.point: He led campaigns against Zhuge Liang, including the defense against the Shu invasion and the standoff at Wuzhangyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: He correctly predicted Zhuge Liang's death and pursued his army, but stopped due to a feigned counterattack.
details.label: included

details.point: He suppressed Gongsun Yuan's rebellion in Liaodong, capturing Xiangping and executing Yuan.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as regent alongside Cao Shuang under Emperor Cao Fang, but conflict arose.
details.label: included

details.point: He feigned illness to deceive Cao Shuang, then staged a coup, deposing Cao Shuang and his faction.
details.label: included

details.point: He suppressed Wang Ling's rebellion, leading to the death of Wang Ling and Cao Biao.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at age 73, posthumously honored as Emperor Xuan of Jin, with a temple name of Gaozu.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Xu's grandfather Yu Jing was a county prison officer who handled cases impartially.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Xu was twelve years old and could read Shangshu; he was an orphan and took care of his grandmother.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Xu declined an official position to care for his grandmother; after her death, he was recruited into Taiwei Li's Mansion.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yongchu 4th year, Deng Zhi proposed abandoning Liangzhou; Yu Xu argued against it, saying it would endanger the capital.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Xu suggested controlling Liangzhou by appointing local leaders' sons as officials to monitor them.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Xu was sent to suppress the Song thief Ning Ji; he used tactics like recruiting thieves and marking their clothes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yu Xu was promoted to prefect of Wudu; he used deception and increased stoves to mislead the Qiang.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Xu used strong crossbows to defeat the Qiang at Chiting and built 180 fortifications.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Xu opened a grain transport channel, saving over 40 million yuan annually.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yu Xu increased the county's households from 10,000 to over 40,000 in two or three years.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Xu as Sili Xiaowei impeached powerful officials like Tai Tu Feng Shi and was hated by them.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Xu was imprisoned for accusing Zhang Fang; Sun Cheng and others petitioned for his release.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yu Xu's son Yu Kai and students protested, leading to Zhang Fang's exile and Yu Xu's release.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yu Xu abolished the practice of 'righteous money' where officials redeemed criminals for money.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Xu defended a chief clerk who complained about a county magistrate, arguing it was not treason.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yu Xu advocated for equal distribution of Shangshu Lang positions across counties and states.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fu Xie was from Beidi; he changed his name to Nanrong after reading the Book of Songs.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fu Xie attacked Zhang Jiao with Huangfu Song; he warned against eunuch power before the campaign.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fu Xie opposed abandoning Liangzhou, arguing it was the country's screen; he criticized Situ Cui Lie.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Xie refused bribery from eunuch Zhao Zhong and was sent to Hanyang as governor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Biao was appointed Governor of Jingzhou after Sun Jian killed the previous governor.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Biao consulted Kuai Yue and Cai Mao on how to pacify Jingzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Kuai Yue advised using strategy to lure and kill bandit leaders, then pacify the region.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Biao implemented Kuai Yue's plan, killing 15 bandit leaders and capturing their troops.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Hu and Chen Li surrendered after being persuaded by Kuai Yue and Pang Ji.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Biao pacified all areas south of the Yangtze River.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Shu and Sun Jian attacked Liu Biao; Sun Jian was killed by a stray arrow.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Jue appointed Liu Biao General of Zhennan and Shepherd of Jingzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Biao accepted Zhang Ji's troops after Zhang Ji was killed, gaining their loyalty.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Biao defeated Zhang Xian and pacified Changsha, Lingling, and Guiyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Biao's territory expanded to connect with Wuling in the south and Han in the north, with over 100,000 troops.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Biao established schools and supported Confucian scholars, producing the 'Houding' commentaries.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Guandu conflict, Liu Biao remained neutral, neither aiding Cao Cao nor Yuan Shao.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Song advised Liu Biao to submit to Cao Cao, but Liu Biao hesitated and sent Han Song as envoy.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Song was appointed by the emperor and praised Cao Cao; Liu Biao imprisoned him for suspected betrayal.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Biao treated Liu Bei well but did not use his abilities.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Biao died of illness in 208 after nearly 20 years in Jingzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Biao favored his younger son Liu Cong over Liu Qi due to the influence of his wife and relatives.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Qi sought advice from Zhuge Liang and requested to govern Jiangxia to protect himself.
details.label: included

details.point: After Liu Biao's death, Liu Cong succeeded and surrendered Jingzhou to Cao Cao.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaojing had thirteen sons who were named kings, born to five mothers.
details.label: included

details.point: Sons of Li Ji: Liu Rong, Liu De, Liu Yanyu.
details.label: included

details.point: Sons of Cheng Ji: Liu Yu, Liu Fei, Liu Duan.
details.label: included

details.point: Sons of Jia Fu: Liu Pengzu, Liu Sheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Son of Tang Ji: Liu Fa.
details.label: included

details.point: Sons of Mrs. Wang: Liu Yue, Liu Ji, Liu Cheng, Liu Shun.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu De, King of Hejian, was a Confucian scholar and attracted many Confucians from Shandong.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Rong, former crown prince, was deposed, made Linjiang King, and died after being summoned for building on temple grounds.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yu, King of Lu, liked building palaces and raising animals, and had a stutter.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Fei, King of Jiangdu, was brave, fought in the Seven Kingdoms rebellion, and was awarded the emperor's banner.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jian, son of Liu Fei, committed suicide after incest, adultery, and involvement in rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Duan, King of Jiaoxi, was cruel, impotent, and manipulated officials; his kingdom was abolished after his death.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Pengzu, King of Zhao, was deceitful and manipulative, causing many officials to be executed or dismissed.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Sheng, King of Zhongshan, was fond of drinking and women, with over 120 descendants.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Fa, King of Changsha, was born to a maid and given a small, poor kingdom.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yue, King of Guangchuan, died after 12 years; his son Liu Qi was accused of incest.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ji, King of Jiaodong, prepared for Huainan rebellion and died of illness; his son Liu Xian succeeded.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Cheng, King of Qinghe, died without heirs; his kingdom became Qinghe Commandery.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Shun, King of Changshan, was favored but arrogant; his kingdom was abolished after succession disputes.
details.label: included

details.point: Later, the Han court reduced the power of princes, sending officials and limiting them to tax revenues.
details.label: included

details.point: Zang Dun's courtesy name was Xuanqing, from Ju, Dongguan.
details.label: included

details.point: His great-great-grandfather Zang Tao was Zuo Guanglu doctor during Song.
details.label: included

details.point: His grandfather Zang Tanzhi was Minister of Zuo Min.
details.label: included

details.point: His father Zang Weizhen was talented and served in Qi and Liang dynasties.
details.label: included

details.point: Zang Weizhen mourned his mother for three years in a thatched cottage.
details.label: included

details.point: Zang Dun studied the Five Classics under Zhuge Gu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuge Zhang praised Zang Dun as a great talent.
details.label: included

details.point: Zang Dun served as Zhongshu General Secretary Shiren and other posts.
details.label: included

details.point: Zang Dun felt severe pain in his left middle finger the night his mother died.
details.label: included

details.point: He mourned his mother for five years, becoming emaciated.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu praised and comforted Zang Dun.
details.label: included

details.point: During a wild elephant incident at Tongtai Temple, Zang Dun remained calm.
details.label: included

details.point: Zang Dun was appointed leader of the army, handling affairs orderly.
details.label: included

details.point: He succeeded Xiao Jing in reputation as leader.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zang Dun died at age 66 in Datong 9th year.
details.label: included

details.point: Zang Jue, Zang Dun's brother, was known for talent and strict law enforcement.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zang Jue was called 'Zang Hu' for harsh punishments.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Qi, from Lingzhou, served as Zhongshu General Secretary Shiren.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Qi opposed peace with Wei, foreseeing Hou Jing's rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Qi predicted Hou Jing would break the covenant, which proved true.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zike was the second son of Xiao Yi, King Wen of Yuzhang in the Qi Dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Yongming era, he was made Marquis of Nankang County as a prince.
details.label: included

details.point: At age twelve, he wrote 'Gaosong Fu' with his cousin, King Jingling of Situ.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as General Ningshuo and Grand Administrator of Jinduo, later as General Fuguo and Grand Administrator of Wujun.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Jiangan period, Wang Jingze rebelled; Xiao Zike fled to the capital, and Emperor Ming did not harm him.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Donghunhou, he became Secretary Supervisor, then Minister.
details.label: included

details.point: In the first year of Tianjian, he was demoted to viscount and appointed as Cavalier Attendant and Infantry Commandant, but not appointed due to illness.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu (Liang Wu) spoke to Xiao Zike's disciples, emphasizing fate and citing examples of past emperors.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu stated that he did not kill the Xiao clan because of shared ancestry and to avoid the mistakes of previous dynasties.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu sent a eunuch to reassure the princes of Beidi about their safety.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiao Zike served as Prefect of Yongjia, then Guanglu Qing, Secretary Supervisor, and other posts.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at age 52 in the third year of Datong; posthumously given Shi Zhong and Zhong Shu Ling, with the posthumous name Gong.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zike had five talented brothers: Zike, Zizhi, Zixian, Ziyun, and Zihui.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zifan, Zike's sixth younger brother, was known for filial piety and literary talent, and compiled the 'Thousand-Character Essay'.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zixian, Zike's eighth younger brother, was tall, learned, and wrote 'Hongxu Fu' and 'History of Qi'.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zixian served as Minister of Civil Affairs and was praised by Emperor Gaozu; he died at 49.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiao Ziyun, Zike's ninth younger brother, was a scholar and calligrapher, known for imitating Zhong Yao and Wang Xizhi.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Ziyun revised the sacrificial music lyrics for the Liang court and wrote 'Book of Jin' (110 volumes).
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Ziyun died of starvation at 63 during Hou Jing's rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: The Liang dynasty treated the Qi imperial clan generously, unlike previous dynasties, as noted in the historian's comment.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/后汉书/列传/王刘张李彭卢列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/王刘张李彭卢列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Wang Chang was a prince from Handan, Zhao State, originally a fortune-teller who believed Hebei had the aura of the Son of Heaven.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Lin, son of King Mu of Zhao, was friendly with Wang Chang and loved magic.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang killed a man claiming to be Liu Ziyu, son of Emperor Cheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Lang falsely claimed to be Liu Ziyu, the true son of Emperor Cheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Lin, Li Yu, and Zhang Shen conspired to support Wang Lang as emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: In December of the first year of Gengshi, Wang Lang was made emperor in Handan.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Lang appointed Liu Lin as Prime Minister, Li Yu as Grand Sima, and Zhang Shen as General.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Lang issued a proclamation claiming to be Liu Ziyu and calling for support.
details.label: included

details.point: Guangwu received Wang Lang's letter and attacked Handan, besieging it for over 20 days.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Lang's officer Li Li opened the city gate; Wang Lang fled and was killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yong, eighth generation grandson of King Xiao of Liang, was made King of Liang by Gengshi.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yong raised troops, captured 28 cities, and allied with Dong Xian and Zhang Bu.
details.label: included

details.point: After Gengshi's failure, Liu Yong proclaimed himself emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Guangwu sent Gai Yan and others to attack Liu Yong; Su Mao rebelled and joined Liu Yong.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yong was defeated and killed; his son Liu Yu was made king by Su Mao and Zhou Jian.
details.label: included

details.point: Pang Meng, originally a trusted general of Guangwu, rebelled and joined Dong Xian.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Guangwu personally attacked Pang Meng and Dong Xian; Dong Xian and Pang Meng were killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Bu occupied Langfu County, was appointed by Liu Yong as King of Qi, and killed Guangwu's envoy.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Bu was defeated by Geng Yan, surrendered, was made Marquis of Anqiu, but later fled and was killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Fang falsely claimed to be Liu Wenbo, great-grandson of Emperor Wu, and was made emperor by the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaowen was the fourth son of Emperor Gaozu of Han, with mother Bo Ji.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 11th year of Gaozu, Chen Xi was executed and the Dai territory pacified; Liu Heng was made King of Dai with capital Zhongdu.
details.label: included

details.point: After Empress Lu's death, the Lü clan plotted to seize power but were killed by Chen Ping, Zhou Bo, Liu Zhang, and others.
details.label: included

details.point: The ministers decided to welcome King Liu Heng of Dai as emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Wu advised against going to the capital, suspecting the ministers' motives.
details.label: included

details.point: Song Chang argued that the Han regime was divinely ordained and the people supported Liu, so the king should go.
details.label: included

details.point: Divination gave a great omen: 'Heaven's king, Xia Qi's glory, ancestor Yao.'
details.label: included

details.point: King Dai sent Bo Zhao to meet Zhou Bo, who confirmed the sincerity of the invitation.
details.label: included

details.point: Song Chang was sent ahead; at Weiqiao, ministers greeted him, and Zhou Bo offered the imperial seal.
details.label: included

details.point: King Dai entered the Dai Palace on the 29th day of the 9th month.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ministers petitioned that the sons of Emperor Xiaohui were not his true sons and asked Liu Heng to be emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Dai Wang declined three times, then accepted after Chen Ping's urging.
details.label: included

details.point: He entered Weiyang Palace that evening, appointed Song Chang as General of the Guard and Zhang Wu as Lang Zhongling.
details.label: included

details.point: He issued a general amnesty, granted ranks and gifts to the people, and rewarded those who killed the Lü clan.
details.label: included

details.point: He restored territories taken by Lü, abolished the law of collective punishment, and established the crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: He granted relief to the elderly, widowed, and poor, with specific rations for those over 80 and 90.
details.label: included

details.point: He abolished the crime of 'libel' and attempted crimes without action, and encouraged agriculture by personally farming.
details.label: included

details.point: He reduced taxes, exempted half of the land rent, and later abolished farmland tax entirely.
details.label: included

details.point: He dealt with rebellions: Jibei king Xingju rebelled and committed suicide; Huainan king Liu Chang rebelled and died in exile.
details.label: included

details.point: He died in Weiyang Palace in the 7th year of his reign, leaving a frugal burial edict, and was buried in Baling.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaowu Liu Che was the second son of Emperor Jing.
details.label: included

details.point: At age seven, he was made crown prince; at sixteen, he succeeded the throne.
details.label: included

details.point: In 141 BC, he ordered recommendations of virtuous and upright people.
details.label: included

details.point: Prime Minister Wei Wan banned recommendations of Legalist and strategist texts.
details.label: included

details.point: In 140 BC, he issued edicts to support the elderly and exempt taxes.
details.label: included

details.point: He established Mingtang and summoned Lu Shen Gong.
details.label: included

details.point: In 139 BC, Zhao Wan and Wang Zang committed suicide; Dou Ying and Tian Fen were dismissed.
details.label: included

details.point: In 138 BC, the Yellow River flooded; Maoling was established.
details.label: included

details.point: In 135 BC, Minyue attacked Dong Ou; Han forces relieved Dong Ou.
details.label: included

details.point: In 136 BC, he abolished three baht coins and issued half liang coins; set up Doctors of the Five Classics.
details.label: included

details.point: In 134 BC, Empress Dowager Dou died; comets appeared.
details.label: included

details.point: In 133 BC, the Mayi ambush failed; Wang Hui committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: In 132 BC, the Yellow River burst; 100,000 soldiers mobilized.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 130 BC, Queen Chen was deposed; witch trials occurred.
details.label: included

details.point: In 129 BC, Wei Qing attacked Xiongnu at Longcheng.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 127 BC, Wei Qing recovered Henan; Shuofang and Wuyuan counties established.
details.label: included

details.point: In 124 BC, Wei Qing defeated Xiongnu; captured 15,000 heads.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 123 BC, Wei Qing again defeated Xiongnu; Su Jian fled; Zhao Xin surrendered.
details.label: included

details.point: In 121 BC, Huo Qubing defeated Xiongnu at Gaolan; captured 8,000 heads.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 119 BC, Wei Qing and Huo Qubing defeated Xiongnu at Mobei; Li Guang committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ping was from Humiao Township, Yangwu County, and his family was poor but he loved studying.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ping's brother Chen Bo farmed while Chen Ping studied abroad.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ping's sister-in-law complained about him, leading Chen Bo to divorce her.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Fu, a rich man, married his granddaughter to Chen Ping despite his poverty.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Fu lent Chen Ping money for the wedding and advised his granddaughter to serve the Chen family respectfully.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ping distributed sacrificial meat evenly, saying he would rule the world like that.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ping served Wei Wang Jiu but left because his advice was ignored and he was slandered.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ping served Xiang Yu, was made Lord Xinwu, but fled after fearing execution.
details.label: included

details.point: During his escape, Chen Ping stripped to show he had no valuables, avoiding murder by boatmen.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Ping surrendered to Han and was appointed captain by Liu Bang, despite generals' objections.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Bo and Guan Ying slandered Chen Ping for having an affair with his sister-in-law and accepting bribes.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Wuzhi defended Chen Ping, saying talent matters more than character.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bang questioned Chen Ping, who explained his moves and was rewarded and made lieutenant.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ping proposed using gold to sow discord among Xiang Yu's ministers, and Liu Bang gave him 40,000 jin.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ping's stratagem caused Xiang Yu to suspect Fan Zeng, who resigned and died.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ping helped Liu Bang escape Xingyang by sending women out the east gate.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ping advised Liu Bang to capture Han Xin by pretending to tour Yunmeng.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ping proposed a secret plan to relieve the siege at Pingcheng, details unknown.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ping was granted the title of Qu Nihou and later increased fiefs six times for his strategies.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Liu Bang's death, Chen Ping pretended to obey Empress Lu but later conspired with Zhou Bo to eliminate the Lu clan and install Emperor Wen.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/三十世家/绛侯周勃世家/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/三十世家/绛侯周勃世家/target.summary.txt

details.point: Zhou Bo was from Peixian County, originally from Juan County.
details.label: included

details.point: He made a living weaving silkworm foil and played flute at funerals.
details.label: included

details.point: He became a warrior and followed Liu Bang (Pei Gong) from the start of his uprising.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Bo fought in many battles, including attacking Huling, Fangyu, and Fengyi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was the first to scale city walls at Xiayi and Zhisang.
details.label: included

details.point: He was granted the title of Fifth Doctor by Gaozu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Xiang Liang's death, Liu Bang and Xiang Yu returned to Dang County.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhou Bo was appointed Huben Ling and later Marquis of Weiwu.
details.label: included

details.point: He followed Liu Bang into Hanzhong and was appointed general.
details.label: included

details.point: He helped pacify the Three Qins and attacked Xiang Yu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Xiang Yu's death, he pacified Chu regions, capturing 22 counties.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He suppressed rebellions of Zang Tu, Han Xin, Chen Xi, and Lu Wan.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Bo was granted the title of Jianghou with 8,180 households.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to Taiwei and later helped annihilate the Lü clan.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Right Chancellor under Emperor Wen but resigned due to fear.
details.label: included

details.point: He was falsely accused of rebellion, imprisoned, and released after bribery and intercession.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Bo died in the 11th year of Emperor Wen, posthumously titled Marquis Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Zhou Yafu inherited the title as Tiaohou and became a famous general.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Yafu suppressed the Rebellion of the Seven States by cutting off Wu-Chu food supplies.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Yafu was falsely accused of rebellion, starved himself to death in prison.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Gui, courtesy name Weiming, was from Linyi, Langxie.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Gui's grandfather Wang Jian was a Taiwei during the Qi Dynasty and was named Nanchang County Duke.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Gui's father Wang Qian served as a doctor in Jinziguanglu and was named Marquis of Nanchang.
details.label: included

details.point: At age eight, Wang Gui's biological mother died; he showed extreme filial piety, moving Taiwei Xu Xiaosi to tears.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Gui's uncle Wang Chen praised him as 'my family's horse'.
details.label: included

details.point: At twelve, Wang Gui understood the Five Classics; he later became eloquent and loved learning.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Gui was promoted as a scholar by the state and served as chief registrar.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Secretary Lang, Prince Sheren, and other posts; in Tianjian 12, he presented 'New Hall Fu'.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Gui served as prefect of Xin'an but resigned due to his father's death.
details.label: included

details.point: After mourning, he was granted Marquis of Nanchang County and appointed Minister of Huangmen of Zhongshu.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor ordered Wang Gui, Yin Gou, Wang Xi, and Zhang Mian to serve Prince Zhaoming, who treated them with courtesy.
details.label: included

details.point: At a banquet, Wang Gui refused to make drinking orders, saying it hadn't happened since Jin moved to Jiangzuo.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Gui predicted disaster for Chen Qingzhi's Northern Expedition, which later came true.
details.label: included

details.point: In the sixth year, Emperor Gaozu admired Wang Gui's poem and appointed him minister in Shao.
details.label: included

details.point: In Datong 3, Wang Gui became Minister of the Fifth Army and infantry captain.
details.label: included

details.point: In Zhongdatong 2, Wang Gui became prefect of Wu County; he treated Rui Zhenzong distantly and was later transferred.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Gui resigned due to illness, built a house in Songxi Temple, and died at age 45.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor posthumously awarded him Sanqi Changshi and Guanglu Doctor, and gave him a Mi title.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Gui's son Wang Bao was a talented writer; at seven he could write articles.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Bao served as Secretary Lang, Marquis of Nanchang, and later surrendered to the Zhou Dynasty after Jiangling fell.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/三十世家/田敬仲完世家/target.txt
