details.point: Chen Wan is the son of Chen Ligong.
details.label: included

details.point: At Chen Wan's birth, a Zhou Taishi divined that his descendants would prosper in a state with the surname Jiang.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Ligong was killed by Chen Lin, who became Duke Zhuang of Chen.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Wan fled to Qi after Prince Yu Kou was killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Huan of Qi appointed Chen Wan as Gongzheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi Yizhong divined that Chen Wan's descendants would prosper after five generations and become equal to Zhengqing after eight.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Wan changed his surname to Tian in Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Wuyu (Tian Huanzi) served Duke Zhuang of Qi and was favored.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Tian Qi (Tian Lizi) used large and small measures to win the people's hearts.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Qi supported Yangsheng as Duke Dao of Qi after killing Yan Ruzi.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Chang (Tian Chengzi) continued the policy of winning people's hearts and killed Duke Jian of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Chang killed many powerful clans and divided Qi land for his fief.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Chang had over 70 sons by allowing guests into his harem.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian He (Taigong) moved Duke Kang of Qi to the seaside and became marquis with Zhou approval.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wei of Qi reformed governance, executed corrupt officials, and made Qi strong.
details.label: included

details.point: Zou Ji advised King Wei on music and governance, and was enfeoffed as Chenghou.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wei considered virtuous ministers as treasures, not pearls.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Qi under King Wei defeated Wei at Guiling and Maling.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Xuan of Qi established the Jixia Academy, attracting many scholars.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Min of Qi was killed by Nao Chi; his son King Xiang restored Qi with Tian Dan's help.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Sengbian was the son of General Wang Shennian.
details.label: included

details.point: He served under King Xiangdong of Xiangdong Kingdom in various military posts.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He suppressed the rebellion in Wuning County.
details.label: included

details.point: He held positions such as General Zhenwei, Prefect of Wuning, and Grand Administrator of Guangping.
details.label: included

details.point: When Hou Jing rebelled, Wang Sengbian was sent with naval troops to aid the capital.
details.label: included

details.point: After the capital fell, he initially surrendered to Hou Jing but later returned to Shizu (Emperor Yuan of Liang).
details.label: included

details.point: Shizu appointed him as leading general.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Sengbian was ordered to attack King Hedong of Xiangzhou but delayed due to insufficient troops.
details.label: included

details.point: Shizu became angry, wounded Wang Sengbian with a sword, and imprisoned him.
details.label: included

details.point: He was later pardoned and replaced Bao Quan to besiege Changsha, capturing Xiangzhou.
details.label: partially_included

details.point: Wang Sengbian defended Baling against Hou Jing's forces and repelled their attacks.
details.label: included

details.point: He was appointed General of the East Conquest and Duke of Changning County.
details.label: included

details.point: He captured Lushan and Yingcheng, defeating Song Zixian.
details.label: included

details.point: He allied with Chen Baxian at Baimaozhou, swearing an oath to destroy Hou Jing.
details.label: included

details.point: They defeated Hou Jing at Stone City; Hou Jing fled and was later killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Sengbian was promoted to Taiwei and General of Chariots and Cavalry.
details.label: included

details.point: He suppressed the rebellion of Lu Na in Xiangzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: After the death of Emperor Yuan, he supported Emperor Jing and accepted Xiao Yuanming as emperor under Qi pressure.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Baxian turned against him, captured and killed Wang Sengbian.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Wang Jie later served in Qi and died of grief after Wang Lin's death.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Zhao was the youngest son of Emperor Wu of Han, born to Zhao Jieyu.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu made Zhao the crown prince at age 8 after Crown Prince Liu Ju was deposed.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang was appointed regent by Emperor Wu to assist the young emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Zhao ascended the throne on February 15, 87 BC, after Emperor Wu's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Princess Eyi was granted the title of Tang Muyi and honored as the eldest princess.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang presided over state affairs with Jin Rixi and Shangguan Jie as deputies.
details.label: included

details.point: In 86 BC, the Xiongnu invaded Shuofang, and troops were sent to garrison Xihe.
details.label: included

details.point: In 85 BC, yellow swans appeared in Taiye Pond, considered auspicious.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Zhao started farming at Goudun Field in 85 BC.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 84 BC, Liu Ze rebelled but was discovered and executed.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin Rixi died in 84 BC.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 83 BC, Huo Guang and Shangguan Jie were made marquises for suppressing rebels.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 82 BC, relief was provided to the poor, and land rent was exempted.
details.label: included

details.point: In 81 BC, a comet appeared, and households were moved to Yunling.
details.label: included

details.point: In 80 BC, the queen was named Shangguan, and wealthy households were moved to Yunling.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 79 BC, Tian Guangming was sent to suppress the Yizhou rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: In 78 BC, the ban on raising mares and crossbows was lifted.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 77 BC, Emperor Zhao farmed at Shanglin, and the salt, iron, and wine monopolies were terminated.
details.label: partially_included

details.point: Su Wu returned after 19 years in Xiongnu captivity and was appointed as a vassal state official.
details.label: included

details.point: In 74 BC, Emperor Zhao died at age 21 and was buried in Pingling.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Taichuan (Gongye) was born in Kaifeng, Henan, great-grandson of Sinong Zheng Zhong.
details.label: included

details.point: He was talented and secretly made friends with heroes during Emperor Ling's reign.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to Xiaolian but refused appointments from three government offices.
details.label: included

details.point: He Jin appointed Zheng as Minister of the Secretariat and Censor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng warned He Jin against recruiting Dong Zhuo, predicting his rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: He Jin ignored the warning; Zheng resigned and He Jin was later killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng conspired with others to appoint Yuan Shao as Prefect of Bohai.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zheng argued against Dong Zhuo's troop expansion, citing virtue over force.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Zhuo initially made Zheng general but later revoked it due to suspicion.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng's family wealth allowed him to host guests and save many during famine.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zheng plotted to kill Dong Zhuo; when leaked, he fled to Yuan Shu.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Shu appointed Zheng Governor of Yangzhou, but he died en route at 41.
details.label: included

details.point: Kong Rong was a 20th-generation descendant of Confucius from Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: At 10, Kong Rong impressed Li Ying by claiming kinship through Confucius and Laozi.
details.label: included

details.point: At 16, Kong Rong hid Zhang Jian, leading to his brother Kong Bao's execution.
details.label: included

details.point: Kong Rong served as Beihai Chancellor, defended against Yellow Turbans, and promoted Confucianism.
details.label: included

details.point: He refused to ally with Yuan Shao or Cao Cao, killing advisor Zuo Chengzu.
details.label: included

details.point: Kong Rong opposed Cao Cao's policies, including alcohol ban and attack on Wuhuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Cao had Kong Rong executed on charges of treason; his children were also killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Yu left Yuan Shao for Cao Cao, becoming his chief strategist.
details.label: included

details.point: Huan Tan was born in Xiangxian County, Peiguo County, and his courtesy name was Junshan.
details.label: included

details.point: He was knowledgeable, read all Five Classics, and excelled in music and playing drums and harp.
details.label: included

details.point: He debated with Liu Xin and Yang Xiong, and was a simple man who disliked secular Confucian scholars.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Ai and Emperor Ping's reigns, his status was low.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised Fu Yan to be cautious and dismiss guests to avoid disaster, which saved the Fu family.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Xian wanted to befriend Huan Tan, but Huan Tan refused due to Dong Xian's improper conduct.
details.label: included

details.point: During Wang Mang's regency, Huan Tan remained silent and did not flatter Wang Mang.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as an official in charge of music under Wang Mang and later as Taizhong under Gengshili.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Under Emperor Guangwu, he was summoned but his advice was not adopted.
details.label: included

details.point: Song Hong recommended Huan Tan, and he became Yilang, submitting a memorial on political affairs.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He argued that wise assistants are crucial for governance, citing King Zhuang of Chu and Sun Shuao.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He criticized the current legal system for inconsistency and proposed unifying laws.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He opposed prophecies and urged the emperor to reject them and uphold the Five Classics.
details.label: included

details.point: He criticized the emperor's military rewards as insufficient, leading to prolonged unrest.
details.label: included

details.point: The emperor was displeased with Huan Tan's memorials.
details.label: included

details.point: When the emperor proposed using prophecies for the spiritual platform, Huan Tan refused and argued against prophecies.
details.label: included

details.point: The emperor ordered Huan Tan beheaded, but he was spared after kowtowing until bleeding.
details.label: included

details.point: He was demoted to Liu'an County Cheng and died of illness on the way, aged over seventy.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote twenty-nine articles titled 'New Treatise' and other works; Ban Gu completed an unfinished chapter.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Suzong honored Huan Tan's tomb during a hunting tour.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Sima Ming's character is from Wen, Hanoi.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Xie was good at 'Three Rites' and served as a doctor of Guozi in Qi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Sima Xian inherited the family business, studied etiquette, and was praised by Liu Xian.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Xian was appointed to study and manage Jiali in early Tianjian.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Xian was proficient in predicting good and bad fortunes and consulted by scholars.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Xian served as infantry school captain, Zhongshu Tongshisheren, and other posts.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Xian died in the 17th year of Tianjian; his works were compiled by Yu Jianwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Maoguan (Daoji) was from Wuyuan, Pengcheng; his father died young, family poor.
details.label: included

details.point: Maoguan was appreciated by Ren Fang and became famous.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Maoguan served as Yushi Zhongcheng, Taifu Qing, and other high offices.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Maoguan was frugal, not fond of sensuality, and had a simple lifestyle.
details.label: included

details.point: Maoguan was favored by Emperor Gaozu, who played chess with him.
details.label: included

details.point: Maoguan became blind in later years and was allowed to recuperate at home.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Maoguan was vegetarian, built a temple, and donated salary to it.
details.label: included

details.point: Maoguan died at 72; his collection of 20 volumes circulated.
details.label: included

details.point: Zijing (Yuanzhao) was smart, served as Zuo Lang and other posts.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zijing wrote poems quickly and was praised by Emperor Gaozu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Xian (Sifang) was a child prodigy from Pei State.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xian was knowledgeable; identified a fragment from 'Book of Zhou'.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xian answered Shen Yue's questions correctly and was admired.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xie Ju was the younger brother of Xie Lan, who was ordered by Zhongshu Ling.
details.label: included

details.point: Xie Ju was eager to learn, could talk about mystical principles, and was as famous as Xie Li.
details.label: included

details.point: Xie Ju served as Secretary Lang, Prince Sheren, and other positions, and was deeply appreciated by Prince Zhaoming.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Fang, the secretary supervisor, valued Xie Ju and wrote a poem for him.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu was pleased when Xie Ju said he was not as good as his ministers in drinking.
details.label: included

details.point: Xie Ju served as General Ningyuan and Internal History of Yuzhang, winning the hearts of the people.
details.label: included

details.point: Xie Ju served as Minister of the Ministry of Personnel three times, a rare honor.
details.label: included

details.point: Xie Ju was especially good at Lao, Zhuang, Xuanli and Buddhist philosophy.
details.label: included

details.point: Xie Ju pointed out mistakes in Lu Guang's lectures, impressing Lu Guang.
details.label: included

details.point: Xie Ju served as Prince Zhan Shi, a position his father held, and begged for a new appointment but was not allowed.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xie Ju held the position of prime minister but was unwilling to participate in current affairs and requested dismissal due to illness.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xie Ju died in the besieged city during Hou Jing's invasion.
details.label: included

details.point: He Jinrong married Princess Changcheng and was awarded the title of Prince Consort.
details.label: included

details.point: He Jinrong served as internal history of Jian'an, known for honest and effective governance.
details.label: included

details.point: He Jinrong was known for his solemn appearance and beautiful clothes.
details.label: included

details.point: He Jinrong was diligent in government affairs, unlike other prime ministers who entertained themselves with literary words.
details.label: included

details.point: He Jinrong was convicted of stealing official rice through his concubine and was dismissed from office.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He Jinrong was warned by Xie Yu to stop seeking reinstatement and to reflect on his mistakes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He Jinrong predicted that Hou Jing would bring chaos to the country.
details.label: included

details.point: He Jinrong died in the besieged capital during Hou Jing's rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Gao (Lu family) gave birth to Emperor Hui and assisted Emperor Gaozu.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Hui succeeded, he honored Empress Lu as Queen Mother.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Mother made daughter of Princess Lu Yuan the Queen; she had no children, so a harem beauty's son was made prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Hui died; the prince became emperor, young, so Empress Dowager Lu ruled and granted amnesty.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager made four of her brother's sons kings and six Zhu Lu princes.
details.label: included

details.point: In first year of Empress Lu's reign, she abolished harsh laws punishing three clans and wrong words as evil words.
details.label: included

details.point: In second year, she ordered ranking of princes by merit and storing merit book in Gaozu's temple.
details.label: included

details.point: In fourth year, young emperor complained about not being empress's biological child; Empress Dowager imprisoned him.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager deposed the young emperor and made Liu Hong (King of Hengshan) emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: In fifth year, Wei Tuo, king of Nanyue, claimed to be Emperor Nanwu.
details.label: included

details.point: In seventh year, Xiongnu invaded Didao and plundered over 2,000 households.
details.label: included

details.point: In seventh year, King Zhao Liu You was imprisoned and died; Liu Hui committed suicide.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In eighth year, Empress Dowager Lu died in Weiyang Palace.
details.label: included

details.point: After her death, Lu Lu and Lu Chan controlled military and political power, conspired to cause chaos.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Xuhou Liu Zhang learned of plot, informed King Qi to raise army westward.
details.label: included

details.point: Taiwei Zhou Bo and Prime Minister Chen Ping conspired to kill Zhu Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Bo used Li Ji to deceive Lu Lu into giving up military power.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Bo entered Northern Army, ordered soldiers to support Liu (left side); all turned left.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Zhang killed Lu Chan and Lu Gengshi; Zhou Bo executed Lu Lu and Lu Xunu.
details.label: included

details.point: Ministers killed young emperor and his brothers, enthroned Emperor Wen.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Gaozu (Liu Bang) was born in Peixian County, with a dragon-like appearance and 72 black moles on his left thigh.
details.label: included

details.point: He was generous, informal, and unwilling to engage in ordinary labor; he served as a minor official and chief of Sishang Pavilion.
details.label: included

details.point: He often drank on credit at Wang Po and Wu Ma's hotels; they waived his debts due to strange phenomena seen on him.
details.label: included

details.point: While on corvee in Xianyang, he saw Qin Shihuang and said, 'A real man should be like this!'
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Gong of Shanfu County, a friend of the Pei magistrate, held a banquet; Liu Bang falsely claimed a gift of 10,000 yuan, impressing Lu Gong.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Gong, skilled in physiognomy, married his daughter (future Empress Lu) to Liu Bang despite his wife's objections.
details.label: included

details.point: An old man predicted that Empress Lu and her children would be noble, and that Liu Bang's fortune was priceless.
details.label: included

details.point: As a pavilion chief, Liu Bang released convicts on the way to Lishan; over ten men followed him.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bang killed a large snake blocking the path; an old woman said it was the son of the White Emperor killed by the son of the Red Emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin Shihuang heard of an emperor's cloud in the southeast; Empress Lu could find Liu Bang by the cloud over his hiding place.
details.label: included

details.point: In 209 BC, Chen She rebelled; the Pei magistrate wanted to join but later reneged; Liu Bang's letter led the elders to kill the magistrate and elect Liu Bang as Duke of Pei.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bang's army grew to 3,000; he adopted red flags, symbolizing the Red Emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Yong Chi rebelled and surrendered Feng to Wei; Liu Bang failed to recapture Feng and later joined Xiang Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: After Xiang Liang's death, King Huai of Chu appointed Liu Bang as Marquis of Wu'an and ordered him to march west; Xiang Yu was sent north to rescue Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bang marched west, capturing cities and accepting surrenders; he defeated Qin forces and entered Guanzhong.
details.label: included

details.point: In 206 BC, Ziying surrendered; Liu Bang entered Xianyang, sealed the treasury, and returned to Bashang; he issued the three chapters of the law.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu, angered by Liu Bang's control of Hangu Pass, planned to attack; the Hongmen Banquet incident occurred, where Liu Bang escaped assassination.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu divided the empire, making Liu Bang King of Han in Ba, Shu, and Hanzhong; Liu Bang later burned the plank road to show no intention of leaving.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bang appointed Han Xin as general; Han Xin advised an eastward campaign; Liu Bang conquered the Three Qins and expanded his territory.
details.label: included

details.point: The Chu-Han Contention ended with the Treaty of Honggou; Liu Bang, advised by Zhang Liang and Chen Ping, broke the treaty and defeated Xiang Yu at Gaixia, unifying China.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Hui was the crown prince of Emperor Gaozu and son of Empress Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: He became emperor on May 17 after Gaozu's death in April of the 12th year.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Lu became empress dowager.
details.label: included

details.point: He rewarded subjects with titles and promotions based on service.
details.label: included

details.point: He reduced land rent to one tax per fifteen people.
details.label: included

details.point: He relaxed punishments for officials and certain relatives.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He exempted officials with salary over 600 dan from corvée except military tax.
details.label: included

details.point: He ordered construction of Gaozu's ancestral temples in each county.
details.label: included

details.point: King Liu Ruyi of Zhao died in December of the first year.
details.label: included

details.point: He allowed atonement for death penalty with 30-level title money.
details.label: included

details.point: He built Chang'an city, starting in the first year.
details.label: included

details.point: King Hui of Qi presented Chengyang County to Princess Lu Yuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Prime Minister Xiao He died in July of the second year.
details.label: included

details.point: He recruited laborers to build Chang'an for 30 days in the third year.
details.label: included

details.point: He married a Liu princess to the Xiongnu chanyu.
details.label: included

details.point: He selected filial and incorruptible persons and exempted them from corvée.
details.label: included

details.point: He held a crown ceremony and granted amnesty in the fourth year.
details.label: included

details.point: He abolished Qin laws against carrying documents.
details.label: included

details.point: Chang'an city was completed in September of the fifth year.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Hui died in Weiyang Palace on August 12 of the seventh year.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuomao, courtesy name Zikang, was from Wan, Nanyang County.
details.label: included

details.point: He studied under Dr. Jiang Weng in Chang'an and mastered Poetry, Li, and Calendar.
details.label: included

details.point: He was known for his tolerance and lack of disputes, once giving his horse to a stranger who mistakenly claimed it.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as magistrate of Mi County, practicing good governance and teaching the people.
details.label: included

details.point: He handled a case of bribery with leniency, emphasizing etiquette over law.
details.label: not_included

details.point: During a locust plague, locusts did not enter Mi County.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang appointed him as minister of the capital; the people of Mi County wept at his departure.
details.label: included

details.point: He resigned due to illness and later served Gengshi, then retired.
details.label: included

details.point: Guangwu visited him and praised his conduct.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuomao was associated with six others who refused to serve Wang Mang, including Kong Xiu who committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Gong, courtesy name Zhongkang, was from Pingling, Fufeng.
details.label: included

details.point: At age 12, he and his brother Lu Pi mourned their father with exceptional filial piety.
details.label: included

details.point: He studied Lu Shi at Taixue and was praised by Confucian scholars.
details.label: included

details.point: As magistrate of Zhongmu, he resolved land disputes through moral persuasion.
details.label: not_included

details.point: A pheasant not being caught by a child impressed an inspector, who reported three wonders of Lu Gong's governance.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He admonished Emperor He against attacking the Xiongnu, citing famine and moral reasons.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Situ and later as Changle Weiwei, advocating for seasonal sentencing.
details.label: included

details.point: He argued against executing prisoners in winter, citing the Moon Order and Yin-Yang principles.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Ba, courtesy name Qiaoqing, was from Jiyin Juyang and known for simplicity and forgiveness.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Kuan, courtesy name Wenrao, was from Hongnong Huayin; he once returned a cow to a mistaken claimant without anger.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yan proposed appointing state shepherds to suppress rebellions.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yan was appointed as the shepherd of Yizhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yan appointed Jia Long as school captain after defeating Ma Xiang.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yan sent Zhang Lu to attack Hanzhong, leading to Zhang Lu's occupation.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yan killed powerful families in Yizhou, causing resentment.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yan's sons Liu Fan and Liu Dan were killed in Chang'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Zhang succeeded Liu Yan as shepherd of Yizhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Zhang was weak and lacked authority, leading to internal strife.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Wei rebelled against Liu Zhang but was defeated.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Lu broke with Liu Zhang and killed his mother and brother.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Zhang allied with Liu Bei to resist Cao Cao.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Bei turned against Liu Zhang and besieged Chengdu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Zhang surrendered to Liu Bei and was later moved to Gong'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Lu established a theocratic state in Hanzhong based on Five Pecks of Rice Taoism.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Lu surrendered to Cao Cao and was granted titles.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Shu claimed the title of emperor based on prophecies.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Shu's tyranny and extravagance led to his downfall.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Sun Ce broke with Yuan Shu over his imperial ambitions.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lu Bu killed Dong Zhuo and later defected to various warlords.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Bu was defeated by Cao Cao at Xiapi and executed.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius was born in Zouyi, Changping Township, Lu State.
details.label: included

details.point: His ancestor was Uncle Kong Fang from the Song Dynasty.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Confucius was born in the 22nd year of Duke Xiang of Lu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: His head was concave at birth, so he was named Qiu, courtesy name Zhongni, surname Kong.
details.label: included

details.point: His father Shu Lianghe died shortly after Confucius was born.
details.label: included

details.point: As a child, Confucius played at setting up sacrificial vessels and learning ritual movements.
details.label: included

details.point: At 17, Meng Lizi on his deathbed told his son to learn from Confucius.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius worked as a clerk managing granaries and pastures for the Ji family.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to Sikong (Minister of Works).
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius was nine feet six inches tall, called 'The Long Man'.
details.label: included

details.point: He traveled to Zhou to learn rites from Laozi.
details.label: included

details.point: At 30, Confucius was asked by Duke Jing of Qi about governance.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius served as governor of Zhongdu, then Sikong, then Grand Minister of Crime (Dasikou).
details.label: included

details.point: At the Jiagu meeting, Confucius forced Qi to return Lu's lands.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius dismantled the city walls of the Three Huan families.
details.label: included

details.point: He killed the official Shaozhengmao for disturbing state affairs.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius left Lu after Ji Huanzi accepted female musicians from Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: He traveled to Wei, Song, Chen, Cai, and other states, facing hardships.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius returned to Lu at age 68 and compiled the Six Classics.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He died at age 73 and was buried north of Lucheng on the shore of Surabaya.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaoai was the grandson of Emperor Yuan of Han and son of Prince Dingtao Gong.
details.label: included

details.point: His mother was Ding Ji.
details.label: included

details.point: He became king at age three and was interested in literature and law.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yuanyan 4th year, he visited Emperor Cheng with all his officials.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng favored him over King Zhongshan for his knowledge and manners.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Mother Fu, his grandmother, bribed Zhao Zhaoyi and Wang Gen.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Zhaoyi and Wang Gen praised him to Emperor Cheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng made him crown prince at age 17.
details.label: included

details.point: He became emperor after Emperor Cheng died in Suihe 2nd year.
details.label: included

details.point: He honored his grandmother as Empress Dowager and mother as Empress Dowager.
details.label: included

details.point: He issued an edict to abolish Yuefu for lewd music.
details.label: included

details.point: He granted titles and lands to relatives and officials.
details.label: included

details.point: He ordered restrictions on land and slave holdings.
details.label: included

details.point: He abolished certain laws and allowed palace women over 30 to marry.
details.label: included

details.point: He exempted old official slaves and banned rare bird offerings.
details.label: included

details.point: He issued amnesty and tax relief after disasters.
details.label: included

details.point: He changed era names based on prophecies but later canceled them.
details.label: included

details.point: He executed or punished those involved in the prophecy incident.
details.label: included

details.point: He restored Ganquan and Fenyin sacrifices, canceling southern and northern suburbs.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at age 20 after reigning 6 years, buried in Yiling.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing succeeded Emperor Wen in 157 BC.
details.label: included

details.point: He honored Empress Dowager Bo and Empress Dowager Dou.
details.label: included

details.point: He ordered the 'Zhao De' dance for Emperor Wen's temple.
details.label: included

details.point: Prime Minister Shentu Jia proposed Emperor Gao as Taizu and Emperor Wen as Taizong.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing encouraged migration to fertile lands.
details.label: included

details.point: He reduced farmland rent by half.
details.label: included

details.point: He reformed laws on official bribery and gifts.
details.label: included

details.point: He set the age for assistant officials at 20.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He enfeoffed several sons as kings in 155 BC.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Dowager Bo died in 155 BC.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shentu Jia died; Xiao Xi was made marquis.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Seven Kingdoms rebellion occurred in 154 BC.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Yafu and Dou Ying suppressed the rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Rebel kings were killed or committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: He deposed Queen Bo in 150 BC.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He made Liu Che crown prince in 150 BC.
details.label: included

details.point: He reformed penal laws, abolishing dismemberment.
details.label: included

details.point: He issued edicts on judicial caution and leniency.
details.label: included

details.point: He emphasized agriculture and reduced commerce.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Jing died in 141 BC and was buried in Yangling.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zong was the second son of Emperor Gaozu, granted Prince of Yuzhang County in 502.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zong suspected he was not Gaozu's biological son due to his mother's past and palace rumors.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zong performed a blood-dripping test on the bones of Qi Shuhunhou and his own son, confirming his paternity doubts.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zong defected to Wei in 527, was appointed high official, and changed his name to Xiao Zuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zong was killed by Wei in 531 while trying to flee to Chang'an.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiao Ji was the eighth son of Emperor Gaozu, named King of Wuling in 516.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Ji proclaimed himself emperor in Shu after Gaozu's death, with reign name Tianzheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Ji killed advisors who warned him, leading to internal dissent.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Ji led an army east in 551 but was defeated by Western Wei and executed.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zhengde was adopted by Gaozu but passed over for crown prince, leading to resentment.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zhengde defected to Wei but returned, later colluded with Hou Jing.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zhengde helped Hou Jing cross the river and was made emperor by Hou Jing.
details.label: included

details.point: After Taicheng fell, Hou Jing demoted and killed Xiao Zhengde.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Yu was the second son of Prince Zhaoming, made King of Hedong in 531.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Yu refused to submit to Shizu during Hou Jing's rebellion, leading to conflict.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shizu sent Bao Quan to attack Xiao Yu; Xiao Yu was defeated and executed.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zong's poems 'Listening to the Ringing of the Bell' and 'Sad Poems on Falling Leaves' expressed his frustration.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Ji's reign name Tianzheng was considered ominous, associated with short rule.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Zhengde's plot with Hou Jing was discovered after his death.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Yu's defeat was preceded by ominous signs like seeing no head in the mirror.
details.label: included

details.point: Pei Ziye was a native of Wenxi, Hedong, and the eighth-generation grandson of Pei Kang.
details.label: included

details.point: He was known as one of the 'Four Peis' with his brothers Pei Li, Pei Kai, and Pei Chuo.
details.label: not_included

details.point: His great-grandfather was Pei Songzhi, a Taizhong doctor in the Song Dynasty.
details.label: not_included

details.point: His mother died after his birth; he was raised by his grandmother, who died when he was nine.
details.label: included

details.point: He was studious and good at writing articles from a young age.
details.label: included

details.point: He began his career as Zuo Changshi of the Wuling Kingdom of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: During mourning for his father, his behavior was exemplary; grass withered where he wept and a white rabbit crouched beside him.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yun praised his conduct but died before reporting to the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Fang resented Pei Ziye because Ziye, as his cousin, did not visit him.
details.label: included

details.point: He was dismissed from office when colleagues signed his name on a document without his presence.
details.label: included

details.point: He refused to litigate to clear his name, saying he could not get a job by litigating.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Zhen recommended him, praising his conduct, learning, and his work 'Song Lue'.
details.label: included

details.point: Some officials blocked his promotion due to insufficient qualifications.
details.label: included

details.point: He later became Minister Bibu Lang and then a county magistrate, where he resolved disputes without whipping.
details.label: included

details.point: He completed 'Song Lue' in twenty volumes, which Shen Yue praised.
details.label: included

details.point: He was appointed as an author to compile national history and daily life notes.
details.label: included

details.point: He correctly identified the origins of the Baiti and Hua kingdoms based on historical records.
details.label: included

details.point: He drafted an edict against Wei quickly, impressing Emperor Gaozu.
details.label: included

details.point: He was known for writing quickly and elegantly, imitating ancient styles.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at age 62, having compiled many works including 'Song Lue', 'Collection of Mourning Clothes', and 'Continued Biography of the Pei Family'.
details.label: included

details.point: Tang Shuyu of Jin was son of King Wu of Zhou and younger brother of King Cheng.
details.label: included

details.point: King Cheng granted Tang to Shuyu after cutting a tung leaf as a token.
details.label: included

details.point: Shuyu's son Xie became Marquis of Jin.
details.label: included

details.point: In 17th year of Jinghou, King Li of Zhou fled, and the 'Republic' period began.
details.label: included

details.point: Mu Hou's son Qiu (Wenhou) killed his uncle and became ruler.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Quwo grew powerful; Huan Shu of Quwo was enfeoffed there.
details.label: included

details.point: Quwo Zhuangbo killed Xiaohou; later Quwo Wugong killed Aihou and Xiaozihou.
details.label: included

details.point: Quwo Wugong destroyed Jin and was recognized as Duke Wu of Jin by King Li.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Xian of Jin favored Li Ji and alienated his sons Shen Sheng, Chong'er, and Yiwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Ji poisoned meat and framed Shen Sheng, who committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Chong'er fled to Di, then to Qi, Cao, Song, Zheng, Chu, and finally Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Xian died; Xi Qi and Daozi were killed by Li Ke.
details.label: included

details.point: Yiwu became Duke Hui of Jin with Qin help but broke promises.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Hui fought Qin at Han Yuan, was captured, but later released.
details.label: included

details.point: Prince Yu (Duke Huai) fled Qin and became ruler; Chong'er returned as Duke Wen.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Duke Wen became hegemon after Chengpu battle and received Zhou king's mandate.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Ling was extravagant; Zhao Dun fled after assassination attempt; Zhao Chuan killed Ling.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Duke Jing defeated Chu at Yanling; later six ministers grew powerful.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Li killed three Que; Luan Shu and Zhongxing Yan imprisoned and killed him.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Jin was partitioned by Zhao, Han, and Wei; Duke Jing became commoner, ending Jin.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Hao was a native of Wuyang, Qianwei County, and his sixth-generation ancestor was Zhang Liang, the Marquis of Liu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Hao served as Shangshu Pushe for eight years and became prime minister of Pengcheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Hao was promoted to Tingwei in the first year of Yongning.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Hao argued against deposing the crown prince but was unsuccessful.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Hao wrote a memorial warning against repeating the mistakes of the Jiang Chong incident.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Shun appointed Zhang Hao as Sikong; he promoted many talents.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Hao persuaded Emperor Shun to reduce the punishment of Zhao Teng and others accused of slander.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Hao died at age 83 and was buried in Henan County.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Hao's son Zhang Gang was proficient in Confucian classics and served as imperial censor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Gang criticized Emperor Shun for indulging eunuchs and urged adherence to old regulations.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Gang buried his wheel in Luoyang, refusing to inspect customs, and denounced Liang Ji.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Gang became prefect of Guangling and persuaded rebel Zhang Ying to surrender with 10,000 followers.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Gang died at age 46; Zhang Ying and 500 people mourned and built his tomb.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Gong served as governor of Qingzhou and impeached corrupt officials.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Gong recommended Huang Xian and Chen Fan; he was promoted to Taiwei.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Gong wrote to criticize eunuchs but was falsely accused; Li Gu helped resolve the issue.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chang served as governor of Nanyang and enforced strict anti-corruption measures.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Chang adopted lenient governance after advice from Zhang Chang.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhong Hao used his inheritance to help the poor and was recommended as filial and incorrupt.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhong Hao served as censor, impeached corrupt officials, and later as governor of Liangzhou and Hanyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Guang was born in Wan County, Nanyang, and was loyal in youth.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Guang was rescued by Liu Ci when Han soldiers tried to kill him for his clothes.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Guang led followers to join Liu Ci, became a partial general, and defeated Wang Xun and Wang Yi.
details.label: included

details.point: Gengshi appointed Ren Guang as governor of Xindu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: When Wang Lang rebelled, Ren Guang alone refused to surrender and executed Ting Ping who tried to persuade him.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Guang sent 4,000 elite soldiers to defend Xindu.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Guangwu (Shizu) came to Xindu after being defeated, and Ren Guang welcomed him.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Guang advised Guangwu to recruit troops by plundering neighboring counties.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Guangwu appointed Ren Guang as General of the Left and Marquis of Wucheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Guang wrote propaganda claiming Guangwu had millions of soldiers, causing Tangyang to surrender.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Guang was later made Marquis of Aling with over 10,000 households.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Zhong was from Huang County, Donglai, and served as a captain under Gengshi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Zhong and Ren Guang jointly served Guangwu, and Li Zhong was made Marquis of Wuguhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Zhong did not plunder, and Guangwu rewarded him specially.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Zhong killed hundreds who had sided with Wang Lang after returning to Xindu.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Zhong became Marquis of Zhongshui and later governor of Danyang, where he established schools and attracted refugees.
details.label: included

details.point: Wan Xiu was from Maoling, Fufeng, and helped defend Xindu, becoming a partial general and Marquis of Yicheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Pi Tong was from Xindu, surrendered to Guangwu, and advised him not to return west, which Guangwu accepted.
details.label: included

details.point: Pi Tong was made Marquis of Wuyi and later Marquis of Lingshou, serving as Taichang and Shaofu.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Zhi from Julu welcomed Guangwu, persuaded Liu Yang of Zhending to surrender, and was made Marquis of Changcheng.
details.label: included

details.point: The text compiles women's deeds into 'Lienv Pian' since the ZTE period.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Ma, Empress Deng, and Empress Liang are recorded in previous 'Queen's Notes'.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Xuan's wife Huan Shaojun returned her dowry and lived frugally with Bao Xuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Xuan became Sili Xiaowei under Emperor Ai.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Ba's wife encouraged him to maintain his integrity despite poverty.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Shi's wife fetched river water for her mother-in-law and was sent away but later returned.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Shi's wife's filial piety led to a spring with carp appearing daily.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Red Eyebrow rebels spared Jiang Shi's home due to his filial piety.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Yu's wife Zhao A committed suicide after being blamed for her husband's behavior.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Zhao (Cao Shishu's wife) completed the 'Book of Han' after Ban Gu's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Zhao taught the empress and nobles, and was called 'Everyone'.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Zhao advised Empress Dowager Deng to allow Deng Zhi to retire.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Zhao wrote 'Female Commandments' in seven chapters.
details.label: included

details.point: Leyangzi's wife persuaded him to return a found gold and to complete his studies.
details.label: included

details.point: Leyangzi's wife committed suicide to protect her mother-in-law from robbers.
details.label: included

details.point: Cheng Wenju's wife Mu Jiang treated her stepchildren kindly, leading to their reform.
details.label: included

details.point: Filial daughter Cao E drowned herself after her father's death and was honored.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Xusheng's wife Lu Rong killed her husband's murderer and later died resisting bandits.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Wei's wife Ma Lun defended her father Ma Rong's reputation.
details.label: included

details.point: Pang Ao's mother Zhao E avenged her father's murder after ten years.
details.label: included

details.point: Zongyang was a native of Nieyang County, Nanyang, and lived in Jiangling for generations.
details.label: included

details.point: Zongyang's grandfather Zong Bing was recruited by the Southern Song as crown prince and concubine but did not accept.
details.label: included

details.point: Zongyang passed the Yingzhou scholar examination at age twenty and served as a regular attendant of King Lin.
details.label: included

details.point: King Situ Jingling of Southern Qi included Zongyang in the portraits of scholars at the West Residence.
details.label: included

details.point: During Yongming, Zongyang and Ren Fang received Wei envoys by imperial order.
details.label: included

details.point: Prince Nanjun appointed Zongyang to manage the secretariat due to his calligraphy and integrity.
details.label: included

details.point: After the Young Emperor's execution, Zongyang and Fu Zhao were spared due to their integrity.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Ming appointed Zongyang to govern Yingzhou, where he was known for competence.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Gaozu appointed Zongyang as Xizhonglang consultant and Biejia, and he was trusted by Xiao Yingzhou.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zongyang died at age forty-nine in the third year of Tianjian.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Tan was a native of Anzhong County, Nanyang, and a seventh-generation grandson of General Liu Qiao.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Tan served as magistrate of Xiaoling County and was known for administrative ability.
details.label: included

details.point: During Liang Gaozu's uprising, Liu Tan became a consultant and joined the army.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Tan recommended himself to govern Xiangzhou and successfully transported 300,000 hu of rice as military supplies.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Tan suppressed the rebellion of Wang Sengken by killing Zhong Baoti and burning incriminating documents.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Tan was enfeoffed as Lord of Yiqiu Shu with 300 households and died at age sixty-two.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Ai was a sixth-generation grandson of Bi Tong and lived in Jiangling for generations.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Ai was recruited by King Yuzhang of Qi as chief administrator and later served as governor of Jingzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Ai restored Jingzhou's official buildings quickly without using common laborers.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Ai served as Yushi Zhongcheng and Dazhongzheng, known for fairness and knowledge, and died in office as General Zhenglu.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Yuan was the son of Emperor Xuan and Queen Gongai Xu.
details.label: included

details.point: He was made prince at age eight.
details.label: included

details.point: He was generous and respected Confucianism, unlike his father who favored legalism.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan criticized Confucian scholars as impractical and predicted the prince would disrupt the Liu family.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan considered replacing him with the King of Huaiyang but did not due to his bond with Queen Xu.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Yuan succeeded to the throne in December of the first year of Huanglong.
details.label: included

details.point: He issued amnesties and relief measures for the poor, including lending land and seeds.
details.label: included

details.point: He sent officials to tour the country to comfort the needy and recruit worthy men.
details.label: included

details.point: He reduced palace expenses and provided disaster relief during famines and plagues.
details.label: included

details.point: He exempted taxes in disaster-stricken areas and lent public lands to the poor.
details.label: included

details.point: He ordered the removal of guards from Ganquan and Jianzhang palaces to reduce labor.
details.label: included

details.point: He established the crown prince in the second year of his reign.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He ordered the suicide of Wangzhi after false accusations by Shi Xian and Honggong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He abandoned the campaign against Zhuya due to famine and focused on disaster relief.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He reduced imperial meals and dismissed entertainments to save costs.
details.label: included

details.point: He restored the Yantieguan and doctorate disciples after abolishing them.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He pardoned the world and canceled debts for the poor.
details.label: included

details.point: He defeated Zhizhi Chanyu through Gan Yanshou and Chen Tang, displaying his head.
details.label: included

details.point: He received Huhanye Chanyu and renamed the era to Jingning to celebrate peace.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He died in Weiyang Palace in May of the first year of Jingning and was buried in Weiling.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng was the son of Emperor Yuan and Empress Wang.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan favored him and named him Taisun.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Yuan once considered deposing him due to his drinking and pleasure-seeking.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Xian protected the prince, and Emperor Xuan's favor prevented deposition.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Yuan died in 33 BC, and Emperor Cheng ascended the throne.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Feng was appointed Grand Marshal and Grand General, controlling the secretariat.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng agreed to stop burying chariots, cattle, horses, and animals.
details.label: included

details.point: A comet appeared in the camp star area.
details.label: included

details.point: A fire at the Gaozu Temple and a comet were seen as divine warnings.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng issued an edict blaming himself and granting amnesty.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chong and other uncles were made marquises.
details.label: included

details.point: Yellow mist and swarms of flies were considered omens.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng established suburban sacrifices in Chang'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Xu was established in 31 BC.
details.label: included

details.point: A false flood rumor caused panic in the capital.
details.label: not_included

details.point: A solar eclipse and earthquake occurred simultaneously in 29 BC.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Yellow River burst at Jindi in Dongjun.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Yanshi repaired the Yellow River, and the era name changed to Heping.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Cheng deposed Queen Xu in 18 BC.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng died in 7 BC and was buried in Yanling.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin and Peng Yue failed to meet Han King at Guling, leading to Han defeat by Xiang Yu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang advised granting territory to Han Xin and Peng Yue to secure their alliance.
details.label: included

details.point: Han King allocated land to Han Xin and Peng Yue, prompting them to join forces.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jia invaded Chu and besieged Shouchun; Zhou Yin defected to Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Han forces surrounded Xiang Yu at Gaixia; Xiang Yu broke out and was pursued.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu died; Lu surrendered after seeing his head; he was buried with Duke of Lu rites.
details.label: included

details.point: Han King entered Han Xin's camp and seized his military power.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin was made King of Chu; Peng Yue was made King of Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: Princes requested Han King to take title of Emperor; he accepted.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu established capital at Luoyang, then moved to Chang'an on Lou Jing's advice.
details.label: included

details.point: General amnesty and demobilization; edicts on land, taxes, and slave emancipation.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu discussed reasons for victory: using Zhang Liang, Xiao He, Han Xin.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Heng fled to island, was pardoned but committed suicide near Luoyang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zang Tu rebelled and was captured; Lu Wan made King of Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin arrested on suspicion of rebellion, demoted to Marquis of Huaiyin.
details.label: included

details.point: Meritorious officials enfeoffed; Zhang Liang advised rewarding Yong Chi to calm fears.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu honored his father as Supreme Emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin (King of Han) surrendered to Xiongnu; Emperor campaigned, was besieged at Pingcheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Xi rebelled; Emperor campaigned, suppressed rebellion with bribery and force.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu died; Empress Lu initially concealed death; he was buried as Emperor Gao.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan was the great-grandson of Emperor Wu and grandson of Prince Ru.
details.label: included

details.point: Prince Ru, his consort, and their son were killed in the witchcraft incident.
details.label: included

details.point: As an infant, Emperor Xuan was imprisoned due to the witchcraft incident.
details.label: included

details.point: Bingji, a Tingwei official, saved Emperor Xuan by ordering female convicts to nurse him.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu ordered execution of all prisoners in Chang'an prison, but Bingji prevented it.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After a general amnesty, Bingji took Emperor Xuan to his grandmother's home.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang He, Yeting official, supported Emperor Xuan's education with personal funds.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan married Xu Guanghan's daughter and studied poetry under Zhong Weng.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Zhao died without heirs; Huo Guang made King Changyi emperor but deposed him.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang recommended Emperor Xuan as successor; he became emperor in 74 BC.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan established Queen Xu and granted amnesty and rewards.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang returned power but Emperor Xuan declined; Huo Guang was rewarded with 17,000 households.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan honored the late crown prince with posthumous title and cemetery.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Xuan ordered construction of Pingling and moved people there.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Xuan sent five generals with 150,000 cavalry to attack Xiongnu in 72 BC.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Queen Xu died in 71 BC; Empress Huo was established in 70 BC.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huo Guang died in 68 BC; Emperor Xuan began personal rule.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Yu and others rebelled in 66 BC; Empress Huo was deposed.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan reduced salt prices and reformed judicial procedures.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan received Huhanxie Chanyu's submission in 51 BC, ending Xiongnu threat.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Tong was a native of Anding Wushi, with a resolute character and love for law.
details.label: included

details.point: In the second year of Gengshi, Liang Tong was appointed governor of Jiuquan.
details.label: included

details.point: After the Red Eyebrow Army entered Chang'an, Liang Tong and Dou Rong raised troops; Liang Tong declined to be commander, and Dou Rong was elected.
details.label: included

details.point: In the fifth year of Jianwu, Liang Tong and others paid tribute to Emperor Guangwu and was granted the title of General Xuande.
details.label: included

details.point: In the eighth year of Jianwu, Liang Tong joined Guangwu in conquering Wei Xiao and was later granted the title of Marquis of Chengyi.
details.label: included

details.point: In the twelfth year, Liang Tong came to the capital as a marquis, was granted Gaoshan Marquis, and served as Taizhong doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Tong advocated for stricter punishments, arguing that lenient laws increased crime.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Tong cited historical precedents from the Five Emperors to Emperor Xuan to support his views on punishment.
details.label: included

details.point: The court rejected Liang Tong's proposal, stating harsh punishments were not urgent.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liang Tong later served as prefect of Jiujiang and died in office.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Ji, courtesy name Bozhuo, was a noble relative known for his cruel and extravagant behavior.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liang Ji served as Yin of Henan and was appointed general after his father Liang Shang's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Ji poisoned Emperor Zhi after the emperor called him a 'domineering general'.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Ji's power grew; he was granted 30,000 households and his wife Sun Shou was made a lord.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Ji and Sun Shou built lavish mansions and gardens, amassing immense wealth.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Ji controlled the court, with all officials required to visit him before accepting posts.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Ji killed officials who opposed him, including Wu Shu and Hou Meng.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Zhu wrote a memorial criticizing Liang Ji's power; Liang Ji had him killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Huan, with eunuchs, plotted against Liang Ji; Liang Ji and Sun Shou committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Ji's property was confiscated, totaling over three billion, used to reduce taxes nationwide.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang was from Yangxia, Chen County.
details.label: included

details.point: His grandfather Yuan Xun was a general and prefect; his father Yuan Hao was a champion general and governor of Yongzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Hao raised troops to support Prince Xun of Jin'an but was defeated and killed.
details.label: not_included

details.point: At age five, Yuan Ang was hidden in Lushan by his wet nurse; he left after pardon and moved to Jin'an.
details.label: included

details.point: At fifteen, he returned to his hometown during the Yuanhui period.
details.label: included

details.point: His father's head was sent to the capital and later returned; Yuan Ang cried and vomited blood.
details.label: included

details.point: His brother Yuan Yuzeng raised him; Yuan Ang mourned and lived by the cemetery.
details.label: included

details.point: In early Qi, he served as chief warden, prince Sheren, and military official's meritorious official.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Wu of Qi changed his name from Qianli to Yuan Ang.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as chief historian of Poyang and Duke of Xunyang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: When his mother died, he mourned according to etiquette.
details.label: included

details.point: His cousin Yuan Tuan died; Yuan Ang mourned for him citing precedents like Maleng and Zhong Yu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After mourning, he became Censor Zhongcheng and impeached Wang Xiang for bribery.
details.label: included

details.point: During a storm while transporting his mother's coffin, he tied himself to it and vowed to sink; the storm stopped.
details.label: included

details.point: At the end of Yongyuan, he defended Wuxing against the righteous army and resisted Emperor Gaozu's letter urging surrender.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote back explaining his loyalty and hesitation; after Jiankang fell, he surrendered and was pardoned.
details.label: included

details.point: He held many high offices under Liang, including Minister of Personnel, Shangshu Ling, and Sikong.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at age 80; posthumous title Mu Zhenggong was granted despite his wish to decline honors.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Yuan Jun was upright and served as governor of Wu County; he submitted to Hou Jing's general Yu Ziyue and died of illness.
details.label: included

details.point: The historian praised Yuan Ang for his loyalty and integrity, comparing him to Boyi and Shuqi.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Huishao, courtesy name Deji, from Yiyang, had military talent in youth.
details.label: included

details.point: During Qi Ming Emperor's reign, he served as Zhihe and garrison commander of Jingling Hengsang.
details.label: included

details.point: In early Yongyuan, his mother died; he returned home for burial.
details.label: included

details.point: He joined Liang Gaozu's righteous army, appointed as Ningshuo general and military leader.
details.label: included

details.point: He defeated Shen Nandang's navy, beheading him and seizing weapons.
details.label: included

details.point: After Jiankang fell, he became auxiliary state general and front army commander.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Gaozu enfeoffed him as Marquis of Shiyang County with 500 households.
details.label: included

details.point: He suppressed a remnant attack on the palace, killing many, and increased his fief by 200 households.
details.label: included

details.point: In Tianjian 4, he captured Suyu city and its lord Ma Chenglong.
details.label: included

details.point: He failed to hold Suyu against Wei reinforcements and fled to Huaiyin.
details.label: included

details.point: In Tianjian 6, he fought at Zhongli under Cao Jingzong, defeating Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as governor of Northern Yanzhou, then Sizhou, and was loved by officials and people.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Bo gained control of the Northern Army; Liu Zhang killed Lu Chan.
details.label: included

details.point: The Lu family was exterminated; Liu Heng, King of Dai, was made Emperor Wen.
details.label: included
