details.point: Fu Zhan was a native of Dongwu, King of Lang, and a descendant of Fu Sheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Zhan taught his father's Confucian teachings and had hundreds of students.
details.label: included

details.point: During Wang Mang's reign, Fu Zhan served as law enforcement in Xiu Yi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: As prefect of Pingyuan, Fu Zhan ate coarse grains and used his salary to relieve the starving people.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Zhan beheaded a corrupt governor and stabilized Pingyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Guangwu appointed Fu Zhan as Sizhi, performing the duties of the Great Situ.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Zhan succeeded Deng Yu as the Great Situ and was granted the title of Marquis of Yangdu.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Zhan advised Guangwu not to personally campaign against Peng Chong, citing King Wen's example.
details.label: included

details.point: The thief Xu Yiqing surrendered to Fu Zhan, and Fu Zhan escorted him to Luoyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Zhan requested to hold a village drinking ceremony, which was approved.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fu Zhan was dismissed from his post for not reporting a dispute in the temple.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Hou Ba was a native of Mi County, Henan, and studied the Guliang Spring and Autumn Annals.
details.label: included

details.point: As magistrate of a border county, Hou Ba killed powerful criminals and pacified the area.
details.label: included

details.point: Hou Ba served as Dayin of Huaiping and was known for his governance.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Hou Ba was appointed Shangshu Ling by Guangwu and established many government regulations.
details.label: included

details.point: Hou Ba succeeded Fu Zhan as the Great Situ and was granted the title of Marquis of Guan Nei.
details.label: included

details.point: Song Hong was a native of Chang'an and served under Emperor Ai, Emperor Ping, and Wang Mang.
details.label: included

details.point: Song Hong recommended Huan Tan to Guangwu but later criticized him for playing music at court.
details.label: included

details.point: Song Hong refused to marry Princess Huyang, saying he would not abandon his wife.
details.label: included

details.point: Cai Mao was a Confucian scholar who refused to serve under Wang Mang and later became Situ.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xin believed Fu Xi received the River Map and created the Eight Trigrams, and Yu received the Luo Shu and created the Hong Fan.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wu of Zhou consulted Jizi, who explained that Heaven gave Yu the nine categories of Hong Fan.
details.label: included

details.point: The nine categories of Hong Fan are: Five Elements, Five Affairs, Eight Policies, Five Disciplines, Royal Perfection, Three Virtues, Examining Doubts, Various Verifications, and Five Blessings and Six Extremes.
details.label: included

details.point: The text of Luo Shu consists of 65 characters, which are the nine categories of the Great Law.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Zhongshu studied Gongyang Chunqiu and explored yin-yang principles, praised by Confucianists.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xiang studied Gu Liang Chunqiu and attached Hong Fan explanations, differing from Dong Zhongshu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Xin studied Zuo Shi Zhuan and his interpretations diverged from his father Liu Xiang's.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The author compiled the Five Elements Chronicle by comparing Dong Zhongshu, Liu Xiang, and Liu Xin, and including other scholars' views, covering twelve dynasties up to Wang Mang.
details.label: included

details.point: The Five Elements are water, fire, wood, metal, and earth, each with specific properties.
details.label: included

details.point: Wood represents the east; improper hunting, drinking, expeditions, and farming cause wood to lose its nature, leading to strange phenomena like wood ice.
details.label: included

details.point: Fire represents the south; abandoning laws, banishing heroes, killing heirs, and taking concubines as wives cause fire to lose its nature, leading to fires in palaces and granaries.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Earth represents the center; building extravagant palaces, sexual immorality, and disrespecting relatives cause earth to lose its nature, leading to agricultural disasters.
details.label: included

details.point: Metal represents the west; militarism, disregarding people, and decorating defenses cause metal to lose its nature, leading to smelting failures and strange events like speaking stones.
details.label: included

details.point: Water represents the north; neglecting ancestral temples, abandoning sacrifices, and going against nature cause water to lose its nature, leading to floods and continuous rains.
details.label: included

details.point: The Spring and Autumn records many fires, such as the fire in the palace granary in 14th year of Duke Huan, interpreted as warnings from Heaven.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Zhongshu interpreted the fire at Gaomiao in Liaodong as Heaven's sign to eliminate unruly princes and ministers.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Xiang linked fires to political events, such as the fire at Weiyang Palace ice room in 4th year of Emperor Hui due to Empress Dowager Lu's actions.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The fire at the White Crane Pavilion in 3rd year of Emperor Yuan was seen as a warning against treacherous ministers like Shi Xian.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Floods in the Spring and Autumn period were often attributed to moral failings, such as Duke Huan of Lu killing his brother or Duke Yan's mother's adultery.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Han dynasty experienced floods during the reigns of Empress Dowager Lu, Emperor Wen, and Emperor Cheng, linked to political corruption and improper rituals.
details.label: included

details.point: The First Emperor was born in Handan in 259 BCE, named Zheng, surname Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: At age 13, he succeeded his father King Zhuangxiang as King of Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Buwei served as prime minister; Li Si and Meng Ao were key officials.
details.label: included

details.point: In 238 BCE, the king held a crown ceremony and wore a sword at age 22.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lao Ai rebelled using the queen mother's seals; the king suppressed it, executed Lao Ai and his clan.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Buwei was removed as prime minister in 237 BCE due to involvement with Lao Ai.
details.label: included

details.point: The king expelled guest officials but revoked the order after Li Si's remonstrance.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Liao advised bribing enemy ministers; the king adopted his strategy.
details.label: included

details.point: In 230 BCE, Qin conquered Han, the first of the six states.
details.label: included

details.point: In 228 BCE, Qin captured the King of Zhao; the First Emperor killed those who had wronged his mother in Handan.
details.label: included

details.point: In 227 BCE, Jing Ke attempted assassination; the king had him executed and attacked Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: In 225 BCE, Qin conquered Wei by flooding Daliang.
details.label: included

details.point: In 223 BCE, Qin conquered Chu; King Jing was captured.
details.label: included

details.point: In 222 BCE, Qin conquered Yan and Dai; King Xi of Yan and King Jia of Dai were captured.
details.label: included

details.point: In 221 BCE, Qin conquered Qi; King Jian was captured, unifying China.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The First Emperor adopted the title 'Shi Huangdi' (First Emperor) and abolished posthumous names.
details.label: included

details.point: He divided the empire into 36 commanderies, standardized laws, weights, measures, and writing.
details.label: included

details.point: He ordered the burning of books and burying of scholars in 213-212 BCE.
details.label: included

details.point: He built the Great Wall, roads, and palaces including Epang Palace and his mausoleum at Mount Li.
details.label: included

details.point: The First Emperor died in 210 BCE during an eastern tour; his death was concealed, and Hu Hai succeeded as Second Emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu spent thirteen years controlling floods and did not enter his house when passing by.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu divided Kyushu, dredged rivers, built embankments, and measured mountains.
details.label: partially_included

details.point: Yu guided the Yellow River from Jishi Mountain through Longmen to Daren Mountain.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu divided the Yellow River into two rivers to reduce water potential.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu's achievements benefited the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties.
details.label: included

details.point: In Chu, ditches connected Moshui and Yunmeng; in Wu, canals connected three rivers and five lakes.
details.label: included

details.point: In Qi, canals connected Zi River and Jishui River.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Bing dug two rivers in Chengdu to avoid Moshui harm.
details.label: included

details.point: Ximen Bao was magistrate of Ye County but did not use Zhangshui for irrigation.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Qi diverted Zhangshui to irrigate Ye County, making Hanoi rich.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Guo built a canal from Jingshui to Luoshui, irrigating 40,000 hectares; Qin became rich and powerful.
details.label: included

details.point: During Han, Yellow River burst at Huzi; Tian Fen advised against blocking, so it was left unblocked.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Dangshi proposed a canal from Chang'an to Wei River, reducing transport time and irrigating farmland.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Xi proposed diverting Fen and Yellow River water to irrigate 5,000 hectares in Hedong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Tang's son Zhang Yin dug Baoxie Road, but water was too fast and rocky for navigation.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yan Xiong proposed Longshou Canal using wells; it took over ten years but had little benefit.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu personally supervised blocking Huzi breach; it was finally blocked and Xuanfang Palace built.
details.label: included

details.point: Bai Gong dug Baiqu canal from Jingshui to Wei River, irrigating 4,500 hectares.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Yanshi blocked Yellow River breach in Shujun using bamboo and stones; he was rewarded.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Rang proposed three strategies: best (relocate people, let river flow north), middle (dig canals), worst (repair old embankments).
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huangdi (Yellow Emperor) was a descendant of the Shaodian tribe, with surname Gongsun and name Xuanyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Xuanyuan practiced military training and conquered rebellious princes, making them submit.
details.label: included

details.point: Chiyou was the most violent prince and could not be conquered initially.
details.label: included

details.point: Xuanyuan fought Emperor Yan at Banquan and defeated him.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangdi fought and killed Chiyou at Zhuolu.
details.label: included

details.point: The princes respected Xuanyuan as emperor, replacing Shennong.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangdi traveled extensively, pacifying disobedient regions.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangdi set up official positions named after clouds and established left and right supervisors.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangdi received a tripod from God, observed the sun, and used yarrow to calculate the calendar.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangdi appointed Fenghou, Limu, Changxian, Dahong to govern.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huangdi had twenty-five sons, fourteen of whom established surnames.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangdi married Leizu, who bore Xuanxiao and Changyi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Huangdi's death, his grandson Gaoyang (Zhuanxu) succeeded him.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuanxu raised crops, calculated seasons, and pacified all regions.
details.label: included

details.point: After Zhuanxu, Gaoxin (Emperor Ku) succeeded, being benevolent and wise.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Ku married and had Fangxun (Yao) and Zhi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Ku's death, Zhi ruled poorly, and Yao succeeded.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yao was kind and wise, ordered Xi and He to create a calendar.
details.label: included

details.point: Yao appointed Gun to control floods, but Gun failed after nine years.
details.label: included

details.point: Yao tested Shun and eventually abdicated to him.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Biao, courtesy name Shupi, was born in Anling, Fufeng.
details.label: included

details.point: His grandfather Ban Kuang served as a captain of the Yue Cavalry School.
details.label: included

details.point: His father Ban Zhi served as prefect of Guangping under Emperor Ai.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Biao had a serious personality and liked traditional culture.
details.label: included

details.point: In his twenties, he followed Wei Xiao to Tianshui after Gengshi's defeat.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xiao asked Ban Biao about the possibility of a new Warring States period.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Biao argued that the Han system of prefectures and counties prevented such fragmentation.
details.label: included

details.point: He stated that the people longed for the Han dynasty, as shown by their support for Liu family leaders.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xiao disagreed, citing the example of Liu Bang's rise from obscurity.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ban Biao wrote 'On the King's Mandate' to persuade Wei Xiao, but failed.
details.label: included

details.point: He then left Wei Xiao and went to Hexi, serving under Dou Rong.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Rong recommended Ban Biao to Emperor Guangwu, who summoned him.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Biao was promoted to Maocai and appointed Prefect of Xuzhou, but could not take office due to illness.
details.label: included

details.point: He later served in the offices of the Three Dukes.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Biao was talented in writing and focused on historical records.
details.label: included

details.point: He criticized later continuations of Sima Qian's 'Records of the Grand Historian' as vulgar.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He wrote dozens of later biographies to continue Sima Qian's work.
details.label: included

details.point: He evaluated Sima Qian's work, praising its narrative but criticizing its ideological flaws.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised on the education of the crown prince, recommending strict selection of tutors.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Biao died at age 52 in office, having written nine fu, treatises, and memorials.
details.label: included

details.point: Sacrificial officials are the third type of government officials in 'Hong Fan'.
details.label: included

details.point: Sacrifices show filial piety, serve ancestors, and understand gods.
details.label: included

details.point: Sage kings established laws and rituals for sacrifices.
details.label: included

details.point: Wizards (male 觋, female 巫) communicate with gods.
details.label: included

details.point: Descendants of sages who understand mountains, rivers, and rituals become wizards; those who understand sacrificial animals and gods become sect members.
details.label: included

details.point: Separation of duties between gods and people ensures good fortune and order.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Shao Hao, the Li family rebelled, causing chaos between people and spirits.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuanxu appointed Nan Zhengzhong for astronomy and Huo Zhengli for geography to restore order.
details.label: included

details.point: Gonggong's son Julong was worshipped as the land god; Lieshan's son Zhu was worshipped as the grain god.
details.label: included

details.point: Shun observed the Xuanji Jade Scale to organize celestial bodies and offered sacrifices to heaven, six sects, mountains, and rivers.
details.label: included

details.point: Shun conducted inspections every five years to the four mountains (Tai, Heng, Hua, Heng) with similar rituals.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Kong Jia liked to worship gods, defiling them; two dragons left.
details.label: included

details.point: Tang conquered Xia Jie and made 'Xia She', demoting Zhu and sacrificing Zhou Guo's son as grain god.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Taiwu saw mulberry and grain trees grow overnight; Yi Zhi said monsters cannot defeat virtue; Taiwu practiced virtue and trees died.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wuding got Fu Yue as prime minister, revived Yin; a pheasant crowed on a tripod; Zu Ji advised cultivating virtue.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Yi neglected gods and was struck by lightning; Emperor Zhou was promiscuous and King Wu crusaded against him.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke of Zhou established rituals and music; emperor worshipped heaven at Mingtang and Piyong; princes at Pangong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Sacrifices to Hou Ji and King Wen matched heaven; emperor sacrificed to famous mountains and rivers; princes to their own; officials to five places; commoners to ancestors.
details.label: included

details.point: King You lost power; King Ping moved east; Duke Xiang of Qin rescued Zhou and built Xizhi to sacrifice to White Emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Wen of Qin dreamed of a yellow snake and built a fortress to worship Baidi; Yongzhou became a center for altars and temples.
details.label: included

details.point: There are 118 star officials and 783 stars, representing states, countries, officials, palaces, and things.
details.label: included

details.point: Celestial phenomena are manifestations of Yin and Yang, born on earth and expressed in the sky.
details.label: included

details.point: A wise king responds to celestial signs by cautious governance and repentance to avert disasters.
details.label: included

details.point: The Purple Palace includes Tianji star (Taiyi), three princes, four hook stars (concubines), and twelve vassal stars.
details.label: included

details.point: The Big Dipper determines seasons, yin-yang, four seasons, five elements, and calendar.
details.label: included

details.point: Wenchang Palace has six stars: General, Second General, Noble Prime Minister, Siming, Si Lu, Si Ban.
details.label: included

details.point: East Palace Canglong includes Heart (emperor's hall) and House (heavenly mansion).
details.label: included

details.point: South Palace Red Bird includes Hengxing (Taiwei enclosure) and Quanxing (Xuanyuan).
details.label: included

details.point: West Palace Xianchi includes Wuhuangxing (garage of Five Emperors).
details.label: not_included

details.point: North Palace Xuanwu includes Xu and Wei (empty and danger).
details.label: not_included

details.point: Jupiter (Sui) governs spring and wood; its movement indicates benevolence and punishment.
details.label: included

details.point: Mars governs summer and fire; its stay indicates chaos, war, famine, and disease.
details.label: included

details.point: Venus governs autumn and metal; its appearance and movement indicate war and military outcomes.
details.label: included

details.point: Mercury governs winter and water; its appearance indicates lunar eclipses, comets, and floods.
details.label: included

details.point: Saturn governs late summer and earth; its position indicates land gain or loss.
details.label: included

details.point: Conjunctions of five stars indicate major events: Jupiter for victory, Mars for prosperity, etc.
details.label: included

details.point: Solar and lunar eclipses symbolize the throne and ministers; cultivation of virtue and regulation of laws.
details.label: included

details.point: Comets and guest stars herald war, destruction, and change of rulers.
details.label: included

details.point: The Milky Way is a metal body with gas emitted; many stars indicate floods, few indicate drought.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Historical examples: five stars gathered at Dongjing when Han Gaozu ascended; Mars in Heart when Emperor Gaozu died.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Xie was born with a deformed jaw and forehead, and his mother wanted to abandon him, but his father kept him.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Xie studied the Book of Songs and the Analects at age ten, and later specialized in the Book of Rites and the Book of Changes.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Xie supported himself by farming and refused to eat food he did not produce himself.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Xie was recommended as filial and incorrupt but declined office, claiming illness.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor An sent gifts to recruit Zhou Xie, but he declined and returned home.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Ye destroyed his carriage and horse, fled to study under Du Fu, and later returned home after more than ten years.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huang Xian was poor, his father was a cattle doctor, and at age 14 he impressed Xun Shu.
details.label: included

details.point: Dai Liang felt inferior after meeting Huang Xian, and Chen Fan said he dared not wear his seal before Huang Xian.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Linzong compared Huang Xian's depth to a thousand hectares of waves, immeasurable.
details.label: included

details.point: Huang Xian was promoted to filial and incorrupt but died at 48 without taking office.
details.label: included

details.point: Xu Zhen was poor, farmed himself, and refused to eat what he did not work for.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Fan set up a special couch for Xu Zhen and hung it up when he left.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Huan tried to recruit Xu Zhen with gifts, but he did not come.
details.label: included

details.point: Xu Zhen traveled to mourn Huang Qiong without revealing his name.
details.label: included

details.point: Xu Zhen left a bunch of mugwort at Guo Linzong's mother's funeral, symbolizing virtue.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Gong and his brothers were famous for filial piety and slept together even after marriage.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Gong taught the Five Classics to over 3,000 students and refused all official positions.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Gong and his brother encountered bandits and offered to die for each other; the bandits released them.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Gong hid from the painter sent by Emperor Huan by covering his face with a quilt.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Tu Pan mourned his father excessively, abstaining from meat and wine for over ten years.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan An was born in Ruyang County, Runan County, and inherited his grandfather Yuan Liang's study of the Book of Changes.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan An refused to deliver a private letter while serving as a county magistrate, demonstrating his integrity.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan An was recommended as Xiaolian and served as magistrate of Yinping and Rencheng counties, earning respect.
details.label: included

details.point: In 69 AD, Yuan An was appointed prefect of Chu County to handle the case of Liu Ying's rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan An released over 400 families from prison by reviewing cases and releasing those without evidence, despite opposition.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan An served as Henan Yin for ten years, maintaining strict governance without bribery cases.
details.label: included

details.point: In 83 AD, Yuan An argued for returning Northern Xiongnu prisoners to maintain peace, and his view was adopted by Emperor Zhang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yuan An became Sikong in 84 AD and Situ in 87 AD.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan An opposed Dou Xian's campaign against the Xiongnu, arguing it was unnecessary and costly.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan An impeached Dou Jing for illegally mobilizing border troops and requested his execution.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan An and Ren Wei reported over 40 corrupt officials, angering the Dou family but avoiding harm due to their integrity.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yuan An opposed appointing A Tong as Northern Chanyu, arguing it violated precedent and would waste resources.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan An's predictions about the Xiongnu rebellion came true after Dou Xian appointed A Tong.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan An died in 92 AD, and after the Dou family fell, his son Yuan Shang was appointed as a gentleman.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Youfu, a descendant of Zhao king Zhang Ao, studied Shangshu and taught it to hundreds of followers.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Youfu served as governor of Dongjun, where he promoted loyal officials like Wang Qing.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Zhang visited Dongjun in 85 AD, had Zhang Youfu lecture on Shangshu, and rewarded him.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Youfu opposed Dou Xian's power, imprisoned Dou Jing's messenger, and later defended Dou Xian's punishment.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Youfu became Taiwei in 93 AD, but was dismissed after a conflict with Sili Xiaowei Yan Cheng.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han Leng, a filial man, secretly managed county affairs for ill prefect Ge Xing and was later pardoned by Emperor Ming.
details.label: included

details.point: The text discusses the importance of food and goods as the foundation of people's livelihood, originating from Shennong.
details.label: included

details.point: Huang Di and his subordinates made adjustments for the people.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Yao ordered officials to inform people of weather and seasons.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Shun appointed Houji to address starvation.
details.label: included

details.point: Dayu quelled floods, stabilized the nine provinces, and regulated fields and taxes.
details.label: included

details.point: The prosperity of Shang and Zhou depended on stabilizing and enriching the people before educating them.
details.label: included

details.point: The Book of Changes states that the great virtue of heaven and earth is life, and the most precious thing for a saint is the throne.
details.label: included

details.point: Property is the basis for emperors to gather people, support the masses, and govern the country.
details.label: included

details.point: The wise king defined the people, built cities, houses, markets, and schools, and established four classes: scholars, farmers, workers, and merchants.
details.label: included

details.point: The method of governing people involved settling them in one place with defined land boundaries and a well-field system.
details.label: included

details.point: Land was distributed based on quality: good land 100 acres, medium 200, poor 300, with rotation for fallow fields.
details.label: included

details.point: Taxes were one-tenth of public land and income from industry and commerce; Fu provided labor for military supplies.
details.label: included

details.point: People received land at age 20 and returned it at 60; grains were mixed to prevent disasters.
details.label: included

details.point: Village organization: 5 families formed a neighbor, 5 neighbors a li, up to 12,500 households in a township.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Education: at 8 entered primary school, at 15 entered university; outstanding students were promoted.
details.label: included

details.point: The general policy of previous emperors was to arrange people according to land quality, enrich them, then educate them.
details.label: included

details.point: After the Zhou decline, tyrants and corrupt officials neglected boundaries, leading to chaos and the 'first tax mu' by Lu Xuangong.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Kui formulated an edict for Wei Wenhou to maximize land productivity and stabilize grain prices.
details.label: included

details.point: Shang Yang abolished well fields, promoted farming and warfare, leading to Qin's dominance but loss of restraint.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Han Dynasty, after initial famine, Emperor Wen implemented frugality and agricultural encouragement based on Jia Yi and Chao Cuo's advice.
details.label: included

details.point: Gaozu was born in Zhongyangli, Fengyi, Peixian County, surname Liu, courtesy name Ji.
details.label: included

details.point: His mother conceived him after dreaming of meeting a god and seeing a dragon on her body.
details.label: included

details.point: Gaozu had a distinctive appearance: high nose, plump forehead, beautiful beard, and 72 black moles on his left leg.
details.label: included

details.point: He was generous, charitable, and broad-minded, not engaging in ordinary production.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as the chief of Sishui Pavilion, often borrowing wine and sleeping drunk, with a dragon seen above him.
details.label: included

details.point: Feizi, a descendant, was granted Qin territory by King Xiao of Zhou for horse breeding.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin Zhong was killed by Xirong; his son Zhuang Gong avenged him with Zhou help.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Gong rescued Zhou from Quanrong and escorted King Ping east; granted land west of Qishan.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Wen moved to the Qin ancestral land and built a city; expanded territory.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Wu buried 66 people alive with him; first recorded human sacrifice in Qin.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Duke Mu (Mugong) reformed, employed Baili Xi and Jian Shu, and dominated Xirong.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Mu rescued Jin from famine, later fought Jin at Han; captured Duke Hui of Jin.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Duke Mu helped Chong'er become Duke Wen of Jin; later Qin attacked Zheng but retreated.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin army defeated by Jin at Xiao; Duke Mu took blame and restored the generals.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Duke Mu used Youyu's strategy to conquer Xirong, expanding territory by a thousand li.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Mu buried 177 people, including three good ministers; criticized for this.
details.label: included

details.point: After Duke Mu, Qin declined; lost Hexi lands to Jin; internal instability.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Duke Xiao reformed with Shang Yang (Wei Yang), moved capital to Xianyang, strengthened Qin.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shang Yang's reforms made Qin powerful; he was executed after Duke Xiao's death.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lu Buwei was a wealthy merchant from Yangzhai.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 40th year of King Zhao of Qin, the crown prince died.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 42nd year, King Zhao made An Guojun crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: An Guojun had over 20 sons and favored concubine Huayang, who had no son.
details.label: included

details.point: Zichu was a middle-ranking son of An Guojun, sent as hostage to Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Zichu was poorly treated in Zhao and lived in hardship.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Buwei saw Zichu as a rare commodity to hoard.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Buwei offered to help Zichu become heir by lobbying An Guojun and Huayang.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Buwei gave Zichu 500 gold for expenses and took 500 gold worth of gifts to Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Buwei persuaded Huayang's sister to convince Huayang to adopt Zichu as heir.
details.label: included

details.point: Huayang convinced An Guojun to make Zichu heir, confirmed by jade talisman.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Buwei gave Zichu a beautiful dancer (Zhao Ji) who was already pregnant with Lu Buwei's child.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Ji gave birth to Ying Zheng (future Qin Shihuang) after 12 months.
details.label: included

details.point: In 257 BCE, Zhao tried to kill Zichu; he escaped with Lu Buwei's help.
details.label: included

details.point: Zichu's wife and son survived in Zhao due to her wealthy family.
details.label: not_included

details.point: An Guojun became King Xiaowen in 251 BCE; Zichu became crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: King Xiaowen died after one year; Zichu became King Zhuangxiang.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Buwei became prime minister and Marquis Wenxin with 100,000 households.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhuangxiang died after 3 years; Ying Zheng became king; Lu Buwei remained prime minister.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Buwei compiled the Lüshi Chunqiu and published it with a reward for anyone who could improve it.
details.label: included

details.point: Chun Shenjun was a native of Chu, named Huang Xie.
details.label: included

details.point: He served King Qingxiang of Chu and was sent as an envoy to Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin planned to attack Chu with Han and Wei.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huang Xie wrote a letter to King Zhao of Qin advising against attacking Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: He argued that attacking Chu would strengthen Han and Wei, which were enemies of Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhao of Qin agreed and stopped the attack, forming an alliance with Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: Huang Xie accompanied Prince Wan of Chu as a hostage in Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: When King Qingxiang fell ill, Huang Xie helped Prince Wan escape back to Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: Huang Xie stayed behind and confessed to King Zhao, who spared him on Fan Ju's advice.
details.label: included

details.point: Prince Wan became King Kaolie of Chu, and Huang Xie was made prime minister and granted the title Lord Chunshen.
details.label: included

details.point: Chun Shenjun governed Huaibei and later moved his fief to Jiangdong.
details.label: included

details.point: He competed with other lords in attracting retainers.
details.label: included

details.point: In 257 BCE, he led Chu troops to relieve the siege of Handan.
details.label: included

details.point: In 256 BCE, he destroyed Lu and appointed Xunqing as magistrate.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chu became powerful again under his administration.
details.label: included

details.point: In 241 BCE, he led a failed allied campaign against Qin at Hangu Pass.
details.label: included

details.point: King Kaolie blamed him, and he was gradually alienated.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Yuan presented his pregnant sister to Chun Shenjun, who then gave her to King Kaolie; she bore a son who became crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Yuan feared Chun Shenjun would reveal the secret and plotted to kill him.
details.label: included

details.point: After King Kaolie's death, Li Yuan assassinated Chun Shenjun at the palace gate and exterminated his family.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Gong, named Zhongsun, was born in Yangzhai, Yingchuan, and his family had been officials for generations.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Gong's father, Guo Hong, studied 'Xiao Du Lv' and served as a judge for thirty years, known for fairness.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Gong inherited his father's business, taught hundreds of disciples, and later became a county official.
details.label: included

details.point: During Yongping period, Guo Gong participated in reviewing the case of Qin Peng, who was accused by Dou Gu of killing people without authorization.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Gong argued that Qin Peng should be beheaded according to law, but the emperor questioned the authority of a deputy commander to kill.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Gong cited military urgency and Han system to justify Qin Peng's actions, and the emperor agreed.
details.label: included

details.point: In a case of brothers committing murder together, the emperor initially ruled the elder brother be severely sentenced and the younger brother commuted.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Zhang mistakenly conveyed the imperial edict, leading to two executions; Guo Gong argued for a fine, distinguishing intentional homicide from manslaughter.
details.label: included

details.point: The emperor suspected Sun Zhang's intent due to proximity, but Guo Gong insisted on the law, and the emperor accepted.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Guo Gong was appointed Tingweizheng, later dismissed for breaking the law, then promoted three times to Tingwei in Yuanhe 3rd year.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Gong's family specialized in law, and he advocated mercy, reporting 41 cases where severe punishment could be mitigated.
details.label: included

details.point: In Zhanghe 1st year, a pardon reduced death penalties but did not cover escaped criminals; Guo Gong argued for their inclusion, and the emperor agreed.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Gong died in office in Yongyuan 6th year; his son Guo Rizhi also understood law and became prefect of Nanyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Chong, courtesy name Zhaogong, was from Pei Kingdom; his great-grandfather Chen Xian served as Minister of Law under Emperor Cheng and Ai.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Xian resigned during Wang Mang's usurpation, hid legal texts in walls, and advised descendants to be lenient in judgments.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Chong learned family law, served as a county official, and was recruited by Situ Bao Yu, for whom he wrote 'Resignation and Litigation Bi'.
details.label: included

details.point: As minister under Emperor Suzong, Chen Chong advocated leniency, submitting a memorial to change harsh Yongping practices.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Chong argued against executing in winter, citing classics and 'Yue Ling', and the emperor accepted his view.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Chong refused to flatter Dou Xian, was sent to be prefect of Taishan and later Guanghan, where he reduced lawsuits and buried unburied bones.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Chong became Tingwei in Yongyuan 6th year, saved many prisoners, and proposed reducing legal codes to 3000 articles to match rites, but it was not implemented.
details.label: included

details.point: Tang Meng was ordered to open Yelang and Fenzhong, levying soldiers from Ba and Shu, causing fear among the people.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor sent Sima Xiangru to blame Tang Meng and inform the people that Tang's actions were not the emperor's intention.
details.label: included

details.point: The emperor's message stated that the barbarians often invaded the border, causing hardship.
details.label: included

details.point: The emperor attacked the Xiongnu in the north; Shanzi surrendered and begged for peace.
details.label: included

details.point: Kangju and other Western Regions countries sent envoys with tributes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Minyue was pacified; the King of Nanyue sent his prince to court.
details.label: included

details.point: Nanyi and Xifen leaders served and contributed, hoping to return to Daoyi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhonglang was sent to make the barbarians submit; 500 soldiers from Ba and Shu were recruited to guard envoys.
details.label: included

details.point: Some recruits committed suicide or ran away; this was not the emperor's original intention.
details.label: included

details.point: The message contrasted the bravery of border soldiers with the cowardice of those who fled.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Tang Meng opened Yelang and built a road to southwestern Yi, recruiting tens of thousands of soldiers; the road took two years and was not completed, with many deaths and huge costs.
details.label: included

details.point: Many in Shu and the Han court said opening the southwest was not good for the country.
details.label: included

details.point: Yinyi and Zha leaders wanted to become vassals; the emperor asked Nuojia, who said the Yi tribes were close to Shu and easy to open.
details.label: included

details.point: The emperor appointed Xiangru as Zhonglang General to envoy to Xiyi, with deputy envoys Wang Ranyu, Hu Chongguo, and Lu Yue.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiangru pacified the southwestern barbarians; Yin, Zha, Ran, Qo, and Siyu submitted to Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Old passes were demolished, new passes expanded; Lingshan Road opened and a bridge built on Sunshui River.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiangru wrote an article to admonish the emperor and announce his decree, using a conversation with the elders of Shu.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiangru was accused of accepting money on his mission and was dismissed; later summoned again as Lang Guan.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiangru suffered from diabetes and often stayed home due to illness; he did not participate in public affairs.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiangru wrote 'Adult Fu' for the emperor, who was delighted and felt like traveling between heaven and earth.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang granted titles and rewards to officials and princes, including Lu Ta and Xian Zhi.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang implemented the land system and five feudal ranks based on classical texts.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang reaffirmed six financial and economic management systems, with severe punishments for violations.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang levied a tax on slaves, causing widespread resentment and uprisings.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Mu, a woman from Langxie, led a rebellion after her son was unjustly killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang forged a copper 'Mighty Dou' to intimidate peasant armies.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang dismissed officials who reported the true causes of rebellions, such as Fei Xing.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang confiscated property from corrupt officials to fund border defense.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Zong, Wang Mang's grandson, was forced to commit suicide for plotting rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: The Red Eyebrow Army, led by Li Zidu and Fan Chong, rose in Langxie due to famine.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang changed the year name and promoted the idea of becoming an immortal to dazzle the people.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang recruited specialists with unique skills to attack the Xiongnu, but many were frauds.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang lured Xiongnu prince Xubutang to Chang'an and planned to replace the Chanyu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yan You advised Wang Mang to focus on internal rebels before attacking the Xiongnu, but was dismissed.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Mang executed Han Bo for ridiculing him with the story of a giant man.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang built nine ancestral temples in Chang'an, causing massive labor and death.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Mang's son Wang Lin plotted to kill him but was discovered and forced to commit suicide.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Green Forest Army rose in Jingzhou, led by Zhang Ba and others.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Mang's army under Wang Yi was defeated at Kunyang by Liu Xiu's forces.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Mang was killed by商人 Du Wu in the Jiantai, and his head was sent to Emperor Gengshi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Dong Zhuo was from Lintao, Longxi, with a rough and scheming temperament.
details.label: included

details.point: He befriended Qiang leaders and gained fame for bravery and chivalry.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Yulin Lang under Zhang Huan, defeating rebellious Qiang and distributing rewards to soldiers.
details.label: included

details.point: He was appointed as Polu General under Zhang Wen to suppress rebellions by Bian Zhang and Han Sui.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Zhuo's army was the only one to return intact after a campaign, earning him the title Marquis of Lianxiang.
details.label: included

details.point: He refused appointments as Shaofu and Bingzhou Shepherd, retaining his troops to observe changes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was summoned by He Jin to lead troops into the capital to intimidate the Empress Dowager.
details.label: included

details.point: He met the young emperor and Prince Chenliu at Beimang, and planned to depose the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: He entered Luoyang with few troops but deceived others into thinking he had a large army.
details.label: included

details.point: He deposed the young emperor and established Emperor Xian, then murdered the Empress Dowager.
details.label: included

details.point: He became Prime Minister, allowed to enter court with sword and shoes, and granted his mother a title.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He indulged his soldiers in looting, raping, and killing in Luoyang, calling it 'prison raids.'
details.label: not_included

details.point: He destroyed five-baht coins, cast small coins, causing inflation and economic chaos.
details.label: included

details.point: He pretended to promote scholars but his cronies held only military positions.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He moved the capital to Chang'an, forcing millions to relocate, and burned Luoyang.
details.label: included

details.point: He dug up imperial tombs and collected treasures, sending Lu Bu to do so.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He defeated Sun Jian initially but was later defeated by him near Luoyang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He built Wansuiwu in Yong, storing 30 years of food, and killed rebels brutally at banquets.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was killed by Lu Bu in a plot with Wang Yun; his body was burned and ashes scattered.
details.label: included

details.point: After his death, his subordinates Li Cui and Guo Si caused chaos, leading to the collapse of central authority.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Qian was from Hanzhong and served as Lang Guan during the Jianyuan period.
details.label: included

details.point: The Xiongnu defeated the Yuezhi and used the Yuezhi king's head as a drinking vessel.
details.label: included

details.point: The Han wanted to ally with the Yuezhi against the Xiongnu and recruited envoys.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Qian was recruited and set out with Gan Fu, but was captured by the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: The Xiongnu Chanyu detained Zhang Qian for over ten years, but he kept his Han envoy status.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Qian escaped westward to Dawan, which helped him reach the Yuezhi via Kangju.
details.label: included

details.point: The Yuezhi had conquered Daxia and were content, refusing to ally against the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Qian returned via the Qiang region but was recaptured by the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: He escaped again after the Chanyu's death and returned to Han with his wife and Gan Fu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Qian was appointed Taizhong Taifu; only he and Gan Fu survived the 13-year journey.
details.label: included

details.point: He reported on the Western Regions, including Dawan, Dayuezhi, Daxia, and Kangju.
details.label: included

details.point: He noted Shu products in Daxia, suggesting a route via Shendu (India) to the Western Regions.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu was pleased and sent envoys to explore routes through Shu, but they were blocked.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Qian served as a captain under Wei Qing, knowing water and grass, and was made Marquis of Bowang.
details.label: included

details.point: He later joined Li Guang but arrived late, was sentenced to death, and redeemed himself as a commoner.
details.label: included

details.point: After the Xiongnu were driven from the Hexi Corridor, Zhang Qian proposed allying with Wusun.
details.label: included

details.point: He led a second mission to Wusun with 300 men and gifts, but failed to secure an alliance.
details.label: included

details.point: He sent deputies to Dawan, Kangju, Yuezhi, and Daxia; Wusun later sent envoys to Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Qian died about a year after returning; his missions opened the Western Regions to Han.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Han later conquered Dawan after two campaigns, securing horses and establishing ties.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius advocated using morality and etiquette to guide people, not just laws and punishments.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Laozi said that strict laws increase thieves, and high virtue does not show formal virtue.
details.label: included

details.point: Tai Shigong commented that laws are tools, not the source of political turmoil.
details.label: included

details.point: After the Han Dynasty, laws were simplified and lenient, leading to good governance.
details.label: included

details.point: During the High Empress era, cruel official Hou Feng was executed after the fall of the Lü clan.
details.label: included

details.point: Chao Cuo was harsh and was killed during the Rebellion of the Seven States.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhi Du was a brave and upright official who killed the leading family in Jinan, ending crime there.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhi Du refused to save Emperor Jing's concubine from a boar, prioritizing the emperor's safety.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhi Du was called 'Goshawk' by nobles for his harsh enforcement against royalty.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhi Du caused King Linjiang to commit suicide by denying him writing materials.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhi Du was executed after Empress Dowager Dou insisted, despite Emperor Jing's reluctance.
details.label: included

details.point: Ning Cheng was a cruel official who bullied superiors and subordinates, later became a wealthy landlord.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Yangyou was tyrannical, bending laws to kill or save people based on personal likes.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yu and Zhang Tang created strict laws, starting the trend of harsh legalism.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Tang was a cunning official who used Confucianism to justify harsh punishments.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Tang handled cases of princes, gaining imperial favor and becoming censor-in-chief.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Tang committed suicide after being accused of corruption and deceit.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Tang's family was poor at his death; his mother refused a lavish burial.
details.label: included

details.point: Yi Zong was a cruel official who killed over 400 people in Dingxiang to instill fear.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Wenshu was a harsh official who killed many, but later committed suicide after his crimes were exposed.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Han was born in Wan County, Nanyang County, to a poor family and served as county pavilion chief.
details.label: included

details.point: During Wang Mang's last years, Wu Han fled to Yuyang after his guests broke the law and made a living selling horses.
details.label: included

details.point: Gengshi Emperor sent Han Hong to recruit in Hebei; Han Hong appointed Wu Han as magistrate of Anle County.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Han wanted to join Guangwu and advised Peng Chong to ally with Guangwu against Wang Lang, but Peng Chong's officials opposed.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Han feigned a letter from Guangwu to persuade Peng Chong, who then sent troops with Wu Han to join Guangwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Han was appointed partial general and later Marquis Jiance after conquering Handan.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Han was known for loyalty but lacked literary talent; Deng Yu recommended him, and Guangwu trusted him.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Han was appointed general to recruit troops from ten counties; he killed Youzhou Mu Miao who opposed him.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Han mobilized troops and joined Guangwu at Qingyang; he offered his troops to Guangwu, impressing the generals.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Han and Cen Peng captured Ye city after persuading Chen Kang to surrender; they ambushed and killed Xie Gong.
details.label: included

details.point: After Guangwu became emperor, Wu Han was made Grand Sima and Marquis of Wuyang.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianwu 2, Wu Han defeated Tanxiang bandits and was made Marquis of Guangping.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Han defeated various bandits and captured cities in Nanyang, then fought Qin Feng and others.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianwu 3, Wu Han defeated Qingdu and surrounded Su Mao; despite injury, he rallied troops and defeated Zhou Jian and Su Mao.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Han helped Gai Yan besiege Liu Yong; after Liu Yong's death, both cities surrendered.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Han defeated five-school bandits and pacified Qinghe and Pingyuan; he persuaded five surnames in Li County to surrender without fighting.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianwu 4, Wu Han repelled a night attack and later captured Qu City, killing Dong Xian and pacifying the east.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianwu 8, Wu Han disobeyed orders to dismiss troops, leading to defeat when Gongsun Shu's forces arrived.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianwu 11-12, Wu Han led forces against Gongsun Shu; after initial setbacks, he defeated Shu forces and killed Gongsun Shu.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Han died in Jianwu 20; he was given a grand funeral and posthumous title Zhonghou.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xian, courtesy name Changru, was born in Zou, State of Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: His ancestor Wei Meng was Fu to King Yuan of Chu and his son King Yi.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Meng admonished Liu Wu with poems and later resigned, moving to Zoudi.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xian was a simple, learned man, proficient in Li and Shangshu, teaching Poetry.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recruited as a doctor, taught Emperor Zhao, and became Guanglu doctor Zhan Shi, then Dahonglu.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xian was made Marquis of Guannei for supporting Emperor Xuan's accession.
details.label: included

details.point: In the third year of Benshi, he became prime minister and Marquis of Fuyang.
details.label: included

details.point: He resigned due to old age and illness, receiving gold and a mansion; his resignation began the practice.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xian died at 82, posthumously named Jiehou.
details.label: included

details.point: He had four sons: Fangshan, Hong, Shun, and Xuancheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xuancheng, youngest son, was known for humility and learning, becoming a Langguan.
details.label: included

details.point: He pretended to be insane to avoid inheriting his father's title, but eventually accepted.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan made him governor of Henan; later he became Taichang.
details.label: included

details.point: He was demoted to Guannei Marquis for a ritual error, then wrote a self-blaming poem.
details.label: included

details.point: He later became prime minister, restoring his father's title and fief.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Xuancheng wrote another poem admonishing descendants about ritual propriety.
details.label: included

details.point: He died in the third year of Jianzhao, posthumously named Gonghou.
details.label: included

details.point: The Wei family had over ten officials of 2000 shi rank.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The text discusses the Han dynasty temple system and debates over temple destruction.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Xin argued for preserving Emperor Wu's temple based on his achievements.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Xuan, also known as Shenggong, was the elder brother of Emperor Guangwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xuan fled to Pinglin after his guests broke the law, and later joined the Pinglin soldiers.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Kuang and Wang Feng from Xinshi became leaders of a group that grew to thousands and hid in the Green Forest Mountains.
details.label: included

details.point: In the second year of Wang Mang's reign, the Green Forest army defeated Jingzhou Mu's forces and captured Jingling.
details.label: included

details.point: In the third year, a plague killed half of the Green Forest army, causing it to split into Xiajiang soldiers and Xinshi soldiers.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xuan was promoted to General Gengshi after defeating Wang Mang's officers.
details.label: included

details.point: On Xinsi day of February, Liu Xuan was made emperor on the beach of Feishui, establishing the Gengshi reign.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gengshi granted titles to generals including Wang Kuang, Wang Feng, Zhu Kun, Liu Bo, and Chen Mu.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gengshi killed Liu Boxheng out of jealousy.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Wang declared himself emperor but was later killed by Gengshi's forces.
details.label: included

details.point: In September, Wang Mang was killed in Chang'an, and his head was sent to Gengshi.
details.label: included

details.point: Gengshi moved his capital to Luoyang, then to Chang'an in February of the second year.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Gengshi was shy and incompetent, entrusting government to Zhao Meng and indulging in drinking.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Meng became dictatorial, and Gengshi killed an official who reported him.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Shu advised Gengshi to reform appointments but was imprisoned.
details.label: included

details.point: In December, the Red Eyebrows entered the pass westward.

details.point: Jia Yi was slandered by nobles and demoted to be tutor of the Prince of Changsha.
details.label: included

details.point: On his way to Changsha, Jia Yi wrote a poem mourning Qu Yuan, comparing himself to him.
details.label: included

details.point: In his third year as tutor, an owl flew into his room; Jia Yi wrote a fu on fortune and fate.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen later summoned Jia Yi back to Chang'an and discussed ghosts and gods with him.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Yi was appointed Taifu of King Huai of Liang, the emperor's youngest son.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Yi submitted multiple memorials on state affairs, including strategies to weaken vassal states.
details.label: included

details.point: He advocated dividing large vassal states into smaller ones to prevent rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Yi criticized the Han's appeasement of the Xiongnu and proposed military action.
details.label: included

details.point: He lamented the decline of social customs and the lack of ritual and moral education.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Yi emphasized the importance of early education for the crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised against making the sons of the rebellious King Li of Huainan kings.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Yi died at age 33; his policies were later partially implemented by Emperor Wen and Jing.
details.label: included

details.point: Huan Rong studied Ouyang Shangshu under Zhu Pu in Chang'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Huan Rong was poor and worked as a servant to support himself.
details.label: included

details.point: Huan Rong did not return home for 15 years, only returning after Wang Mang's usurpation.
details.label: included

details.point: Huan Rong built his teacher Zhu Pu's grave and taught hundreds of disciples.
details.label: included

details.point: During Wang Mang's fall, Huan Rong fled with students and continued teaching despite hunger.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianwu 19, Huan Rong was appointed Grand Situ at over 60.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Guangwu summoned Huan Rong to teach the crown prince after He Tang named him as teacher.
details.label: included

details.point: Huan Rong was made Yilang and given 100,000 cash to teach the prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Huan Rong declined the position of Dr. Ouyang, recommending Peng Hong and Gao Hong instead.
details.label: included

details.point: Huan Rong was known for his gentle, respectful, and erudite manner in debates.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Guangwu praised Huan Rong as a true Confucian scholar.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huan Rong recommended his disciple Hu Xian as lecturer for the crown prince.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huan Rong was appointed Junior Tutor to the crown prince alongside Zhang Yi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huan Rong attributed his success to the power of classical studies.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huan Rong requested retirement after the prince's studies were complete, but was retained.
details.label: included

details.point: Huan Rong was made Taichang in Jianwu 30.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Ming personally visited Huan Rong during illness and called him 'Master'.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huan Rong was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guannei with 5,000 households.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Huan Rong's death, Emperor Ming changed clothes and buried him with honors.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ding Hong studied Ouyang Shangshu under Huan Rong at age 13 and mastered it in 3 years.
details.label: included

details.point: The rise and fall of Xia, Yin, and Zhou dynasties were linked to the influence of empresses and consorts.
details.label: included

details.point: The Han dynasty established a hierarchy of imperial consorts with titles and ranks.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Lü was the wife of Emperor Gaozu and mother of Emperor Hui; she was resolute and assisted in pacifying the realm.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu favored Consort Qi and considered replacing Crown Prince Liu Ying with her son Ruyi.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Gaozu's death, Empress Dowager Lü imprisoned and killed Consort Qi and her son King Zhao Ruyi.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Lü appointed Lü Chan and Lü Lü as generals, consolidating power for the Lü clan.
details.label: included

details.point: After Empress Dowager Lü's death, ministers led by Zhou Bo and Chen Ping exterminated the Lü clan and installed Emperor Wen.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Zhang of Emperor Hui was the daughter of Princess Lu Yuan; she had no children and adopted a son from a palace maid.
details.label: included

details.point: Consort Bo, mother of Emperor Wen, was rarely favored by Emperor Gaozu, which allowed her to escape persecution by Empress Lü.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dou, wife of Emperor Wen and mother of Emperor Jing, was originally a palace maid sent to the Dai kingdom.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dou's brother Dou Guangguo was lost as a child and later reunited with her after she became empress.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Dowager Dou favored Huang-Lao teachings and required Emperor Jing and the Dou family to study Laozi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Bo of Emperor Jing was deposed because she had no sons and was not favored.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Wang, mother of Emperor Wu, was originally married to Jin Wangsun but was sent to the crown prince's harem after a divination.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Chen, daughter of Princess Guantao, was deposed for using witchcraft and jealousy.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Wei Zifu, originally a singer, became empress after giving birth to a son; she later committed suicide during a witchcraft scandal.
details.label: included

details.point: Consort Li, sister of musician Li Yannian, was favored by Emperor Wu but died young; she was posthumously made empress.
details.label: included

details.point: Consort Gouyi, mother of Emperor Zhao, was favored by Emperor Wu; she died after being scolded, and her son became crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Shangguan, granddaughter of Huo Guang, became empress at age six; she was not deposed after her family's rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Xu, first wife of Emperor Xuan, was poisoned by Huo Guang's wife; her son became crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaoxuan had five sons.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress gave birth to Emperor Xiaoyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Jiantun gave birth to King Xian of Huaiyang, Liu Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Weijie gave birth to King Xiao of Chu, Liu Xiao.
details.label: included

details.point: Gongsun Jie gave birth to King Si of Dongping, Liu Yu.
details.label: included

details.point: Rong gave birth to King Ai of Zhongshan, Liu Tong, who died early.
details.label: included

details.point: Huaiyang Xianwang Liu Qin was established in the third year of Yuankang.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan favored Zhang Jiantun and considered making her queen and Liu Qin crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan chose Wang Jiantun as queen to protect the crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Xuan died, Emperor Yuan ordered Liu Qin to go to his fief.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Bo, Liu Qin's uncle, corresponded with Liu Qin, encouraging him to seek an audience and criticizing the court.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Bo and his brother Zhang Guang were arrested for leaking palace conversations and misleading the prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Yuan pardoned Liu Qin but sent Wang Jun to admonish him.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Qin apologized and reformed; Zhang Bo and Jingfang were exiled.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng later allowed Liu Qin to repatriate Zhang Bo's family.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Qin died in his 36th year; his son Liu Xuan succeeded.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xiao, King of Chu, was known for filial piety; Emperor Cheng granted his son Liu Xun a marquisate.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yu, King of Dongping, had conflicts with his mother and was admonished by Emperor Yuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yu's son Liu Yun was deposed and committed suicide after being accused of cursing the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaoyuan had three sons: Emperor Cheng, Liu Kang (King of Dingtao), and Liu Xing (King of Zhongshan).
details.label: included
