details.point: Sima Ranju is a descendant of Tian Wan.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin and Yan attacked Qi; Qi was defeated.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi Jinggong worried; Yan Ying recommended Rangju.
details.label: included

details.point: Rangju said he was humble and requested a trusted minister as supervisor.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi Jinggong sent Zhuang Jia as supervisor.
details.label: included

details.point: Rangju agreed with Zhuang Jia to meet at the camp gate at noon.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuang Jia was late due to farewell drinking.
details.label: included

details.point: Rangju executed Zhuang Jia for being late.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi Jinggong sent a messenger to pardon Zhuang Jia.
details.label: included

details.point: Rangju refused the pardon, citing general's authority in the army.
details.label: included

details.point: Rangju executed the messenger's servants and damaged the chariot.
details.label: included

details.point: Rangju cared for soldiers, shared food, and inspected camp.
details.label: included

details.point: After three days, the army was ready and soldiers were eager to fight.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin army withdrew upon hearing of Rangju's discipline.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan army retreated north across the Yellow River.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Qi army recovered lost territory and returned in triumph.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi Jinggong appointed Rangju as Grand Sima.
details.label: included

details.point: Officers Bao, Gao, and Guo slandered Rangju; he was dismissed and died of illness.
details.label: included

details.point: Later, Tian Chang killed Duke Jian and exterminated Gao and Guo families.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian He became King Qi Wei and used Rangju's methods; his art of war was included in 'Sima's Art of War'.
details.label: included

details.point: Guangwu was born among the people and knew their hardships.
details.label: included

details.point: He abolished Wang Mang's complicated methods and restored Han's lenient policies.
details.label: included

details.point: Guangwu wore rough clothes, avoided luxury, and treated everyone equally.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianwu 13, foreign gifts of fine horses and swords were given to charioteers and knights.
details.label: included

details.point: He reduced officials and abolished traveling and hunting.
details.label: included

details.point: His handwritten letters were in ten lines of small characters.
details.label: included

details.point: Diligence and frugality prevailed in the court.
details.label: included

details.point: He inquired about people's sufferings and collected folk songs.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Local governors like Du Shi, Ren Yan, and Xiguang achieved remarkable political results.
details.label: included

details.point: During Jianwu and Yongping, politics were too strict, and governors were replaced on rumors.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Fu and Zhong Zhengtong gave advice but were not adopted.
details.label: included

details.point: From Emperor Zhang and He, officials like Lu Gong, Wu You, and Liu Kuan used benevolence and honesty.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Tang and Chen Chong appointed virtuous people, and politics were managed naturally.
details.label: included

details.point: Bian Feng and Yan Du were compared to Zhao Guangmo and Zhang Chang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Huan and Ren Jun as Luoyang orders punished evil and improved officialdom.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Sa built schools, rectified education, and formulated marriage etiquette in Guiyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Sa dug mountain roads, built inns, and set up post offices, reducing labor.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Sa established iron casting officials, increasing annual income by over 5 million.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Yan taught farming in Jiuzhen, increasing cultivated land and self-sufficiency.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Yan established marriage regulations, resulting in over 2,000 marriages.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/平原君虞卿列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/平原君虞卿列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Zhao Sheng, Lord of Pingyuan, was a virtuous and talented young master of Zhao who hosted thousands of guests.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as prime minister under Kings Huiwen and Xiaocheng, leaving and returning to the post three times.
details.label: included

details.point: A lame man complained that Lord Pingyuan's concubine laughed at him; Lord Pingyuan initially refused to kill her.
details.label: included

details.point: Over half of Lord Pingyuan's guests left because he valued beauty over scholars.
details.label: included

details.point: Lord Pingyuan then beheaded the concubine and apologized to the lame man, causing guests to return.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Qin siege of Handan, Lord Pingyuan was sent to Chu to form an alliance.
details.label: included

details.point: He needed twenty followers but could only find nineteen; Mao Sui recommended himself.
details.label: included

details.point: Lord Pingyuan initially dismissed Mao Sui for lack of reputation, but Mao Sui argued he would have shown his talent if placed in a pocket.
details.label: included

details.point: Lord Pingyuan took Mao Sui; the other nineteen laughed at him.
details.label: included

details.point: In Chu, Mao Sui persuaded the King of Chu to form an alliance by threatening him and citing Chu's past humiliations by Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: The alliance was sealed with a blood oath; Mao Sui's eloquence made Zhao's status more noble than the Nine Tripods.
details.label: included

details.point: Lord Pingyuan admitted his failure in recognizing talent and treated Mao Sui as a distinguished guest.
details.label: included

details.point: Chu and Wei sent reinforcements, but Handan was still in danger; Li Tong advised Lord Pingyuan to distribute resources to the people.
details.label: included

details.point: Lord Pingyuan followed Li Tong's advice, raising 3,000 volunteers; Li Tong died in battle, pushing Qin back thirty li.
details.label: included

details.point: Reinforcements arrived, and the Qin army withdrew, saving Handan.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Qing proposed increasing Lord Pingyuan's fief; Gongsun Long argued against it, and Lord Pingyuan rejected the proposal.
details.label: included

details.point: Lord Pingyuan died in the 15th year of King Xiaocheng; his descendants inherited until Zhao's fall.
details.label: included

details.point: Lord Pingyuan initially favored Gongsun Long but dismissed him after Zou Yan refuted his 'Li Jian Bai' proposition.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Qing advised King Zhao against ceding six cities to Qin after Changping, proposing instead to ally with Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhao eventually followed Yu Qing's advice, sending him to Qi; Qin envoys arrived in Zhao, and Lou Huan fled.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/张释之冯唐列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/张释之冯唐列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Zhang Shizhi was from Duyang, courtesy name Ji, served Emperor Wen of Han as a langzhong for ten years without promotion.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang recommended Zhang Shizhi to Emperor Wen, who appointed him as a visitor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Shizhi advised Emperor Wen to avoid promoting a sharp-tongued tiger keeper, citing Qin's downfall due to such practices.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen cancelled the promotion and appointed Zhang Shizhi as bus commander.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Shizhi stopped the prince and King Liang from entering Simamen without dismounting, reporting them for disrespect.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Bo pardoned the princes, and Emperor Wen promoted Zhang Shizhi to zhonglang general.
details.label: included

details.point: At Baling, Zhang Shizhi argued that a secure tomb depends on lack of valuables, not stone coffins.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Shizhi became tingwei and fined a man who startled the emperor's horse, despite the emperor's anger.
details.label: included

details.point: He sentenced a thief of Gaozu Temple's jade ring to death, not execution of relatives, convincing the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Yafu and Wang Tiankai admired Zhang Shizhi's impartiality.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Emperor Wen's death, Zhang Shizhi feared Emperor Jing and used Wang Sheng's strategy to apologize.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Sheng publicly asked Zhang Shizhi to tie his garters to enhance Zhang's reputation.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Shizhi was demoted to prince of Huainan and died later; his son Zhang Zhi was dismissed for not currying favor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Feng Tang, known for filial piety, served as zhonglang director under Emperor Wen.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Tang said Emperor Wen could not use generals like Lian Po and Li Mu, angering the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Tang explained that ancient kings trusted generals fully, unlike Han's strict laws and punishments.
details.label: included

details.point: He cited Li Mu's success under Zhao and Wei Shang's unjust punishment for minor reporting errors.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen pardoned Wei Shang and appointed Feng Tang as chariot and cavalry captain.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Emperor Jing, Feng Tang became prime minister of Chu but was dismissed; under Emperor Wu, he was too old to serve.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian praised Zhang Shizhi and Feng Tang for their integrity and adherence to law.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/韩信卢绾列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/韩信卢绾列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: King Han Xin of Han was the concubine grandson of King Xiang of Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Liang made Hancheng King of Han to appease the former Korean territory.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin was appointed general of Korea by Pei Gong (Liu Bang).
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin persuaded Liu Bang to march east from Hanzhong to compete for the world.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bang made Han Xin King of Han after pacifying the Three Qins.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiang Yu made Zheng Chang King of Han to resist Han Xin.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin defeated Zheng Chang and became King of Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin surrendered to Chu at Xingyang but later returned to Liu Bang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han Xin was officially enfeoffed as King of Han with fief in Yingchuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu moved Han Xin to Taiyuan to resist Xiongnu; Han Xin moved capital to Mayi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han Xin surrendered to Xiongnu after being besieged and suspected by Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin led Xiongnu to attack Han; Emperor Gaozu defeated him at Tongdan.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin fled to Xiongnu; his generals supported Zhao Li as king.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu was besieged at Pingcheng by Xiongnu but escaped after bribing the Xiongnu queen.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han Xin continued raiding Han borders for Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin was killed by General Chai after refusing to surrender.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Wan was a close childhood friend of Liu Bang and served as Taiwei.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Wan was made King of Yan after Zang Tu's surrender.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Wan was suspected of colluding with Chen Xi and Xiongnu; he fled to Xiongnu after Gaozu's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Xi rebelled as King of Dai; was defeated and killed by Han forces.
details.label: included

details.point: Huhanxie Shanyu stopped war, appointed his brother Hutuwusi as King Zuoguli, and ordered nobles to kill King Youxian.
details.label: included

details.point: Dulongqi and King Youxian supported Zhu Wanglian as Kenzhouliyu and attacked Huhanxie.
details.label: included

details.point: Huhanxie was defeated; Tuqi Chanyu returned to court and appointed his sons as kings.
details.label: included

details.point: Tuqi Chanyu appointed King Youaota and others as Wujie Captains to guard against Huhanxie.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Hujie slandered King Youxian, leading Tuqi to kill him; later Tuqi killed Weili.
details.label: included

details.point: King Hujie fled and declared himself Hujie Chanyu; King Youao Tartar declared himself Cheli Chanyu; Wujiu Duwei declared himself Wujii Chanyu, resulting in five chanyus.
details.label: included

details.point: Tuqi attacked Cheli and Wujii; both fled to join Hujie, totaling 40,000 troops.
details.label: included

details.point: Huhanxie sent his brother to attack Tuqi's forces, killing 10,000; Tuqi attacked Huhanxie but was defeated and committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Huhanxie's general Dan Quli surrendered to Han; Huhanxie returned to court with only tens of thousands left.
details.label: included

details.point: Runzhen Chanyu and Zhizhi Chanyu emerged; Zhizhi killed Runzhen and attacked Huhanxie.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zuoyi Zhizi advised Huhanxie to surrender to Han; Huhanxie agreed despite opposition, sent his son as hostage.
details.label: included

details.point: Huhanxie visited Han emperor in 51 BCE, received lavish gifts and was treated with high honor.
details.label: included

details.point: Han sent troops to escort Huhanxie and provided grain; Zhizhi also sent tribute but was treated less favorably.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhizhi moved west, attacked Wusun, conquered Jiankun and Dingling, established capital at Jiankun.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhizhi killed Han envoy Gu Ji; Han later learned of this.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han envoys Han Chang and Zhang Meng made a blood alliance with Huhanxie, but Han court criticized it.
details.label: included

details.point: Huhanxie returned north; Zhizhi was killed by Han forces under Gan Yanshou and Chen Tang.
details.label: included

details.point: After Zhizhi's death, Huhanxie visited Han again; Emperor Yuan gave him Wang Zhaojun as wife.
details.label: included

details.point: Huhanxie offered to guard the border; Han debated but kept border defenses due to Hou Ying's ten objections.
details.label: included

details.point: Huhanxie died after 28 years; succession disputes led to a series of chanyus, with Wang Mang's interference causing conflict.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius said that when the world is at peace, political power is not in the hands of officials.
details.label: included

details.point: With the decline of the Zhou royal family, princes began to control ritual and military affairs.
details.label: included

details.point: After Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin, officials gained exclusive power.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Warring States period, princes abandoned propriety and fought with force.
details.label: included

details.point: The Four Lords (Xinling, Pingyuan, Mengchang, Chunshen) relied on noble authority and attracted retainers.
details.label: included

details.point: Prime Minister Yu Qing left his state to save his friend Wei Qi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lord Xinling stole the military talisman to relieve Zhao from Qin siege.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After the Han dynasty, bans were loose, and the practice of keeping retainers continued.
details.label: included

details.point: King Liu Bi of Wu and King Liu An of Huainan each had thousands of guests.
details.label: included

details.point: Civilians like Ju Meng and Guo Xie became powerful knights-errant.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Xie was a calm and brave man who reformed his behavior but remained chivalrous.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Xie's nephew was killed; Guo Xie blamed his nephew and let the killer go.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Xie secretly helped a man who disrespected him avoid military duty.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Xie mediated a feud in Luoyang but gave credit to local mediators.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Xie was forced to move to Maoling despite being poor; General Wei Qing spoke for him.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Guo Xie was executed for treason after a Confucian scholar was killed by his followers.
details.label: included

details.point: Lou Hu was a doctor's son who became an official and served the five Wang brothers.
details.label: included

details.point: Lou Hu distributed gifts worth a hundred gold to relatives during an envoy mission.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Zun was a flamboyant official who loved drinking and entertaining guests.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yuan She returned funeral donations, mourned three years, and became a famous knight-errant.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Yi was a native of Wei and studied lobbying under Mr. Gui Guzi with Su Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Su Qin thought himself inferior to Zhang Yi in talent.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Yi was falsely accused of stealing jade while drinking with the Prime Minister of Chu and was tortured.
details.label: included

details.point: After torture, Zhang Yi asked his wife if his tongue was still there, indicating his reliance on rhetoric.
details.label: included

details.point: Su Qin secretly helped Zhang Yi by providing resources and goading him to go to Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Yi became a guest minister of King Hui of Qin and discussed attacking the feudal lords.
details.label: included

details.point: Su Qin's retainer revealed that Su Qin had orchestrated Zhang Yi's rise to secure Qin's non-aggression.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Yi became prime minister of Qin and warned the Chu prime minister he would take Chu cities.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Yi and Sima Cuo debated whether to attack Shu or Han; Zhang Yi advocated attacking Han.
details.label: included

details.point: King Hui of Qin chose Sima Cuo's advice to attack Shu, which enriched Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Yi persuaded King Wei of Wei to ally with Qin, leading to Wei ceding Shangjun and Shaoliang.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Yi served as Qin's prime minister for four years and supported King Hui's claim to kingship.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Yi went to Wei as prime minister to promote Qin's interests but faced resistance.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Yi persuaded King Ai of Wei to break the vertical alliance and submit to Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Yi went to Chu as prime minister and promised King Huai 600 li of Shangyu land in exchange for breaking with Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Zhen warned King Huai that Zhang Yi would deceive Chu, but the king ignored him.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Qin and Qi attacked Chu after Chu broke with Qi, defeating Chu and seizing Danyang and Hanzhong.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Yi was imprisoned by Chu but freed through the influence of Zheng Xiu and Jin Shang.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Yi persuaded Chu, Han, Qi, Zhao, and Yan to submit to Qin through separate diplomatic missions.
details.label: included

details.point: After King Wu of Qin ascended, Zhang Yi fell out of favor and went to Wei, where he died as prime minister.
details.label: included

details.point: During Wang Mang and Gengshi, rituals and documents were in disarray.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Guangwu revived classical learning, collected texts, and scholars gathered in the capital.
details.label: included

details.point: Fourteen doctors of the Five Classics were established, each teaching a family tradition.
details.label: included

details.point: In 29 CE, the Imperial Academy was built with ancient ritual implements.
details.label: included

details.point: In 56 CE, the Piyong, Mingtang, and Lingtai were constructed.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Ming personally performed rituals and lectured, with many attending.
details.label: included

details.point: Schools were established for descendants of officials and the Xiongnu sent children to study.
details.label: included

details.point: The White Tiger Hall conference produced the 'White Tiger Tongyi'.
details.label: included

details.point: Ancient texts like 'Guwen Shangshu' and 'Zuo Shi Chun Qiu' were taught but not given doctors.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Deng's regency led to scholarly decline.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Shun rebuilt the academy with 240 rooms and 1850 buildings.
details.label: included

details.point: By Emperor Huan's time, students exceeded 30,000, but scholarship declined.
details.label: included

details.point: The Xiping Stone Classics were carved in 175 CE to standardize the Five Classics.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Dong Zhuo's relocation caused massive loss of texts; only 70 carts survived.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Kun taught rituals and was imprisoned by Wang Mang for unauthorized ceremonies.
details.label: included

details.point: Wa Dan taught 'Meng's Yi' and wrote 'Yi Tong Lun'.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren An studied 'Meng's Yi' and Hetu talismans, refused official posts.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Zheng rescued Fan Sheng's son by petitioning the emperor, gaining fame.
details.label: included

details.point: Dai Ping debated at court, sat on over 50 seats in scripture discussions.
details.label: included

details.point: Ouyang She, an eighth-generation doctor, was imprisoned for corruption; students pleaded for him.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Zhong, named Yiwu, was from Yingshang.
details.label: included

details.point: He often interacted with Bao Shuya, who recognized his talent.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Zhong often took advantage of Bao Shuya, but Bao Shuya was kind and had no complaints.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Shuya served young master Xiaobai; Guan Zhong served young master Jiu.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiaobai became Duke Huan of Qi and had Prince Jiu killed; Guan Zhong was imprisoned.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Shuya recommended Guan Zhong to Duke Huan.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Zhong became prime minister and helped Duke Huan become overlord, uniting the princes.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Zhong explained that Bao Shuya understood him in poverty, failure, and disgrace.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Shuya was willing to serve under Guan Zhong after recommending him.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Shuya's descendants received fiefs and many became famous officials.
details.label: included

details.point: People praised Bao Shuya for recognizing talent more than Guan Zhong's abilities.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Zhong made Qi rich and strong by circulating goods and sharing likes/dislikes with the people.
details.label: included

details.point: He emphasized that warehouses full of food lead to understanding etiquette; abundance leads to honor/disgrace.
details.label: included

details.point: He advocated that government decrees should flow like water and align with people's desires.
details.label: included

details.point: He was skilled at turning disaster into fortune and weighing priorities.
details.label: included

details.point: He used Duke Huan's desire to attack Cai to instead attack Chu for not paying tribute to Zhou.
details.label: included

details.point: He used Duke Huan's campaign against Shanrong to make Yan restore Zhou's political system.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He persuaded Duke Huan to keep a treaty forced by Cao Mo, gaining submission of princes.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Zhong's wealth rivaled the monarch's, but the people did not consider him extravagant.
details.label: included

details.point: After Guan Zhong's death, Qi followed his policies and remained strong.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/后汉书/列传/宗室四王三侯列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/宗室四王三侯列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Liu Yan, courtesy name Bosheng, was Guangwu's eldest brother.
details.label: included

details.point: He was resolute, generous, and used his family property to make friends with heroes.
details.label: included

details.point: He planned to restore the Han dynasty during Wang Mang's usurpation.
details.label: included

details.point: He raised troops with Deng Chen, Guangwu, Li Tong, and Li Yi.
details.label: included

details.point: He mobilized 7-8,000 disciples from Chongling, calling them the Zhutiandu tribe.
details.label: included

details.point: He allied with Xinshi and Pinglin soldiers, capturing Changju, Tangzixiang, and Jiyang.
details.label: included

details.point: At Xiaochang'an, the Han army was defeated in dense fog; his sister Liu Yuan and brother Liu Zhong were killed.
details.label: included

details.point: He regrouped at Jiyang and defeated Zhenfu and Liangqiuci at Lanxiang, beheading them.
details.label: included

details.point: He defeated Yan You and Chen Mao at Yuyang, then besieged Wancheng, calling himself General Zhutian.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang offered a huge reward for killing Liu Yan and had his image shot with arrows.
details.label: included

details.point: After the victory, over 100,000 people surrendered daily.
details.label: included

details.point: The generals wanted to establish Liu Yan as emperor, but Xinshi and Pinglin generals favored Liu Xuan (Gengshi) due to Liu Yan's strictness.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yan advised against immediate enthronement, citing Chen Sheng and Xiang Ji as examples, but was overruled.
details.label: included

details.point: Gengshi was enthroned; Liu Yan was made Grand Situ and Marquis of Han Xin.
details.label: included

details.point: Gengshi and his ministers conspired to kill Liu Yan; Li Yi and Zhu Kun urged Gengshi to arrest him.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yan was killed on the same day as his cousin Liu Ji.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianwu 2, Guangwu made Liu Yan's eldest son Liu Zhang King of Taiyuan, later moved to Qi; second son Liu Xing King of Lu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Xing was a wise administrator, served as magistrate and prefect, later became King of Beihai.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Liang, Guangwu's uncle, initially opposed the uprising but later joined; was made King of Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Zhi, son of Liu Chang, was imprisoned by Wang Mang but later became King of Chengyang under Guangwu.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/后汉书/列传/李陈庞陈桥列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/李陈庞陈桥列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Li Xun studied 'Han Shi' and taught hundreds of students.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Xun was appointed as a meritorious official but failed to take up the post.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Xun mourned for three years after Li Hong's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Xun was promoted to imperial censor and described mountains and rivers in over a hundred volumes.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Xun was appointed governor of Yanzhou and later Zhangye, gaining a prestigious reputation.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Xun was dismissed by Dou Xian for not practicing rituals and gifts.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Xun was made Chijie captain of the Western Regions and refused gifts from envoys and merchants.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Xun offered a reward, beheaded the Xiongnu commander, and cleared the road.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Xun was dismissed from Wuwei prefect, walked home, and lived in seclusion.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Xun was captured by Qiang but released due to his reputation.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Xun refused grain from officials during a famine and died at 96.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Chan was a meritorious officer who did good and punished evil.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Chan was arrested for investigating a governor accused of bribery and endured torture without changing his confession.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Chan became governor of Hanzhong and barbarians surrendered upon hearing his reputation.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Chan criticized the performance of foreign illusions at court and was demoted.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Chan became governor of Liaodong and the Xiongnu retreated hundreds of miles.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Chan was dismissed due to association with Deng Zhao, later became Sili Xiaowei, and died in office.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Pang Can began as an official, was promoted to Xiaolian, and became Zuo Xiaoling.
details.label: included

details.point: Pang Can wrote a letter advising against distant campaigns and was recommended by Fan Zhun.
details.label: included

details.point: Pang Can was promoted from exile to visitor and supervised military camps in the west.
details.label: included

details.point: The east is called barbarians (Yi), divided into nine branches: Yi, Yu, Fang, Huang, Bai, Chi, Xuan, Feng, Yang.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius wanted to live in the Jiuyi area.
details.label: included

details.point: Xia Emperor Taikang lost virtue, causing Yi to rebel; later Yi submitted and presented music and dance.
details.label: partially_included

details.point: Shang Tang pacified Xia; during Zhongding, Lan Yi invaded; Yi fluctuated between submission and rebellion.
details.label: partially_included

details.point: King Wu of Zhou destroyed Shang; Sushen contributed arrows; Guan and Cai rebelled with Yi Di; Zhou Gong pacified Shu Yi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xu Yi usurped title, led nine barbarians to attack Zongzhou; King Mu of Zhou separated eastern princes, appointed King Xu Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: King Mu sent Zaofu to Chu; Chu destroyed Xu; King Xu Yan was kind but failed, died at Xushan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Li was cruel; Huaiyi invaded; Guo Zhong failed; King Xuan sent Duke Zhao to pacify Huaiyi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King You was debauched; barbarians invaded; Duke Huan of Qi repelled them.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Chu Ling allied with Huaiyi; Yue moved to Langye, fought Huaiyi; Qin annexed six states, Huaiyi scattered.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen She revolted; Weiman of Yan fled to Korea and ruled it; Emperor Wu of Han destroyed Korea.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fuyu country: north of Xuantu, flat land, produces famous horses, jade; has walls, palaces, prisons; customs include severe punishment, levirate marriage, human sacrifice.
details.label: included

details.point: Yilou: northeast of Fuyu, cold, cave dwellings, pig raising, use poison arrows, good at plundering.
details.label: included

details.point: Gaoguli: five tribes, originally Xiaonu tribe king, later Guilou tribe; customs include worship, ASEAN festival, no prisons, severe punishment.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Gouli (Gaoguli) resisted Wang Mang; later submitted to Han; conflicts with Han continued; palace invaded Liaodong; eventually peace.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Woju: fertile land, good at farming, foot combat; funeral customs with large coffins; later under Gouli rule.
details.label: included

details.point: Korea: Jizi taught etiquette and farming, established eight prohibitions; later Weiman ruled; Han established four counties.
details.label: included

details.point: Han divided into Mahan, Chenhan, Benchen; Mahan largest, joint king; Chenhan descendants of Qin refugees; produce iron used as currency.
details.label: included

details.point: Japan (Wa): islands southeast of Korea; king of Yamatai; customs include tattooing, long life, many women; Queen Himiko ruled after chaos.
details.label: included

details.point: Jizi's influence brought morality to Korea; later Wei Man disturbed customs; Confucius considered Jiuyi not despicable.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/后汉书/列传/朱景王杜马刘傅坚马列/target.txt

details.point: Zhu You was a native of Wan County, Nanyang, and lost his father young.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu You served as guard for Bo Sheng and later as army guard for Shizu (Liu Xiu).
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu You accompanied Shizu to Hebei, fought bravely, and was made a partial general and Marquis of Anyang.
details.label: included

details.point: After Shizu ascended the throne, Zhu You was appointed General Jianyi and later blocked Yanghou.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu You was captured by Deng Feng but later surrendered and was restored by the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu You defeated Yancen and beheaded Zhang Cheng, receiving ninety-seven seals and ribbons.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu You besieged Qin Feng in Liqiu; Qin Feng surrendered and was beheaded in Luoyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu You was simple, upright, liked Confucianism, and forbade plundering.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianwu 13, Zhu You's fief was increased to 7,300 households as Lihou.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu You suggested changing all kings to dukes, which the emperor adopted.
details.label: included

details.point: Jing Dan was from Yueyang, studied in Chang'an, and was promoted under Wang Mang.
details.label: included

details.point: Jing Dan and Geng Kuang resisted Wang Lang and led troops south to Shizu.
details.label: included

details.point: Jing Dan was made a partial general and Marquis Fengyi, and later Hussar General.
details.label: included

details.point: Jing Dan was granted Marquis of Yueyang, his hometown, by the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Jing Dan died of illness after being appointed governor of Hongnong to suppress thieves.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Liang was from Yuyang, served as county official, and led troops to Shizu.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Liang was made Grand Sikong and Marquis Wuqiang, but was nearly executed for disobeying orders.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Liang opened a canal to divert water into Luoyang, but the project failed.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Mao was from Nanyang, became a general under Shizu, and was granted Marquis of Lexiang.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Mao guarded the northern border against Xiongnu, built forts and beacon towers.
details.label: included

details.point: The Sima family descended from the Zhuanxu-era astronomers Zhong and Li, later serving as Zhou historians.
details.label: included

details.point: During King Xuan of Zhou, the family lost its astronomical post and adopted the surname Sima.
details.label: included

details.point: The Sima family served as Zhou historians for generations, later scattering to Jin, Wei, Zhao, and Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Cuo of Qin argued with Zhang Yi about conquering Shu and became its governor.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Cuo's grandson Sima Qi served under Bai Qi and died in the Changping campaign.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Tan served as Grand Historian under Emperor Wu of Han and studied astronomy, the Yijing, and Daoism.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Tan discussed the six schools of thought: Yin-Yang, Confucianism, Mohism, Legalism, Mingjia, and Daoism.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Tan lamented not participating in the Fengshan ceremony and urged his son Sima Qian to continue the historical work.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian traveled extensively in his youth, studied in Qi and Lu, and served as an envoy to the southwest.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian became Grand Historian after his father's death and began compiling historical records.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian defended Li Ling to Emperor Wu, was accused of defaming the emperor's brother-in-law, and was sentenced to castration.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian endured humiliation to complete his historical work, inspired by earlier figures like Confucius and Qu Yuan.
details.label: included

details.point: The work covers history from the Yellow Emperor to Emperor Wu, comprising 130 chapters and 526,500 characters.
details.label: included

details.point: The book includes 12 basic annals, 10 chronological tables, 8 treatises, 30 hereditary houses, and 70 biographies.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian's letter to Ren An explains his reasons for not committing suicide: to complete his historical work.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian argues that death can be heavier than Mount Tai or lighter than a feather, depending on one's achievements.
details.label: included

details.point: After Sima Qian's death, his grandson Yang Yun published the work during Emperor Xuan's reign.
details.label: included

details.point: The text criticizes Sima Qian for favoring Daoism over Confucianism and for praising wealth and power.
details.label: included

details.point: Despite criticisms, Sima Qian is praised as a fine historian for his clear narrative and simple style.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The work is known as the Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian) and is a foundational text of Chinese historiography.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Shan studied under his grandfather Jia Qu and wrote 'Zhi Yan' using Qin as an example to discuss governance.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Shan criticized Qin's tyranny, excessive construction of palaces and roads, and the lavish Lishan Mausoleum.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Shan argued that Qin's harsh punishments and lack of remonstrance led to its downfall.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Shan advised Emperor Wen to encourage remonstrance and avoid excessive hunting.
details.label: included

details.point: Maishan remonstrated against private coinage, arguing it gave the people control over wealth.
details.label: included

details.point: Zou Yang advised King Wu of Wu against rebellion, using Qin's fall as a warning.
details.label: included

details.point: Zou Yang was imprisoned by King Liang Xiao due to slander but wrote a letter defending his loyalty.
details.label: included

details.point: Zou Yang's letter cited historical examples of loyal ministers being misunderstood.
details.label: included

details.point: Zou Yang argued that trust between ruler and minister is essential for good governance.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Liang Xiao released Zou Yang after reading his letter and made him a guest.
details.label: included

details.point: Zou Yang helped King Liang avoid punishment by persuading Wang Changjun to intercede with the emperor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Mei Cheng advised King Wu of Wu against rebellion, warning of the Han's superior strength.
details.label: included

details.point: Mei Cheng compared Wu's wealth to Han's but argued rebellion would still fail.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Mei Cheng's advice was ignored; Wu was defeated in the Seven Kingdoms Rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Mei Cheng became famous after the rebellion and was later summoned by Emperor Wu but died en route.
details.label: included

details.point: Mei Gao, Mei Cheng's son, became a court poet favored by Emperor Wu for his quick wit.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lu Wenshu wrote to Emperor Xuan advocating lenient punishments and criticizing harsh prison officials.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Wenshu argued that Qin's harsh legalism was a major fault that persisted in Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Wenshu's advice was appreciated; he was promoted and later became a prefect.
details.label: included

details.point: The text concludes that the descendants of these remonstrators prospered due to their righteous speech.
details.label: included

details.point: Since ancient times, only those who have received destiny can become kings.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Divination was prevalent in the Zhou Dynasty and continued into the Qin and Han Dynasties.
details.label: included

details.point: Lord Sima Ji, from Chu State, practiced divination in the east city of Chang'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Song Zhong and Jia Yi, both doctors, visited Sima Ji to observe diviners.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Ji explained the principles of heaven, earth, yin and yang, and good and bad luck.
details.label: included

details.point: Song Zhong and Jia Yi questioned why Sima Ji, despite his wisdom, held a lowly position.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Ji criticized officials for being corrupt, self-serving, and harming the people.
details.label: included

details.point: He argued that diviners follow moral principles and help people without seeking reward.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Ji cited Fuxi, King Wen, and King Gou Jian as examples of using divination for governance.
details.label: included

details.point: He stated that divination brings benefits such as healing, avoiding disasters, and success.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Sima Ji quoted Laozi and Zhuangzi to defend the virtue of diviners.
details.label: included

details.point: He compared diviners favorably to lobbyists who use flattery and deception.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Ji said gentlemen stay humble to avoid harm and help others without seeking status.
details.label: included

details.point: Song Zhong and Jia Yi were humbled and left speechless after Sima Ji's speech.
details.label: included

details.point: Later, Song Zhong was convicted for a failed mission to the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Yi died of hunger strike after King Huai of Liang fell from a horse.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Ji was a wise official of Chu, proficient in the Book of Changes and Huang-Lao teachings.
details.label: included

details.point: The text notes that many diviners were famous for their skills and had high moral character.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaowu consulted various divination experts on an auspicious day for marriage.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The emperor adopted the advice of the Five Elements school to avoid death taboos.
details.label: not_included

summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/第五钟离宋寒列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Fifth Lun, courtesy name Boyu, was from Changling, Jingzhao, with ancestors surnamed Tian from Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: During Wang Mang's late reign, Fifth Lun built a fortress and defended against bandits like Bronze Horse and Red Eyebrow.
details.label: included

details.point: Fifth Lun served as a battalion commander under Xianyu Bao, who later recommended him to Yan Xing.
details.label: included

details.point: Fifth Lun rectified scales and measures in Chang'an market, ensuring fair trade.
details.label: included

details.point: In 51 AD, Fifth Lun was promoted to Xiaolian and became chief medical officer of Huaiyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Guangwu summoned Fifth Lun and was impressed by his governance advice.
details.label: included

details.point: Fifth Lun became governor of Kuaiji, where he banned excessive sacrifices and cow killings.
details.label: included

details.point: In 62 AD, Fifth Lun was transferred due to a legal violation; people blocked his departure.
details.label: included

details.point: Fifth Lun was released and returned to farming, later became magistrate of Danqu County.
details.label: included

details.point: As governor of Shu, Fifth Lun dismissed corrupt officials and promoted the virtuous.
details.label: included

details.point: Fifth Lun became Sikong in 75 AD and criticized the power of the Ma clan.
details.label: included

details.point: He submitted memorials warning against the Ma family's influence and recommending caution.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fifth Lun advocated for lenient governance and criticized harsh officials.
details.label: included

details.point: He warned against the Dou clan's growing power and advised restricting their associations.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fifth Lun was known for his integrity and selflessness, refusing gifts and favoring merit.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhongli Yi, courtesy name Zi'a, was from Shanyin, Kuaiji, and served as a county governor.
details.label: included

details.point: During a plague in Kuaiji, Zhongli Yi provided medical aid and relief.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhongli Yi released a prisoner to bury his mother, then reported the case and saved him.
details.label: included

details.point: As a minister, Zhongli Yi refused stolen pearls and criticized Emperor Ming's hunting.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhongli Yi remonstrated against palace construction during a drought, leading to rain.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Guang was a native of Longxi County, descendant of Qin general Li Zhi.
details.label: included

details.point: He joined the army in 14th year of Emperor Wen, became a Langguan due to archery skills.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen regretted Li Guang was not born in Emperor Gao's era to be a marquis.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Guang served as Cavalry General under Emperor Jing, fought in the Rebellion of the Seven States.
details.label: included

details.point: He was not rewarded because the King of Liang gave him a general's seal privately.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Guang served as prefect of Shanggu, fought many battles with Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Kunxie praised Li Guang's talent, feared he would die in battle.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Guang with 100 cavalry faced thousands of Xiongnu, used bluff to avoid attack.
details.label: included

details.point: He shot a Xiongnu general on a white horse, then dismounted to show no fear.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Guang served as prefect of Longxi, Beidi, Yanmen, Yunzhong.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Emperor Wu, Li Guang was Weiyang Palace Guard; Cheng Bushi was Changle Guard.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Guang's army was informal but effective; soldiers loved him; Huns feared his strategy.
details.label: included

details.point: In 129 BC, Li Guang attacked from Yanmen, was outnumbered and captured.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Guang escaped by jumping on a Xiongnu boy's horse, shot pursuers.
details.label: included

details.point: He was sentenced to death for losing troops, but redeemed himself and became a commoner.
details.label: included

details.point: Later, as Right Beiping governor, he killed the Baling Lieutenant who had humiliated him.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Guang shot an arrow into a stone, thinking it was a tiger.
details.label: included

details.point: In 121 BC, Li Guang with 4000 cavalry was surrounded by 40,000 Xiongnu; he held them off.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Guang's cousin Li Cai became marquis and prime minister, but Li Guang never got a title.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Guang committed suicide in 119 BC after losing his way on a campaign, rather than face trial.
details.label: included

details.point: Suihong studied Spring and Autumn with Ying Gong and became a Yilang.
details.label: included

details.point: In 3rd year of Yuanfeng, a boulder stood up in Mount Tai, white crows gathered, dead trees revived, and willow leaves formed words 'Gongsun Bing has been established'.
details.label: included

details.point: Suihong interpreted these omens as signs that commoners would become emperors and the Gongsun clan would revive.
details.label: included

details.point: Suihong urged Emperor Zhao to abdicate in favor of a worthy successor.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang executed Suihong for treason.
details.label: included

details.point: Five years later, Emperor Xuan rose from the people and recruited Suihong's son as Lang.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiahou Shichang predicted the fire at Bailiang Terrace and served as tutor to King Changyi.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiahou Sheng studied Shangshu and Hong Fan's Five Elements, and was expert in disasters.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiahou Sheng warned King Changyi of a plot against the emperor, citing Hong Fan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huo Guang and Zhang Anshi deposed King Changyi and established Emperor Xuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiahou Sheng taught Shangshu to the Empress Dowager and was made Marquis of Guannei.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiahou Sheng opposed honoring Emperor Wu with temple music, citing his harm to the people.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiahou Sheng was imprisoned for slandering Emperor Wu but later pardoned after an earthquake.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiahou Sheng died at 90; the Empress Dowager mourned him for five days.
details.label: included

details.point: Jingfang studied Yijing under Jiao Yanshou and was expert in disasters and music.
details.label: included

details.point: Jingfang warned Emperor Yuan about the dangers of eunuch Shi Xian's power.
details.label: included

details.point: Jingfang recommended a system to inspect officials' performance, but was opposed by Shi Xian.
details.label: included

details.point: Jingfang was appointed prefect of Wei County but was later executed for conspiracy.
details.label: included

details.point: Yi Feng studied Qi Shi and used yin-yang and calendar to advise Emperor Yuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Yi Feng proposed moving the capital to Chengzhou to reform the dynasty.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/孟子荀卿列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/孟子荀卿列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Tai Shigong sighed about profit being the beginning of troubles after reading Mencius.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Confucius rarely discussed profit to prevent its source.
details.label: included

details.point: Mencius was from Zou and studied with Zisi's disciples.
details.label: included

details.point: Mencius lobbied King Xuan of Qi but was not appointed.
details.label: included

details.point: Mencius went to Wei but King Hui of Liang found his ideas unrealistic.
details.label: included

details.point: At that time, states like Qin, Chu, Wei, and Qi implemented reforms and became strong.
details.label: included

details.point: Mencius promoted virtues of ancient sage-kings, which did not meet contemporary needs.
details.label: included

details.point: Mencius returned home and wrote the book 'Mencius' with seven chapters.
details.label: included

details.point: After Mencius, scholars like Zou Yan appeared.
details.label: included

details.point: Zou Yan observed yin-yang and wrote about strange changes, totaling over 100,000 words.
details.label: included

details.point: Zou Yan's theories started from small things and extended to infinity.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He traced history from the present back to the Yellow Emperor and beyond.
details.label: included

details.point: He described China as Chixian Shenzhou, one of 81 parts of the world.
details.label: included

details.point: He proposed the five virtues (metal, wood, water, fire, earth) cycle corresponding to dynastic changes.
details.label: included

details.point: Zou Yan's theories ultimately emphasized benevolence, righteousness, frugality, and proper relationships.
details.label: included

details.point: Zou Yan was highly respected in Qi, Wei, Zhao, and Yan, receiving great honors.
details.label: included

details.point: Chunyu Kun was a knowledgeable Qi scholar who observed the king's mind and remained silent when distracted.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chunyu Kun later conversed with King Hui of Liang for three days and nights but declined the prime minister position.
details.label: included

details.point: Xunqing (Xunzi) was from Zhao, studied in Qi, and became the oldest master at Jixia.
details.label: included

details.point: Xunqing served as Lanling magistrate in Chu, taught Li Si, and wrote works criticizing dark politics.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/后汉书/列传/朱冯虞郑周列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/朱冯虞郑周列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Zhu Fu served as chief secretary under Guangwu, later became general, and followed him to conquer Handan.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Fu was appointed Youzhou Mu and guarded Jicheng, settling the northern border.
details.label: included

details.point: In 26 AD, Zhu Fu was made Marquis of Wuyang with three counties.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Fu recruited former Wang Mang officials, angering Peng Chong, who refused to comply.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Fu slandered Peng Chong, leading to Peng Chong's rebellion and attack on Zhu Fu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Fu wrote a letter rebuking Peng Chong, comparing him to a Liaodong pig.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Feng, governor of Zhuo, also rebelled; Zhu Fu felt abandoned by the emperor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhu Fu fled after Geng Kuang's rescue; his wife was killed; city surrendered to Peng Chong.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Fu was replaced as Jin Wu by Jia Fu and made Marquis of Chengdu.
details.label: included

details.point: In 30 AD, Zhu Fu submitted a memorial criticizing hasty appointments and advocating gradual governance.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Fu's memorial led to reduced mobilization of Mu Shou officials.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Fu criticized the emperor for bypassing the Three Dukes and relying on personal envoys.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 34 AD, Zhu Fu became a servant and proposed expanding the selection of doctors.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Fu was executed during Yongping period after being accused without evidence.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Li rescued Shentu Ji from Yu Duwei, gaining respect and establishing his own camp.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Li was appointed magistrate of Yu County and later Jia County, known for strict governance.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Feng Li suppressed Yingchuan bandits, pardoning them and using them as informants.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Li served as Wei commandery prefect, then as Sikong, and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guannei.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Yan, as Luoyang magistrate, tortured Ma Cheng despite pleas from the Yin family, earning the emperor's respect.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yu Yan committed suicide after failing to report Liu Ying's rebellion; his family was poor.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/后汉书/列传/杜栾刘李刘谢列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/杜栾刘李刘谢列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Du Gen was from Dingling County, Yingchuan County.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Gen's father Du An was known for his integrity and sealed letters from nobles without opening them.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Gen was elected Xiaolian in the first year of Yongchu and became a doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Gen and others wrote a letter urging Emperor An to take charge, angering Empress Dowager Deng.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Gen was beaten and left for dead, but survived by feigning death with maggots in his eyes.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Gen hid as a busboy for 15 years until Empress Dowager Deng was executed.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Gen was later recruited as an imperial censor and served as prefect of Jiyin.
details.label: included

details.point: Cheng Yishi defended the deposed crown prince during Yanguang period.
details.label: included

details.point: Cheng Yishi was recommended by Zhang Hao and became Yilang under Emperor Shun.
details.label: included

details.point: Luan Ba was from Huang County, Wei County, and practiced Taoism.
details.label: included

details.point: Luan Ba served as a eunuch but requested to leave and became a doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: As governor of Guiyang, Luan Ba established schools and promoted education.
details.label: included

details.point: Luan Ba destroyed shrines and eliminated witches in Yuzhang using Taoist skills.
details.label: included

details.point: Luan Ba was imprisoned for remonstrating about tombs at Xianling Mausoleum.
details.label: included

details.point: Luan Ba committed suicide after being arrested for defending Chen Fan and Dou Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Tao was from Yingyin County, Yingchuan County, descendant of Liu Bo.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Tao submitted a memorial criticizing Emperor Huan's rule and recommending Zhu Mu and Li Ying.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Tao argued against minting big money, emphasizing food over currency.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Tao captured Zhang Jiao's followers and warned about the rebellion.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Tao was imprisoned and died after being framed by eunuchs.
details.label: included
