summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/桓谭冯衍列传下/target.summary.txt

details.point: Feng Yan served as Shangshu in the last years of Jianwu.
details.label: included

details.point: He compared Gaozu's talents and Chen Ping's wisdom, noting that slander alienates and praise brings close.
details.label: included

details.point: He contrasted Emperor Wen's wisdom and Wei Shang's loyalty, where justice makes criminals and virtue makes heroes.
details.label: included

details.point: He cited Dong Zhongshu's emphasis on morality and jealousy from Gongsun Hong.
details.label: included

details.point: He mentioned Li Guang's hard fighting against the Huns and rejection by Wei Qing.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yan considered himself a humble minister without recommendations or talents.
details.label: included

details.point: His ancestor Feng Shen was loyal and caused trouble in his private family.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yan encountered disturbances and did not seek benefits; his servants and generals had no evil plans.
details.label: included

details.point: He associated with Wei Wei Yinxing, who was respectful and careful.
details.label: included

details.point: Yin Xing offered money to establish Feng Yan's livelihood, but he refused.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Gengshi period, he held power in Taiyuan for over 20 years, but his property decreased.
details.label: included

details.point: He faced resentments and ridicule during the Qingming period.
details.label: included

details.point: He submitted a book but it was not used due to previous mistakes.
details.label: included

details.point: He retired to write poems, commenting on virtue and change with the times.
details.label: included

details.point: He lamented that his strategies could not be used and he was stuck in a small official role.
details.label: included

details.point: He suffered hunger and cold, and lost his eldest son.
details.label: included

details.point: He designated a cemetery east of Xinfeng, above Hongmen, in Shouan.
details.label: included

details.point: He retreated to seclusion, closed the door to lecture on morality, and watched Confucius and Laozi.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote fifty articles including various genres, valued by Suzong.
details.label: included

details.point: He died poor and old at home; his son was Feng Bao.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/屈原贾生列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/屈原贾生列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Qu Yuan served as left disciple of King Huai of Chu and was trusted.
details.label: included

details.point: Shangguan official slandered Qu Yuan, causing King Huai to alienate him.
details.label: included

details.point: Qu Yuan wrote 'Li Sao' out of grief over injustice.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Yi deceived Chu into breaking alliance with Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Chu attacked Qin, was defeated at Danyang and Xishui, losing 80,000 soldiers.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei attacked Chu while Chu was fighting Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi refused to rescue Chu due to broken alliance.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Huai refused land, demanded Zhang Yi; Zhang Yi bribed Zheng Xiu and Jin Shang to escape.
details.label: included

details.point: Qu Yuan advised to kill Zhang Yi but was too late.
details.label: included

details.point: Allied states defeated Chu, killed general Tang Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Qu Yuan advised against King Huai meeting King Zhao of Qin; Zilan persuaded otherwise.
details.label: included

details.point: King Huai was detained by Qin, died in Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: King Qingxiang exiled Qu Yuan due to slander by Zilan and Shangguan.
details.label: included

details.point: Qu Yuan met a fisherman, expressed his purity and refusal to compromise.
details.label: included

details.point: Qu Yuan wrote 'Huai Sha' expressing despair.
details.label: included

details.point: Qu Yuan drowned himself in the Miluo River.
details.label: included

details.point: After Qu Yuan's death, Chu weakened and was eventually destroyed by Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Yi wrote a poem to commemorate Qu Yuan while crossing the Xiang River.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Yi served as Grand Tutor of Changsha, wrote 'Ode to the Birds'.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Yi died at age 33 after grieving for King Liang Huai.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Sheng and Wu Guang led 900 conscripts to Yuyang but were delayed by rain, facing execution.
details.label: included

details.point: They decided to rebel, citing widespread suffering under Qin rule.
details.label: included

details.point: They pretended to be Fusu and Xiang Yan to gain support.
details.label: included

details.point: They used omens like fish belly silk and fox cries to inspire troops.
details.label: included

details.point: They killed the escorting officers and declared an uprising.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Sheng proclaimed himself king of Zhang Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Guang was appointed acting king to attack Rongyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Sheng sent Zhou Wen to attack Qin, but Zhou Wen was defeated by Zhang Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Guang was killed by his own generals under Chen Sheng's orders.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Sheng's army was defeated by Zhang Han; Chen Sheng was killed by his charioteer Zhuangmai.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Liang and Xiang Yu raised troops in Kuaiji after Chen Sheng's death.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiang Liang supported King Huai of Chu's grandson as figurehead.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiang Liang was killed in battle; Xiang Yu became leader.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu killed Song Yi and took command to rescue Zhao at Julu.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu defeated Zhang Han at Julu, becoming leader of the allied forces.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiang Yu killed 200,000 surrendered Qin soldiers at Xin'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu entered Xianyang, burned palaces, and killed Ziying.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu divided the empire, making himself Hegemon-King of Western Chu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiang Yu and Liu Bang fought for supremacy; Xiang Yu was defeated at Gaixia.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiang Yu committed suicide at the Wu River.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/魏豹彭越列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/魏豹彭越列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Wei Bao was originally the son of the Wei Kingdom during the Six Kingdoms period.
details.label: included

details.point: After Qin destroyed Wei, Wei Bao was exiled and became a commoner.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Sheng rebelled and made Wei Jiu, Wei Bao's brother, king of Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Han defeated Wei Jiu, who surrendered and then set himself on fire.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Bao fled to Chu and was given troops by King Huai of Chu to recapture Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu made Wei Bao king of Wei after he captured over 20 cities.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu moved Wei Bao to Hedong and titled him King of Western Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Bao surrendered to the King of Han and followed him to attack Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: After the Han defeat, Wei Bao returned home and betrayed the King of Han.
details.label: included

details.point: The King of Han sent Li Sheng to persuade Wei Bao, but he refused.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin captured Wei Bao and escorted him to Xingyang; Wei Bao was later killed by Zhou Ke.
details.label: included

details.point: Peng Yue was a fisherman and robber who became a leader of a band.
details.label: included

details.point: Peng Yue led followers and gathered over a thousand soldiers.
details.label: included

details.point: Peng Yue assisted Peigong (Liu Bang) in attacking Changyi.
details.label: included

details.point: Peng Yue joined the King of Han with 30,000 troops and was made prime minister of Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: After Han's defeat, Peng Yue operated independently along the Yellow River.
details.label: included

details.point: Peng Yue captured cities and grain, aiding the Han army.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang advised the King of Han to promise Peng Yue kingship to secure his aid.
details.label: included

details.point: Peng Yue joined the Han at Gaixia and defeated Chu; he was made King of Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: Peng Yue was accused of rebellion, arrested, and executed by Empress Lü.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Since the Han Dynasty, sycophants and favored ministers who flattered the emperor and gained favor continued to appear.
details.label: included

details.point: In Emperor Gaozu's dynasty, there were registered children; in Emperor Xiaohui's dynasty, there were Hong children.
details.label: included

details.point: These two had no outstanding talents, just flattered the emperor and gained wealth and favor.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Hui's ministers decorated their hats with feathers, belts with shells, and applied makeup due to their influence.
details.label: included

details.point: Later favorites included Deng Tong, Zhao Tan, Beigong Bozi (Emperor Wen); Han Yan, Li Yannian (Emperor Wu); Hong Gong, Shi Xian (Emperor Yuan); Zhang Fang, Chun Yuchang (Emperor Cheng); Dong Xian (Emperor Ai).
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing, Zhao, and Xuan had no favorite ministers.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Tong was a native of Nan'an, Shu County, known as Huangtoulang because he could row a boat and wear a yellow hat.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen dreamed of a yellow-headed man pushing him to heaven; he found Deng Tong matching the dream and favored him greatly.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen rewarded Deng Tong with tens of thousands of dollars multiple times, making him a high official.
details.label: included

details.point: A fortune teller said Deng Tong would die of poverty; Emperor Wen gave him Tongshan Mountain to mint coins, making him rich.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Tong sucked Emperor Wen's abscesses; the prince was ashamed and hated Deng Tong.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Jing ascended, Deng Tong was dismissed, convicted for minting coins, and died penniless.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Yan studied with Emperor Wu, was good at riding and archery, and became favored; he was killed by the Empress Dowager for adultery.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Yannian was a musician; his sister Mrs. Li was favored by Emperor Wu; Li Yannian became Xielu Captain; later he and his brother were killed for promiscuity.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Xian was a eunuch who became Zhongshu Ling under Emperor Yuan; he monopolized power and persecuted officials like Xiao Wangzhi.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Xian cleverly manipulated the emperor, confessed faults to gain trust, and was supported by Emperor Yuan; after Emperor Cheng ascended, he lost power and died on the road.
details.label: included

details.point: Chun Yuchang was favored by Emperor Cheng for helping make Feiyan empress; he became Marquis of Dingling, but was convicted for adultery with deposed Empress Xu and died in prison.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Xian was favored by Emperor Ai for his appearance; he became Grand Sima at age 22, with power equal to the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Ai once cut his sleeve to avoid waking Dong Xian; Dong Xian's family received immense rewards and built a grand mansion.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Ai died, Wang Mang forced Dong Xian to commit suicide; his family was exiled, and his property confiscated.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaoming had nine sons, including Emperor Zhang and Liu Chang of Liangjie.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jian, Qiancheng Ai King, was enfeoffed in Yongping 3rd year, died childless the next year.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xian, Chen Jing Wang, was enfeoffed as Guangping King in Yongping 3rd year.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianchu 3rd year, Liu Xian and others were ordered to fiefs but stayed in capital due to Suzong's affection.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianchu 2nd year, household registrations were equalized, annual rent was 80 million.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Xian was a scholar who debated at White Tiger Temple.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In Yongping 7th year, Liu Xian was renamed Xiping King, later changed to Chen King by posthumous edict.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xian died at age 37, succeeded by his son Liu Jun.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Gong, Pengcheng Jing Wang, was enfeoffed as Lingshou King in Yongping 9th year.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Gong was renamed Julu King, then Jiangling King, then Liu'an King, finally Pengcheng King by posthumous edict.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Gong was dignified and respected; his son Anu was made marquis in Yongchu 6th year.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yuanhe 3rd year, Liu Gong's son Liu Youfu committed suicide after angering him.
details.label: included

details.point: Prime Minister Zhao Mu falsely accused Liu Gong of treason; investigation cleared Liu Gong, Zhao Mu imprisoned.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Gong died at age 46, succeeded by his son Liu Dao.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Dang, Chengxiao King of Jing, was enfeoffed as Chongxi King in Yongping 9th year.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Dang was intelligent, studied Historical Records, and was close to Suzong.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianchu 4th year, eight counties were added to Lecheng Kingdom.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Dang broke law by having affair with palace woman Ai Zhi and killing her husband Zhang Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Dang died at age 25, succeeded by his son Liu Chong.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yan, Xia Pi Hui Wang, was enfeoffed in Yongping 15th year, had good looks, favored by Suzong.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang was from Yangwu and served as a censor under Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang was pardoned from execution by Wang Ling's intercession.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang followed Pei Gong (Liu Bang) and later served as governor of Changshan.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang captured Chen Yu and became prime minister of Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang was granted the title of Marquis of Beiping in 201 BC.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang served as chief accountant and was proficient in calculations, music, and calendars.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang assisted Liu Chang as prime minister of Huainan.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang was promoted to imperial censor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Chang was from Peixian and served as a flag officer under Liu Bang.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Ke was killed by Xiang Yu after refusing to surrender.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Chang was appointed imperial censor after Zhou Ke's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou昌 was granted the title of Marquis of Fenyin in 201 BC.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhou Chang was known for his bluntness and once compared Liu Bang to Jie and Zhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Chang opposed the deposition of the crown prince and was thanked by Empress Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yao suggested Zhou Chang as prime minister of Zhao to protect Liu Ruyi.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Chang became prime minister of Zhao and later died after Liu Ruyi was killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yao became imperial censor and was later stripped of his title by Empress Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Ao became imperial censor after Zhao Yao; he had helped Empress Lu earlier.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang succeeded as prime minister after Guan Ying and revised music and calendars.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang resigned after a proposal about the Han dynasty's virtue was accepted.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han Dynasty reversed Qin's bad governance, allowing people to recuperate.
details.label: included

details.point: Prime ministers Xiao He and Cao Shen were models of generous and quiet governance.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Hui and Empress Lu ruled without action, leading to peace and agricultural prosperity.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperors Wen and Jing saw changes in customs.
details.label: included

details.point: Officials like Wu Gong and Wen Weng were strict and just, influencing people without coercion.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu's external wars and internal legal revisions exhausted the people.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Zhongshu, Gongsun Hong, and Ni Kuan were Confucian scholars valued by Emperor Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Zhao was young; Huo Guang governed, maintaining stability after wars.
details.label: included

details.point: During Shiyuan and Yuanfeng, Xiongnu surrendered, people prospered, and reforms were made.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan, from humble origins, worked hard, personally interviewed officials, and emphasized justice.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan believed good county governors were key to peace and stability.
details.label: included

details.point: Many upright officials emerged during Emperor Xuan's reign, known as the Zhongxing period.
details.label: included

details.point: Wen Weng, as Shu prefect, selected students to study in Chang'an and established schools.
details.label: included

details.point: Wen Weng's educational reforms transformed Shu's culture, leading to many scholars.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Cheng attracted over 80,000 refugees and was rewarded, but later accused of exaggeration.
details.label: included

details.point: Huang Ba was known for lenient governance, reducing crime and increasing household registration.
details.label: included

details.point: Huang Ba's detailed local governance included issuing edicts, supporting widows, and promoting agriculture.
details.label: included

details.point: Huang Ba became prime minister but his performance declined; he was criticized for hypocrisy.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Yi was an honest official who recommended talents and lived frugally; he was buried in Tongxiang.
details.label: included

details.point: Gong Sui pacified Bohai by pardoning farmers and promoting agriculture; Zhao Xinchen improved irrigation and promoted thrift.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang presented the Imperial Seal to the Empress Dowager and removed the name of the Han Dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang married a daughter of the Wang family and made her queen.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang had four sons: Wang Zi, Wang Huo, Wang An, and Wang Lin.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Lin was made crown prince; Wang An was made Jiapi.
details.label: included

details.point: Six sons were given the title of king: Wang Qian, Wang Shou, Wang Ji, Wang Zong, Wang Shi, and Wang Li.
details.label: included

details.point: An amnesty was announced for the whole world.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang deposed Liu Ying, granting him the title of Ding'an Gong and establishing the Ding'an Principality.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Xiaoqian was named the Queen Mother of Ding'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang appointed four assistants, three dukes, and four generals.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang changed official titles and renamed palaces and cities.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang established a system of officials and ranks.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang set up flags of suggestions, wooden signs of criticism, and drums around the palace.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Mang granted titles to relatives of the royal family and changed the titles of princes to gong.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang sought descendants of ancient sage emperors and granted them titles.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang built ancestral temples for Huangdi and Yushun.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang declared that people with the surnames Yao, Ma, Chen, Tian, and Wang were his clan.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang repaired tombs of ancient emperors and established sacrifices.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang abolished the Han ancestral temples in the capital and changed the status of the Liu family.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang recast coins and banned private possession of copper and charcoal.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Mang implemented the well-field system and banned private sale of land and slaves.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xun Shu was a native of Yingyin, Yingchuan, and the 11th generation grandson of Xun Qing.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Shu was known for his noble virtues and knowledge, but was looked down upon by vulgar scholars.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Shu was recruited as a doctor during Emperor An's reign and later promoted to Tu Chang.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Shu criticized powerful relatives and eunuchs, leading to his transfer by Liang Ji.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Shu was called the 'divine king' for his upright governance.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Shu had eight sons, known as the 'Eight Dragons', and their neighborhood was renamed Gaoyangli.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Shu's sons Xun Yu and Xun Tan fought against eunuchs and died in the struggle.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Shuang, son of Xun Shu, was known for his learning and was recommended as filial and incorrupt.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Shuang's memorial criticized the lack of three-year mourning for officials and the improper marriage system.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Shuang proposed sending away excess palace women to save expenses and balance yin and yang.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Shuang lived in seclusion during the party ban and wrote many books, becoming a great Confucian.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Shuang served under Dong Zhuo but plotted against him, dying of illness at 63.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Yue, son of Xun Jian, was known for his learning and wrote 'Shenjian' discussing governance.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Yue's 'Shenjian' outlined the 'four troubles' and 'five policies' for good government.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Yue compiled 'Han Ji' in 30 chapters, a concise history of the Han dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Shao, as county magistrate, opened granaries to aid refugees despite opposition.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhong Hao was known for his virtue and was praised by Li Ying as a teacher in virtue.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Shi was known for his fairness and moral influence, even reforming a thief.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Shi voluntarily imprisoned himself during the party arrests to protect others.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Shi's son Chen Ji was known for his virtue and opposed Dong Zhuo's relocation of the capital.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Tuo was from Zhending and appointed magistrate of Longchuan during Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Xiao, Nanhai commandery governor, appointed Zhao Tuo as acting governor on his deathbed.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Tuo cut off roads, killed Qin officials, and appointed his own men.
details.label: included

details.point: After Qin fell, Zhao Tuo annexed Guilin and Xiang commanderies and declared himself King Wu of Nanyue.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu of Han recognized Zhao Tuo as King of Nanyue in 196 BCE.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Lü banned iron trade with Nanyue, prompting Zhao Tuo to declare himself Emperor Wu of Nanyue.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Tuo attacked Changsha border; Han general Zhou Zao failed due to heat and illness.
details.label: included

details.point: After Lü's death, Zhao Tuo expanded territory by bribing Minyue, Xiou, and Luoyue.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen of Han honored Zhao Tuo's ancestors and sent Lu Jia as envoy.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Tuo apologized, renounced imperial title, and became a Han vassal, but secretly kept imperial trappings.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Tuo died in 137 BCE; his grandson Zhao Hu succeeded.
details.label: included

details.point: Minyue attacked Nanyue; Zhao Hu requested Han intervention; Han sent troops and Minyue surrendered.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Hu sent his son Yingqi to Han court as hostage.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yingqi married a Han woman, Xi, and had son Zhao Xing.
details.label: included

details.point: Yingqi succeeded as king, refused to visit Han court, and died; Zhao Xing became king with Xi as queen mother.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Mother Xi had affair with Han envoy Anguo Shaoji; she advocated full submission to Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Prime Minister Lü Jia opposed submission, killed Zhao Xing, Queen Mother, and Han envoys.
details.label: included

details.point: Lü Jia installed Zhao Jiande as king; Han sent Han Qianqiu with 2000 troops, all killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu launched massive invasion in 112 BCE; Han forces captured Panyu; Lü Jia and Zhao Jiande fled but were captured.
details.label: included

details.point: Nanyue was annexed and divided into nine Han commanderies after 93 years of existence.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan was a native of Di County and a member of the Qi royal Tian family.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan killed the Di County magistrate and proclaimed himself King of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan raised troops and seized Qi lands after Zhou Shi's withdrawal.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin general Zhang Han defeated and killed Tian Dan at Linji.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan's cousin Tian Rong fled to Dong'a with remaining troops.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi people made Tian Jia king, Tian Jiao prime minister, and Tian Jian general.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Liang defeated Zhang Han at Dong'a, rescuing Tian Rong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Tian Rong attacked and drove out King Tian Jia due to anger over his appointment.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Rong made Tian Dan's son Tian Shi king of Qi and himself prime minister.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Rong refused to send troops to Xiang Liang unless Chu killed Tian Jia and Zhao killed Tian Jiao and Tian Jian.
details.label: included

details.point: Chu and Zhao refused, and Zhang Han defeated and killed Xiang Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu divided Qi after conquering Qin: Tian Shi as King of Jiaodong, Tian Du as King of Qi, Tian An as King of Jibei.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Rong attacked and killed Tian Du, Tian Shi, and Tian An, then proclaimed himself King of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu attacked Qi, defeated Tian Rong, who was killed by the people of Pingyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Heng gathered troops, counterattacked Xiang Yu, and made Tian Guang king of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Heng, as prime minister, controlled Qi's government.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han Xin attacked Qi after Li Shiqi's peace mission, capturing Linzi.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Guang and Tian Heng killed Li Shiqi, believing they were betrayed.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin defeated the Qi-Chu coalition, killed Long Qie, and captured Tian Guang.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Heng fled to an island with 500 followers; after being summoned by Liu Bang, he committed suicide near Luoyang, and his followers also died.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi was a native of Fucheng County, Yingchuan County, and was familiar with Zuo's Spring and Autumn Annals and Sun Tzu's Art of War.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi initially served Wang Mang as a county magistrate and resisted the Han army.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi was captured by Han soldiers and later recommended to Guangwu by his cousin and fellow villagers.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi persuaded Miao Meng to surrender to Guangwu, citing Guangwu's virtuous conduct.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi opened the city gate and welcomed Guangwu, who appointed him as a principal.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi recommended several capable men to Guangwu, who made them governors.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Feng Yi advised Guangwu to cultivate relations with Cao Xu, which helped during the northern campaign.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi comforted Guangwu after his brother's death and urged him to act independently and show kindness.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi provided food and firewood to Guangwu during a difficult journey, earning his gratitude.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi was known as 'General Big Tree' for his humility and refusal to boast about his achievements.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi wrote to Li Yi, urging him to surrender, and Li Yi ceased hostilities, allowing Feng Yi to pacify many counties.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi reported Li Yi's cooperation to Guangwu, who revealed the letter, leading to Li Yi's assassination.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Feng Yi advised Guangwu to ascend the throne, citing a dream as a sign of destiny.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi was sent to pacify the three auxiliary regions and instructed to avoid plundering.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi defeated Chimei at Huayin and later at Guodi, with a clever ambush using identical clothing.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi pacified Guanzhong, defeating various bandit leaders and restoring order.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi was suspected of disloyalty but wrote a letter to Guangwu expressing his loyalty, and Guangwu trusted him.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi visited the capital and was honored by Guangwu, who recalled his past services.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi defended Xunyi against Wei Xiao's forces, using a surprise attack to defeat them.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Yi died of illness in the army and was posthumously honored; his descendants continued his legacy.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaowen had four sons: Empress Dou gave birth to Emperor Xiaojing and King Xiao of Liang Wang Wu, and Zhu Ji gave birth to Prince Xiao Shen and King Huai of Liang Yi.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Wu was first King of Dai, then King of Huaiyang, and finally King of Liang in the 12th year of Emperor Xiaowen.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing casually offered to pass the throne to King Xiao of Liang, who was pleased but resigned.
details.label: included

details.point: In the spring of the 7th year of Emperor Jing, the seven kingdoms rebelled and attacked Liang; King Xiao defended Suiyang and held off Wu and Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu and Chu were defeated after three months; Liang and Han forces killed roughly equal numbers of enemy troops.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liang was a large, fertile kingdom with over 40 cities, stretching from Mount Tai to Gaoyang.
details.label: included

details.point: King Xiao built a grand garden and palace, exceeding regulations, and recruited many retainers like Yang Sheng and Gongsun Gui.
details.label: included

details.point: King Xiao had vast wealth, including hundreds of thousands of crossbows and millions in cash.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 29th year, King Xiao entered court and was treated with great honor, riding with Emperor Jing.
details.label: included

details.point: After the emperor deposed Prince Li, the Queen Mother wanted King Xiao as heir, but ministers opposed and the idea was dropped.
details.label: included

details.point: King Xiao conspired with Yang Sheng and Gongsun Gui to assassinate Yuan An and other ministers; the plot failed.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing investigated and forced King Xiao to surrender Yang Sheng and Gongsun Gui, who committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: King Xiao later hid in the eldest princess's garden, causing the Queen Mother to think the emperor killed him; they reconciled.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing became distant from King Xiao and stopped riding with him.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 35th year, King Xiao died of fever after a hunting trip; he was very filial to the Queen Mother.
details.label: included

details.point: After King Xiao's death, the Queen Mother refused to eat until Emperor Jing divided Liang into five kingdoms for his sons.
details.label: included

details.point: King Xiao's property at death included over 400,000 kilograms of gold and other valuables.
details.label: included

details.point: King Xiao's sons were all made kings: Liu Mai (Liang Gong), Liu Ming (Jichuan), Peng Li (Jidong), Liu Xuan (Shanyang), and Pi Yao (Nadan Mu).
details.label: included

details.point: Later generations of Liang kings faced scandals, including adultery and murder, leading to reductions in territory or depositions.
details.label: included

details.point: The historian's praise notes King Xiao's wealth and grandeur but criticizes his excesses and tragic end.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Tang was from Duling and his father was a county magistrate.
details.label: included

details.point: As a child, Zhang Tang interrogated a rat that stole meat, impressing his father with his legal skills.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Tang served as a county official in Chang'an after his father's death.
details.label: included

details.point: He helped Zhou Yanghou Tiansheng while imprisoned, leading to a friendship and introductions to important people.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Tang was recommended by Ning Cheng and served in the Prime Minister's Office under Marquis Wu'an.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to Taizhong doctor after investigating Queen Chen's witchcraft case.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Tang and Zhao Yu formulated strict laws for officials.
details.label: included

details.point: He became a court captain and treated Zhao Yu like an elder brother.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Tang colluded with wealthy merchants Tian Jia and Yu Wengshu.
details.label: included

details.point: He pretended to respect Confucian scholars while disagreeing with them.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Tang studied 'Shangshu' and 'Spring and Autumn' to align laws with ancient principles.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He tailored legal decisions to please the emperor, taking credit for successes and blaming subordinates for failures.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Tang handled cases differently based on the defendant's status: harsh on the powerful, lenient on the poor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He gained a good reputation by caring for friends and poor relatives despite his harsh methods.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Tang investigated rebellions of Huainan, Hengshan, and Jiangdu kings thoroughly.
details.label: included

details.point: He argued against pardoning Yan Zhu and Wu Bei, leading to their execution.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Tang was promoted to imperial censor and proposed minting coins, monopolizing salt and iron, and suppressing wealthy merchants.
details.label: included

details.point: He dominated state affairs, causing unrest and blame from ministers and commoners.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Tang debated against peace with the Xiongnu, leading to the death of Dr. Dishan.
details.label: included

details.point: He was eventually framed by three chief ministers and committed suicide; his family was poor, and his mother insisted on a simple burial.
details.label: included

details.point: Uncle Tian was a native of Xingcheng, Zhao State, descendant of the Tian family of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: He studied Huang-Lao teachings at Le Jugong's residence.
details.label: included

details.point: Recommended by Zhao people to Prime Minister Zhao Wu, who praised him to King Zhao Zhang Ao, who appointed him as a doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Gaozu's campaign against Chen Xi, King Zhao served respectfully but was insulted by the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Wu and others plotted rebellion, but King Zhao refused; Guan Gao secretly planned to kill the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: The plot was discovered; Zhao Wu committed suicide, Guan Gao was imprisoned.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu decreed that anyone following King Zhao to the capital would be punished with three clans.
details.label: included

details.point: Meng Shu, Tian Shu, and others shaved their heads, wore prison clothes, and pretended to be King Zhao's slaves to accompany him to Chang'an.
details.label: included

details.point: After Guan Gao's rebellion was clarified, King Zhao was released and deposed as Marquis of Xuan Ping.
details.label: included

details.point: Uncle Tian was recommended and appointed as governor of Hanzhong County for over ten years.
details.label: included

details.point: After Empress Gao's death and Emperor Wen's ascension, Uncle Tian recommended Meng Shu as a loyal elder.
details.label: included

details.point: Meng Shu had been dismissed for failing to resist Xiongnu raids, but Uncle Tian argued he spared exhausted soldiers.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen reinstated Meng Shu as governor of Yunzhong County.
details.label: included

details.point: Uncle Tian later lost his position due to a crime.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing sent Uncle Tian to investigate Liang King's assassination of Yuan Ang; he confirmed it but advised leniency.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing appointed Uncle Tian as prime minister of Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: As Lu prime minister, Uncle Tian punished accusers of King Lu and refused to repay debts on the king's behalf.
details.label: included

details.point: Uncle Tian discouraged King Lu from excessive hunting by refusing to rest in pavilions.
details.label: included

details.point: Uncle Tian died as Lu prime minister; his son Tian Ren refused gold offerings to preserve his father's reputation.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Ren became General Wei Qing's retainer, later a doctor, and eventually Si Zhi, but was executed for letting the prince escape during the prince's rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangfu Gui was from Anding County, grandson of a Liao general and son of a Fufeng commander.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yonghe 6th year, Western Qiang invaded; General Ma Xian failed to defeat them.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangfu Gui predicted Ma Xian's defeat and wrote to the court.
details.label: included

details.point: He led 800 soldiers to repel Qiang and was appointed planner.
details.label: included

details.point: He criticized border generals for corruption and false reports, causing rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: He requested 5,000 troops to pacify Qiang but was refused.
details.label: included

details.point: During Empress Dowager Liang's regency, he criticized eunuchs and Liang Ji in a countermeasure.
details.label: included

details.point: Liang Ji hated him and forced him to resign; he taught for 14 years.
details.label: included

details.point: After Liang Ji's death, he was summoned but declined; later became Taishan prefect and pacified bandits.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yanxi 4th year, he was appointed Zhonglang General to suppress Qiang, defeating Lingwu and beheading 800.
details.label: included

details.point: Over 100,000 Qiang surrendered due to his prestige.
details.label: included

details.point: He reported corrupt officials; eunuchs slandered him for bribing Qiang.
details.label: included

details.point: He defended himself in a letter, citing precedents and denying bribery.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recalled as Yilang but denied bribes to eunuchs, leading to imprisonment.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was released after amnesty, recommended Zhang Huan as successor.
details.label: included

details.point: He later served as Xiongnu Zhonglang General and General of Liao.
details.label: included

details.point: He requested retirement but was refused; died at 71.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote 27 works including poems and inscriptions.
details.label: included

details.point: Historian praised his integrity and ability to yield position to worthy men.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was known as one of 'Liangzhou Sanming' along with Zhang Huan and Duan Jiong.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Rong was from Pingling County, Fufeng, and his courtesy name was Duke of Zhou.
details.label: included

details.point: His seventh-generation ancestor Dou Guangguo was the younger brother of Queen Xiaowen.
details.label: included

details.point: During Wang Mang's reign, Dou Rong served as Sima under Wang Jun and was named Jianwu Nan for military merits.
details.label: included

details.point: He was known for chivalry and righteousness, and cared for his mother, elder brother, and weak younger brother.
details.label: included

details.point: After Wang Mang's defeat, Dou Rong surrendered to Zhao Meng of Gengshi and was made a school captain.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Rong requested to be sent to Hexi, becoming Captain of Zhangye's vassal state.
details.label: included

details.point: He befriended local heroes and ethnic minorities, gaining popularity in Hexi.
details.label: included

details.point: After Gengshi's failure, Dou Rong was elected General of the Five Counties of Hexi.
details.label: included

details.point: He appointed prefects for the five counties and supervised them, maintaining peace and prosperity.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Rong repelled Qiang and Hu invasions, and refugees from other commanderies returned.
details.label: included

details.point: When Guangwu ascended, Dou Rong considered joining him but was initially swayed by Wei Xiao's envoy.
details.label: included

details.point: After deliberation, Dou Rong decided to support Guangwu and sent Liu Jun with a letter and horses.
details.label: included

details.point: Guangwu appointed Dou Rong as Liangzhou Mu and gave him gold and a seal.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Rong wrote to rebuke Wei Xiao for his rebellion, but Wei Xiao refused to change.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Rong and the five prefects attacked and defeated Xianling Qiang Feng He.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Dou Rong met Guangwu at Gaoping First City and was treated with special etiquette.
details.label: included

details.point: He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Anfeng, and his brother Dou You as Marquis of Xianqin.
details.label: included

details.point: After pacifying Long and Shu, Dou Rong returned to the capital and was promoted to Da Sikong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Dou Rong repeatedly sought to resign due to fear of overreaching, but Guangwu refused.
details.label: included

details.point: The Dou family became extremely powerful, with one prince, two marquises, three princesses, and many officials.
details.label: included

details.point: Jun Buyi was a native of Bohai County, proficient in Spring and Autumn, and served as county literary official.
details.label: included

details.point: In the late years of Emperor Wu, Baoshengzhi was appointed Zhizhi envoy to suppress thieves.
details.label: included

details.point: Jun Buyi refused to remove his sword when visiting Baoshengzhi, citing it as a gentleman's weapon.
details.label: included

details.point: Baoshengzhi respected Jun Buyi and recommended him to the emperor, who appointed him governor of Qingzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Jun Buyi discovered and arrested Liu Ze's rebellion, was promoted to Jing Zhaoyin.
details.label: included

details.point: Jun Buyi's mother influenced his judicial decisions by asking about rehabilitated prisoners.
details.label: included

details.point: In the fifth year of Emperor Zhao, a man claiming to be Prince Wei appeared; Jun Buyi arrested him, citing Confucian principles.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Zhao and Huo Guang praised Jun Buyi for using classics to uphold justice.
details.label: included

details.point: Jun Buyi refused Huo Guang's offer of marriage and later died at home.
details.label: included

details.point: Shu Guang served as Taifu to the crown prince, and his nephew Shu Shou as Shaofu.
details.label: included

details.point: Shu Guang advised against appointing Xu Shun to supervise the prince's household, gaining Emperor Xuan's respect.
details.label: included

details.point: After five years, Shu Guang and Shu Shou retired together, citing contentment and avoiding danger.
details.label: included

details.point: Shu Guang used the gold given by the emperor to feast with clan and guests, not leaving it to descendants.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Dingguo's father Yu Gong was a fair judge; a filial woman was wrongly executed, causing a drought.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Dingguo studied law, became Tingwei, and was known for fair judgments, praised as not causing injustice.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Dingguo served as prime minister under Emperor Yuan, but resigned after disasters and criticism.
details.label: included

details.point: Xue Guangde served as censor doctor, advised Emperor Yuan to stop hunting and return to palace.
details.label: included

details.point: Xue Guangde threatened suicide to prevent the emperor from crossing a river by boat; the emperor took a bridge instead.
details.label: included

details.point: Ping Dang advised on restoring imperial mausoleums and temple gardens, and was promoted to prime minister.
details.label: included

details.point: Peng Xuan was dismissed as General Zuo due to being from a vassal kingdom, later recalled, and resigned under Wang Mang.
details.label: included

details.point: Bian Que was from Miao, Bohai County, surname Qin, given name Yue.
details.label: included

details.point: He was a guesthouse manager and treated Chang Sangjun with respect.
details.label: included

details.point: Chang Sangjun gave Bian Que a secret medical prescription and medicine.
details.label: included

details.point: After taking the medicine for 30 days, Bian Que could see through walls.
details.label: included

details.point: Bian Que diagnosed Zhao Jianzi's coma and predicted his recovery in 3 days.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Jianzi woke up and described his journey to the Emperor of Heaven.
details.label: included

details.point: Bian Que revived the prince of Guo, who was thought dead from corpse disease.
details.label: included

details.point: He used acupuncture and moxibustion to treat the prince, who recovered in 20 days.
details.label: included

details.point: Bian Que warned Qi Huanhou about a disease progressing from skin to marrow.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi Huanhou ignored the warnings and died when the disease reached the marrow.
details.label: included

details.point: Bian Que listed six incurable conditions, including arrogance and superstition.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He adapted his practice to local customs: women in Handan, elderly in Luoyang, children in Xianyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Xi, the Qin imperial physician, had Bian Que assassinated out of jealousy.
details.label: included

details.point: Chunyu Yi was from Lingan, studied medicine with Gongcheng Yangqing.
details.label: included

details.point: Chunyu Yi's daughter Tiying petitioned Emperor Wen to pardon her father.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen pardoned Chunyu Yi and abolished corporal punishment that year.
details.label: included

details.point: Chunyu Yi accurately diagnosed and treated many patients, predicting outcomes.
details.label: included

details.point: He used pulse diagnosis and facial color observation to determine diseases.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chunyu Yi recorded his cases and explained his diagnostic reasoning.
details.label: included

details.point: Bian Que and Chunyu Yi are both renowned for their medical skills and pulse diagnosis.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor ordered a grand hunt in Changyang to impress barbarians with animal abundance.
details.label: included

details.point: Hunt involved recruiting people from Baoxie, Hongnong, and Hanzhong to catch various animals.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Animals were transported to Changyang Shooting Bear Pavilion for barbarians to fight bare-handed.
details.label: included

details.point: Farmers could not harvest crops due to the hunt.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Xiong accompanied the emperor and later presented 'Ode to Chang Yang' to satirize the hunt.
details.label: included

details.point: In the ode, Zimo Keqing criticizes the hunt for harassing farmers and being an entertainment trip.
details.label: included

details.point: Hanlin master defends the hunt as a display of power and a precaution against danger.
details.label: included

details.point: Hanlin master recounts past military campaigns against barbarians and the pacification of distant lands.
details.label: included

details.point: The hunt is framed as a way to train troops and maintain readiness in peacetime.
details.label: included

details.point: The ode concludes with a return to proper governance and agricultural peace.
details.label: not_included

details.point: During Emperor Ai's reign, Ding, Fu, and Dong Xian held power; Yang Xiong wrote 'Tai Xuan' in seclusion.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Xiong wrote 'Explanation of Mockery' to defend his reclusive lifestyle.
details.label: included

details.point: In 'Explanation of Mockery', Yang Xiong contrasts chaotic times with stable Han rule.
details.label: included

details.point: He argues that in peaceful times, mediocre scholars suffice, and he chooses to remain obscure.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang Xiong wrote 'Tai Xuan' based on celestial phenomena, with 81 divisions and 729 praises.
details.label: included

details.point: 'Tai Xuan' corresponds to the Taichu and Zhuanxu calendars and is used for divination.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang Xiong wrote 'Fayan' in 13 chapters, imitating the Analects, to correct contemporary scholarship.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang Xiong served in Huangmen alongside Wang Mang and Liu Xin but was not promoted under Cheng, Ai, or Ping.
details.label: not_included

details.point: During Wang Mang's usurpation, Yang Xiong was implicated in a talisman case and attempted suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Xiong died at 71; his works 'Fayan' became popular, but 'Tai Xuan' remained obscure.
details.label: included
