details.point: Fu Kuan followed Pei Gong Liu Bang as a cavalry officer and started an uprising in Hengyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Kuan defeated Qin generals Zhao Bi and Yang Xiong, capturing twelve enemy heads.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Kuan was granted the title of Qing and later Gongdejun.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Kuan followed Liu Bang into Hanzhong and was promoted to right cavalry general.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Kuan helped pacify the Three Qin Dynasties and was given Diaoyin County.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Kuan attacked Xiang Yu and was granted the title of Marquis of Tongde.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Kuan captured an enemy cavalry general at Aocang Mountain, increasing his food supply.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Kuan served under Han Xin and defeated Qi's garrison at Lixia and general Tian Jie.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Kuan served under Cao Shen and conquered Bo County of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Kuan was granted the title of Marquis of Yangling with 2,600 households.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Kuan served as right prime minister of Qi and guarded against Tian Heng's rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Kuan attacked Chen Xi under Zhou Bo and defeated him.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Kuan was transferred to Dai Guo Xiangguo and led troops to garrison border counties.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fu Kuan died in the fifth year of Emperor Hui of Han, posthumous title Jinghou.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin She followed Pei Gong as an attendant and raised troops in Wanqu.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin She defeated Qin general Li You and killed a general with a thousand cavalry.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin She was granted the title of Lord Linping and later Marquis of Jianwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin She pacified six counties in Longxi, killing many Qin commanders.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin She defeated Chu general Xing Shuo, capturing over 4,000 enemy soldiers.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin She was granted the title of Marquis of Xinwu with 4,600 households.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/后汉书/列传/隗嚣公孙述列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/隗嚣公孙述列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Wei Xiao was from Chengji County, Tianshui County, and served as a state and county official under Wang Mang.
details.label: partially_included

details.point: After Liu Xin's death, Wei Xiao returned home; his uncle Wei Cui planned to raise troops to support the Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xiao was recommended as general by Wei Cui, Yang Guang, and Zhou Zong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Xiao built a temple for Gaozu, Taizong, and Shizong, and conducted a blood covenant with 31 generals.
details.label: included

details.point: The covenant declared support for Liu Zong and condemned Wang Mang's crimes.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xiao led 100,000 troops, killed Yongzhou shepherd Chen Qing, and captured Anxi.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xiao captured Longxi, Wudu, Jincheng, Wuwei, Zhangye, Jiuquan, and Dunhuang.
details.label: included

details.point: In the second year of Gengshi, Wei Xiao was appointed Right General; later he reported Wei Cui and Wei Yi's rebellion and became Imperial Censor.
details.label: included

details.point: After Gengshi's fall, Wei Xiao fled to Tianshui and called himself General Xizhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xiao gathered many scholars and became famous in Xizhou and Shandong.
details.label: included

details.point: In the second year of Jianwu, Deng Yu appointed Wei Xiao as General of Xizhou, controlling Liangzhou and Shuofang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Xiao defeated Chimei and accepted titles from Deng Yu, but later refused to go to the capital.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Guangwu corresponded with Wei Xiao, but Wei Xiao hesitated to fully submit.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xiao killed Gongsun Shu's envoys and defeated Shu forces, but later refused to attack Shu.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xiao's generals Wang Yuan and Wang Jie advised him to resist Guangwu; Wei Xiao agreed.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xiao sent his son Wei Xun as hostage but still planned to dominate.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Xiao resisted Guangwu's forces, was defeated, and later surrendered to Gongsun Shu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Xiao died of illness and anger in the ninth year of Jianwu; his son Wei Chun was made king by Wang Yuan.
details.label: included

details.point: The next year, Wei Chun surrendered; Wei Xiao's family was later killed when trying to flee.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The historian comments that Wei Xiao's conduct was admirable but he failed due to circumstances.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Heng was from Xi'e County, Nanyang.
details.label: included

details.point: His grandfather Zhang Kan served as prefect of Shu County.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Heng studied in Sanfu and Taixue, mastering the Five Classics and Six Arts.
details.label: included

details.point: He was modest and indifferent, not liking to interact with common people.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recommended as Xiaolian but did not accept, and declined several government recruitments.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote 'Ode to Two Capitals' over ten years to satirize extravagance.
details.label: included

details.point: General Deng Zhi admired him but Zhang Heng did not respond to his summons.
details.label: included

details.point: He was skilled in mechanics, astronomy, yin-yang, and calendar calculation.
details.label: included

details.point: He admired Yang Xiong's 'Tai Xuan Jing' and discussed its significance.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor An appointed him as a doctor and later Taishi Ling.
details.label: included

details.point: He built an armillary sphere and wrote 'Lingxian' and 'Suanwang Lun'.
details.label: included

details.point: He invented the seismoscope in 132 AD, which detected earthquakes accurately.
details.label: included

details.point: The seismoscope was made of fine copper with eight dragons holding bronze balls.
details.label: included

details.point: During an earthquake, a dragon would release a ball into a toad's mouth.
details.label: included

details.point: The device successfully detected an earthquake in Longxi, gaining admiration.
details.label: included

details.point: He submitted a memorial criticizing political decline and urging the emperor to retain power.
details.label: included

details.point: He argued against prophecies (chenwei), calling them fabricated and deceptive.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as prime minister of Hejian, where he suppressed lawlessness and gained respect.
details.label: included

details.point: He requested retirement after three years but died at age 62 in 139 AD.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote 32 works including poems, fu, and scientific treatises.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban's ancestors were descendants of Chu's Ling Yin Ziwen, named after a tiger nursing him.
details.label: included

details.point: During Qin's conquest of Chu, the Ban family moved between Jin and Dai, adopting Ban as their surname.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Yi raised livestock in Loufan at the end of Qin Shihuang's reign.
details.label: included

details.point: In early Han, the Ban family prospered in border areas, with Ban Yi living over a hundred years.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Yi's son Ban Ru was known for chivalry.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Ru's son Ban Chang served as Shanggu Prefect.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Chang's son Ban Hui was a county magistrate.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Hui's son Ban Kuang served as a captain and was promoted to Zuo Caoyue's cavalry school.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Kuang's daughter became Emperor Cheng's Jieyu; he retired to Changling.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Kuang had three sons: Ban Bo, Ban Si, and Ban Zhi.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Bo studied the Book of Songs with Shi Dan and was recommended by Wang Feng as a regular attendant.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Bo served as prefect of Dingxiang, capturing all thieves within ten days.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Bo was summoned by the emperor, visited his ancestral home, and distributed gold to his clan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ban Bo suffered a stroke and later died at age 38.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Si was knowledgeable, served as Yilang, and collated books with Liu Xiang.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Zhi served as Huangmen Langzhong, was upright, and later demoted by Emperor Ai.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Zhi had a friendly relationship with Wang Mang but did not present carols during his reign.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Zhi's son Ban Biao studied with Ban Si and wrote 'The Theory of King's Mandate' to counter Wei Xiao.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Biao fled to Hexi and served under Dou Rong, but resigned due to illness.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Biao's son Ban Gu wrote 'Ode to You Tong' and later served as Lang, collating imperial books.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Gu wrote the Book of Han covering 230 years from Emperor Gaozu to Wang Mang.
details.label: included

details.point: The Han Dynasty inherited the legacy of Tang Yao.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian privately wrote the Records of the Grand Historian, ranking Han after the Hundred Kings.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu inherited Yao's virtues and overthrew the Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu betrayed the covenant and was defeated by Gaozu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiao He, Cao Shen, Han Xin, Zhang Liang, and Chen Ping helped Gaozu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Hui's reign was short; Empress Lü controlled the government.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Wen was frugal and virtuous, leading to prosperity.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Jing suppressed the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Wu expanded territory and promoted Confucian classics.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Zhao relied on loyal ministers and punished rebels.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Xuan was wise and received submission from the Xiongnu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Yuan was kind but relied on eunuchs, harming his virtue.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng favored Zhao Feiyan and entrusted power to the Wang family.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Ai deposed the Wangs but appointed Dong Xian, leading to crisis.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Ping was a puppet; Wang Mang usurped the throne.
details.label: included

details.point: The Han established feudal lords and meritorious officials, recorded in tables.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Han succeeded the Qin with changes in official positions.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Han compiled ancient and modern names in a table.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Han recorded laws, rituals, music, astronomy, and geography in treatises.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Yi's ancestor Le Yang served Wei Wenhou and captured Zhongshan.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Yang was enfeoffed at Lingshou, where his descendants settled.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Yi was a virtuous man fond of military affairs, recommended in Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: After King Wuling of Zhao died, Le Yi left Zhao for Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Yi heard King Yan Zhao wanted revenge on Qi and went to Yan as envoy.
details.label: included

details.point: King Yan Zhao treated Le Yi with guest rites; Le Yi became a minister.
details.label: included

details.point: King Min of Qi was powerful but arrogant, causing resentment among states.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Yi advised King Yan Zhao to ally with Zhao, Chu, Wei to attack Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Yi formed alliances; King Yan Zhao made him general of allied forces.
details.label: included

details.point: The allied forces defeated Qi at Jishui; other states withdrew, Yan pursued.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Yi captured Linzi, seized Qi's treasures and ritual objects for Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: King Yan Zhao rewarded Le Yi with Changguo and title of Changguojun.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Yi captured over 70 Qi cities in five years; only Ju and Jimo held out.
details.label: included

details.point: King Yan Zhao died; King Yan Hui, who disliked Le Yi, succeeded.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan used counterintelligence, spreading rumors that Le Yi would rebel.
details.label: included

details.point: King Yan Hui replaced Le Yi with Qi Jie; Le Yi feared death and fled to Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao enfeoffed Le Yi at Guanjin with title Wangzhujun.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Tian Dan defeated Qi Jie and recovered all Qi cities.
details.label: included

details.point: King Yan Hui regretted and apologized; Le Yi replied with a letter explaining his actions.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Yi later traveled between Zhao and Yan, serving as guest minister in both.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/鲁仲连邹阳列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/鲁仲连邹阳列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Lu Zhonglian was a native of Qi, skilled in grand strategies, and unwilling to serve as an official.
details.label: included

details.point: He visited Zhao during the siege of Handan by Qin after Bai Qi killed 400,000 Zhao soldiers at Changping.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Anli of Wei sent General Jin Bi to rescue Zhao, but he stalled at Tangyin out of fear of Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei sent Xinyuan Yan to suggest Zhao honor King Zhao of Qin as emperor to make Qin withdraw.
details.label: included

details.point: Pingyuan Jun was hesitant; Lu Zhonglian criticized him and offered to confront Xinyuan Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Zhonglian told Xinyuan Yan he would rather die than be a subject of Qin, and he would help Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: He argued that Qin's emperor would depose and replace officials, endangering Wei's king and Xinyuan Yan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xinyuan Yan was convinced, apologized, and left Zhao, no longer advocating for Qin's emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: The Qin army withdrew fifty li upon hearing this, and Lord Wuji of Wei rescued Zhao, ending the siege.
details.label: included

details.point: Pingyuan Jun offered Lu Zhonglian a reward, but he refused, saying he did not act for profit.
details.label: included

details.point: More than twenty years later, a Yan general held Liaocheng; Lu Zhonglian wrote him a letter.
details.label: included

details.point: The letter urged the general to either return to Yan or surrender to Qi, citing historical examples.
details.label: included

details.point: The general hesitated, then committed suicide; Tian Dan then took Liaocheng and massacred it.
details.label: included

details.point: The King of Qi wanted to ennoble Lu Zhonglian, but he fled to the seaside and lived in seclusion.
details.label: included

details.point: Zou Yang, a native of Qi, traveled to Liang and was slandered by Yang Sheng and Gongsun Gui.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Xiao of Liang imprisoned Zou Yang and planned to execute him.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zou Yang wrote a letter from prison arguing that loyalty is often misunderstood and slandered.
details.label: included

details.point: He cited historical figures like Bian He, Li Si, and Bigan to illustrate the dangers of slander.
details.label: included

details.point: He urged the king to be open-minded and not be swayed by flatterers.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Xiao of Liang released Zou Yang and made him an honored guest.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Wu was a great-great-grandson of a marquis and known for Confucian virtues.
details.label: included

details.point: His daughter became empress, and he was promoted to marquis and city gate captain.
details.label: included

details.point: He was honest, refused bribes, and used his rewards to aid the poor and students.
details.label: included

details.point: He reprimanded his nephew Dou Shao for extravagance and requested his removal.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Wu memorialized against eunuch power, defending Li Ying and other party members.
details.label: included

details.point: He recommended virtuous officials like Chen Fan and criticized eunuch corruption.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Huan's death, Dou Wu supported Liu Hong (Emperor Ling) as emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Wu became general and planned with Chen Fan to kill eunuchs like Cao Jie.
details.label: included

details.point: The Empress Dowager refused to abolish all eunuchs, only allowing execution of criminals.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Dou Wu's plan leaked; eunuchs counterattacked, accusing him of treason.
details.label: included

details.point: Eunuchs seized the emperor and empress dowager, and Dou Wu's troops defected.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Wu and his brother committed suicide; their clans were exterminated.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Wu's grandson Dou Fu escaped with help from Hu Teng and later died in battle.
details.label: included

details.point: He Jin rose through his half-sister becoming empress and was made general.
details.label: included

details.point: He Jin suppressed the Yellow Turban rebellion and was made marquis.
details.label: included

details.point: He Jin and Yuan Shao plotted to kill eunuchs after Emperor Ling's death.
details.label: included

details.point: The Empress Dowager opposed killing all eunuchs; He Jin hesitated.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Shao urged He Jin to summon Dong Zhuo to threaten the court.
details.label: included

details.point: Eunuchs killed He Jin in the palace; his followers retaliated, burning palaces.
details.label: included

details.point: The eunuchs kidnapped the emperor; Yuan Shao killed over 2,000 eunuchs.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang was the younger brother of Huo Qubing, born from his father Zhong Ru's affair with maid Wei Shaoer.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Qubing brought Huo Guang to Chang'an at age 10 and appointed him as Lang.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang served Emperor Wu for over 20 years, cautious and trusted.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu appointed Huo Guang as Grand Sima General to assist the young Emperor Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang, Jin Rixi, Shangguan Jie, and Sang Hongyang received orders to assist the young emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang executed Shangguan Jie, Shangguan An, Sang Hongyang, and Ding Wairen for plotting rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Zhao died without heir; Huo Guang deposed King Changyi Liu He for licentious behavior.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang established Emperor Xuan, a great-grandson of Emperor Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang's wife Xian poisoned Empress Xu to make her daughter Chengjun empress.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang concealed the poisoning, but after his death, the truth emerged.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan gradually stripped power from the Huo family after Huo Guang's death.
details.label: included

details.point: The Huo family plotted rebellion but was discovered; Huo Yu, Huo Shan, Huo Yun committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: The Huo clan was exterminated; Empress Huo was deposed.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang was posthumously honored as Xuanchenghou and buried with imperial honors.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin Rixi, a Xiongnu prince, became a trusted official of Emperor Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin Rixi killed his own son for fornication with palace servants.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin Rixi helped suppress the Mang Heluo rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin Rixi refused to be regent, deferring to Huo Guang due to his foreign origin.
details.label: included

details.point: Jin Rixi's descendants served as chamberlains for seven generations.
details.label: included

details.point: The Huo family's downfall was attributed to arrogance and lack of restraint.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang Wangsun was from the time of Emperor Wu of the Han Dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Wangsun learned the art of Huang Lao and practiced health preservation.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Wangsun ordered a naked burial to return to nature.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Wangsun's son consulted Qi Hou about the burial instructions.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi Hou wrote to Yang Wangsun arguing against naked burial, citing filial piety and the Book of Filial Piety.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Wangsun replied that lavish burials are wasteful and harmful, and naked burial corrects social trends.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Wangsun argued that the dead are unconscious and should return to the earth.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Wangsun was finally buried naked after his death.
details.label: included

details.point: Hu Jian was a military official during the Tianhan period of Emperor Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Hu Jian killed a censor who illegally built a shop in the military fortress.
details.label: included

details.point: Hu Jian cited military law to justify the killing and was praised by the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Hu Jian later became magistrate of Weicheng County.
details.label: included

details.point: Hu Jian arrested an assassin for Princess Gaichang's lover Ding Wairen.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Hu Jian was forced to commit suicide after being framed by Shangguan Jie.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Yun was a brave man who later studied the Book of Changes and the Analects.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Yun debated Wulu Chongzong and became a doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Yun requested a sword to kill sycophant minister Zhang Yu, but was spared after Xin Qingji pleaded.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Yun retired and taught students, dying at home in his seventies.
details.label: included

details.point: Mei Fu wrote many letters to Emperor Cheng criticizing the Wang family's power and urging reforms.
details.label: included

details.point: Mei Fu advocated for establishing Confucius' descendants as heirs of the Yin dynasty, which was eventually done.
details.label: included

details.point: Since ancient times, sage kings used divination to establish countries and achieve good deeds.
details.label: included

details.point: The rise of Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties was based on auspicious omens from divination.
details.label: included

details.point: Dayu's marriage to the Tushan daughter was auspicious, leading to Xia Qi's establishment of the Xia dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: Jian Di swallowed a swallow's egg, leading to the rise of the Yin (Shang) dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: Houji's skill in sowing grains led to the Zhou dynasty's kingship.
details.label: included

details.point: Kings referred to turtle divination for difficult decisions, an unchanging tradition.
details.label: included

details.point: Barbarian tribes also practiced divination using various materials.
details.label: included

details.point: During Xia and Yin, yarrow and turtle shells were discarded after use; Zhou preserved them.
details.label: included

details.point: Divination methods varied by dynasty but served the same purpose of predicting the future.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu followed Qin's system and established diviners.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Emperors Xiaohui, Xiaowen, and Xiaojing, divination's subtle methods were lost.
details.label: included

details.point: The current emperor (Han Wudi) recruited skilled diviners and rewarded them heavily.
details.label: included

details.point: Divination contributed to military campaigns against Xiongnu, Dawan, and Baiyue.
details.label: included

details.point: Diviners like Qiu Ziming gained wealth and favor, but later their false accusations led to their execution.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Zhou's divination helped King Wu recover from illness; King Zhou's divination was unlucky.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Wen of Jin's divination predicted success in restoring King Zhou Xiang.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Xian of Jin's divination for attacking Li Rong was unlucky, leading to disaster.
details.label: included

details.point: King Ling of Chu's divination for betraying Zhou was unlucky, leading to defeat.
details.label: included

details.point: The 'Hongfan' chapter of 'Shangshu' includes divination as one of five methods for solving difficulties.
details.label: included

details.point: Turtles live a thousand years; yarrow has hundreds of stems; both are used for divination.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius had 77 disciples proficient in the six arts.
details.label: included

details.point: Disciples outstanding in virtue: Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu, Zhong Gong.
details.label: included

details.point: Disciples good at political affairs: Ran You, Ji Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: Disciples skilled in language: Zaiwo, Zigong.
details.label: included

details.point: Disciples erudite in literature: Ziyou, Zixia.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Hui (Yan Yuan) was Confucius' favorite disciple, known for virtue and poverty.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Hui died prematurely at age 29.
details.label: included

details.point: Min Ziqian was known for filial piety.
details.label: included

details.point: Ran Boniu died of an incurable disease.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhong Gong was recommended for high office despite his father's low status.
details.label: included

details.point: Ran Qiu (Zi You) served as Ji family retainer.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhong You (Zi Lu) was brave and straightforward, died in Wei civil war.
details.label: included

details.point: Zaiwo (Zi Wo) questioned the three-year mourning period.
details.label: included

details.point: Zigong (Duanmu Ci) was a skilled diplomat and wealthy merchant.
details.label: included

details.point: Zigong's diplomatic mission saved Lu, disrupted Qi, destroyed Wu, strengthened Jin, and enabled Yue's dominance.
details.label: included

details.point: Ziyou (Yan Yan) served as Wucheng governor, promoted music education.
details.label: included

details.point: Zixia (Bu Shang) taught in Hexi after Confucius' death.
details.label: included

details.point: Zizhang (Zhuan Sun) asked about official salary and enlightenment.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zeng Shen (Zengzi) wrote the Book of Filial Piety.
details.label: included

details.point: Tantai Mieming (Ziyu) was initially judged by appearance but later proved virtuous.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Fengshi was a native of Lu County, Shangdang County, later moved to Duling.
details.label: included

details.point: His ancestor Feng Ting dedicated Shangdang to Zhao and died at Changping.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Fengshi was elected as a Langguan during Emperor Wu's reign.
details.label: included

details.point: He studied Spring and Autumn and military strategy, recommended by Han Zeng.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as an envoy to escort Dawan guests and encountered Shache's rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Shache killed King Wannian and Han envoy Xi Chongguo.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Fengshi mobilized 15,000 troops from various states and captured Shache city.
details.label: included

details.point: King Shache committed suicide; Feng Fengshi's reputation shocked the Western Regions.
details.label: included

details.point: He obtained a famous horse from Dayuan and returned to Chang'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan rewarded him as Guanglu Doctor and Captain Shuiheng despite Xiao Wangzhi's opposition.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Yuan appointed him Jinwu, then Right General of Dian Kingdom.
details.label: included

details.point: He became Guang Luxun and later led troops against Qiang rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: He argued for 40,000 troops but only got 12,000 initially.
details.label: included

details.point: After initial defeat, he requested 36,000 more troops; Emperor sent 60,000 under Ren Qianqiu.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Fengshi defeated the Qiang, beheading thousands.
details.label: included

details.point: He was granted Marquis of Guannei with 500 households and 60 kg gold.
details.label: included

details.point: He died of illness after serving as a general for ten years.
details.label: included

details.point: His daughter Feng Yuan became Emperor Yuan's Zhaoyi and mother of Prince Xiao of Zhongshan.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Feng Yewang became a high official but was dismissed due to being the emperor's uncle.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Shen, another son, was made Marquis of Yixiang but later committed suicide after being framed.
details.label: included

details.point: Ranghou Wei Ran was the younger brother of Queen Mother Xuan, mother of King Zhao of Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: After King Wu of Qin died without sons, his younger brother became King Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Mother Xuan was originally a palace woman called Mi Bazi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Ran supported King Zhao's succession against rival brothers.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhao appointed Wei Ran as general to guard Xianyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Ran suppressed a rebellion and expelled Queen Wu to Wei.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Ran's prestige shocked Qin; Queen Mother Xuan presided over court while King Zhao was young.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In year 7 of King Zhao, Qin sent Lord Jingyang as hostage to Qi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhao envoy Qiu Lie, advised by Song Gong, successfully lobbied to make Wei Ran prime minister.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In year 14, Wei Ran appointed Bai Qi as general; they defeated Han and Wei at Yique, killing 240,000.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Ran captured cities of Wan and Ye from Chu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Ran was granted Rangdi and later Taoyi, becoming Marquess of Rang.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Ran led attacks on Wei, forcing surrender of 400 li east of the river and capturing over 60 cities.
details.label: included

details.point: In year 19, King Zhao claimed West Emperor, Qi Min East Emperor; titles were soon dropped.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Ran served as prime minister three times; he recommended Bai Qi, who became Lord Wu'an.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Marquess of Rang's wealth exceeded the monarch's family.
details.label: included

details.point: In year 32, Wei Ran besieged Daliang; Wei official Xu Jia persuaded him to withdraw.
details.label: included

details.point: In year 33, Wei Ran attacked Wei, killing 40,000 and taking three counties.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In year 34, Wei Ran, Bai Qi, and Hu Yang defeated Zhao, Han, Wei at Huayang, killing 100,000.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Sui criticized Queen Mother Xuan and Marquess of Rang's power; King Zhao removed Ranghou from office.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/淮南衡山列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/淮南衡山列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Liu Chang was the youngest son of Emperor Gaozu of Han.
details.label: included

details.point: His mother was a concubine of Zhang Ao, former king of Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Chang's mother committed suicide after giving birth to him.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Chang was raised by Empress Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: In 196 BC, Liu Chang was made King of Huainan.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Chang killed Piyang Hou Shenshi to avenge his mother.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen pardoned Liu Chang for the murder.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Chang became arrogant and imitated the emperor's behavior.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Chang plotted rebellion with Chai Qi and others.
details.label: included

details.point: The rebellion was discovered, and Liu Chang was summoned to Chang'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Chang was sentenced to exile in Shu County.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Chang went on a hunger strike and died in Yong County.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen mourned and buried Liu Chang with honors.
details.label: included

details.point: In 164 BC, Emperor Wen enfeoffed Liu Chang's sons as kings.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu An, son of Liu Chang, became King of Huainan.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu An plotted rebellion, inspired by Tian Fu's suggestion.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu An's rebellion was exposed by his grandson Liu Jian.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu An committed suicide before arrest.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ci, King of Hengshan, also plotted rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Both Huainan and Hengshan kingdoms were abolished after the rebellions.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Guangwu had eleven sons, including Liu Qiang, Liu Fu, Liu Kang, Liu Yan, Liu Yan, Liu Cang, Liu Ying, Liu Jing, Liu Shang, Liu Heng, and Liu Jing.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Qiang was initially crown prince but was deposed when his mother Empress Guo was deposed in 41 AD.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Qiang was made King of Donghai in 43 AD and given preferential treatment including 29 counties.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Qiang repeatedly requested to return his territory but was refused by Emperor Guangwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Qiang died in 58 AD; his funeral was lavish with many nobles attending.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Fu, King of Pei, was known for his love of classics and wrote the 'Treatise on the Five Classics'.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Fu was cautious and disciplined, called a wise king; he died after 46 years of reign.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ying, King of Chu, was fond of Huang-Lao and Buddhism, and performed fasting and sacrifices.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ying was accused of treason in 70 AD, deposed, and moved to Danyang where he committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: The Chu prison case implicated many, leading to thousands of deaths and exiles.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Kang, King of Jinan, was extravagant with many slaves and horses, and was admonished by He Chang.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Kang did not reform his ways despite admonishment; he died after 59 years of reign.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Cang, King of Dongping, was intelligent and loved by Emperor Ming; he served as General of Hussars.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Cang advised Emperor Ming against hunting during farming season, and the emperor returned.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Cang repeatedly requested to resign his post and return to his fiefdom, which was eventually allowed.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Cang was consulted on political matters and his advice was often adopted.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Cang died in 83 AD; his funeral was grand with many gifts and honors.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Yan, King of Fuling, was arrogant and harsh; he was implicated in treason and demoted to marquis.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yan was later restored as king of Fuling by Emperor Zhang.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jing, King of Guangling, was treacherous and plotted rebellion; he committed suicide after being exposed.
details.label: included

details.point: Eunuchs have served in the imperial court since ancient times, as recorded in the Book of Changes, Rites of Zhou, and other classics.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Han Dynasty, eunuchs were initially used for palace duties, but their power gradually expanded.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Zhong, a eunuch under Emperor He, helped eliminate the Dou Xian faction and was enfeoffed, marking the beginning of eunuch power.
details.label: included

details.point: Cai Lun, a eunuch, invented paper using tree bark, hemp, rags, and fishing nets, known as 'Caihou paper'.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Cheng led a coup to depose the Yan Xian faction and establish Emperor Shun, resulting in the enfeoffment of nineteen eunuchs.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Teng served four emperors without error, recommended worthy officials, and was known for his integrity.
details.label: included

details.point: Shan Chao, Xu Huang, Ju Yuan, Zuo Guan, and Tang Heng (the 'Five Marquises') helped Emperor Huan eliminate Liang Ji and gained immense power.
details.label: included

details.point: Hou Lan abused his power, extorted bribes, and built lavish tombs; he was eventually forced to commit suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Jie and Wang Fu falsely accused and killed Dou Wu and Chen Fan, consolidating eunuch control under Emperor Ling.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Qiang was a loyal eunuch who advised Emperor Ling to curb corruption and amnesty party members; he was falsely accused and committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Rang and Zhao Zhong were powerful eunuchs under Emperor Ling, known for corruption and influence; they were called 'father' and 'mother' by the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: The 'Ten Regular Attendants' (including Zhang Rang and Zhao Zhong) dominated the court, leading to widespread corruption and the Yellow Turban Rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Ling collected heavy taxes and built palaces, with eunuchs profiting from the construction.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Ling's death, Yuan Shao persuaded He Jin to kill eunuchs, but the plan leaked, leading to He Jin's murder.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Shao then massacred eunuchs, killing all regardless of age.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Rang and others fled with the emperor, eventually committing suicide by drowning in the Yellow River.
details.label: included

details.point: The historian comments that the fall of the Eastern Han was due to eunuchs, similar to how previous dynasties fell due to other causes.
details.label: included

details.point: Eunuchs were trusted because they were close to the emperor and familiar with palace affairs, but their power led to corruption and chaos.
details.label: included

details.point: Loyal eunuchs existed, but many were deceitful, and their growing numbers led to the persecution of upright officials.
details.label: included

details.point: The eunuch problem developed gradually, not overnight, as warned by the Book of Changes.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/后汉书/列传/张法滕冯度杨列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/张法滕冯度杨列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Zhang Zongchuan led 300-400 people to seize territory during Wang Mang's fall.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Zong was appointed partial general by Emperor Gengshi.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Zong volunteered to stay and defend against Red Eyebrows when others drew lots.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Zong repelled Red Eyebrows and was admired for bravery.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Zong was wounded in the arm while attacking Red Eyebrows at night.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Zong served under Guangwu as capital auxiliary captain and later Henan captain.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Zong became governor and senior official in Taizhong in 30 AD.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Zong suppressed bandits in Yingchuan, Qingzhou, and Jizhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Zong pacified Langyi and Beibu bandits in 40 AD.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Zong died in office in 59 AD.
details.label: included

details.point: Faxiong was a descendant of King Qi Xiang Fa Zhang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Faxiong served as magistrate of Wanling and was promoted by Bao Yu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Faxiong and Wang Zong suppressed Zhang Bolu rebellion in 109 AD.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Faxiong advised against immediate attack, leading to bandit surrender.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Faxiong defeated bandits in Donglai in 111 AD.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Faxiong reduced tiger attacks by banning hunting in Nanjun.
details.label: included

details.point: Teng Fu served as magistrate of Zhuo County and managed six counties.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Teng Fu defeated Fan Rong, Zhou Sheng, and Ma Mian in 144 AD.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Teng Fu pacified southeast and was appointed Zhonglang General.
details.label: included

details.point: Teng Fu was deposed by eunuchs and died at home.
details.label: included

details.point: Qiao Xuan was from Langzhong, Ba County, studied Yi and Spring and Autumn, and was recommended as filial and incorrupt.
details.label: included

details.point: Qiao Xuan admonished Emperor Cheng about the importance of heirs and criticized his indulgence in women.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Qiao Xuan served as an embroidered messenger under Emperor Ping but fled when Wang Mang took power.
details.label: included

details.point: Gongsun Shu tried to recruit Qiao Xuan with poison; Qiao Xuan refused, citing Xu You and Boyi as models.
details.label: included

details.point: Qiao Xuan's son Qiao Wangying offered money to save his father; Qiao Xuan hid until Gongsun Shu's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Ye from Zitong, Guanghan, studied Lu Shi and refused to serve Wang Mang, feigning illness.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Ye was forced by Gongsun Shu to serve; he chose to drink poison rather than submit.
details.label: included

details.point: Gongsun Shu regretted Li Ye's death and sent condolences; Li Ye's son refused gifts.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Hao and Wang Jia from Shu County refused Gongsun Shu's recruitment; Wang Hao committed suicide, Wang Jia was killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Yong and Feng Xin feigned blindness to avoid Gongsun Shu; after his death, they regained sight and their adulterous partners committed suicide.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Mao from Taiyuan carried the prefect Sun Fu on his back to escape Red Eyebrows, hiding for over 100 days.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Mao was recommended for his righteousness and served as Yilang and Zong Zhengcheng.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yan Shuo died fighting Xianbei; Wei Fu and Xu Xian died protecting the prefect Zhang Xian.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Suo Fu died in place of Liu Xiong when captured by bandits; the court rewarded his family.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wen Xu from Taiyuan was recommended by Gongsun Shu, served as censor, and was killed by Gou Yu after refusing to betray Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Peng Xiu at age 15 saved his father from robbers by threatening them with a sword.
details.label: included

details.point: Peng Xiu died covering the prefect from arrows during a bandit attack; the bandits killed the shooter.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Suo Lufang offered his life to save the prefect from execution by a Gengshi envoy.
details.label: included

details.point: Suo Lufang served as Luoyang Order, known for ability, and was later carried to court by Guangwu due to illness.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhou Jia's ancestor Zhou Yan died on hunger strike after being tortured for refusing to execute an innocent man.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Xiongnu ancestor was Chunwei, a descendant of the Xiahou family.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiongnu lived by nomadic herding, moving with water and grass, without cities or agriculture.
details.label: included

details.point: They had no written language, using oral agreements for management.
details.label: included

details.point: Men were trained in archery from youth; strong men served as armored cavalry.
details.label: included

details.point: In war, they attacked when advantageous and retreated when not, without shame in flight.
details.label: not_included

details.point: They valued the strong and disdained the weak; young ate well, old ate leftovers.
details.label: included

details.point: Levirate marriage was practiced: sons married stepmothers, brothers married widows.
details.label: included

details.point: The Xiongnu had no taboo on names or posthumous titles.
details.label: included

details.point: The Zhou dynasty declined, and Rong and Di tribes frequently invaded the Central Plains.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin and Jin became powerful; Duke Mu of Qin subdued the Xirong, and Duke Wen of Jin expelled Rong Di.
details.label: included

details.point: The Xiongnu were bordered by three Warring States: Qin, Zhao, and Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin Shihuang sent Meng Tian to attack the Xiongnu, recovering the Ordos and building the Great Wall.
details.label: included

details.point: After Meng Tian's death, the Xiongnu regained strength under Modu Chanyu.
details.label: included

details.point: Modu killed his father Touman and became Chanyu, then defeated the Donghu, Yuezhi, and others.
details.label: included

details.point: Modu's Xiongnu had over 300,000 archers and became a major threat to the Han.
details.label: included

details.point: The Han dynasty initiated heqin (marriage alliance) with the Xiongnu, sending princesses and gifts.
details.label: included

details.point: Modu wrote an insulting letter to Empress Lü, but she responded diplomatically.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Laoshang Chanyu, the Xiongnu broke the heqin and invaded Han borders.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu of Han launched large-scale campaigns against the Xiongnu, led by Wei Qing and Huo Qubing.
details.label: included

details.point: After decades of war, the Xiongnu weakened and eventually split, with Huhanye submitting to the Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang's ancestors were Korean prime ministers for five generations.
details.label: included

details.point: After Qin conquered Han, Zhang Liang used his wealth to hire an assassin to kill the Qin emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang and an assassin ambushed the Qin emperor at Bolangsha but hit the wrong carriage.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang fled to Xiapi after the failed assassination.
details.label: included

details.point: An old man on a bridge tested Zhang Liang by making him pick up his shoes.
details.label: included

details.point: The old man gave Zhang Liang the 'Tai Gong's Art of War' and said he would become a teacher of kings.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang studied the book and later became a strategist for Liu Bang (Pei Gong).
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang advised Liu Bang to avoid attacking Qin's strong army and instead bribe the Qin general.
details.label: included

details.point: After Qin's surrender, Zhang Liang persuaded Liu Bang to leave Qin's palace and camp at Bashang.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang helped Liu Bang survive the Hongmen Banquet by enlisting Xiang Bo's help.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang advised Liu Bang to burn the plank road to show no intention of returning east.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang recommended Han Xin, Peng Yue, and Ying Bu as key allies against Xiang Yu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang opposed enfeoffing the six kingdoms' descendants, arguing it would undermine Liu Bang's support.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang persuaded Liu Bang to grant Han Xin the title of King of Qi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Liang was enfeoffed as Marquis of Liu, declining 30,000 households.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang advised Liu Bang to enfeoff Yong Chi first to calm generals' fears of rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang advocated building the capital in Guanzhong rather than Luoyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang recruited the Four Whitebeards to support the crown prince, preventing his replacement.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang studied Daoism and sought immortality after the Han was established.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Liang died and was buried with the yellow stone from the old man, whom he believed was Huangshi Gong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang Zhen, styled Boqi, was from Hongnong Huayin.
details.label: included

details.point: His eighth-generation ancestor Yang Xi was granted Marquis of Chiquan under Emperor Gaozu.
details.label: included

details.point: His father Yang Bao studied Ouyang Shangshu and refused officialdom under Emperors Ai and Ping.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Guangwu admired Yang Bao's integrity.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Zhen studied Ouyang Shangshu under Taichang Huanyu and was known as 'Confucius of Kansai'.
details.label: included

details.point: He did not accept official invitations for decades until age 50.
details.label: included

details.point: A crested sparrow with three fish was interpreted as an omen of his promotion.
details.label: included

details.point: General Deng Zhi recommended him as Maocai; he became Governor of Jingzhou and Donglai.
details.label: included

details.point: He refused Wang Mi's nighttime bribe of ten pounds of gold, saying 'Heaven knows, Earth knows, I know, you know'.
details.label: included

details.point: He was known for honesty and did not accept personal requests; his descendants lived frugally.
details.label: included

details.point: He said he wanted his descendants to be called 'descendants of an innocent official'.
details.label: included

details.point: In 121 AD, he became a servant and then Taichang; he recommended worthy scholars like Yang Lun.
details.label: included

details.point: In 120 AD, he replaced Liu Kai as Situ.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He memorialized against Wang Sheng and Bo Rong's corruption, citing historical precedents.
details.label: included

details.point: He opposed the enfeoffment of Liu Gui, who married Bo Rong, as against Han law.
details.label: included

details.point: In 122 AD, he replaced Liu Kai as Taiwei.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He refused to recommend Li Gui's brother at Geng Bao's request, and also refused Yan Xian's request.
details.label: included

details.point: He criticized the extravagant construction of a house for the wet nurse, citing disasters and waste.
details.label: included

details.point: He attributed an earthquake to the overreach of eunuchs and officials, and urged reform.
details.label: included

details.point: He was dismissed and forced to return home; he committed suicide by poison at age 70.
details.label: included

details.point: King Weiman of North Korea was originally from the state of Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: When Yan was powerful, it conquered Zhenfan and North Korea, making them part of Yan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Qin destroyed Yan, North Korea became a border region outside Liaodong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Early Han dynasty, the border was set at the Xishui River under Yan's jurisdiction.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Weiman fled with over a thousand followers, crossed the Xu River, and settled in Shangxiazhang.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Hui and Empress Gao's time, Weiman was made a Han foreign minister to protect the border.
details.label: included

details.point: Weiman used his power to conquer Zhenfan and Lintun, controlling a vast area.
details.label: included

details.point: Weiman's grandson Youqu refused to visit the Han emperor and blocked other states from doing so.
details.label: included

details.point: In 128 BC, Han sent Shehe to reprimand Youqu, but Youqu rejected the edict.
details.label: included

details.point: Shehe assassinated a Korean general on his way back and was rewarded by Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Korea retaliated by killing Shehe.
details.label: included

details.point: Han sent General Yang Pu with 50,000 troops by sea and General Xun Zhi by land to attack Korea.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Pu's initial attack on Wangxian City failed; he fled and regrouped.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Zhi failed to break the Korean defense west of the Xu River.
details.label: included

details.point: Han envoy Weishan negotiated with Youqu, who agreed to surrender but later backed out.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun Zhi defeated Korea at Haishui River and besieged Wangxian City; Yang Pu joined from the south.
details.label: included

details.point: The two generals disagreed on strategy; Yang Pu favored surrender, Xun Zhi favored attack.
details.label: included

details.point: Han sent Gongsun Sui to mediate; he arrested Yang Pu on Xun Zhi's suspicion of treason.
details.label: included

details.point: Korean officials killed King Youqu and surrendered to Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Han established four counties in Korea; Xun Zhi was executed for rivalry, Yang Pu became a commoner.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao He was from Peidi and served as an official under Pei Lord.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao He supported Gaozu (then a commoner) in official affairs and gave him 500 yuan when others gave 300.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao He was the best in the Qin examination but refused a court recruitment.
details.label: included

details.point: When Gaozu became Duke of Pei, Xiao He was appointed prime minister and governor.
details.label: included

details.point: In Xianyang, Xiao He collected Qin's legal books, enabling Gaozu to know the empire's details.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao He governed Ba and Shu, pacifying the people and supplying food for the army.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Han-Chu conflict, Xiao He stayed in Guanzhong, established laws, and supplied troops and grain.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao He sent his family to the army to alleviate Gaozu's suspicion.
details.label: included

details.point: After Xiang Yu's death, Gaozu ranked Xiao He first among meritorious officials, citing his strategic role like a hunter.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao He was granted the title of Marquis of Feng with 8,000 households.
details.label: included

details.point: E Jun argued Xiao He's merit was eternal, so he was ranked first over Cao Shen.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao He followed Zhao Ping's advice to refuse rewards and fund the army to avoid suspicion.
details.label: included

details.point: During Yingbu's rebellion, Xiao He damaged his reputation by buying land to ease Gaozu's fears.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao He was imprisoned for requesting Linyuan for the people but was released after Wang Weiwei's defense.
details.label: included

details.point: On his deathbed, Xiao He recommended Cao Shen as his successor.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao He's descendants were enfeoffed multiple times, continuing until Wang Mang's era.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Shen was from Peidi, served as a jailer, and followed Gaozu from the beginning.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Shen had numerous military victories, including capturing Wei's king and pacifying Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: As Prime Minister of Qi, Cao Shen ruled with Huang-Lao principles of tranquility.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Shen succeeded Xiao He as Han prime minister, maintained his policies, and drank daily, arguing that following established laws was sufficient.
details.label: included
