summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/万石张叔列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Wan Shijun, originally named Shi Fen, was from Zhao and moved to Wen County after Zhao's fall.
details.label: included

details.point: At 15, Shi Fen served Emperor Gaozu as a minor official and was liked for his respectful caution.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Fen's sister became a palace beauty, and his family moved to Chang'an.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shi Fen rose to high office under Emperor Wen through merit, despite limited Confucian knowledge.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He became the prince's tutor (future Emperor Jing) after Zhang Xiangru was dismissed.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Emperor Jing, Shi Fen was appointed Jiuqing and later prime minister of the princes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shi Fen's four sons all held 2,000-shi posts, leading Emperor Jing to call him 'Wan Shijun' (Lord of Ten Thousand Stones).
details.label: included

details.point: In late Emperor Jing's reign, Shi Fen retired with a doctor's salary but attended court ceremonies.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Fen showed extreme respect: dismounting at palace gates, greeting the emperor's carriage, and wearing court clothes to receive descendants.
details.label: not_included

details.point: When descendants erred, Shi Fen would refuse to eat until they repented and corrected themselves.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Fen's family was renowned for filial piety and prudence, surpassing even Confucian scholars of Qi and Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianyuan 2, Empress Dowager appointed Shi Fen's eldest son Shi Jian as doctor's order and youngest son Shi Qing as internal historian.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shi Jian, while a doctor, secretly washed his father's clothes and spoke candidly to the emperor when alone.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Qing once entered the inner gate drunk without dismounting; Shi Fen refused to eat until Shi Qing repented.
details.label: included

details.point: Wan Shijun died in Yuanshuo 5; Shi Jian died a year later from excessive grief.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Jian was extremely cautious, once panicking over a missing stroke in a memorial.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Qing, the most casual son, still counted horses with a whip before reporting six.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shi Qing became prime minister and Marquis Muqiu in Yuanding 5, but was overshadowed by other officials during Emperor Wu's campaigns.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shi Qing served nine years as prime minister without major reforms; he was blamed for social turmoil and offered to resign, but was rebuked by the emperor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Shi Qing's death, the family's filial tradition declined as descendants lost positions due to crimes.
details.label: included

details.point: Qingbu (Yingbu) was from Liuxian County, surname Ying, a common man in Qin Dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: As a child, a fortune-teller said he would be king after being tortured.
details.label: included

details.point: He was sentenced to tattooing (qing) and laughed, recalling the prophecy.
details.label: included

details.point: He was sent to Lishan as a hard labor prisoner among hundreds of thousands.
details.label: included

details.point: When Chen Sheng rebelled, Yingbu joined Wu Rui, magistrate of Fan County, to rebel against Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Magistrate Fan married his daughter to Yingbu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yingbu defeated Qin forces at Qingbo and later joined Xiang Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: Yingbu was brave in battle, often ranked first, and was named Dangyang Lord by Xiang Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: After Xiang Liang's death, Yingbu served under King Huai of Chu and later Xiang Ji (Xiang Yu).
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Ji sent Yingbu to cross the Yellow River first to attack Qin; they defeated Zhang Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Yingbu commanded the army to defeat many with fewer troops, impressing the princes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yingbu buried alive over 200,000 surrendered Qin soldiers at Xin'an under Xiang Ji's orders.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu named Yingbu King of Jiujiang with capital at Liu County.
details.label: included

details.point: Yingbu, under Xiang Yu's secret order, sent troops to kill Emperor Yi (King Huai of Chu).
details.label: included

details.point: Yingbu excused himself from aiding Xiang Yu against Qi due to illness, causing resentment.
details.label: included

details.point: Sui He, sent by Liu Bang, persuaded Yingbu to betray Chu and join Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Yingbu killed the Chu envoy and attacked Chu, but was defeated by Long Ju.
details.label: included

details.point: Yingbu fled to Liu Bang, who later made him King of Huainan.
details.label: included

details.point: Yingbu rebelled after seeing the execution of Han Xin and Peng Yue, fearing for himself.
details.label: included

details.point: Yingbu was defeated by Liu Bang's army and killed by Fan Yang people while fleeing.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Rong, courtesy name Ji Chang, was born in Maoling, Fufeng, son of Ma Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: He studied under Jingzhao Zhixun, who taught Confucianism in seclusion in Nanshan.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhixun admired Ma Rong's talent and married his daughter to him.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yongchu 2nd year, Deng Zhi summoned Ma Rong as a minister; he refused and lived in Liangzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Due to Qiang raids and famine, Ma Rong regretted his refusal and accepted Deng Zhi's call.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yongchu 4th year, he became a collator at Dongguan, collating secret books.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Deng and Deng Zhi brothers governed; they stopped military training, causing unrest.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Rong criticized the neglect of military affairs and wrote 'Guangcheng Ode' to satirize.
details.label: included

details.point: The ode offended Deng, so Ma Rong was kept at Dongguan without promotion for ten years.
details.label: included

details.point: He resigned after his brother's son died; Empress Dowager banned him from office.
details.label: included

details.point: After Empress Dowager's death, Emperor An recalled Ma Rong as a lang and lecturer.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as stable chief of the King of Hejian, then wrote 'Ode to the Eastern Tour' for Emperor An.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor An appreciated the ode and made him a doctor; later he became a meritorious official.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yangjia 2nd year, he was recommended as xiaolian, passed exam, became Yilang, then Zhonglang, then governor of Wudu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: During Xiqiang rebellion, Ma Rong submitted a memorial predicting defeat and offering to lead troops, but the court did not use his plan.
details.label: included

details.point: His predictions of Qiang and Wuhuan invasions came true.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Emperor Huan, he was governor of Nanjun; he offended Liang Ji, was accused of corruption, exiled to Shuofang, later pardoned.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Rong was a great scholar with many students, including Lu Zhi and Zheng Xuan.
details.label: included

details.point: He was free-spirited, fond of luxury, taught with female musicians behind a gauze screen.
details.label: included

details.point: He annotated many classics and wrote various works; he died at 88, buried simply.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Shen of Lu received poems from Fuqiu Bo and wrote exegesis, called 'Shi of Lu'.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yuan Gusheng of Qi explained 'Shi of Qi'.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han Ying of Yan explained 'Shi of Han'.
details.label: included

details.point: All three schools (Lu, Qi, Han) have Ph.D.
details.label: included

details.point: Mao Chang from Zhao explained 'Mao Shi' and did not establish a doctorate.
details.label: included

details.point: Gao Xu taught 'Lu Shi' and refused to serve Wang Mang, later served under Guangwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Xian studied 'Lu Shi' and 'The Analects', taught the crown prince, and wrote chapters for the Analects.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Ying studied 'Lu Shi', taught many disciples, and participated in the Baihu Temple conference.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Gong studied 'Qi Shi', served as Sikong, and simplified his father's chapters.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Mo studied 'Qi Shi', carried his friend's funeral, and died on the way to his teacher's funeral.
details.label: included

details.point: Jing Luan studied 'Qi Shi', wrote many works including 'Yi Shuo' and 'Poetry Interpretation'.
details.label: included

details.point: Xue Han studied 'Han Shi', compiled prophecies, and was imprisoned to death.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Fu studied 'Han Shi' from Xue Han, taught many disciples, and wrote 'Poem Titles and Meanings'.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Xun studied 'Han Shi', served as Henan Yin, and died in office.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Ren studied 'Han Shi', served as Beigong Guards Order, and advised on lenient government.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Ye studied 'Han Shi' from Du Fu, cut off contact for 20 years, and died at home.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Hong studied 'Mao's Poems' from Xie Manqing, wrote 'Preface to Mao's Poems', and also studied 'Guwen Shangshu'.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Jun studied 'Qingshi Rites', served as doctor, and consulted on rituals.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Xuan studied 'Xiao Dai Li', annotated 'Zhou Guan' and 'Book of Rites', forming 'Three Rites'.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ding Gong studied 'Gongyang Yan's Spring and Autumn Annals', taught thousands, and served as Shaofu.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji Bu was a native of Chu known for chivalry and served as a general under Xiang Yu.
details.label: included

details.point: After Xiang Yu's defeat, Emperor Gaozu offered a reward for Ji Bu's capture and threatened to punish those who harbored him.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji Bu hid at Zhou's house in Puyang; Zhou disguised him as a criminal and sold him to the Zhu family in Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Jia recognized Ji Bu and bought him, then went to Luoyang to persuade Xiahou Ying to intercede with the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Jia argued that pursuing Ji Bu would drive talented men to enemy states like the Xiongnu or South Vietnam.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiahou Ying relayed Zhu Jia's words to Liu Bang, who pardoned Ji Bu and appointed him a doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Hui's reign, Ji Bu became Zhonglang General.
details.label: included

details.point: When the Xiongnu Chanyu insulted Empress Lu, Fan Kuai proposed a 100,000-man campaign; Ji Bu opposed, citing Emperor Gaozu's defeat at Pingcheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji Bu argued that Fan Kuai's proposal was deceitful and would destabilize the realm; Empress Lu dropped the campaign.
details.label: included

details.point: Later, Ji Bu served as governor of Hedong County.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen summoned Ji Bu to be a censor but sent him back after hearing he was willful; Ji Bu criticized the emperor for being swayed by praise and slander.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen was ashamed and kept Ji Bu as governor of Hedong.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Qiusheng, a rhetorician, sought Ji Bu's favor; Ji Bu initially disliked him but was won over by Cao's flattery.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Qiusheng promoted Ji Bu's reputation, leading to the saying 'better to get Ji Bu's promise than a hundred catties of gold.'
details.label: included

details.point: Ji Bu's younger brother Ji Xin was a brave and chivalrous man in Guanzhong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ji Bu's half-brother Ding Gong, a former Xiang Yu general, once spared Liu Bang in battle but was later executed by Liu Bang for disloyalty.
details.label: included

details.point: Luan Bu, from Liang, was a friend of Peng Yue; after Peng Yue was executed, Luan Bu mourned him and was arrested.
details.label: included

details.point: Luan Bu defended Peng Yue's loyalty and argued that executing him would endanger other meritorious officials; Emperor Gaozu released him and made him a captain.
details.label: included

details.point: Uncle Tian, a native of Zhao, was a chivalrous man who followed King Zhang Ao to Chang'an after a rebellion plot; he was later appointed a county governor.
details.label: included

details.point: Uncle Tian recommended Meng Shu as an honest official; Meng Shu was reinstated as governor of Yunzhong after Uncle Tian's defense.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Shiqi was born in Gaoyang, Chenliu County, and was poor but studious.
details.label: included

details.point: He initially hid from narrow-minded rebel generals.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shiqi sought to meet Pei Gong (Liu Bang) through a fellow villager cavalryman.
details.label: included

details.point: Pei Gong was initially rude, washing his feet while receiving Li Shiqi.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shiqi criticized Pei Gong for not respecting elders if he wanted to overthrow Qin.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Pei Gong apologized and consulted Li Shiqi, who advised capturing Chenliu for its food stores.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shiqi persuaded the Chenliu magistrate to surrender, and Pei Gong captured Chenliu.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shiqi was granted the title Lord of Guangye and recommended his brother Li Shang.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Chu-Han conflict, Li Shiqi advised holding Aocang and key strategic points.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shiqi persuaded the King of Qi, Tian Guang, to submit to Han, leading to Qi's surrender.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin attacked Qi despite the surrender, causing Tian Guang to kill Li Shiqi.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Jia was a Chu native known for eloquence, serving as envoy to South Vietnam.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lu Jia convinced Wei Tuo (Zhao Tuo) to submit to Han by arguing Han's superiority.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lu Jia debated with Emperor Gaozu that ruling requires civil governance, not just military force.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Jia wrote 'New Speeches' on statecraft at Gaozu's request.
details.label: included

details.point: During Empress Lü's regency, Lu Jia advised Chen Ping to ally with Zhou Bo to counter the Lü clan.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Jia helped secure the succession of Emperor Wen and later re-envoyed to South Vietnam.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhu Jian was a clean official who refused to associate with the corrupt Marquis of Piyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Jian advised the emperor's favorite to save Marquis Piyang, but later died on a mission to the Xiongnu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lou Jing (Liu Jing) advised Gaozu to establish the capital in Guanzhong for strategic advantage.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Du, named Jiya, was born in Duling, Jingzhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Du's great ancestor was Du Yannian, a censor under Emperor Xuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Du was knowledgeable but not well-treated by villagers.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Du was arrested by Meiyang Ling and sent to the capital.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Du wrote an edict in prison that impressed Guangwu, who gave him silk and exempted him from punishment.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Du wrote 'Fu on the Capital' arguing against rebuilding Luoyi.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Du served as a county literature official but did not go to the capital for over 20 years due to eye disease.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Du's maternal great-grandfather was Xin Wuxian, famous for military strategies.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Du Du died in battle at Shegu Mountain while serving as lieutenant to Ma Fang.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Du wrote 18 articles including fu, elegy, and 'Nv's Commandments'.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Long, courtesy name Wenshan, was from Yunyang, Feng Yi.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Long served as Lang under Wang Mang, then fled to Hexi and served Dou Rong.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Long became magistrate of Xinji County in Jianwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Long wrote 26 poems, inscriptions, and books.
details.label: included

details.point: Xia Gong, named Jinggong, was from Meng, Liang State.
details.label: included

details.point: Xia Gong studied 'Han Shi' and 'Mencius' Book of Changes' and had thousands of disciples.
details.label: included

details.point: Xia Gong defended his area during Wang Mang's reign and was praised by Guangwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Xia Gong wrote 20 fu, odes, poems, and 'Encouraging Learning'.
details.label: included

details.point: Xia Gong died in office at age 49, posthumously named 'Xuanmingjun'.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Yi imitated the 'Qing Temple' to write ten 'Xianzong Odes' for Emperor Xiaoming.
details.label: included

details.point: The ancient hierarchical system from emperor to slaves ensured orderly society.
details.label: included

details.point: Land and water resources were classified for agriculture and livestock.
details.label: included

details.point: Production followed seasonal rules; resources were not exploited before certain times.
details.label: included

details.point: Young plants and animals were protected to allow reproduction.
details.label: included

details.point: Scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants specialized in their occupations.
details.label: included

details.point: The Book of Changes and Guanzi emphasized proper governance and division of labor.
details.label: included

details.point: The Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties succeeded through moral guidance and ritual.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhou decline led to ritual violations by Duke Zhuang of Lu and others.
details.label: included

details.point: The three families of Lu used improper music and poems in rituals.
details.label: included

details.point: Decline spread after Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin, causing social disorder.
details.label: included

details.point: Merchants sold rare goods, artisans made useless items, scholars sought wealth.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Rich decorated houses with silk; poor lacked basic necessities.
details.label: included

details.point: King Gou Jian of Yue used Ji Ran's strategies to enrich the state and defeat Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Li (Lord Zhu) became wealthy through trade at Taoyi.
details.label: included

details.point: Zigong (Duanmu Ci) became rich through business between Cao and Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Bai Gui advocated buying when others sell and selling when others buy.
details.label: included

details.point: Yidun, Guo Zong, and Wu Shiying amassed fortunes through iron, livestock, and trade.
details.label: included

details.point: The widow Qing of Ba preserved her cinnabar mine and was honored by Qin Shihuang.
details.label: included

details.point: Wealthy families like the Zhuo, Kong, and Dao Xian profited from iron, salt, and slaves.
details.label: included

details.point: The Ren family of Xuanqu became rich by hoarding grain during the Qin-Han war.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Shengzhuan, named Yanzhen, was grandson of Zhang Fang, Marquis of Fuping.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Sheng acted willfully and made friends based on shared ambition, regardless of status.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Sheng served as acting county official and executed corrupt officials.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Sheng defended his harshness by citing Confucius' example.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Sheng was killed after speaking out during a party conflict at age 49.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yi, courtesy name Yuanshu, was from Xixian, Hanyang, tall and imposing.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yi was arrogant and rejected by his community, wrote 'Explanation'.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yi nearly executed but rescued by friends; wrote 'Ode to a Poor Bird' and 'Ode to the Diseases of the World'.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yi impressed Situ Yuan Feng by bowing only slightly and citing Li Shiqi.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yi forced his way into Yin Yangzhi's home, cried loudly, and gained Yangzhi's respect.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhao Yi was recommended by Yuan Feng and Yang Zhi, became famous in the capital.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yi offended Prefect Huangfu Gui by leaving without meeting; Gui apologized in a letter.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yi replied to Huangfu Gui, criticizing his arrogance and declining further contact.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yi died at home after refusing multiple summons from prefectures and commanderies.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Liang, named Manshan, from Ningyang, Dongping, lost father young, sold books for living.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Liang wrote 'On Breaking the Group' to criticize partisan behavior.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Liang served as Chief of Beixin City, promoted Confucian education and lectured disciples.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Liang was promoted to Shangshu Lang and later Ye Wang Ling, died of illness.
details.label: included

details.point: Bian Rang, courtesy name Wenli, from Chenliu, was knowledgeable and good at debate.
details.label: included

details.point: Bian Rang was recommended by Cai Yong to He Jin as a talent deserving high position.
details.label: included

details.point: Chuilizi, named Ji, was the younger brother of King Hui of Qin, born to a different mother.
details.label: included

details.point: Chuilizi was eloquent and resourceful, called 'the wise man' by the people of Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: In the eighth year of King Hui, Chuilizi was granted the title of Yougeng and led an army to attack Quwo in Wei, annexing the land to Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: In the twenty-fifth year of King Hui, Chuilizi attacked Zhao, capturing General Zhuang Bao and Linyi.
details.label: included

details.point: The next year, he assisted Wei Zhang in defeating Chu, capturing Hanzhong.
details.label: included

details.point: King Hui granted Chuilizi the title Yan Jun.
details.label: included

details.point: After King Hui's death, King Wu expelled Zhang Yi and Wei Zhang, appointing Chuilizi and Gan Mao as left and right prime ministers.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wu sent Chuilizi with a hundred chariots to the Zhou capital; the Zhou king greeted him respectfully, angering the Chu king.
details.label: included

details.point: You Teng persuaded the Chu king that the Zhou king's actions were precautionary, not disrespectful.
details.label: included

details.point: After King Wu's death, King Zhao came to the throne and Chuilizi was even more respected.
details.label: included

details.point: In the first year of King Zhao, Chuilizi attacked Pucheng in Wei but was persuaded by Hu Yan to withdraw.
details.label: included

details.point: Chuilizi died in the seventh year of King Zhao and was buried east of Zhangtai, south of the Wei River.
details.label: included

details.point: Before his death, he prophesied that an emperor's palace would flank his tomb, which later came true with the Han palaces.
details.label: included

details.point: Gan Mao was from Xiacai, studied under Mr. Shi Ju, and was introduced to King Hui by Zhang Yi and Chuilizi.
details.label: included

details.point: King Hui sent Gan Mao to help Wei Zhang seize Hanzhong.
details.label: included

details.point: After King Wu ascended, he appointed Gan Mao as left prime minister and Chuilizi as right prime minister.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wu wanted to see the Zhou capital; Gan Mao proposed attacking Yiyang in Han, and after initial difficulty, captured it with reinforcements.
details.label: included

details.point: After King Zhao's accession, Gan Mao advised sending troops to rescue Han from Chu, which succeeded.
details.label: included

details.point: Gan Mao fled to Qi due to slander from Xiang Shou and Gongsun Shi, but was later honored by both Qin and Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Gan Luo, Gan Mao's grandson, at age 12 persuaded Zhang Tang to go to Yan and then convinced the Zhao king to give Qin five cities, leading to Zhao attacking Yan and Qin gaining territory.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang claimed descent from the Yellow Emperor and Yu Shun.
details.label: included

details.point: The Wang family surname originated from Tian An, who was called 'Wang Family' by the people of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang He (Wengru) was a censor under Emperor Wu who saved over ten thousand lives.
details.label: included

details.point: A divination predicted that a virtuous woman would appear in Shalu after 645 years.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Zhengjun was born to Wang Jin and the Li family; her mother dreamed of the moon falling into her belly.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Zhengjun entered the palace at age 18 and became consort of the future Emperor Yuan.
details.label: included

details.point: She gave birth to Emperor Cheng, the first grandson of Emperor Xuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Zhengjun became empress and her father Wang Jin was made Marquis of Yangping.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Yuan considered deposing the crown prince but was dissuaded by Shi Dan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Emperor Yuan's death, Emperor Cheng ascended and Wang Feng became regent.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Feng and his brothers were made marquises, leading to the 'Five Marquises'.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Feng dominated the court; Emperor Cheng feared him and could not act independently.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Zhang criticized Wang Feng and was executed; his family exiled.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Feng recommended Wang Yin as his successor; Wang Yin served as regent.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Mang inherited the title of Marquis of Xindu after his father Wang Man.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Mang became regent after Emperor Ai's death, with Empress Dowager Wang's support.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Mang usurped the throne and established the Xin dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Wang refused to give the imperial seal to Wang Mang but eventually threw it.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang changed her title to Xinshi Wenmu and severed her connection with Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Wang died at age 84 and was buried with Emperor Yuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Su Qin was from Luoyang, Eastern Zhou, and studied under Mr. Guiguzi.
details.label: included

details.point: After traveling, he returned home impoverished and was ridiculed by his family.
details.label: included

details.point: He studied the 'Yin Fu' text and developed a strategy to persuade kings.
details.label: included

details.point: He first lobbied King Xian of Zhou but was rejected due to courtiers' disdain.
details.label: included

details.point: He went to Qin but King Hui of Qin refused him, as Qin hated lobbyists after Shang Yang's execution.
details.label: included

details.point: He went to Zhao but was rejected by Lord Fengyang.
details.label: included

details.point: He went to Yan and persuaded Yan Wenhou to ally with Zhao for protection.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Wenhou funded Su Qin to travel to Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: After Lord Fengyang's death, Su Qin lobbied Zhao Suhou to form a vertical alliance against Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: He argued that the six states combined were stronger than Qin and proposed a mutual defense pact.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Suhou agreed and provided resources for Su Qin to persuade other states.
details.label: included

details.point: Su Qin then persuaded Han Xuanwang to join the alliance, warning against ceding land to Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: He persuaded King Wei of Wei, emphasizing Wei's strength and the folly of serving Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: He persuaded King Xuan of Qi, highlighting Qi's wealth and Qin's inability to attack Qi effectively.
details.label: included

details.point: He persuaded King Wei of Chu, arguing that Chu should lead the alliance to become king.
details.label: included

details.point: The six states formed the vertical alliance, and Su Qin became the leader and prime minister of all six.
details.label: included

details.point: Su Qin returned to Luoyang in glory, and his family treated him with respect.
details.label: included

details.point: He distributed gold to relatives and repaid debts.
details.label: included

details.point: The alliance held for 15 years, preventing Qin from attacking east of Hangu Pass.
details.label: included

details.point: Later, the alliance collapsed due to Qi and Wei attacking Zhao, and Su Qin's subsequent actions led to his assassination.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Xu of Emperor Cheng was daughter of Xu Jia.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Yuan betrothed Xu Jia's daughter to crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Xu gave birth to a son and a daughter, both died in infancy.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng appointed Wang Feng as Grand Marshal alongside Xu Jia.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Qin advised Wang Feng to respect Xu Jia.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng dismissed Xu Jia with gold and special status.
details.label: included

details.point: Xu Jia died and was given posthumous title.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Xu was intelligent and favored, but later lost favor.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xiang and Gu Yong blamed disasters on the harem.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng reduced expenses for the queen's palace.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Xu petitioned against restrictions, citing old practices.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng responded citing solar eclipses and disasters as signs.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Xu was deposed after her sister Xu Ye cursed others.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng later pitied Xu family and allowed return.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Xu died after being forced to commit suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Jieyu refused to ride with Emperor Cheng, praised by Empress Dowager.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Jieyu recited poems and acted according to ancient rites.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Feiyan and her sister rose from humble origins to great favor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Feiyan falsely accused Empress Xu and Ban Jieyu.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Jieyu defended herself and retired to serve Empress Dowager.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaowu had six sons: Prince Ru, Emperor Xiaozhao, Liu Hong, Liu Dan, Liu Xu, and Liu Ai.
details.label: included

details.point: Prince Liu Ju was made crown prince at age 7 in the first year of Yuanshou.
details.label: included

details.point: Crown prince Liu Ju studied Gongyang and Guliang Chunqiu under Duke Xiaqiu Jiang.
details.label: included

details.point: In later years, Emperor Wu suspected witchcraft and Jiang Chong exploited this against the prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Chong planted evidence of witchcraft in the prince's palace.
details.label: included

details.point: Prince Liu Ju, advised by Shi De, arrested and killed Jiang Chong.
details.label: included

details.point: The prince raised an army against Prime Minister Liu Quli but was defeated and fled.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu was initially furious but later realized the prince was innocent after a letter from a Huguan elder.
details.label: included

details.point: Prince Liu Ju hanged himself in Hu County after being discovered.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu executed Jiang Chong's family and built the Palace of Thoughts for the prince.
details.label: included

details.point: The prince's grandson later became Emperor Xuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan posthumously honored his grandfather as Prince Ru and built a mausoleum.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Hong, King of Qi, died without heirs after 8 years.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Dan, King of Yan, plotted rebellion after being passed over as heir, eventually hanged himself.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xu, King of Guangling, also plotted rebellion and hanged himself after witchcraft curses were exposed.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu He, King of Changyi, was made emperor after Emperor Zhao's death but deposed after 27 days for lewd behavior.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu He was later made Marquis of Haihun by Emperor Xuan.
details.label: included

details.point: The witchcraft case led to widespread deaths and destruction in Chang'an.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The text attributes the disasters to the prolonged wars during Emperor Wu's reign.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Che Qianqiu is praised for revealing the truth of the witchcraft case and clearing the prince's name.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Wuzhu of Minyue and King Yao of Yuedonghai were descendants of King Goujian of Yue, surname Zou.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin abolished their titles and established Minzhong County.
details.label: included

details.point: During Qin rebellion, Wuzhu and Yao led Yue people to join Wu Rui and helped destroy Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Ji did not make them kings, so they did not join Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: They assisted Han in attacking Xiang Ji.
details.label: included

details.point: In 202 BC, Wuzhu was re-established as King of Minyue, capital Dongye.
details.label: included

details.point: In 192 BC, Yao was appointed King of Donghai, capital Dongou, known as King of Dongou.
details.label: included

details.point: During Wu Liu Bi's rebellion, Minyue refused to join; Dongou joined but later killed Wu Bi.
details.label: included

details.point: Ziju, son of Wu Bi, fled to Minyue and urged attacks on Dongou.
details.label: included

details.point: In 138 BC, Minyue besieged Dongou; Dongou sought Han aid.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Fu advised against intervention; Zhuang Zhu argued for rescue.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Wu sent Zhuang Zhu to mobilize troops from Kuaiji; Minyue withdrew before arrival.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongou requested relocation to Jianghuai area.
details.label: included

details.point: In 135 BC, Minyue attacked South Vietnam; South Vietnam reported to Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Han sent Wang Hui and Han Anguo; Yu Shan killed King Ying and surrendered.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu made Yao Junchou king of Yue Yao and Yu Shan king of Dongyue.
details.label: included

details.point: In 112 BC, Yu Shan pretended to aid Han against South Vietnam but stopped at Jieyang.
details.label: included

details.point: In 111 BC, Yu Shan rebelled, killed Han officers; Han sent multiple generals.
details.label: included

details.point: In 110 BC, Han forces attacked; Wu Yang and others killed Yu Shan and surrendered.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han relocated Dongyue people to Jianghuai, leaving the area empty.
details.label: included

details.point: Wuhuan originated from the Donghu tribe.
details.label: included

details.point: After Maodun of Xiongnu defeated Donghu, remnants guarded Wuhuan Mountain and took Wuhuan as their tribal name.
details.label: included

details.point: Wuhuan people were skilled in horseback riding and archery, engaged in hunting and nomadic herding.
details.label: included

details.point: They lived in felt tents with doors facing east, ate meat and dairy, and made clothes from animal hair.
details.label: included

details.point: Wuhuan society valued youth over elders; killing father or brothers was allowed but not mother.
details.label: included

details.point: Leaders were chosen based on bravery and ability, not hereditary; each town had a small leader.
details.label: included

details.point: Marriage involved bride abduction, bride price, and the groom serving the wife's family for 1-2 years.
details.label: included

details.point: They practiced levirate marriage (stepmother and sister-in-law) but buried them with original husbands.
details.label: included

details.point: Wuhuan listened to women's advice in strategy but decided in battle; men shaved heads, women grew hair after marriage.
details.label: included

details.point: They used coffins, had mourning rituals, and burned a dog with the deceased to escort the soul to Chishan.
details.label: included

details.point: They worshipped gods and spirits, sacrificed cattle and sheep, and burned offerings.
details.label: included

details.point: Punishments included death for disobeying the leader and blood feuds redeemable with livestock.
details.label: included

details.point: After Maodun's defeat, Wuhuan became weak and often submitted to Xiongnu, paying tribute.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu moved Wuhuan to five commanderies to spy on Xiongnu; Wuhuan captains were established.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Emperor Zhao, Wuhuan grew strong and dug up Xiongnu Chanyu's tomb; Xiongnu attacked them.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Mingyou attacked Wuhuan after Xiongnu retreated, killing over 6,000 and capturing three princes.
details.label: included

details.point: During Wang Mang's reign, Wuhuan rebelled due to forced garrison; Xiongnu lured them to join.
details.label: included

details.point: In early Guangwu, Wuhuan and Xiongnu invaded border; Baishan Wuhuan was most powerful.
details.label: included

details.point: In 25 CE, Wuhuan leader Hao Dan and 922 people submitted to Han; emperor appointed 81 leaders as princes.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Cao defeated Wuhuan at Liucheng in 207 CE, killed Tadun, and moved over 10,000 towns to Central Plains.
details.label: included

details.point: Tai Shigong states that laws guide good and punishments prevent evil.
details.label: included

details.point: When laws were incomplete, good people still self-restrained because officials behaved well.
details.label: included

details.point: Officials can govern by example without severe punishments.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Shuao was a hermit from Chu recommended by Yu Qiu to King Zhuang.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Shuao became state minister in three months and governed with leniency, stopping prohibitions.
details.label: included

details.point: He encouraged seasonal wood cutting and river transport for people's convenience.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhuang changed small coins to large coins, causing market chaos.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Shuao advised restoring old currency, and the market returned to normal in three days.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhuang wanted to raise low carriages; Sun Shuao suggested raising thresholds instead.
details.label: included

details.point: After half a year, people raised carriages naturally due to higher thresholds.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Shuao was not complacent in office three times and had no regrets leaving three times.
details.label: included

details.point: Zichan became prime minister of Zheng after chaos under Xu Zhi.
details.label: included

details.point: After Zichan's rule, libertines stopped, elderly didn't carry loads, children didn't work fields.
details.label: included

details.point: After two years, market prices were fair; after three years, no theft; after five years, no military service needed.
details.label: included

details.point: Zichan died after 26 years; people mourned deeply, saying who will they rely on.
details.label: included

details.point: Gongyixiu, prime minister of Lu, obeyed laws and did not change regulations.
details.label: included

details.point: He refused a gift of fish, saying accepting could lead to losing his position and future fish.
details.label: included

details.point: He threw away mallow vegetables and burned his wife's loom to avoid competing with farmers and weavers.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi She, prime minister of Chu, let his father go after he committed murder, then imprisoned himself.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi She refused King Zhao's pardon and committed suicide to uphold law and filial piety.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Chun inherited the title of Marquis Fuping and served as a minister under Emperors Ai, Ping, and Wang Mang.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Chun retained his title under Wang Mang due to honesty and compliance with the law.
details.label: included

details.point: In the early Jianwu period, Zhang Chun restored his state and became a doctor in Taizhong.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Chun led troops to farm in Nanyang and was promoted to General of the Five Gentlemen.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Guangwu renamed Zhang Chun as Wu Shihou and gave him half of Fuping County's salary.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Chun was consulted on rituals due to his familiarity with old affairs.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Chun and Zhu Fu memorialized to establish the ancestral temple system, proposing to abolish the Qin Temple.
details.label: included

details.point: The emperor adopted the proposal to replace the ancestral temple with the five emperors and four generations.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Chun replaced Zhu Fu as imperial servant and later replaced Du Lin as Grand Minister of Works.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Chun opened the Yang Canal to divert the Luo River for water transportation, benefiting the people.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Chun established the rituals for the Di and Xia sacrifices, held every three and five years respectively.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Chun proposed building a Mingtang and Piyong, which was approved by the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Chun submitted a memorial for the Fengshan ceremony, and the emperor performed it in the first year of Zhongyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Chun died in March of the first year of Zhongyuan and was given the posthumous title Jiehou.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Bao inherited his father Cao Chong's study of the Qingshi Rites and was knowledgeable in etiquette.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Bao was recruited as a doctor and later ordered to compile Han rituals, producing 150 articles.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Bao's Han Rites was not implemented due to opposition from officials like Zhang Youfu and Zhang Min.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Cao Bao served as governor of Hanoi, alleviated drought, and brought a good harvest.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Xuan studied under various teachers, including Ma Rong, and became proficient in the classics.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Xuan was imprisoned during the party prohibition and later wrote refutations of He Xiu's works.
details.label: included

details.point: Gongsun Hong was from Xue County, Qi Prefecture.
details.label: included

details.point: He worked as a prison officer but was dismissed for crimes.
details.label: included

details.point: He herded pigs due to poverty.
details.label: included

details.point: He studied the Spring and Autumn Annals in his forties.
details.label: included

details.point: He was filial to his stepmother.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recruited as a virtuous person at age 60 and became a doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: He was dismissed after a mission to the Xiongnu displeased Emperor Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recommended again in Yuanguang 5th year and his countermeasure was ranked first by Emperor Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: He inspected the southwestern Yi and advised against the policy, but was ignored.
details.label: included

details.point: He was known for frugality, covering himself with a quilt and eating simple meals.
details.label: included

details.point: He mourned his stepmother for three years.
details.label: included

details.point: He avoided arguing in court and let the emperor decide.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to Zuo Neishi within two years.
details.label: included

details.point: He broke agreements with ministers to follow the emperor's will, leading to Ji An's rebuke.
details.label: included

details.point: He became imperial censor in Yuanshuo 3rd year.
details.label: included

details.point: He opposed the southwestern Yi, Canghai, and Shuofang policies but was overruled.
details.label: included

details.point: He apologized for his frugality when accused of fraud by Ji An.
details.label: included

details.point: He became prime minister and was granted the title Marquis of Pingjin.
details.label: included

details.point: He was outwardly generous but inwardly vengeful, causing the deaths of Dong Zhongshu and others.
details.label: included

details.point: He died as prime minister; his son Gongsun Du inherited the title but later lost it for breaking the law.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Gu was from Nanzheng, Hanzhong, son of Situ Li Hui.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Gu was known for his peculiar appearance with protruding head bones and turtle inscriptions on his feet.
details.label: included

details.point: He was eager to learn, traveled far for teachers, and befriended many wise men.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recommended as Xiaolian and Sikongpu but did not take office.
details.label: included

details.point: In 133 CE, he responded to an imperial edict about disasters, criticizing current politics.
details.label: included

details.point: He argued that officials today are chosen for wealth, not virtue, and harsh punishments are favored.
details.label: included

details.point: He criticized the enfeoffment of Empress Dowager's family and the power of Liang Ji's relatives.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised reducing the power of eunuchs and restoring proper governance.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Shun adopted many of his suggestions, but eunuchs framed Li Gu, leading to his dismissal.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Gu later served as magistrate of Luo County but resigned and returned home.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote to Liang Shang urging reform, but Liang Shang did not listen.
details.label: included

details.point: As governor of Jingzhou, he pardoned bandits and pacified the region within half a year.
details.label: included

details.point: He reported corrupt officials, leading to bribery by Liang Ji, and was transferred to Taishan.
details.label: included

details.point: In Taishan, he dismissed most soldiers and used kindness to quell bandits.
details.label: included

details.point: He recommended many worthy officials, including Yang Lun and Huang Qiong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He opposed concealing Emperor Chong's death and insisted on immediate mourning.
details.label: included

details.point: He advocated for establishing an older, virtuous emperor, but Liang Ji chose the young Liu Zuan.
details.label: included

details.point: He dismissed over a hundred improperly appointed officials, earning enemies.
details.label: included

details.point: He was falsely accused and imprisoned, but released due to public outcry.
details.label: included

details.point: He was eventually killed by Liang Ji at age 54; his disciple Guo Liang mourned him.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ping, originally named Kuang, changed to Ping after becoming emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: During Wang Mang's time, Liu Ping served as a county official and was praised for his ability.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ping abandoned his biological son to save his orphaned niece during a thief attack.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ping encountered a hungry thief, asked to feed his mother first, then returned to be killed; the thief spared him.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ping risked his life to protect Sun Meng, suffering seven stab wounds, and gave his own blood to Sun Meng when thirsty.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ping served as Prime Minister of Jiyin County, where there were no prisoners during inspections.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ping was recommended by Zhongliyi and later served as Yilang, Minister, and Zongzheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Xiao, son of Zhao Pu, served as Lang during Wang Mang's reign and traveled humbly.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Xiao offered himself to hungry thieves to save his brother Zhao Li; the thieves released them.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Xiao was promoted to Xiaolian and served as Admonishing Official and Changle Guardsman.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xianzong treated Zhao Xiao and his brother Zhao Li specially, allowing them to meet every ten days.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chunyu Gong, skilled in Laozi, helped thieves harvest fruit and hid to avoid shaming a seedling thief.
details.label: included

details.point: Chunyu Gong offered to replace his brother Chunyu Chong when bandits were about to cook him; both were spared.
details.label: included

details.point: Chunyu Gong raised his brother's orphans and taught them by beating himself when they misbehaved.
details.label: included

details.point: Chunyu Gong was summoned by Emperor Suzong, served as Counsellor and Cavalry Captain, and died in office.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Ge fled with his mother on his back during chaos, crying to thieves to spare them for his mother's sake.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Ge pulled his mother's cart himself without oxen or horses, earning the nickname 'Jiang Da Duozi'.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Ge refused gifts from nobles Ma Liao and Dou Xian, and was praised by the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Suzong granted Jiang Ge the title 'Ju Xiao' and ordered annual gifts of grain and wine.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Ban, descendant of Emperor Xuan, was known for benevolence; his father Liu Yu died of grief after his brother's death.
details.label: included
