details.point: Gai Kuanrao was from Weijun, proficient in classics, and became a Langguan through filial piety and integrity.
details.label: included

details.point: He impeached Peng Zu for refusing to get out of the carriage at the palace gate, but was demoted for misrepresentation.
details.label: included

details.point: As Sima of the Guards, he reformed protocols, ending the practice of Hou and Sima bowing to Weiwei.
details.label: included

details.point: He personally cared for soldiers, leading thousands to request to stay for another year.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan appointed him Taizhong doctor and later Sili Xiaowei; he impeached many officials.
details.label: included

details.point: At Xu Bo's housewarming, Kuanrao sat alone facing east and criticized the entertainment.
details.label: included

details.point: He impeached Changxin Shaofu for performing a monkey dance, but the emperor dropped the case after Xu Bo apologized.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Kuanrao was upright but liked to frame others, offending powerful people and the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Sheng advised him to be cautious, but Kuanrao ignored the advice.
details.label: included

details.point: Kuanrao submitted a memorial criticizing the emperor's reliance on eunuchs and quoting the Han Shi Yi Zhuan.
details.label: included

details.point: The emperor considered it treason; Kuanrao committed suicide at the North Tower.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuge Feng was from Langxie, known for independence and integrity, became Sili Xiaowei.
details.label: included

details.point: He pursued Xu Shizhong for breaking the law, but the emperor confiscated his talisman, ending the Sili's talisman privilege.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuge Feng wrote letters defending his actions but was eventually demoted to commoner and died at home.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Fu, a royal family member, opposed Emperor Cheng's plan to make Tang Jiandan queen.
details.label: included

details.point: He was imprisoned but later released after ministers interceded; he died at home.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zheng Chong, from a wealthy family, served as Minister of Public Affairs and opposed ennobling Fu Shang.
details.label: included

details.point: He was imprisoned and died after being accused of collusion.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Bao, from Tibei, served as governor of Yizhou and Jizhou, known for integrity.
details.label: included

details.point: He was dismissed for releasing a condemned criminal but later reinstated; he died at home.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Dong Zhongshu was from Guangchuan and studied the Spring and Autumn Annals.
details.label: included

details.point: He became a doctor during Emperor Jing's reign and lectured behind a curtain.
details.label: included

details.point: He did not look at his garden for three years due to intense study.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu asked him to respond to policy questions as a virtuous scholar.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Zhongshu argued that Heaven sends disasters to warn rulers of moral failings.
details.label: included

details.point: He emphasized that the ruler must work hard to cultivate virtue and knowledge.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He stated that music and ritual education are essential for good governance.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He criticized the Qin dynasty for abandoning moral education and using harsh punishments.
details.label: included

details.point: He advocated for establishing a national university to cultivate talent.
details.label: included

details.point: He recommended that local officials annually recommend two talented individuals.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He argued that promotion should be based on merit, not seniority.
details.label: included

details.point: He proposed that only Confucian teachings should be promoted, suppressing other schools.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as prime minister to the kings of Jiangdu and Jiaoxi, governing with propriety.
details.label: included

details.point: He was nearly executed for a draft memorial on disasters but was pardoned.
details.label: included

details.point: He resigned due to fear of punishment and spent his later years writing.
details.label: included

details.point: His works include over 100,000 words on the Spring and Autumn Annals.
details.label: included

details.point: He is credited with promoting Confucianism and establishing the recommendation system.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xiang praised him as comparable to Yi Yin and Lü Wang.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xin argued Dong Zhongshu was not as great as Yi Yin and Lü Wang but surpassed Guan Zhong and Yan Ying.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Zhongshu's teachings unified Confucian classics after the Qin book burning.
details.label: not_included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/廉颇蔺相如列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/廉颇蔺相如列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Lian Po was a Zhao general who conquered Qi and was named Shangqing.
details.label: included

details.point: Lin Xiangru was a retainer of eunuch Miao Xian.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhao of Qin offered 15 cities for He's Bi.
details.label: included

details.point: Lin Xiangru was sent as envoy to Qin with He's Bi.
details.label: included

details.point: Lin Xiangru saw King Qin had no intention to give cities, so he retrieved the jade by claiming a flaw.
details.label: included

details.point: Lin Xiangru threatened to smash the jade and his head against a pillar.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Qin apologized and promised to give cities, but Lin Xiangru suspected deception.
details.label: included

details.point: Lin Xiangru demanded King Qin fast 5 days and hold a nine-guest ceremony.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lin Xiangru sent He's Bi back to Zhao via a small road.
details.label: included

details.point: At the ceremony, Lin Xiangru told King Qin the jade was already in Zhao and accepted punishment.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Qin spared Lin Xiangru and let him return; Zhao made Lin Xiangru a senior大夫.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin attacked Zhao, killing 20,000 soldiers.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Zhao of Qin invited King Zhao of Zhao to a meeting in Mianchi.
details.label: included

details.point: At Mianchi, King Qin asked King Zhao to play the harp; Lin Xiangru demanded King Qin play a fou.
details.label: included

details.point: Lin Xiangru threatened to splash blood on King Qin; King Qin played the fou.
details.label: included

details.point: Lin Xiangru was named Shangqing, ranking above Lian Po.
details.label: included

details.point: Lian Po threatened to humiliate Lin Xiangru; Lin Xiangru avoided him for national unity.
details.label: included

details.point: Lian Po apologized with a thorn stick; they became friends.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao She, a tax official, killed Pingyuan Jun's retainers for non-payment; Pingyuan Jun recommended him.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao She led troops to rescue Yanyu, using a surprise march and capturing the north hill to defeat Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius said natures are similar but habits differ, emphasizing education's role.
details.label: included

details.point: Virtuous people teach cultivation of character and caution in friendships.
details.label: included

details.point: In chaotic times, customs become hypocritical and discipline lax.
details.label: included

details.point: People use benevolence and loyalty for personal gain.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu of Han rose with sword, promoting martial values.
details.label: included

details.point: From Emperor Wu, Confucianism flourished, with debates at Shiqu Pavilion.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang usurped Han; loyalists refused to serve him.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Emperors Huan and Ling, eunuchs controlled the court, leading to scholar protests.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Pang, Zhang Jian, etc., suffered in the Party禁锢 disaster.
details.label: included

details.point: Party names began with Ganling division into northern and southern parts.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Ying executed Zhang Cheng's son despite amnesty, angering eunuchs.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor arrested party members; over 200 were implicated.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After petitions, prisoners were released but banned from office.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Party members were categorized as Sanjun, Bajun, Bagu, Baji, Bachu.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Wu, Liu Shu, Chen Fan were 'Three Lords' (Sanjun).
details.label: included

details.point: Li Ying, Xun Yi, Du Mi, etc., were 'Eight Heroes' (Bajun).
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Jian's enemy Zhu Bing accused him of forming a clique.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Ling arrested former party members; over 100 died in prison.
details.label: included

details.point: Party ban extended to five generations; later lifted after Yellow Turban revolt.
details.label: included

details.point: The party incidents lasted over 20 years, affecting many good people.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/郦生陆贾列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/郦生陆贾列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Li Shiqi was from Gaoyang, Chenliu, and worked as a lowly clerk due to poverty.
details.label: included

details.point: He was known as 'Kangsheng' and local officials dared not employ him casually.
details.label: included

details.point: He initially hid from rebel generals because they were narrow-minded.
details.label: included

details.point: He sought to join Pei Gong (Liu Bang) after hearing of his strategies.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shiqi advised the cavalryman to introduce him as a 'madman' to Pei Gong.
details.label: included

details.point: Pei Gong disliked Confucians and initially received Li Shiqi while washing his feet.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shiqi criticized Pei Gong's disrespect and Pei Gong apologized.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shiqi proposed capturing Chenliu by persuading the magistrate or using internal support.
details.label: included

details.point: Pei Gong captured Chenliu and made Li Shiqi Lord of Guangye.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shiqi recommended his brother Li Shang to lead troops for Pei Gong.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Chu-Han conflict, Li Shiqi advised Pei Gong to hold Aocang and key fortresses.
details.label: included

details.point: He volunteered to persuade the King of Qi to surrender to Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shiqi convinced King Tian Guang of Qi to submit, removing defenses.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin attacked Qi despite the surrender, leading to Li Shiqi's execution by boiling.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shiqi's son Li Shi was later enfeoffed as Marquis of Gaoliang.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Jia was a Chu native and eloquent envoy for Emperor Gaozu.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Jia persuaded Zhao Tuo, King of South Vietnam, to submit to Han.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lu Jia argued that ruling requires both force and civil governance, not just military.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He wrote 'Xin Yu' (New Discourses) on statecraft at Gaozu's request.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lu Jia helped Chen Ping and Zhou Bo ally against the Lü clan during Empress Lü's regency.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Hui, courtesy name Wen Ji, was from Wan, Nanyang.
details.label: included

details.point: At age 13, during Wang Mang's fall, Zhu Hui protected his grandmother from bandits by drawing his sword.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Guangwu summoned Zhu Hui due to old friendship with his father.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Hui refused gifts from Xinyang Houyin, who admired his integrity.
details.label: included

details.point: As a county official, Zhu Hui refused to sell a maid to Prefect Ruan Kuang but later sent gifts after Ruan's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Hui tricked a chief clerk into giving him a jade token and delivered it to Liu Cang, earning praise.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Hui served as Prefect of Linhuai, known for strict justice and a folk song praising him.
details.label: included

details.point: During a famine, Zhu Hui distributed his family property to the poor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Hui fulfilled a promise to Zhang Kan by providing for his widow.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Hui recommended Chen You over his own son for an official post.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Hui opposed Zhang Lin's economic policies, leading to his imprisonment and later pardon.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Hui retired from politics at age 80, refusing to participate further.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhu Mu, courtesy name Gongshu, was known for filial piety and intense study.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhu Mu advised Liang Ji to reform and avoid disaster, but Liang Ji ignored him.
details.label: included

details.point: As Governor of Jizhou, Zhu Mu impeached corrupt officials and executed bandit leaders.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Mu exhumed eunuch Zhao Zhong's father's tomb, leading to his imprisonment and release after student protests.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Mu proposed dismissing eunuchs from power, but the emperor refused.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Mu died at 64, leaving no wealth; he was posthumously honored.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Hui, courtesy name Boqi, saved his father from execution by crying at the county gate at age 11.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Hui attended the funeral of a disgraced prefect and later promoted his slanderer's son as filial and incorrupt.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan was a distant descendant of the Tian family in Qi State.
details.label: included

details.point: During King Qi Min's reign, Tian Dan was a minor official in Linyi.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan general Le Yi attacked Qi; King Qi Min fled to Jucheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan fled to Anping and had axles sawed and wrapped in iron.
details.label: included

details.point: Anping fell; Tian Dan and his clan escaped due to reinforced axles.
details.label: included

details.point: Only Ju and Jimo cities remained unconquered by Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: Minister Nao Chi killed King Qi Min in Jucheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan army besieged Jimo; the city's defender was killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Jimo soldiers and civilians elected Tian Dan as general.
details.label: included

details.point: King Yan Hui succeeded King Yan Zhao; rift with Le Yi.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan sent spies to Yan to sow discord, leading to Le Yi's replacement by Qi Jie.
details.label: included

details.point: Le Yi fled to Zhao; Yan soldiers resented the change.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan used birds to create a divine aura, claiming a godly teacher.
details.label: included

details.point: A soldier pretended to be the teacher; Tian Dan treated him with respect.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Tian Dan provoked Yan to cut off noses of Qi captives, angering Jimo defenders.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan provoked Yan to dig up Qi ancestral graves, enraging the people.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan prepared for battle: hid elite troops, used women and elderly on walls, feigned surrender.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan bribed Yan general with gold to spare families, making Yan complacent.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Dan used fire oxen with knives and torches to attack Yan camp at night.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi army defeated Yan, killed Qi Jie, and recovered over 70 cities; Tian Dan welcomed King Xiang back to Linzi.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/卫将军骠骑列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/卫将军骠骑列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Wei Qing was born in Pingyang County, son of Zheng Ji and Wei Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Qing's half-sister Wei Zifu became favored by Emperor Wu of Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Qing was a servant of the Pingyang Hou family and later a cavalryman.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Zifu's pregnancy led to Queen Chen's jealousy; Wei Qing was arrested but rescued by Gongsun Ao.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu appointed Wei Qing as Jianzhang supervisor and Shizhong.
details.label: included

details.point: In 129 BC, Wei Qing led a cavalry attack on the Xiongnu from Shanggu, killing hundreds.
details.label: included

details.point: In 127 BC, Wei Qing captured the Henan area, driving away the Xiongnu kings, and was made Changping Hou.
details.label: included

details.point: In 124 BC, Wei Qing surrounded the Xiongnu Right Wise King, capturing 15,000 people and millions of livestock.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Qing was appointed Grand General; his three sons were made marquises but he declined.
details.label: included

details.point: In 123 BC, Wei Qing attacked the Xiongnu from Dingxiang, killing over 10,000.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhao Xin surrendered to the Xiongnu; Su Jian lost his army but returned and was spared.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huo Qubing, Wei Qing's nephew, became a favored general and was made Champion Hou.
details.label: included

details.point: In 121 BC, Huo Qubing attacked the Xiongnu from Longxi, capturing the golden statue of King Xiutu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huo Qubing defeated the Xiongnu at the Qilian Mountains, capturing many kings and nobles.
details.label: included

details.point: In 121 BC, the Hunye King surrendered to the Han; Huo Qubing managed the surrender.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 119 BC, Wei Qing and Huo Qubing led 50,000 cavalry each against the Xiongnu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Qing fought the Chanyu, killing 19,000, but failed to capture him; Li Guang committed suicide.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huo Qubing killed 70,443 Xiongnu, including many nobles, and was granted 5,800 households.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After the campaign, Huo Qubing's power rose while Wei Qing's declined; Huo Qubing died in 117 BC.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Qing died in 106 BC; his marquisate was later lost due to legal violations.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Qing was born from an affair between Zheng Ji and a servant named Wei Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Qing's sister Wei Zifu became favored by Emperor Wu, leading Wei Qing to assume the surname Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Qing was treated as a slave in his childhood and herded sheep.
details.label: included

details.point: A prisoner predicted Wei Qing would become a marquis.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Qing became a knight of the Pingyang Hou family and followed Princess Pingyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Princess Chen's mother, the eldest princess, arrested Wei Qing out of jealousy, but Gongsun Ao rescued him.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu appointed Wei Qing as a eunuch of Jianzhang Palace and later as a minister.
details.label: included

details.point: In 129 BC, Wei Qing led a cavalry attack on the Xiongnu, reaching Longcheng and killing hundreds, earning the title of Marquis of Guannei.
details.label: included

details.point: In 127 BC, Wei Qing led 30,000 cavalry to attack the Xiongnu, annihilating thousands and recovering the Hetao region, establishing Shuofang Commandery.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Qing was granted the title of Marquis of Changping with 3,800 households.
details.label: included

details.point: In 124 BC, Wei Qing led a surprise night attack on the Xiongnu Right King, capturing 15,000 people and tens of thousands of livestock.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Qing was appointed General-in-Chief, and his three sons were made marquises, but he declined the titles for his sons.
details.label: included

details.point: In 123 BC, Wei Qing attacked the Xiongnu from Dingxiang, annihilating over 10,000 enemies.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhao Xin surrendered to the Xiongnu, and Su Jian's army was destroyed; Wei Qing spared Su Jian's life.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Qubing, Wei Qing's nephew, emerged as a brilliant commander, becoming a marquis after his first campaign.
details.label: included

details.point: In 121 BC, Huo Qubing attacked the Xiongnu in the Hexi Corridor, capturing the golden statue of King Xiutu and killing 8,960 enemies.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Qubing accepted the surrender of the Hunxie King, killing 8,000 who tried to flee, and settled the surrendered Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: In 119 BC, Wei Qing and Huo Qubing each led 50,000 cavalry in a massive campaign; Wei Qing defeated Shanyu but failed to capture him.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Qubing's campaign against the Left King was highly successful, killing 70,443 enemies, and he was granted 5,800 households.
details.label: included

details.point: After Huo Qubing's death, Wei Qing's influence waned; he died in 106 BC, and his descendants lost their marquisates.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Mo, a general of Lu, threatened Duke Huan of Qi with a dagger at the Ke Di alliance.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Huan of Qi promised to return occupied Lu lands after Cao Mo's threat.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Zhong advised Duke Huan to keep the promise to maintain credibility.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuan Zhu assassinated King Liao of Wu by hiding a dagger in a grilled fish.
details.label: included

details.point: Prince Guang became King Helu of Wu after the assassination.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Rang attempted to assassinate Zhao Xiangzi to avenge his master Zhibo.
details.label: included

details.point: Yu Rang failed and committed suicide after stabbing Zhao Xiangzi's clothes.
details.label: included

details.point: Nie Zheng assassinated Xia Lei, the prime minister of Han, for Yan Zhongzi.
details.label: included

details.point: Nie Zheng disfigured himself to protect his family before dying.
details.label: included

details.point: Nie Zheng's sister Nie Rong identified his body and died of grief.
details.label: included

details.point: Jing Ke was a retainer of Prince Dan of Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: Prince Dan planned to kidnap or kill the King of Qin to stop Qin's expansion.
details.label: included

details.point: Jing Ke requested Fan Yuqi's head and a map of Dukang to gain Qin's trust.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Yuqi committed suicide to provide his head for the plan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Jing Ke and Qin Wuyang went to Qin; Qin Wuyang showed fear at court.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Jing Ke presented the map and revealed a dagger; he grabbed the King of Qin.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The King of Qin escaped, drew his sword, and wounded Jing Ke.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Jing Ke threw the dagger but missed; he was killed by guards.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin invaded Yan; Prince Dan was killed by his father to appease Qin.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Gao Jianli attempted to assassinate Qin Shi Huang with a lead-filled zhu but failed.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang was the nephew of Empress Xiaoyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: His father Wang Man died early and was not granted a title.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang lived simply and studied the Rites and Zhou Rites under Chen Shen.
details.label: included

details.point: He served his mother, widowed sister-in-law, and orphaned nephew with care.
details.label: included

details.point: He attended his uncle Wang Feng during illness, leading to his appointment as Huangmenlang and later Shesheng Xiaowei.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Shang and others recommended Wang Mang, leading Emperor Cheng to consider him virtuous.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yongshi 1st year, Wang Mang was made Marquis of Xindu with 1,500 households.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to Cavalry Commandant and Guanglu大夫, serving as palace guard.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang distributed his wealth to guests and supported famous people, gaining a reputation surpassing his uncles.
details.label: included

details.point: He secretly bought a maidservant for Zhu Ziyuan to appear selfless.
details.label: included

details.point: He exposed Chunyuchang's crimes, leading to Chunyu's execution and Wang Mang's promotion to Grand Sima in Suihe 1st year at age 38.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Cheng's death, Wang Mang resigned but was retained by the Empress Dowager.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He clashed with Empress Dowager Fu over seating at a banquet, leading to his resignation and return to his fief.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Ai's death, Wang Mang was reinstated as Grand Sima and chose Liu Kan (Emperor Ping) as emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: He eliminated rivals like Ding, Fu, and Dong Xian families, and forced Wang Li to return to his fief.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang received the title Anhan Gong and was granted 28,000 households, but initially refused.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He gave his daughter in marriage to Emperor Ping to consolidate power.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang's son Wang Yu was forced to commit suicide for plotting against him.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang became regent (acting emperor) for the infant Emperor Ruzi.
details.label: included

details.point: He accepted the mandate of heaven and founded the Xin dynasty, declaring himself emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu had eight sons, including Empress Lu's son Emperor Xiaohui and Lady Qi's son Liu Ruyi.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Fei, King Hui of Qi, was Gaozu's eldest son and was enfeoffed with over seventy cities.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Hui honored Liu Fei as elder brother at a banquet, angering Empress Dowager Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Lu attempted to poison Liu Fei, but failed.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Fei dedicated Chengyang County to Princess Lu Yuan to appease Empress Dowager Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ruyi, King of Zhao, was killed by Empress Dowager Lu after Gaozu's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu You, King of Zhao, was starved to death by Empress Dowager Lu after his Lu wife slandered him.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Hui, King of Zhao, committed suicide after his favorite concubine was poisoned by his Lu queen.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jian, King of Yan, died and his son was killed, ending his line.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Zhang, Zhu Xuhou, killed a Lu family member at a banquet under military law, intimidating the Lus.
details.label: included

details.point: After Empress Dowager Lu's death, the Lu family plotted rebellion but were killed by Liu Zhang, Zhou Bo, and Chen Ping.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xiang, King Ai of Qi, succeeded Liu Fei; during his reign, Empress Dowager Lu divided Qi territory.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ze, King of Langye, was tricked by Qi and later helped decide the emperor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The ministers chose Liu Heng, King of Dai, as Emperor Wen over Liu Xiang due to the Qi queen's family's ferocity.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen returned Qi's separated territories and enfeoffed Liu Zhang and Liu Xingju as kings.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xingju, King of Jibei, rebelled and committed suicide after defeat.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Rebellion of the Seven States, four Qi-related kings rebelled; King Xiao of Qi initially hesitated and later committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing established Liu Shou as King Yi of Qi after King Xiao's death.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Li of Qi committed adultery with his sister and was investigated by Zhufu Yan, leading to his suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: The Qi state was eventually divided and its territories reverted to the Han dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: Bai Qi was from Yidi and served King Zhao of Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 13th year of King Zhao, Bai Qi became Zuo Shu Zhang and attacked Xincheng.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In Yique, Bai Qi killed 240,000 Han-Wei allies and captured Gongsun Xi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Bai Qi captured 61 Wei cities and later attacked Chu, capturing Yan and Deng.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Bai Qi captured Ying, the Chu capital, burned royal tombs, and Chu moved to Chen.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin established Nanjun; Bai Qi was named Lord Wu'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Bai Qi killed 130,000 at Huayang and sank 20,000 Zhao soldiers.
details.label: included

details.point: Bai Qi attacked Xingcheng, killed 50,000, and blocked Taihang Road.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shangdang governor Feng Ting surrendered to Zhao, triggering the Changping campaign.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao accepted Shangdang; Qin sent Wang He to attack, and Zhao sent Lian Po.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Qin used counterintelligence to replace Lian Po with Zhao Kuo.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Kuo attacked; Qin feigned retreat and cut off Zhao's supply lines.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao army was surrounded for 46 days; Zhao Kuo was killed in a breakout attempt.
details.label: included

details.point: Bai Qi buried 400,000 Zhao soldiers alive; total Zhao losses were 450,000.
details.label: included

details.point: Su Dai persuaded Ying Hou to stop the siege of Handan, fearing Bai Qi's rise.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin made peace with Han and Zhao; Bai Qi resented Ying Hou.
details.label: included

details.point: Bai Qi refused to lead the attack on Handan, citing difficulties and losses.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhao forced Bai Qi to commit suicide; Bai Qi regretted the Changping massacre.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jian served Qin Shihuang, conquered Zhao, Yan, and Chu with 600,000 troops.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jian's grandson Wang Li was captured by Xiang Yu, fulfilling the 'three generations' curse.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Fan, courtesy name Zhongju, was from Pingyu, Runan.
details.label: included

details.point: As a child, Chen Fan said he wanted to sweep away the rubbish in the world, not just clean his room.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Fan served as Prefect of Le'an and was known for his integrity.
details.label: included

details.point: He recruited Zhou Chu, a recluse, and respected him by hanging a special bed after he left.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Fan exposed Zhao Xuan's false filial piety and punished him.
details.label: included

details.point: He beat a messenger from General Liang Ji to death and was sentenced to military service.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Fan advised against military action against bandits, blaming corrupt officials.
details.label: included

details.point: He was dismissed for defending Li Yun, who had been sentenced to death for remonstrance.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Fan criticized Emperor Huan for excessive titles and rewards, leading to release of 500 palace women.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised against hunting at Guangcheng Garden, citing the 'Three Empties' (fields, court, warehouses).
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Fan and Huang Wan were dismissed for not favoring the powerful in official selections.
details.label: included

details.point: He defended Liu Wangzhi, Cheng Jin, Zhai Chao, and Huang Fu against eunuch persecution.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Fan wrote a memorial defending Li Ying and other party members, comparing the persecution to Qin's book burning.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Huan's death, Empress Dowager Dou appointed Chen Fan as Grand Tutor.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Fan and General Dou Wu planned to eliminate eunuchs, but the plot was exposed.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Fan led officials to storm the palace but was arrested and killed in prison.
details.label: included

details.point: His friend Zhu Zhen buried him and hid his son Chen Yi.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Yun, courtesy name Zishi, was from Taiyuan; Guo Linzong praised him as having talent for a king's assistant.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Yun killed the eunuch Zhao Jin and was imprisoned but later released.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Yun conspired with Lu Bu to assassinate Dong Zhuo, but later refused to pardon Dong Zhuo's followers, leading to his death when Li Jue and Guo Si rebelled.
details.label: not_included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/后汉书/列传/南蛮西南夷列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/南蛮西南夷列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Panhu, a five-colored dog, brought the head of Quan Rong general Wu, earning the emperor's daughter as wife.
details.label: included

details.point: Panhu and the emperor's daughter lived in Nanshan, producing six sons and six daughters who intermarried.
details.label: included

details.point: Their descendants became known as barbarians, with customs like colorful clothes and tail-shaped garments.
details.label: included

details.point: During Zhou, barbarians grew strong; King Xuan sent Fang Shu to conquer them.
details.label: included

details.point: King Ping moved east; barbarians invaded Central Plains; Wen of Jin and Cai Gong defeated them.
details.label: included

details.point: Chu annexed barbarians after King Zhuang's reign; later Qin set up Qianzhong Commandery.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han changed Qianzhong to Wuling; barbarians paid cloth tax (yuan cloth).
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 23 CE, Xiang Shancheng rebelled; Liu Shang's army was annihilated.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Yuan defeated Xiang Shancheng in 25 CE; barbarians surrendered.
details.label: included

details.point: In 47 CE, Wuling barbarians rebelled; Chen Feng killed 3,000, surrendered 2,000.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 157 CE, Changsha barbarians rebelled; Du Shang pacified them.
details.label: included

details.point: In 40 CE, Trung Sisters revolted in Jiaozhi; Ma Yuan suppressed them in 43 CE.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 100 CE, Rinan barbarians attacked; Li Gu advised against large expedition; Zhang Qiao pacified them.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lin Jun, from Ba clan, became king by hitting sword target and floating clay boat; later turned into white tiger.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin annexed Ba; Ba leaders married Qin women; taxes and corvée were regulated.
details.label: included

details.point: Banmei barbarians helped Han Gaozu; their dance became Bayu Dance.
details.label: included

details.point: In 180 CE, Banmei rebelled due to harsh taxes; Cheng Bao advised leniency; they surrendered.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yelang king born from bamboo; Han set up Zangke Commandery; later killed Yelang king.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ailao people originated from woman Shao Yi; King Xianli surrendered in 51 CE; Yongchang Commandery established.
details.label: included

details.point: In 69 CE, Ailao king Liumaung submitted with 550,000 people; Yongchang Commandery expanded.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Wangzhi was born in Lanling, Shuhai, later moved to Duling, and studied the Qi Shi and other classics under Houcang, Bai Qi, and Xia Housheng.
details.label: included

details.point: During Huo Guang's regency, Xiao Wangzhi refused to be searched and held hostage before meeting him, advising Huo Guang to treat scholars with courtesy.
details.label: included

details.point: Huo Guang did not appoint Xiao Wangzhi, who became a Langguan after passing the A-level exam, serving as Xiaoyuan East Gate Marquis.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Wangzhi was dismissed due to his younger brother's crime, later became a county official, then was appointed as Minister of Ceremonies of Daxing by Wei Xiang.
details.label: included

details.point: After Huo Guang's death, Xiao Wangzhi memorialized Emperor Xuan about a hailstorm, blaming the disaster on the concentration of power in one family (the Huo clan).
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan appointed Xiao Wangzhi as a visitor, and he was promoted three times in a year to an official of two thousand stone level.
details.label: included

details.point: After the Huo family's treason, Xiao Wangzhi became more important, but was sent as Governor of Pingyuan, which he disliked; he memorialized to be recalled.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was recalled to manage Shaofu, then appointed Zuo Fengyi to test his administrative ability; he initially feared demotion but took office after an imperial decree.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Xiqiang rebellion, Xiao Wangzhi opposed Zhang Chang's proposal to allow criminals to donate grain to atone for sins, arguing it would harm justice and education.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Wangzhi served as Zuo Fengyi for three years with praise, then promoted to Dahonglu; he opposed marrying a princess to Wusun's Yuan Guimi, deeming it unreliable.
details.label: included

details.point: When Wusun's king died and Kuang Wang broke the agreement, Xiao Wangzhi advised against sending the princess, and the emperor recalled her.
details.label: included

details.point: In the third year of Shenjue, Xiao Wangzhi replaced Bingji as imperial censor; during the Huns' civil strife, he advised against attacking, advocating aid and benevolence.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan followed Xiao Wangzhi's advice to aid Huhanxie Chanyu, establishing Han's virtue among barbarians.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiao Wangzhi opposed Geng Shouchang's proposal for Changpingcang, and criticized the prime minister's incompetence, leading to Emperor Xuan's displeasure.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was demoted to Crown Prince Tutor due to accusations of arrogance and misconduct, including failing to visit the ill prime minister and sending officials for personal errands.
details.label: included

details.point: As tutor, he taught the crown prince the Analects and Etiquette; he argued that the Huns Chanyu should be treated as an equal guest, above princes, which the emperor adopted.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Xuan's death, Xiao Wangzhi was appointed former general and Guang Luxun, serving as a key advisor to Emperor Yuan along with Zhou Kan and Liu Gengsheng.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiao Wangzhi recommended replacing eunuchs in Zhongshu with scholars, conflicting with Shi Gao, Hong Gong, and Shi Xian; he was later framed for plotting to depose the emperor's relatives.
details.label: included

details.point: He was imprisoned, then pardoned and made Marquis of Guannei, but after his son Xiao Ji complained, he was pressured to commit suicide by drinking poison, despite the emperor's intent to spare him.
details.label: included

details.point: The emperor mourned Xiao Wangzhi deeply, punished the eunuchs, and honored his grave annually; Xiao Wangzhi had eight sons, several becoming high officials.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Xiaohui's reign, Hongru and Jiru gained favor through flattery and slept with the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Ministers wore bird-feather hats and applied makeup due to the influence of Hongru and Jiru.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Xiaowen's reign, favored ministers included Deng Tong, Zhao Tong, and Beigong Bozi.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Tong was a Huangtou Lang from Shu County who rowed boats.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen dreamed of a yellow-headed man pushing him to heaven, and later found Deng Tong matching the dream.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen favored Deng Tong, promoted him to senior doctor, and gave him hundreds of millions in rewards.
details.label: included

details.point: A fortune teller predicted Deng Tong would die of poverty, but Emperor Wen gave him Tongshan to mint coins.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Tong sucked pus from Emperor Wen's carbuncle, and the prince resented him for it.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Jing ascended, Deng Tong was dismissed and later convicted of minting coins, his wealth confiscated.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Tong died in poverty, living in others' homes without a penny.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Jing's reign, only Zhou Ren was favored, but not deeply.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Wu's reign, favored ministers included Han Yan and eunuch Li Yannian.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Yan was a calligraphy classmate of Emperor Wu and became close when he was prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Yan learned Hu weapons and formations, was promoted to senior official, and slept with the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: King Jiangdu of Jiangdu mistook Han Yan for the emperor and complained to the Queen Mother.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han Yan committed suicide after being ordered by the Queen Mother for adultery with concubines.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Yannian was a singer and dancer from Zhongshan, castrated for breaking the law.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Yannian's sister became Emperor Wu's favorite and gave birth to a son.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Yannian was favored, wore official seal of two thousand stones, and slept with the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: After his sister's death, Li Yannian's favor waned, and he was arrested and killed for lewd behavior.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Yu was from Xinye County, Nanyang County.
details.label: included

details.point: At thirteen, he could recite poems and studied in Chang'an, where he befriended Guangwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Yu refused offers from Gengshi's heroes, pledging loyalty to Guangwu.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised Guangwu to recruit heroes, please the people, and build a great cause.
details.label: included

details.point: Guangwu appointed Deng Yu as General Deng and kept him for strategic discussions.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Yu recruited troops and attacked Leyang County for Guangwu.
details.label: included

details.point: He recommended capable generals and was trusted by Guangwu for knowing people.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Deng Yu defeated the Bronze Horses at Qingyang and captured their general.
details.label: included

details.point: Guangwu sent Deng Yu as former general to lead the western expedition with 20,000 elite troops.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianwu year 1, Deng Yu entered Hedong, defeated Fan Shen, and beheaded him.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Yu's army was initially defeated by Wang Kuang, but he regrouped and defeated them, pacifying Hedong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Guangwu appointed Deng Yu as Grand Minister (Situ) and Marquis of Zan at age 24.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Yu entered Guanzhong, where people welcomed him due to his disciplined troops.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised against attacking Chang'an directly, instead securing northern commanderies for supplies.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Yu's subordinate Feng Yi killed Zong Xin and rebelled; Guangwu predicted Huang Fang would arrest Feng Yi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In Jianwu year 2, Deng Yu was made Marquis of Liang; he worshipped at Gaozu Temple in Chang'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Yu was defeated by Red Eyebrows at Lantian and later at Gaoling, suffering heavy losses.
details.label: included

details.point: He returned his seal as Situ and Marquis of Liang in apology after a major defeat.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Yu later defeated Yan Cen with other generals and was made Marquis of Gaomi in Jianwu 13.
details.label: included

details.point: Deng Yu died in Yongping year 1 at age 57, posthumously named Yuan Hou.
details.label: included

details.point: Shentu Gang was a native of Maoling, Fufeng County, and his seventh-generation ancestor was a prime minister under Emperor Wen.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shentu Gang was upright and admired the conduct of Chief Shi Yu and Ji An.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Ping's reign, Wang Mang isolated the Feng and Wei clans, which Shentu Gang resented.
details.label: included

details.point: Shentu Gang wrote a countermeasure criticizing Wang Mang's policies, including suppressing speech and separating relatives.
details.label: included

details.point: Shentu Gang compared Wang Mang's regency unfavorably to the Duke of Zhou's regency.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shentu Gang warned that Wang Mang's actions would lead to disaster, citing the Huo Guang case.
details.label: included

details.point: Shentu Gang's memorial angered Wang Mang, who ordered him dismissed and sent home.
details.label: included

details.point: After Wang Mang usurped the throne, Shentu Gang fled to Hexi and Bashu for over 20 years.
details.label: included

details.point: Shentu Gang advised Wei Xiao not to rebel against Han and submit to Gongsun Shu, but Wei Xiao refused.
details.label: included

details.point: Shentu Gang was summoned by Emperor Guangwu in 31 AD and appointed imperial censor, then ministerial order.
details.label: included

details.point: Shentu Gang once stopped Guangwu from traveling by placing his head on the carriage wheel.
details.label: included

details.point: Shentu Gang repeatedly advised Guangwu to appoint virtuous guardians for the crown prince, but was ignored.
details.label: included

details.point: Shentu Gang was demoted to Pingyin magistrate and later resigned as Taizhong doctor, dying at home.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Yong, courtesy name Junchang, was from Tunliu, Shangdang, and studied Ouyang's Shang Shu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Bao Yong divorced his wife for scolding a dog in front of his stepmother.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Yong was protected by Governor Gou Jian after Wang Mang sought to kill him for his father Bao Xuan's loyalty to Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Yong stopped Governor Zhao Xing from visiting a false Shizhong, gaining fame when Wang Mang sought the impostor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Bao Yong served under Gengshi, was granted the title Marquis of Zhongyang, but dismissed his troops when surrendering to Guangwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Yong persuaded the governor of Huai County to surrender to Guangwu, and was appointed admonishing doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Yong as governor of Lu County killed rebel leaders Peng Feng and others, and was made Marquis of Guannei.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius studied the Six Arts and used them to clarify the Tao, correct human relations, and achieve governance.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius lamented the decline of Zhou Dao and the lack of wise rulers.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius traveled to various states, was threatened in Kuang and starved in Chen, and sought employment with over seventy rulers.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius revised music, making Ya and Song find their proper places.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius praised Yao and Zhou, and compiled the Book of Documents starting with Yao Dian.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius wrote the Spring and Autumn Annals based on Lu records, using civil and military methods as standards.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius studied the Yi in his later years, wearing out the binding cords, and wrote commentaries.
details.label: included

details.point: After Confucius's death, his disciples scattered and some became teachers to princes.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Warring States, Confucianism was denounced, but Mencius and Xunzi upheld Confucius's teachings.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin Shi Huang burned the Books and killed scholars, causing the Six Arts to become incomplete.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucian scholars from Lu took ritual vessels to Chen She, who appointed Kong Jia as a doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Emperor Gao of Han, Confucian scholars began to study classics and teach rituals.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu established the Five Classics Erudites and initiated the selection of disciples.
details.label: included

details.point: Gongsun Hong became prime minister through studying the Spring and Autumn Annals, promoting Confucianism.
details.label: included

details.point: The number of Erudite disciples increased over time, reaching 3,000 under Emperor Cheng.
details.label: included

details.point: The Yi tradition was transmitted from Confucius through various scholars, including Tian He and Ding Kuan.
details.label: included

details.point: The Book of Documents was preserved by Fu Sheng, who taught it to Zhang Sheng and Ouyang Sheng.
details.label: included

details.point: The Shi (Poetry) tradition included the Lu, Qi, and Han schools, with Shen Gong and Yuan Gu as key figures.
details.label: included

details.point: The Li (Rites) tradition was transmitted by Gao Tangsheng, Hou Cang, and the Dai brothers.
details.label: included

details.point: The Spring and Autumn Annals had Gongyang, Guliang, and Zuo traditions, with Dong Zhongshu and Hu Wusheng as key figures.
details.label: included

details.point: Xue Xuan was a native of Tan County, Shuhai.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as secretary of Tingwei and history of the capital ship prison.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhao Gong, prefect of Langye, admired Xue Xuan and let him follow on inspections.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xue Xuan was promoted to Lelang Duweicheng and later became Wanjuling.
details.label: not_included

details.point: General Wang Feng recommended Xue Xuan as Chang'an Order.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xue Xuan became Censor Zhongcheng under Emperor Cheng.
details.label: included

details.point: He submitted a memorial criticizing harsh officials and urging moral governance.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor approved his memorial.
details.label: included

details.point: Xue Xuan served as prefect of Linhuai and Chenliu, suppressing robbers.
details.label: included

details.point: He became Zuo Fengyi and handled corrupt officials Yang Zhan and Xie You.
details.label: included

details.point: Xue Xuan transferred county magistrates Yin Shang and Xue Gong to improve governance.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was promoted to Shaofu and then to imperial censor.
details.label: included

details.point: Gu Yong recommended Xue Xuan as imperial censor, praising his talents.
details.label: included

details.point: Xue Xuan became prime minister and was granted Marquis of Gaoyang.
details.label: included

details.point: He was dismissed as prime minister due to disasters and banditry.
details.label: included

details.point: Later he was recalled as Tejin and involved in political affairs.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was dismissed again for friendship with Chunyu Chang.
details.label: included

details.point: Xue Xuan's son Xue Kuang injured Shen Xian and was exiled.
details.label: included

details.point: Xue Xuan died at home after being dismissed as civilian.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Bo, from Duling, rose from humble origins to become prime minister.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ban Chao was the youngest son of Ban Biao, from Pingling, Fufeng.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yongping 5, Ban Chao and his mother followed his brother Ban Gu to Luoyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Chao supported his mother by copying documents for officials.
details.label: included

details.point: He aspired to emulate Fu Jiezi and Zhang Qian to achieve merit in foreign lands.
details.label: included

details.point: A fortune teller predicted Ban Chao would become a marquis of a distant land.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Ming appointed Ban Chao as Lantai Lingshi, but he was later dismissed.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yongping 16, Ban Chao served as a fake Sima under Dou Gu against the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Chao was sent as an envoy to the Western Regions with Guo Xun.
details.label: included

details.point: In Shanshan, Ban Chao deduced Xiongnu envoys were present and captured them.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Chao led 36 men to attack and kill the Xiongnu envoys at night.
details.label: included

details.point: Shanshan submitted and sent a hostage to Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Chao was appointed Army Sima and sent again to the Western Regions.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yutian, Ban Chao killed a wizard and intimidated King Guangde into submitting.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Chao captured Douti in Shule and installed Zhong as king.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Ming's death, Ban Chao was isolated but defended Shule for over a year.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Chao was recalled but returned to Shule after pleas from the people.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Chao defeated Weitou and stabilized Shule.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Chao requested more troops to conquer Kucha and pacify the Western Regions.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Zhang approved and sent Xu Qian with troops to assist Ban Chao.
details.label: included

details.point: Ban Chao defeated Fan Chen and beheaded over a thousand rebels.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Guanghan was a native of Liwu County, Zhuo County, known for integrity and savvy.
details.label: included

details.point: He was elected Maocai and served as Yangdi Order, then promoted to Lieutenant of Jingfu acting as Jing Zhaoyin.
details.label: included

details.point: He executed Du Jian for illegal activities despite intercession from powerful figures.
details.label: included

details.point: He participated in deposing King of Changyi and establishing Emperor Xuan, receiving title of Marquis of Guannei.
details.label: included

details.point: As Yingchuan governor, he killed Yuan and Chu leaders and broke up powerful family alliances.
details.label: included

details.point: He used informants and a snitch bucket to control crime, gaining reputation even among Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Jing Zhaoyin, attributing success to subordinates and using hook distance method.
details.label: included

details.point: He solved a kidnapping case by negotiating with robbers and treating them well before execution.
details.label: included

details.point: He revealed private affairs like a god, such as knowing about a pavilion chief's message.
details.label: included

details.point: He increased salaries of traveling wardens to prevent arbitrary arrests.
details.label: included

details.point: After Huo Guang's death, he raided Huo Yu's residence, offending relatives and ministers.
details.label: included

details.point: He was executed after being convicted of insulting the prime minister and killing innocents.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yin Wenggui was a prison clerk familiar with law, later became market official controlling Huo family slaves.
details.label: included

details.point: He was appointed Hedong postal supervisor, then Hongnong Lieutenant, and Donghai governor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: As Donghai governor, he arrested cunning gentry like Xu Zhongsun, executing him to pacify the county.
details.label: included

details.point: He became You Fufeng, using registration books to track crimes and punishing powerful offenders.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He died in office with no extra property; emperor granted gold to his son for sacrifices.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Yanshou was promoted after his father Han Yi died admonishing King of Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: As Yingchuan governor, he changed customs by promoting etiquette and using elders to set rituals.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He resolved a land dispute between brothers by blaming himself, leading to their reconciliation.
details.label: included
