details.point: Sima Xiangru was born in Chengdu, Shu County, courtesy name Changqing.
details.label: included

details.point: He admired Lin Xiangru and changed his name to Xiangru.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as a Langguan under Emperor Jing but resigned due to dislike of the post.
details.label: included

details.point: He lived in Liang State and wrote 'Zixu Fu'.
details.label: included

details.point: After King Liang Xiao died, he returned to Chengdu poor.
details.label: included

details.point: He lived in Linqiong at the invitation of magistrate Wang Ji.
details.label: included

details.point: At a banquet hosted by Zhuo Wangsun, he played the qin to attract Zhuo Wenjun.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhuo Wenjun eloped with Sima Xiangru to Chengdu.
details.label: included

details.point: They returned to Linqiong and opened a wine shop; Zhuo Wangsun eventually gave them wealth.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu read 'Zixu Fu' and summoned Xiangru.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiangru wrote 'Shanglin Fu' which praised the emperor's hunting and advocated frugality.
details.label: included

details.point: He was appointed Langguan after presenting the fu.
details.label: included

details.point: He was sent to blame Tang Meng and reassure Ba and Shu people.
details.label: included

details.point: He was appointed Zhonglang General to pacify the southwestern barbarians.
details.label: included

details.point: He successfully brought Qiong, Zuo, and others under Han control.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He wrote a rebuttal to critics of the southwestern campaign.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was dismissed after accusations of bribery but later reinstated as Langguan.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised the emperor against dangerous hunting in a memorial.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote 'Adult Fu' about immortals to please the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: He left a book on fengshan sacrifices, which was presented after his death.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/樊郦滕灌列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/樊郦滕灌列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Fan Kuai was a native of Peixian County and made a living by killing dogs and selling meat.
details.label: included

details.point: He followed Liu Bang (Emperor Gaozu) from the beginning, raising troops in Fengyi and capturing Peixian.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Kuai repeatedly took the lead in assaults, beheading many enemies and earning promotions.
details.label: included

details.point: At the Hongmen Banquet, Fan Kuai broke into the camp and rebuked Xiang Yu, saving Liu Bang's life.
details.label: included

details.point: After Xiang Yu's defeat, Fan Kuai was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wuyang with 5,400 households.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Kuai married Empress Lü's sister Lü Xu, making him close to the imperial family.
details.label: included

details.point: During Gaozu's illness, Fan Kuai forced his way into the palace to remonstrate, citing the Zhao Gao precedent.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Kuai was slandered and nearly executed, but was saved by Chen Ping and later released by Empress Lü.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Kuai died in the sixth year of Emperor Hui, posthumously titled Marquis Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Fan Kang and later descendants inherited the title, but it was eventually abolished due to crimes.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shang from Gaoyang led 4,000 men to join Liu Bang and was made Xinchengjun.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shang pacified many counties and was enfeoffed as Zhuohou with 5,000 households.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shang served as Right Prime Minister and helped pacify rebellions, including Yingbu.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Shang's son Li Ji was involved with the Lü clan and later lost his title for plotting marriage.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiahou Ying was a stable keeper in Peixian who became close to Liu Bang and served as his charioteer.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiahou Ying saved Liu Bang's children during the defeat at Pengcheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiahou Ying was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ruyin with 6,900 households and served as Taipu.
details.label: included

details.point: He helped depose the young emperor and welcome Emperor Wen to the throne.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Guan Ying was a silk merchant who joined Liu Bang and became a cavalry commander.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Ying played a key role in defeating Xiang Yu, capturing many enemies, and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yingyin.
details.label: included

details.point: The five kings of Chu were brothers of the same father.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jiao studied the 'Poetry' with Mu Sheng, Bai Sheng, Shen Gong, and Fu Qiu Bo.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu of Han made Liu Jiao the King of Chu and Liu Jia the King of Jing.
details.label: included

details.point: Gaozu's sister-in-law once scraped the pot to drive away guests, causing Gaozu to resent her.
details.label: included

details.point: Gaozu later enfeoffed Liu Bo's son Liu Xin as Genjiehou.
details.label: included

details.point: King Yuan of Chu appointed Mu Sheng, Bai Sheng, and Shen Gong as middle-level officials.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Gong wrote a commentary on the 'Poetry' called 'Lu Shi'.
details.label: included

details.point: King Yuan's son Ying Ke succeeded as King Yi of Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wu of Chu rebelled during Emperor Jing's reign and committed suicide after defeat.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Jing established Liu Li as King Wen of Chu after the rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu De, a descendant of Chu, served as Zongzheng and was known for his generosity.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Xiang (Gengsheng) presented the 'Pillow Book of Hongbaoyuan' to Emperor Xuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xiang was imprisoned for failing to make gold but later pardoned.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Xiang wrote 'Hong Fan's Five Elements Biography' to warn against the Wang family's power.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Xiang compiled 'Biography of Women', 'New Preface', and 'Shuo Yuan'.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Xiang warned Emperor Cheng about the Wang family's growing power.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Xin discovered the ancient text 'Zuo Shi Chun Qiu' and advocated for its official status.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Xin wrote a letter to the doctors, criticizing their conservatism.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Mang valued Liu Xin and appointed him to high positions.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Han historian praised Liu Xiang, Liu Xin, and others for their scholarship.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yi countries wear hair in buns, cultivate fields, live in towns.
details.label: included

details.point: Xi and Kunming people move with livestock, no fixed residence or commander.
details.label: included

details.point: Northeast of Wei, many rulers; Yi and Zuo most powerful.
details.label: included

details.point: Northeast of Zuo, many rulers; Ran Zhen most powerful.
details.label: included

details.point: Northeast of Ranjun, many kings; Baima most powerful, same kind as Di.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wei of Chu sent Zhuang Qi up Yangtze, captured areas west of Bajun, Shujun, Qianzhong.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuang Qi arrived at Dianchi Lake, radius 300 li, fertile flat land.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuang Qi pacified Dian, made it subordinate to Chu; road blocked by Qin, became king of Dian.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin's Chang Yan opened Five Feet Road, set officials in these countries.
details.label: included

details.point: After Qin perished, Han abandoned these countries, used Shu boundaries as fortresses.
details.label: included

details.point: Bajun and Shujun people traded for Zuo horses, Bo servants, yaks; became wealthy.
details.label: included

details.point: In 6th year of Emperor Wu, Wang Hui attacked Dongyue; Dongyue killed king Ying.
details.label: included

details.point: Tang Meng learned from Nanyue that wolfberry sauce came via Zangke River.
details.label: included

details.point: Tang Meng proposed attacking Nanyue via Yelang with 100,000 elite soldiers.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu appointed Tang Meng, who entered Yelang, met Yelang Hou Duotong, set officials.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yelang changed to Qianwei County; road built from Bo to Zangke River.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Xiangru told emperor Qiong and Zuo could be counties; set up captain and counties.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Road building failed; barbarians rebelled; Gongsun Hong advised stopping development.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Qian saw Shu cloth and Qiong bamboo in Daxia; suggested road to Shendu via Shu.
details.label: included

details.point: Han envoys blocked by Kunming; Dian king asked 'Which is bigger, Han or Dian?'
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/后汉书/列传/杨李翟应霍爰徐列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/杨李翟应霍爰徐列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Yang Zhong was from Chengdu, Shu County, and studied 'Spring and Autumn' in the capital.
details.label: included

details.point: During a severe drought in the first year of Jianchu, Yang Zhong memorialized against harsh punishments and border settlements.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Zhong argued that the immigration law should be abolished, citing historical precedents.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Suzong accepted Yang Zhong's advice and stopped border settlements.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Zhong proposed a conference like the Shiqu Pavilion to discuss the classics.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Zhong participated in the White Tiger Temple conference after being pardoned.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Zhong was ordered to abridge 'Tai Shi Gong Shu' to over 100,000 words.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Zhong advised Ma Liao to be cautious and educate his son, but Ma Liao did not listen.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang Zhong's brother Yang Feng was involved in a case, and Yang Zhong lobbied for Lian Fan, resulting in exile.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang Zhong wrote twelve chapters of 'Spring and Autumn Annals' and died as a doctor in the twelfth year of Yongyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Fa was from Hanzhong, known for uprightness, and was dismissed for criticizing the government.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Fa refused to explain his criticisms, citing Mencius, and later served as governor of Runan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhai Youfu was from Guangluo, skilled in 'Laozi' and astronomy, and became a minister.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhai Youfu warned Emperor An against excessive favor to relatives and eunuchs.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhai Youfu defeated Qiang rebels as governor of Jiuquan and later served as Jing Zhaoyin.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhai Youfu was falsely accused and died at home; he wrote twelve chapters on 'Yuan Shen' and 'Gou Ming Jie Xie'.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhai Youfu proposed repairing the Imperial Academy, which was approved.
details.label: included

details.point: Ying Feng was from Runan, known for his memory, and served as prefect of Wuling, pacifying rebels.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ying Feng advised Emperor Huan against making Tian Guiren queen, and the emperor adopted his advice.
details.label: included

details.point: Ying Shao, son of Ying Feng, was a scholar and official who wrote extensively on laws and customs.
details.label: included

details.point: Gongsun Hong was born in Xue County, Sichuan State.
details.label: included

details.point: He worked as a jailer, was dismissed for a crime, and herded pigs on the beach.
details.label: included

details.point: In his forties, he began studying Spring and Autumn and miscellaneous treatises.
details.label: included

details.point: At age 60, he became a doctor as a virtuous and literary person under Emperor Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: He was sent as envoy to the Huns but displeased the emperor and was dismissed.
details.label: included

details.point: In the fifth year of Yuanguang, he was recommended again and came to Taichang.
details.label: included

details.point: He responded to an imperial policy exam and was ranked lower by Taichang, but the emperor selected his strategy as first.
details.label: included

details.point: He was appointed as a doctor and later promoted to Zuo Neishi within a year.
details.label: included

details.point: He was known for not arguing in court and often followed the emperor's intentions.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji An accused him of hypocrisy for reneging on agreements, but the emperor favored him.
details.label: included

details.point: He served his stepmother filially and mourned three years after her death.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He became imperial censor and later prime minister, replacing Xue Ze.
details.label: included

details.point: He was granted the title Marquis of Pingjin, starting the practice of enfeoffing prime ministers.
details.label: included

details.point: He built a guesthouse to host scholars, but was jealous and vengeful towards rivals.
details.label: included

details.point: He was involved in the deaths of Zhufu Yan and Dong Zhongshu's demotion.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Huainan and Hengshan rebellions, he fell ill and offered to resign, but the emperor refused.
details.label: included

details.point: He died in office as prime minister at age 80.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Gongsun Du succeeded the marquis but was later sentenced to hard labor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In the first year of Yuanyuan, the emperor praised Gongsun Hong's frugality and granted his descendants a title.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Bu Shi and Ni Kuan were also noted as virtuous ministers of the era.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Yuan was a native of Maoling, Fufeng, and his ancestor Zhao She was a general of Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: During Wang Mang's reign, Ma Yuan served as the Grand Yin of Xincheng.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Wang Mang's defeat, Ma Yuan stayed in Xizhou and was appointed General Suide by Wei Xiao.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Yuan was sent to observe Gongsun Shu in Shu and concluded he was a frog in a well.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Yuan went to Luoyang in 28 AD and was received by Emperor Guangwu, whom he compared favorably to Gaozu.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Yuan advised Wei Xiao to submit to Guangwu, but Wei Xiao later rebelled.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ma Yuan wrote letters to persuade Wei Xiao's generals to defect, but Yang Guang did not reply.
details.label: included

details.point: In 32 AD, Ma Yuan used rice to model terrain for Emperor Guangwu, leading to victory over Wei Xiao.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ma Yuan was appointed Governor of Longxi in 35 AD and defeated the Xianling Qiang.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Yuan advocated retaining Jincheng and helped resettle refugees and develop agriculture.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Yuan suppressed the rebellion of Li Guang in 40 AD.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In 40 AD, Ma Yuan was appointed Fubo General to conquer Jiaozhi, defeating the Trung sisters.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ma Yuan established Han administration in Jiaozhi, digging canals and revising laws.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ma Yuan cast a bronze horse model based on classical physiognomy and presented it to the emperor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ma Yuan famously said, 'A man should die in the wilderness, wrapped in horsehide.'
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ma Yuan was sent against the Wuxi barbarians in 48 AD at age 62, despite initial refusal.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Yuan died of illness during the campaign in 49 AD.
details.label: included

details.point: After his death, Ma Yuan was falsely accused of bringing back pearls and rhino horn; his marquisate was revoked.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Yuan's daughter became empress in 60 AD, but he was omitted from the Yuntai portraits due to her status.
details.label: included

details.point: Ma Yuan was posthumously rehabilitated and granted the title Marquis Zhongcheng in 78 AD.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/后汉书/列传/郑范陈贾张列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/郑范陈贾张列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Zheng Xing studied Gongyang Chunqiu and Zuo Shi Zhuan, and taught Liu Xin.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Xing advised Emperor Gengshi to move west to Chang'an, citing Spring and Autumn.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Xing dissuaded Wei Xiao from claiming kingship, citing Zhou and Han examples.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Xing stopped Wei Xiao from setting up excessive official positions.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Xing requested to return home to bury his parents, and Wei Xiao allowed him.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Xing was recommended by Du Lin and became Taizhong doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Xing submitted a memorial on solar eclipse, citing Spring and Autumn.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Xing declined to use prophecies for suburban sacrifice, angering Emperor Guangwu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zheng Xing was demoted for buying slaves privately while on mission.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Xing was an expert in Zuo Shi and Zhou Guan, and was considered the ancestor of Zuo Shi studies.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Sheng criticized Wang Mang's policies to Wang Yi, but was not heeded.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Sheng declined the title of doctor, recommending Liang Gong and Lu Qiang instead.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fan Sheng argued against establishing a doctor for Zuo Shi Zhuan, debating with Han Xin.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Sheng submitted a memorial opposing the establishment of Zuo Shi and Fei Shi.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Sheng was accused by his divorced wife and imprisoned, later died at home.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Yuan defended Zuo Shi Zhuan in a memorial, arguing for its establishment.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Yuan debated Fan Sheng ten times, and Zuo Shi was established with Chen Yuan as doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Yuan advised against using Sili Xiaowei to supervise the Three Dukes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Jia Kui wrote exegesis of Zuo Shi Zhuan and Guoyu, presented to Emperor Ming.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Jia Kui explained the divine bird as an omen of Hu surrender, and wrote an ode.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Xiong was from Chengdu, Shu County, with ancestors descending from Zhou Boqiao.
details.label: included

details.point: The Yang family took the surname from the food town of Yang in Jin.
details.label: included

details.point: During the decline of Zhou, some Yangs were marquises (Yanghou).
details.label: included

details.point: Yanghou fled to Chuwu Mountain during the Jin ministers' struggle.
details.label: included

details.point: During Chu-Han contention, the Yang family moved to Bajiang Prefecture.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Jiguan became prefect of Lujiang.
details.label: included

details.point: In Han Dingjian period, an ancestor moved to Pi, south of Laoshan, farming silkworms.
details.label: included

details.point: From Ji to Xiong, only one son per generation for five generations.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Xiong was eager to learn, not studying chapters but well-read.
details.label: included

details.point: He was easy-going, stuttered, silent, contemplative, not pursuing wealth or fame.
details.label: included

details.point: Family property under ten pieces of gold; he was content despite poverty.
details.label: included

details.point: He admired Sima Xiangru's fu and imitated him.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote 'Reverse Lisao' to refute Qu Yuan's suicide, mourning him.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote 'Ode to Sweet Springs' to satirize Emperor Cheng's extravagance at Ganquan Palace.
details.label: included

details.point: The ode described the grand procession and palace, comparing it to the Purple Palace.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote 'Hedong Fu' after the emperor's sacrifice at Fenyin, satirizing the tour.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote 'Xiao Xie Fu' to satirize the emperor's hunting, advocating frugality.
details.label: included

details.point: The hunting ode described the vast hunting grounds and military display.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He criticized the extravagance of Shanglin Park and advised returning to simple virtues.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Xiong's works aimed to remonstrate through praise and comparison to ancient ideals.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji An was born in Puyang County, his ancestors served as ministers for generations.
details.label: included

details.point: He became Prince Xima during Emperor Jing's reign due to his father's recommendation.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu appointed him as official of the audience after succeeding the throne.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji An was sent to inspect conflicts between Minyue and Ouyue but turned back at Wuxian, deeming it unworthy of imperial attention.
details.label: included

details.point: He inspected a fire in Hanoi County and reported it as accidental, not needing concern.
details.label: included

details.point: In Henan County, he saw flood and drought victims and ordered grain distribution without authorization, then requested punishment.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu exempted him and transferred him to Xingyang County Magistrate, but Ji An resigned claiming illness.
details.label: included

details.point: He was summoned as a senior official, then released as Prefect of Donghai County.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji An admired Taoism, governed by delegating to capable officials, and achieved peace in Donghai.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recalled as Lord Commander and treated like Jiuqing, but was arrogant and outspoken.
details.label: included

details.point: He criticized Emperor Wu for having many desires while pretending to practice benevolence.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji An opposed Zhang Tang's legal reforms and argued with him in court.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He advocated peace with the Xiongnu instead of military campaigns.
details.label: included

details.point: He slandered Gongsun Hong and Zhang Tang as treacherous and was hated by them.
details.label: included

details.point: Gongsun Hong recommended Ji An as Right Internal History to remove him from court.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji An treated General Wei Qing as an equal despite his rising status.
details.label: included

details.point: King of Huainan feared Ji An's integrity and said he could not be tempted.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji An complained to Emperor Wu about later officials being promoted over him, comparing it to stacking firewood.
details.label: included

details.point: He opposed harsh treatment of surrendered Xiongnu and merchants, leading to his dismissal.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji An was later appointed Prefect of Huaiyang County, governed well, and died seven years later.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Zhang had eight sons: Liu Qing, Liu Zhao, Liu Shou, Liu Kai, and four others.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Qing was born to Noble Consort Song and was initially crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dou framed Noble Consort Song, leading to her suicide and Liu Qing's deposition.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Zhao, son of Liang Guiren, became crown prince and later Emperor He.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Qing was made King of Qinghe and treated with favor by Emperor He.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Qing died at 29; his son Liu Hu succeeded.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Hu's son Liu Lian was considered for emperor but opposed by eunuchs.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Lian was implicated in a rebellion and demoted to marquis, then committed suicide.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Shou, King of Jibei, was granted title in Yongyuan 2nd year.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Shou's son Liu Deng succeeded; his grandson Liu Ci was praised for filial piety.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Kai, King of Hejian, was granted title in Yongyuan 2nd year.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Kai's son Liu Zheng was corrected by prime minister Shen Jing.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Zheng's son Liu Jian succeeded; later Liu Li, then Liu Ye.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yi, son of Liu Kai, was made Marquis of Duxiang, later King of Pingyuan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Yi's son Liu Zhi became Emperor Huan.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Huan honored Liu Kai as Emperor Xiaomu.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Shu, son of Liu Kai, was made Marquis of Jiedu Ting; his son Liu Hong became Emperor Ling.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Ling honored Liu Shu as Emperor Xiaoyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Wansui, King of Guangzong, died without heir; state abolished.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Sheng, King of Pingyuan, died without heir; state later abolished.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/张耳陈馀列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/张耳陈馀列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Zhang Er was a native of Daliang, Wei State, and was a guest of Wei Gongzi Wuji.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Er married a wealthy woman who left her husband on advice, enabling him to attract guests.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Yu was also from Daliang, loved Confucianism, and served Zhang Er like a father.
details.label: included

details.point: After Qin destroyed Wei, Zhang Er and Chen Yu fled to Chendi and worked as guards.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Yu was whipped but Zhang Er stopped him from resisting, advising patience.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen She revolted and Zhang Er and Chen Yu advised him not to become king too early.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen She ignored their advice and proclaimed himself king of Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen She sent Wu Chen with Zhang Er and Chen Yu as captains to seize Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Chen followed Kuai Tong's advice to reward Fan Yangling, leading to many surrenders.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Er and Chen Yu advised Wu Chen to become King of Zhao, which he did.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen She was angry but later congratulated Wu Chen, moving their families to the palace.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Er and Chen Yu advised Wu Chen not to attack west but to expand north and south.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wu Chen was captured by Yan, but a soldier tricked Yan into releasing him.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Liang killed Wu Chen's sister and rebelled, killing Wu Chen and Shao Sao.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Er and Chen Yu gathered troops and made Zhao Xie King of Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Er was besieged in Julu; Chen Yu refused to rescue due to insufficient troops.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Er and Chen Yu fell out after Zhang Er believed Chen Yu killed Zhang Yan and Chen Ze.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiang Yu defeated Qin at Julu, and Zhang Er later followed Xiang Yu into Guanzhong.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu made Zhang Er King of Changshan and Chen Yu a marquis, causing Chen Yu's resentment.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Yu defeated Zhang Er, who then joined Han; later Han killed Chen Yu and made Zhang Er King of Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wu Liu Bi was the son of Liu Zhong, brother of Emperor Gaozu.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bi was made King of Wu after suppressing Yingbu's rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu warned Liu Bi of a possible rebellion in the southeast.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu had copper mines and salt production, making it wealthy.
details.label: included

details.point: The Crown Prince of Wu was killed in a chess game by the Han crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bi feigned illness and refused to attend court after his son's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen pardoned Liu Bi and gave him a staff, relaxing tensions.
details.label: included

details.point: Chao Cuo advised reducing the fiefs of rebellious kings.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing reduced the lands of Chu, Zhao, and Jiaoxi.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bi feared further reductions and planned rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bi allied with Jiaoxi and other kingdoms to rebel.
details.label: included

details.point: The Seven Kingdoms (Wu, Chu, Zhao, Jiaoxi, Jiaodong, Jinan, Sichuan) rebelled.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bi conscripted all men aged 14 to 62, raising 200,000 troops.
details.label: included

details.point: The rebels cited killing Chao Cuo as their goal.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing killed Chao Cuo to appease the rebels.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Ang was sent to negotiate but was detained by Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Yafu used a strategy to cut off Wu's supply lines.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu's army was defeated due to starvation and desertion.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bi fled to Dongyue but was assassinated by Dongyue forces.
details.label: included

details.point: The rebellion was crushed by March; all rebel kings died or committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: King Li of Huainan was the youngest son of Emperor Gao of Han.
details.label: included

details.point: King Li's mother was a beauty presented to Emperor Gao by King Zhang Ao of Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: King Li's mother was imprisoned after the Zhao rebellion and gave birth to King Li in prison.
details.label: included

details.point: King Li's mother committed suicide after giving birth; Emperor Gao regretted and had Empress Lu raise King Li.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 11th year of Han, after suppressing Yingbu's rebellion, Emperor Gao made Liu Chang King of Huainan.
details.label: included

details.point: King Li resented Piyanghou for not saving his mother but dared not show it.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Wen's reign, King Li was arrogant and called the emperor 'big brother'.
details.label: included

details.point: King Li killed Piyanghou with an iron spine, citing three crimes including failing to save his mother.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen pardoned King Li for avenging his mother.
details.label: included

details.point: King Li became more arrogant, made his own laws, and used imperial-style guards.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen's uncle Bo Zhao admonished King Li in a letter, listing eight faults.
details.label: included

details.point: King Li ignored the admonition and plotted rebellion with 70 men, contacting Minyue and Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: The rebellion was discovered; King Li was summoned to Chang'an and charged with multiple crimes.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen spared King Li's life but deposed him and exiled him to Shu.
details.label: included

details.point: King Li starved to death on the way to exile; Emperor Wen mourned and executed the officials who failed to feed him.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen later enfeoffed King Li's four sons as marquises.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 16th year, Emperor Wen made three of King Li's sons kings in Huainan.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu An, King of Huainan, was a scholar who compiled the Huainanzi and was respected by Emperor Wu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu An plotted rebellion, fearing Emperor Wu had no heir; his plot was exposed and he committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: King Hengshan Liu Ci also plotted rebellion but committed suicide; both kingdoms were abolished as commanderies.
details.label: included

summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/后汉书/列传/皇甫嵩朱俊列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Huangfu Song was a Han general who suppressed the Yellow Turban Rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recommended as Xiaolian and Maocai, and served as Yilang and governor of Beidi.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Jiao founded the Way of Taiping, using talisman water to cure diseases and gaining followers.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Jiao organized followers into 36 fangs, each with a general, and spread the prophecy 'Cang Tian is dead, Huang Tian should be established'.
details.label: included

details.point: The rebellion was planned for March 5, but was betrayed by Tang Zhou, leading to Ma Yuanyi's execution.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Jiao and his brothers Zhang Bao and Zhang Liang led the Yellow Turbans, wearing yellow scarves.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangfu Song proposed lifting the party ban and was appointed Left Zhonglang General to suppress the rebellion.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Huangfu Song defeated Bo Cai at Changshe using a night fire attack, with help from Cao Cao and Zhu Jun.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun pacified Runan, Chen, and Dongjun, capturing Bu Ji alive.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangfu Song defeated Zhang Liang at Guangzong, killing him and drowning many rebels in the Yellow River.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Jiao died of illness; Huangfu Song beheaded his corpse and sent it to the capital.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangfu Song killed Zhang Bao at Xiaquyang, capturing over 100,000 rebels.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangfu Song was appointed General of Left Chariot and Cavalry, and Governor of Jizhou.
details.label: included

details.point: He petitioned to reduce land rent in Jizhou to help the hungry, and was praised by the people.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangfu Song refused Yan Zhong's advice to rebel against the Han, remaining loyal.
details.label: included

details.point: He was later recalled and demoted due to slander by eunuchs Zhao Zhong and Zhang Rang.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangfu Song and Dong Zhuo defended Chencang; Huangfu Song refused to attack prematurely, waiting for the enemy to weaken.
details.label: included

details.point: He defeated the kingdom's army after the siege failed, beheading over 10,000, earning Dong Zhuo's jealousy.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Zhuo later tried to kill Huangfu Song, but his son Huangfu Jianshou pleaded for his life.
details.label: included

details.point: Huangfu Song died of illness after serving as Taiwei and other posts; he was known for benevolence and not publicizing his good deeds.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Yuan Jing Yu, named Meng Mu, was from Jiyang Waihuang and died in the sixth year of Yongjia at age 35.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Yuan posthumously honored her as queen and built a temple at her mausoleum.
details.label: included

details.point: The Xun family of Yuzhang Jun, favored by Emperor Yuan, gave birth to Emperor Ming and King Langxie Sima Sui, but was hated by Empress Yu.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Mu Yu of the Ming Dynasty, named Wenjun, was from Yanling, Yingchuan, and became empress when Emperor Ming ascended the throne.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng revered Empress Mu Yu as empress dowager and she served as regent.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Cheng Gong Du, named Lingyang, was from Jingzhao and married Emperor Cheng in the second year of Xiankang.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Cheng Gong Du died at age 21 with no children; Emperor Cheng ordered a simple burial.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Taifei Zhou, favored by Emperor Cheng, gave birth to Emperor Ai and Duke Haixi, and was honored as imperial concubine.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Kang Xian Chu, named Suanzi, was from Yangzhai, Henan, and became empress when Emperor Kang ascended the throne.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Kang Xian served as regent for Emperor Mu and later for Emperor Ai and Duke Haixi.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Mu Zhang He, named Fa Ni, was from Lujiang and became empress in the first year of Shengping.
details.label: included

details.point: During Huan Xuan's usurpation, Empress Mu Zhang He was demoted and later returned to Kyoto.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Ai Jing, named Kuizhi, was the daughter of Wang Sui and became empress of Emperor Ai, reigning for three years with no sons.
details.label: included

details.point: The deposed Emperor Xiao Yu's empress was demoted to Mrs. Haixi after his deposition.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Jian Wen Xuan Zheng, named Achun, was from Xingyang, Henan, and married Emperor Yuan as a widow.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Jian Wen Xuan Zheng gave birth to King Langye Mou and Emperor Jianwen.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Jian Wen Shun, named Jian Ji, was from Jinyang, Taiyuan, and was deposed with her son Daosheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Li Xiao Wu Wen, named Lingrong, was a palace servant who gave birth to Emperor Xiaowu and King Wenxiao.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Xiao Wu Ding, named Fahui, was the niece of Empress Ai Jing and married Emperor Xiaowu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Dowager An De Chen, named Songzi, gave birth to Emperors An and Gong, and was posthumously honored as empress dowager.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Hong's ancestor was granted the title of Fan, becoming a prominent surname.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Hong's father Fan Zhong was good at farming and breeding.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Zhong lived together for three generations, respected by descendants.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fan Zhong's business thrived, opening over 300 hectares of land.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Zhong built high halls, pavilions, ponds, and canals.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Zhong planted Ziqi lacquer for utensils, later used by those who mocked him.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fan Zhong provided relief to support the clan and village.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Zhong settled his grandsons' property dispute with two hectares of land.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Zhong was recommended as the third elder by the county.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fan Zhong died at age eighty; Fan Hong burned debt deeds worth millions.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Hong declined Gengshi's offer to be a general, citing lack of military knowledge.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Hong built a camp to defend against rebels; over a thousand followed him.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Hong sent gifts to Red Eyebrows, who spared his camp due to his benevolence.
details.label: included

details.point: When Shizu ascended, Fan Hong became Dr. Guanglu, second only to the Three Dukes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fan Hong was granted the title of Changluohou in 29 AD.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Hong was modest and cautious, warning his son against excessive wealth.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Hong arrived early at court; the emperor ordered him not to come too early.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Hong destroyed drafts of his memorials and avoided confrontation.
details.label: included

details.point: On his deathbed, Fan Hong wished for his descendants to live in a small village.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fan Hong was buried lightly per his will; the emperor praised his virtue.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Tzu, named Wu, was from the state of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: King Helu of Wu tested Sun Tzu's military command on 180 palace women.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Tzu executed the king's two favorite concubines for disobeying orders.
details.label: included

details.point: King Helu appointed Sun Tzu as general after the drill.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Tzu contributed to Wu's victories over Chu, Qi, and Jin.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Bin was a descendant of Sun Wu and studied with Pang Juan.
details.label: included

details.point: Pang Juan, jealous of Sun Bin, had his feet cut off and face tattooed.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi envoys smuggled Sun Bin to Qi, where he became a strategist.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Bin advised Tian Ji to win a horse race by strategic matching.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Bin used the strategy of 'besieging Wei to rescue Zhao'.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Bin defeated Wei at Guiling, lifting the siege of Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Bin used the 'reduce stoves' ruse to deceive Pang Juan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Sun Bin ambushed and killed Pang Juan at Maling.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Bin captured Wei crown prince Shen.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wu Qi killed his wife to gain command of Lu's army against Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Qi served Wei, captured five cities from Qin.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wu Qi shared hardships with soldiers and sucked a soldier's sore.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Qi argued that state security depends on virtue, not terrain.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Qi fled Wei after being suspected and became prime minister of Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Qi was killed by nobles after King Mourning's death; his assassins were executed.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu You dissuaded his father from writing scriptures on bamboo slips, citing suspicion of transporting valuables.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu You herded pigs after his father's death despite poverty, refusing gifts.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu You was promoted to Xiaolian and befriended Huang Zhen at a farewell ceremony.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu You recognized Gongshamu's talent while he was pounding rice and befriended him.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu You befriended Dai Hong after hearing him chant in the garden.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu You governed with benevolence, settling disputes through moral persuasion.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu You pardoned Sun Xing who stole to buy clothes for his father.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu You allowed Guanqiu Chang to impregnate his wife before execution.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu You argued for Li Gu against Liang Ji, then resigned and retired.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Du learned Zuo Shi Zhuan in ten days and studied under Ma Rong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yan Du repaired Gong Sui's tomb and selected his descendants for office.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Du killed Liang Ji's guests who sought to sell bezoars in Jingzhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Du discussed benevolence and filial piety, arguing they share the same root.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Du declined Li Wende's recommendation, describing his daily scholarly routine.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shi Bi warned Emperor Huan about Bohai King Kui's misconduct.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Shi Bi refused to report party members in Pingyuan, saving over a thousand people.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Bi beat Hou Lan's messenger to death for seeking favors in elections.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Bi was framed by Hou Lan, sentenced to death, but saved by bribery.
details.label: included

details.point: Lu Zhi studied under Ma Rong without distraction, earning his respect.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lu Zhi advised Dou Wu to resign rewards and strengthen the imperial clan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Yi, courtesy name Zhongxiong, was from Ye, Donglai, a descendant of Liu Zhang, King of Yangjing.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yi was filial and upright, known for criticizing people and fearing no nobles.
details.label: included

details.point: As a meritorious official under Prefect Du Shu, he eliminated over a hundred corrupt officials.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recommended as Xiaolian and served as Sili Duguan, bringing order to the capital.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yi impeached Yin of Henan despite Sili's objection, showing his integrity.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recommended by Wang Ji for his uprightness and honesty.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yi declined official positions due to illness, fearing persecution for loyalty to Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu appointed him as minister and prince-in-law, valuing his loyalty.
details.label: included

details.point: As Sili Xiaowei, he suppressed powerful families, causing officials to resign in fear.
details.label: included

details.point: He compared Emperor Wu to Emperors Huan and Ling of Han, criticizing the sale of offices.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu laughed at his frankness, and Zou Zhan praised his directness.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yi opposed congratulating the emperor on a dragon appearing in a well, citing historical precedents.
details.label: included

details.point: He submitted a memorial criticizing the Nine-Rank Zhongzheng system, listing eight drawbacks.
details.label: included

details.point: The memorial argued that the system failed to select talents and caused corruption.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Yi was known for strictness, even punishing his wife for visiting him during fasting.
details.label: included

details.point: He retired at age 70 but was later recommended as Qingzhou Zhongzheng, though initially declined.
details.label: included

details.point: After his death, Emperor Wu mourned him as a famous official and granted posthumous honors.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Liu Tun inherited his integrity and served as Sili Xiaowei five times.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Tun was killed by Shi Le after being captured while delivering a letter to Cao Yi.
details.label: included

details.point: Other figures like He Qiao, Wu Yi, Ren Kai, Cui Hong, Guo Yi, Hou Shiguang, and He Pan were also noted for their integrity and service.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Shizhi bought a position as a knight and served Emperor Wen of Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Shizhi advised Emperor Wen against promoting a fluent tiger-keeper, citing Qin's downfall due to eloquence.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Shizhi stopped the prince and King of Liang from entering Sima Gate without dismounting, accusing them of disrespect.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Shizhi argued against Emperor Wen's plan for an impregnable tomb, saying greed would still lead to theft.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Shizhi, as Tingwei, fined a man who startled the emperor's horse, upholding the law despite the emperor's anger.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Shizhi sentenced a thief of Gaozu Temple artifacts to beheading, not execution of his clan, as per law.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Shizhi tied Wang Sheng's stockings at his request, which Wang Sheng did to enhance Zhang's reputation.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Shizhi was demoted to Prince of Huainan's chancellor and died of old age.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Feng Tang told Emperor Wen that Li Qi was inferior to Lian Po and Li Mu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Feng Tang said Emperor Wen could not use Lian Po or Li Mu due to overly strict laws and light rewards.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Tang cited Wei Shang's punishment for a minor discrepancy in enemy counts as evidence.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen pardoned Wei Shang and appointed Feng Tang as chariot and cavalry captain.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji An was sent to inspect Dongyue but returned without going, saying their conflicts were not worth imperial attention.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji An distributed grain to flood victims in Hanoi without authorization, and the emperor pardoned him.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji An governed Donghai by quiet non-action, achieving great order.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ji An criticized Emperor Wu for having many desires while pretending to practice benevolence.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ji An argued with Zhang Tang over legal reforms, accusing him of harming future generations.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ji An opposed the costly reception of surrendered Xiongnu and the execution of merchants who traded with them.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ji An was appointed prefect of Huaiyang and governed effectively until his death.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zheng Zhuang recommended scholars, treated guests humbly, and had no private property.
details.label: included

source_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/translated/史记/七十列传/刘敬叔孙通列传/target.txt
summary_file: Classical-Chinese-Summarization/data/processed/summary_clean/史记/七十列传/刘敬叔孙通列传/target.summary.txt

details.point: Liu Jing, a native of Qi, advised Emperor Gao to establish the capital in Guanzhong rather than Luoyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jing argued that the Han Dynasty's rise differed from the Zhou Dynasty's, which relied on accumulated virtue.
details.label: included

details.point: He emphasized Guanzhong's natural defenses and fertile land as a strategic advantage.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gao initially hesitated due to ministers' opposition but followed Liu Jing's advice after Zhang Liang's support.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jing was rewarded with the surname Liu, the title Fengchun Jun, and the position of doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: In 200 BCE, Liu Jing warned against attacking the Xiongnu, suspecting a trap, but was ignored and imprisoned.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gao was besieged at Pingcheng for seven days, then released Liu Jing and rewarded him.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jing proposed the heqin policy: marrying a Han princess to the Xiongnu chanyu to secure peace.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gao agreed but sent a palace maid instead of his daughter due to Empress Lü's opposition.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jing was sent to conclude the peace treaty with the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: He recommended relocating powerful clans (e.g., Tian of Qi, Zhao, Qu, Jing of Chu) to Guanzhong to strengthen central control.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gao approved and moved over 100,000 people to Guanzhong.
details.label: included

details.point: Shusun Tong, a Confucian scholar, served under Qin II and flattered him by calling rebels mere thieves.
details.label: included

details.point: He fled to Xue County and later served Xiang Yu, then surrendered to Liu Bang in 205 BCE.
details.label: included

details.point: Shusun Tong changed from Confucian robes to short Chu-style coats to please Liu Bang.
details.label: included

details.point: He formulated court rituals to address disorderly behavior among ministers after the Han unification.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gao approved simplified rituals, and Shusun Tong trained officials for the New Year ceremony in 200 BCE.
details.label: included

details.point: After the ceremony, Emperor Gao remarked, 'Only today do I know the dignity of being an emperor.'
details.label: included

details.point: Shusun Tong was appointed Taichang and rewarded with 500 jin of gold; he secured official posts for his disciples.
details.label: included

details.point: He later served as crown prince's tutor and successfully dissuaded Emperor Gao from replacing the prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongfang Shuo was born in Yanci County, Pingyuan County.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu of Han sought scholars with talents such as integrity, virtuousness, and literature.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongfang Shuo wrote a self-recommending letter to Emperor Wu, boasting of his abilities and knowledge.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu ordered Dongfang Shuo to stay in the Gongche Mansion but gave him a meager salary.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongfang Shuo tricked the dwarfs into thinking the emperor wanted to kill them, leading to a confrontation with Emperor Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu laughed at Dongfang Shuo's explanation and promoted him to wait for Shao Jin Mamen.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongfang Shuo correctly guessed the gecko under a basin using the Yi Jing, earning silk rewards.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongfang Shuo correctly guessed the parasitic thing under a pot, leading to Guo Sheren being whipped.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongfang Shuo answered Guo Sheren's riddle with clever wordplay, impressing everyone.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Wu appointed Dongfang Shuo as Chang Shilang, gaining his favor.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongfang Shuo cut meat without waiting for the order, then humorously blamed himself, earning more rewards.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu began traveling incognito for hunting, causing conflicts with farmers and local officials.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu planned to build Shanglin Garden, compensating farmers with wasteland.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongfang Shuo admonished against building Shanglin Garden, citing three reasons: loss of fertile land, destruction of homes, and waste of resources.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu still built Shanglin Garden but promoted Dongfang Shuo to Taizhong doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongfang Shuo congratulated Emperor Wu for executing Zhaopingjun despite family ties, citing impartial justice.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongfang Shuo was demoted for urinating in the palace but later reinstated as Zhonglang.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Yan, favored by Princess Guantao, was introduced to Emperor Wu and became prominent.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongfang Shuo accused Dong Yan of three crimes deserving death, leading to restrictions on Dong Yan's access.
details.label: included

details.point: Dongfang Shuo advised Emperor Wu to curb luxury by citing Emperor Wen's frugality, but Emperor Wu did not fully comply.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hu was born in Nancheng, Mount Tai, into a family of officials for nine generations.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hu was the grandson of Cai Yong and younger brother of Queen Jingxian.
details.label: not_included

details.point: At age 12, Yang Hu's father died; he showed filial piety beyond etiquette.
details.label: included

details.point: An old man prophesied Yang Hu would achieve great things before age 60.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang Hu was erudite, handsome, and good at talking; Xiahou Wei married his niece to him.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hu refused multiple official appointments, showing prescience by avoiding Cao Shuang's faction.
details.label: included

details.point: After Cao Shuang's failure, Yang Hu's foresight was acknowledged.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hu maintained relations with his wife despite her father Xiahou Ba's defection to Shu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang Hu served as Zhongshu Minister, Shizhong, and Huangmenlang under Emperor Wen.
details.label: included

details.point: He was granted the title of Marquis of Guanzhong and later Jupingzi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang Hu was appointed Zuopushe and General Wei, but remained humble before peers.
details.label: included

details.point: As commander in Jingzhou, Yang Hu reduced border troops, opened schools, and accumulated grain.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hu's lenient policies won over Wu people; he returned captives and compensated for crops.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hu and Wu general Lu Kang maintained mutual respect, exchanging gifts and medicine.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hu advocated for conquering Wu, recommending Wang Jun to build a navy.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hu's memorials urged immediate attack on Wu, citing Sun Hao's tyranny.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hu burned drafts of his memorials to avoid seeking credit.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang Hu died at 58; his death caused widespread mourning in both Jin and Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Yu, born in Duling, was knowledgeable and married Princess Gaolu.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Yu annotated laws, emphasizing simplicity and clarity.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu was the second brother of Emperor Xuan of Jin.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu and his six brothers were known as the 'Eight Da' (eight talents).
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu was gentle, honest, upright, modest, and widely read.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu advised Cao Zhi, who initially disagreed but later admitted his mistakes.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Wu of Wei died, Sima Fu advised the crown prince to stop excessive crying and assume control.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu dismissed the weeping ministers and organized the funeral and succession of Emperor Wen.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu recommended talents instead of allowing the prince's old attendants to appoint themselves.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Sima Fu advised the emperor to treat Sun Quan leniently regarding hostages and Yu Jin's return.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu proposed selecting 20,000 infantry and cavalry as reserves to counter Zhuge Liang's invasions.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu sent 5,000 farmers to Shangying to practice battle formations and manage agriculture, ensuring food surplus.
details.label: included

details.point: During Cao Shuang's rule, Sima Fu kept a low profile to avoid harm.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu helped Emperor Xuan execute Cao Shuang and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Changshe County.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu commanded 200,000 troops to defend against Wu general Zhuge Ke, using delay tactics to make Wu flee.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu argued that the emperor's coffin flags should not bear the state name or surname, based on classical principles.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Gao Gui was killed, Sima Fu wept over his body and requested a royal burial, which was granted.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu was cautious and humble, not participating in the planning of deposing or establishing emperors.
details.label: included

details.point: When Emperor Wu accepted abdication, Sima Fu bid farewell to the Chenliu king, weeping and vowing loyalty to Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu was made King of Anping with 40,000 households and given special honors by Emperor Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu remained humble despite honors, and his will requested a simple burial in everyday clothes.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Fu died at age 93 in the 8th year of Taishi, and the emperor mourned deeply.
details.label: included

details.point: Geng Yan was from Maoling County, Fufeng County, and his ancestors migrated from Julu.
details.label: included

details.point: His father Geng Kuang was a doctor proficient in Confucian classics and studied with Wang Mang.
details.label: included

details.point: Geng Yan became interested in generalship after observing county captains' military exercises.
details.label: included

details.point: At age 21, Geng Yan left his father to seek advancement and brought tributes to consolidate himself.
details.label: included

details.point: He refused to join Wang Lang's rebellion, calling him a deceitful thief.
details.label: included

details.point: Geng Yan persuaded his father Geng Kuang and Kou Xun to mobilize troops from Yuyang and Shanggu.
details.label: included

details.point: He led forces from the two commanderies south, killing over 400 of Wang Lang's officers and capturing many seals.
details.label: included

details.point: Geng Yan's forces defeated Wang Lang's troops across 22 counties before joining Guangwu.
details.label: included

details.point: Guangwu was delighted and promoted Geng Yan and his father, granting them titles.
details.label: included

details.point: Geng Yan advised Guangwu to ignore Gengshi's order to stop fighting and instead recruit more troops.
details.label: included

details.point: He killed Gengshi-appointed officials Wei Shun and Cai Chong in Shanggu.
details.label: included

details.point: Geng Yan served as vanguard in battles against Chimei and other rebel groups.
details.label: included

details.point: After Guangwu became emperor, Geng Yan was made General Jianwei and later Marquis of Haoju.
details.label: included

details.point: He defeated Yan Cen and Du Hong in Nanyang, capturing thousands.
details.label: included

details.point: Geng Yan attacked Zhang Bu, using a feint to lure Fei Yi and defeating him.
details.label: included

details.point: He captured Linzi by surprise, causing Zhang Lan to flee, then defeated Zhang Bu's main army.
details.label: included

details.point: Despite being wounded by an arrow, Geng Yan continued fighting and defeated Zhang Bu again.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Bu eventually surrendered, and Geng Yan pacified the entire Qi region.
details.label: included

details.point: Geng Yan conquered 46 counties and 300 cities in his lifetime without defeat.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at age 56, posthumously titled Minhou, and his descendants held various positions.
details.label: included

details.point: The Western Regions began communication with the Central Plains under Emperor Wu of Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Originally 36 countries, later divided into more than 50 kingdoms west of Xiongnu and south of Wusun.
details.label: included

details.point: The region is bounded by Yumen Pass and Yang Pass in the east, Congling in the west.
details.label: included

details.point: The Tarim River originates from Congling and Khotan, flows into Puchang Sea (Yanze).
details.label: included

details.point: Two main routes: South Road via Shanshan to Yarkand and beyond; North Road via Cheshi to Shule and beyond.
details.label: included

details.point: Most Western Regions states were settled, with cities and agriculture, unlike Xiongnu and Wusun.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiongnu controlled the Western Regions through a boy servant captain stationed in Yanqi.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Dynasty established Jiuquan, Wuwei, Zhangye, and Dunhuang commanderies after defeating Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Guangli's campaign against Dayuan in 104-101 BC intimidated Western Regions states.
details.label: included

details.point: Han built pavilions and barriers from Dunhuang to Yanze, stationed field soldiers in Luntai and Quli.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Ji became the first Protector General (Duhu) in 60 BC after King Rizhu's surrender.
details.label: included

details.point: The Protector General was stationed in Wulei City, monitoring Wusun, Kangju, and other states.
details.label: included

details.point: Shanshan (formerly Loulan) was a key state; King Loulan was assassinated by Fu Jiezi in 77 BC.
details.label: included

details.point: Shanshan requested Han military garrison at Yixun for protection.
details.label: included

details.point: Jibin (Kashmir) was a large state not under the Protectorate; its king killed Han envoys.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Qin advised against engaging with Jibin due to distance and danger.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Anxi (Parthia) was a large empire; Han envoys were greeted by 20,000 cavalry.
details.label: included

details.point: Dayuezhi migrated west after defeat by Xiongnu, conquered Daxia, and established five xihou.
details.label: included

details.point: Kangju was a powerful state; its king was arrogant and refused to bow to Han envoys.
details.label: included

details.point: Dayuan (Ferghana) was famous for horses; Han campaigns secured tribute of two horses per year.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen, courtesy name Chudao, was born in Jinyang, Taiyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen was adopted by his cousin Sikong Wang Chang after losing his father, and was known for filial piety.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen served under Cao Shuang and was dismissed after Cao Shuang's execution.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen co-wrote the 'Book of Wei' with Xunjie and Ruan Ji, but was criticized for not recording truthfully.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen and Wang Ye reported Duke Gaogui of Wei's plot to Emperor Wen, earning the title Marquis of Anping.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen was criticized for disloyalty to his master.
details.label: included

details.point: As governor of Yuzhou, Wang Chen issued teachings encouraging criticism and rewards for advice.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen implemented good governance and promoted education in Yuzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen was promoted to General Zhenglu and Commander-in-Chief of military affairs north of the Yangtze River.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen guarded the border during the Wu invasion and the enemy retreated.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Wu ascended, Wang Chen became Imperial Censor and was involved in founding discussions.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen was granted the title Duke of Boling County but refused, later promoted to County Duke with 1,800 households.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen died in the second year of Taishi; the emperor mourned and gave generous posthumous gifts.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen was known for honesty and frugality, leaving no property.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jun, Wang Chen's son, was initially despised but later became heir.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jun served as governor of Youzhou and allied with Xianbei and Wuhuan for safety.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jun killed He Yan and occupied Youzhou, then led forces against Sima Ying.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jun's troops looted Yecheng; Xianbei women were thrown into Yishui River.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jun became arrogant, killed advisors, and planned to become emperor based on prophecies.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Le pretended to surrender, captured Wang Jun, and executed him.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Zhou was born in Du Yan County, Nanyang County.
details.label: included

details.point: Yi Zong recommended Du Zhou to Zhang Tang as an official historian.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Zhou investigated losses in border counties, convicting and executing many.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Zhou served as Zhongcheng for over ten years, trusted by the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Zhou was taciturn and slow-tempered but kind-hearted.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Zhou governed following Zhang Tang's example and observed the emperor's intentions.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Zhou adjusted judgments based on the emperor's wishes, framing or releasing accordingly.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Zhou argued that laws and decrees are based on the monarch's will, not fixed.
details.label: included

details.point: As Tingwei, Du Zhou handled many cases, imprisoning thousands.
details.label: included

details.point: Cases involved torture and confessions, leading to many deaths and escapes.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Zhou was deposed but later served as Jinwu, harshly interrogating rebels.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Zhou was promoted to imperial censor for his diligence.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Zhou's family wealth accumulated to hundreds of millions.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Yannian, Du Zhou's son, was kind-hearted and well-versed in law.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Yannian reported the rebellion of Shangguan Jie and others, becoming Marquis of Jianping.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Yannian argued for leniency in the case of Hou Shiwu, balancing the court.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Yannian advised Huo Guang to promote frugality and abolish monopolies.
details.label: partially_included

details.point: Du Yannian persuaded Huo Guang to establish Emperor Xuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Yannian was dismissed due to association with Huo Guang but later became governor.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Yannian served as censor, lived in his father's residence, and died of illness.
details.label: included

details.point: Su Jing, courtesy name Bo Kuang, was born in Pingling, Fufeng County.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Ping's reign, Su Jing lectured on the Book of Changes and served as a doctor of wine.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was skilled in drawing and understood texts from various schools of thought.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Wang Mang, he worked with Liu Xin to compile books and was appointed Lieutenant of Daijun.
details.label: included

details.point: Su Jing kept Daijun safe during Xiongnu troubles on the northern frontier.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Guangwu appointed him Governor of Daijun and he requested to strengthen the frontier against the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: In winter of Jianwu 5th year, Lu Fang plundered northern counties; Su Jing was ill and handed over troops to his brother, then went to the capital to apologize.
details.label: included

details.point: He was appointed as a servant but dismissed due to illness after a few months.
details.label: included

details.point: Su Jing wrote to Liu Gong, Liu Xin's nephew, advising him to surrender from bandit Deng Zhongkuang.
details.label: included

details.point: He cited historical examples like Zhiguo and Chen Ping to persuade Liu Gong to avoid rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Su Jing argued that Guangwu's restoration was legitimate and Wang Mang's usurpation failed.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He interpreted astronomical signs as portents of punishment for rebels like Dong Xian and Peng Chong.
details.label: included

details.point: He described a white rainbow and meteor as omens of rebellion and urged Liu Gong to surrender.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Su Jing also wrote to Deng Zhongkuang, leading to their surrender.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Gong was from Chang'an, skilled in argumentation, and respected by Ma Yuan and Ban Biao.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Su Jing did not take credit, devoted himself to Taoism, and wrote 'Records of Teachings'.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at home at age seventy.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hou, courtesy name Zhonghuan, was from Xindu, Guanghan County.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Hou learned prophecy and astronomy from his father Yang Tong and others.
details.label: included

details.point: He predicted disasters and advised the court, but was dismissed when his response displeased Empress Dowager Deng.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Xuan was from Niyang in the north, courtesy name Xiu Yi.
details.label: included

details.point: His grandfather Fu Xie was prefect of Hanyang in Han; his father Fu Qian was governor of Fufeng in Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Xuan was erudite, good at writing, and knew music; he had a strong and upright character.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recommended as Xiaolian twice and recruited by Taiwei but did not take up the post.
details.label: included

details.point: He passed the scholar examination, became a doctor, and compiled Wei books with Mushi.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as prefect of Hongnong and captain of Diannong School, and was granted Baron Quail.
details.label: included

details.point: Under Emperor Wu of Jin, he became Prince Consort and Commander-in-Chief, and jointly served as admonishment officer with Huangfu Tao.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Xuan submitted a memorial criticizing the decline of benevolence and the ills of Qin, urging promotion of moral integrity.
details.label: included

details.point: He proposed a system to divide people into scholars, farmers, workers, and merchants with fixed quotas.
details.label: included

details.point: He advocated that idle officials should farm to ensure food sufficiency.
details.label: included

details.point: He recommended long tenure for officials to establish good governance.
details.label: included

details.point: He emphasized respecting Confucianism and selecting Confucian scholars.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was promoted to Attendant and later Yushi Zhongcheng in the fourth year of Taishi.
details.label: included

details.point: He submitted five proposals on agriculture, water conservancy, and border security.
details.label: included

details.point: He was dismissed from office after a dispute over seating at a mourning ceremony.
details.label: included

details.point: He wrote the book 'Fu Zi' with over 100 volumes, praised by Wang Shen.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Fu Xian inherited his title and was known for uprightness.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Xian criticized excessive official positions and advocated for agriculture.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Xian impeached powerful officials and was feared by nobles.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Xian died at age 56, posthumously titled Zhen.
details.label: included
