details.point: Dou Ying was the son of the cousin of Empress Dou, Emperor Wen's empress.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Wen's reign, Dou Ying served as Prime Minister of Wu State but was dismissed due to illness.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing promised to pass the throne to his brother Liang Xiao Wang, but Dou Ying opposed, angering Empress Dowager Dou.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Ying resigned as Zhan Shi due to the smallness of the post and was expelled from the palace by Empress Dowager Dou.
details.label: not_included

details.point: During the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms (154 BC), Emperor Jing appointed Dou Ying as General; Dou Ying recommended Yuan Ang and Luan Bu.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Ying displayed the gold reward in the corridor for subordinates to take, keeping none for himself.
details.label: included

details.point: After suppressing the rebellion, Dou Ying was made Marquis of Weiqi.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Ying served as tutor to Prince Li, but when the prince was deposed, Dou Ying argued in vain and feigned illness.
details.label: included

details.point: Gao Sui persuaded Dou Ying to return to court, warning that his retirement would publicize the emperor's fault.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Jing refused to appoint Dou Ying as Prime Minister, citing his pride and carelessness.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Fen, half-brother of Emperor Jing, rose to prominence and became Marquis of Wu'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Fen recommended Dou Ying as Prime Minister and himself as Taiwei, following Ji Fu's advice.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Dou Ying and Tian Fen promoted Confucianism, which conflicted with Empress Dowager Dou's preference for Huang-Lao.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Dou dismissed Dou Ying and Tian Fen after Zhao Wan suggested the emperor not report to her.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Empress Dowager Dou's death, Tian Fen became Prime Minister and grew arrogant, controlling appointments.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Fu, originally named Guan Meng, became famous for charging into Wu forces during the rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Fu served as Prime Minister of Yan but was dismissed for legal violations; he lived in Chang'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Fu and Dou Ying became close allies after both lost power.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Fen insulted Dou Ying and Guan Fu at a banquet, leading to Guan Fu's arrest and execution.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Ying was executed for allegedly forging an imperial edict; Tian Fen died later, haunted by ghosts of Dou Ying and Guan Fu.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiqiang originated from Sanmiao, a branch of the Jiang surname.
details.label: included

details.point: The Western Qiang Kingdom is near Nanyue.
details.label: included

details.point: Shun exiled four stubborn people to Sanwei, the Qiang area southwest of Heguan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xiqiang people had no fixed residences and migrated with water and grass.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiqiang customs included clans using father's name and mother's surname, intermarriage after twelve generations, and levirate marriage.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiqiang had no king or ministers; strong leaders became chiefs, weak ones became subordinates.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiqiang soldiers were skilled in valley fighting but not on plains; death in battle was auspicious.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiqiang people endured cold and hardship; women gave birth without shelter.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Xia Dynasty, Taikang lost the world and barbarians rebelled; later prime minister conquered Yiyi.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Yin Dynasty, Wuding conquered Xirong and Guifang.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wen of Zhou repulsed Rong and Di, and all Rong and Di surrendered.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Wu of Zhou attacked Shang with Qiang and Zhang troops at Muye.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Mu of Zhou marched westward against Quanrong, captured five kings, and moved Rong to Taiyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: During King Yi's reign, Zhou was weak; Duke Guo attacked Rong in Taiyuan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Li was cruel; Rong and Di invaded and killed Qin Zhong's family.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Xuan sent Qin Zhong to attack Rong, but Qin Zhong was killed.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King You was fatuous; Rong invaded, killed King You at Mount Li, and Zhou moved east to Luoyi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: During the Spring and Autumn period, Rong entered the Central Plains; Duke Mu of Qin dominated Xirong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: During the Warring States period, Yiqu and Dali were powerful; Qin eventually destroyed Yiqu.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuanren, a Qiang ancestor, escaped slavery, taught farming and livestock, and became chieftain.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhai Fangjin, courtesy name Ziwei, was from Shangcai, Runan.
details.label: included

details.point: His father Zhai Gong was a county scholar; Fangjin became an orphan at 12-13 and worked as a minor historian.
details.label: included

details.point: Cai's father told him he had the bone image of a feudal lord and should study Confucian classics.
details.label: included

details.point: He went to Chang'an with his stepmother, who knitted shoes to support his studies; he studied 'Spring and Autumn' under a doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: He became proficient in classics, attracted many disciples, and passed the imperial examination as a top candidate.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to Mingjing and became a Gentleman (Yilang).
details.label: not_included

details.point: Hu Chang was jealous of Fangjin's talent, but Fangjin humbly sought his teachings, and they became friends.
details.label: not_included

details.point: During the Heping period, Fangjin became a doctor; later served as Governor of Shuofang and then Prime Minister Sizhi.
details.label: included

details.point: He impeached Sili Xiaowei Chen Qing for disrespect and had him dismissed.
details.label: included

details.point: He impeached Sili Xiaowei Juanxun for arrogance and disrespect, leading to his demotion.
details.label: included

details.point: As Jing Zhaoyin, he attacked the powerful and was feared in the capital.
details.label: included

details.point: He became Prime Minister and Marquis of Gaoling, known for impartiality and strict law enforcement.
details.label: included

details.point: He impeached and dismissed Chen Xian and Feng Xin for corruption and association with Chen Tang.
details.label: included

details.point: He later impeached Chen Xian again when he was recommended as a Fangzheng candidate.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He impeached Hongyang Hou Li and his associates (Zhu Bo, Sun Hong, Chen Xian) for treachery.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fangjin studied 'Guliang Zhuan' but loved 'Zuo Shi Zhuan' and astronomy; he taught Liu Xin and Tian Zhongshu.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as prime minister for nine years; in the second year of Suihe, Mars entered the heart constellation, and he was blamed for disasters.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Cheng sent a reproachful edict; Fangjin committed suicide that day.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Zhai Yi later rebelled against Wang Mang, proclaiming Liu Xin emperor, but was defeated and killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Mang destroyed Zhai Yi's family, dug up Fangjin's grave, and killed all relatives of the three clans.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Feizi criticized Confucian scholars and chivalrous men for disturbing the rule of law.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji Ci and Yuan Xian were poor but virtuous scholars, remembered by disciples for centuries.
details.label: included

details.point: Rangers keep their word, sacrifice for others, and do not boast of their merits.
details.label: included

details.point: Tai Shigong listed ancient sages who suffered disasters, showing that even virtuous people face hardships.
details.label: included

details.point: Secular saying: 'Those who benefit are virtuous'; Boyi starved for honor, while tyrants were praised.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Those who steal small things are executed, but those who steal states become marquises with benevolence.
details.label: included

details.point: Commoner knights value morality and fulfill promises, even at the cost of their lives.
details.label: included

details.point: Ancient civilian knights are not recorded; modern ones like Yanling Jizi and the Four Lords were nobles.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Commoner knights like Zhu Jia, Tian Zhong, Ju Meng, and Guo Xie are commendable despite violating laws.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Jia saved hundreds of heroes and ordinary people, lived frugally, and refused to see Ji Bu after saving him.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Zhong served Zhu Jia like a father and was known for chivalry.
details.label: included

details.point: Ju Meng of Luoyang was sought by Zhou Yafu during the Rebellion of the Seven States.
details.label: included

details.point: Ju Meng's mother's funeral had thousands of mourners; he died poor.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Xie changed his behavior after youth, repaying hatred with kindness and saving lives.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Xie's sister's son was killed; Guo Xie blamed his nephew and let the murderer go.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Guo Xie secretly exempted a rude man from military service, earning his apology.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Guo Xie mediated a feud in Luoyang but deferred to local mediators.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Xie was moved to Maoling despite poverty; Emperor Wu noted his influence.
details.label: included

details.point: Guo Xie was executed for treason after a Confucian scholar was killed by his followers.
details.label: included

details.point: Later knights like Fan Zhongzi were respectful, while others like the Yao family were thieves.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Guan, courtesy name Boyu, was born in Anyi, Hedong Province.
details.label: included

details.point: His father Wei Jian was Minister of Wei; Wei Guan inherited the title of Marquis of Yuexiang.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Guan served as an official under Wei, known for competence and fairness.
details.label: included

details.point: He was sent to supervise Deng Ai and Zhong Hui during the conquest of Shu.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Guan arrested Deng Ai under imperial edict, then pretended to support Deng Ai's cause to pacify his generals.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhong Hui rebelled; Wei Guan feigned illness, then organized troops to defeat and kill Zhong Hui.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Guan ordered Tian Xu to kill Deng Ai and his son, avenging a personal grudge.
details.label: included

details.point: He refused credit for conquering Shu, attributing it to generals.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Guan held high offices under Jin, including General of Zhenxi and Sikong.
details.label: included

details.point: He proposed abolishing the nine-rank system and restoring rural recommendation, but was not implemented.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Guan hinted to Emperor Wu that Crown Prince Hui was unfit to rule, angering Empress Jia.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was forced to retire due to slander, but later restored under Emperor Hui.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Guan and Sima Liang were killed by Sima Zhang under false edict from Empress Jia.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Guan's son Wei Heng was a calligrapher who wrote 'Four Body Scripts'.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Heng was killed alongside his father; his sons Wei Zao and Wei Jie survived.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Jie was a famous handsome and witty scholar, died young at 27.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Hua, courtesy name Maoxian, was a learned official from Fanyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Hua supported the conquest of Wu and was rewarded with a marquisate.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Sikong and opposed the deposition of the crown prince.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Hua was executed by Sima Lun; his extensive library and knowledge were renowned.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius advocated using morality and rituals to govern, not punishments.
details.label: included

details.point: Laozi distinguished superior virtue (natural) from inferior virtue (subjective).
details.label: included

details.point: The text argues that strict laws increase crime, not reduce it.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Dynasty's broad legal framework led to peace and order.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhidu was a harsh official under Emperor Jing, known for integrity and fearlessness.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhidu killed the chief culprit of the Kun clan in Jinan, restoring order.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhidu refused to bow to Prime Minister Tiaohou, showing his defiance.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhidu was called 'Goshawk' for his harshness toward nobles.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhidu prevented King Linjiang from writing to the emperor, leading to his suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Dowager Dou caused Zhidu's execution despite Emperor Jing's reluctance.
details.label: included

details.point: Ningcheng was a cruel official who succeeded Zhidu but was less honest.
details.label: included

details.point: Ningcheng was sentenced to tweezers, escaped, became a wealthy chivalrous man.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Yangyou was a harsh official who killed based on personal likes/dislikes.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yu was honest but harsh, and was not trusted by Zhou Yafu.
details.label: included

details.point: Yi Zong was a cruel official who killed over 400 people in Dingxiang.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Wenshu was a cruel official who killed over a thousand in Hanoi.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Wenshu committed suicide after being accused of crimes.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Yannian was a harsh official who killed many, called 'Butcher'.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Yannian's mother warned him against excessive killing, predicting his downfall.
details.label: included

details.point: Yin Shang used 'tiger caves' to kill hundreds of criminals in Chang'an.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan An is from Linmiao.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan An wrote a letter criticizing luxury and advocating frugality.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan An argued that luxury leads to dissatisfaction, crime, and social decay.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan An proposed laws to curb extravagance and promote harmony.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan An discussed the decline of Zhou and the rise of the Five Hegemons.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan An described the Warring States period and the unification by Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan An criticized Qin's harsh laws and expansionist policies.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yan An noted that Qin's fall was due to military violence and inability to adapt.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yan An warned against Han's expansionist plans, citing risks.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan An was appointed as the riding order.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhongjun (Zhong Jun) was from Jinan, known for eloquence.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhongjun wrote a letter to Emperor Wu about auspicious signs.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhongjun interpreted the white unicorn and strange tree as omens.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhongjun recommended changing the reign name to Yuanshou.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhongjun interrogated Xu Yan for acting under false orders.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhongjun volunteered to envoy to South Vietnam and was killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Bao was from Shu, summoned by Emperor Xuan for poetry.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Bao wrote odes praising wise rulers and ministers.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Ganzhi advised against attacking Zhuli County.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Ganzhi was executed for deceit and leaking palace words.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius said the Six Classics govern the country: Li regulates, Music promotes harmony, Book records deeds, Poetry expresses emotions, Yi spies on changes, Spring and Autumn weighs right and wrong.
details.label: included

details.point: Chunyu Kun was a short, funny, eloquent son-in-law of Qi who never failed on missions.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wei of Qi indulged in drinking and neglected state affairs, endangering the country.
details.label: included

details.point: Chunyu Kun used an argot about a big bird that didn't fly or scream for three years to admonish King Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wei responded that the bird would soar and amaze if it flew or screamed, then he rewarded one official, killed another, and repelled invaders, restoring Qi's prestige for 36 years.
details.label: included

details.point: When Chu invaded, Chunyu Kun was sent to Zhao with insufficient gifts; he laughed at a farmer praying for much with little.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wei increased gifts to a thousand gold, ten pairs of white jade, and a hundred chariots; Zhao sent 100,000 troops and 1,000 chariots, causing Chu to withdraw.
details.label: included

details.point: Chunyu Kun explained to King Wei that he could drink from one dou to one shi depending on the occasion, warning against extremes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Wei stopped nightly drinking and appointed Chunyu Kun as guest official.
details.label: included

details.point: You Meng was a tall, eloquent Chu performer who used jokes to advise King Zhuang.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhuang wanted to bury his favorite horse with a doctor's funeral; You Meng sarcastically suggested a king's funeral, then advised burying it like an animal, which King Zhuang accepted.
details.label: included

details.point: Sun Shuao, Chu prime minister, treated You Meng well; on his deathbed, he told his son to seek You Meng if poor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Sun Shuao's son became poor; You Meng imitated Sun Shuao and told King Zhuang that being an upright official like Sun Shuao left his son destitute.
details.label: included

details.point: King Zhuang granted Sun Shuao's son the city of Qiuqiu with 400 households for ancestral sacrifices, continuing for ten generations.
details.label: included

details.point: You Zhan was a short Qin performer who used jokes to advise Qin Shihuang and Qin II.
details.label: included

details.point: You Zhan got guards' duty halved by joking about their wet condition during rain.
details.label: included

details.point: You Zhan dissuaded Qin Shihuang from expanding the hunting ground by saying elk could repel invaders.
details.label: not_included

details.point: You Zhan dissuaded Qin II from painting city walls by joking about the difficulty of drying them.
details.label: included

details.point: Tai Shigong praised Chunyu Kun, You Meng, and You Zhan for their wise advice.
details.label: included

details.point: Chu Shaosun added six more funny stories, including those of Guo Sheren, Dongfang Shuo, Mr. Dongguo, and Ximen Bao.
details.label: included

details.point: Meng Tian's ancestor was from Qi State.
details.label: included

details.point: Meng Tian's grandfather, Meng Ao, came to Qin from Qi and became a high official under King Zhao of Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Meng Ao served as a general, attacking Han, Zhao, and Wei, capturing cities and establishing commanderies.
details.label: included

details.point: Meng Ao died in the seventh year of Qin Shihuang's reign.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Meng Tian's father, Meng Wu, served as a general and attacked Chu with Wang Jian, killing Xiang Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: Meng Wu later captured the King of Chu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Meng Tian had a younger brother named Meng Yi.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 26th year of Qin Shihuang, Meng Tian became a general, attacked Qi, and was appointed Neishi.
details.label: included

details.point: After unification, Meng Tian led 300,000 troops to drive away the Rong and Di and recover land south of the Yellow River.
details.label: included

details.point: He built the Great Wall from Lintao to Liaodong, over 10,000 li.
details.label: included

details.point: He crossed the Yellow River, occupied Yangshan, and stationed in Shangjun for over ten years, intimidating the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin Shihuang trusted the Meng family; Meng Yi served as a high official and advisor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Gao, a eunuch, was promoted by Qin Shihuang for his legal expertise.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Gao committed a crime; Meng Yi sentenced him to death, but Qin Shihuang pardoned him.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin Shihuang sent Meng Tian to build a road from Jiuyuan to Ganquan, 1,800 li, but it was not completed.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Qin Shihuang died on a tour; Meng Yi was away praying. Li Si, Hu Hai, and Zhao Gao plotted to make Hu Hai crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: They forged an order forcing Fusu to suicide and imprisoning Meng Tian.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Gao slandered the Meng brothers; Hu Hai imprisoned Meng Yi and killed him despite Ziying's advice.
details.label: included

details.point: Meng Tian was ordered to suicide; he argued his loyalty but eventually swallowed poison.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian criticized Meng Tian for not admonishing the First Emperor and for building the Great Wall, causing suffering.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Si was a native of Shangcai, State of Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: He learned from Xunzi about how emperors govern the world.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Si went west to Qin to lobby the King of Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: He became a retainer of Lu Buwei and then a Lang Guan.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Si advised the King of Qin to seize the opportunity to unify the world.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin Shihuang appointed Li Si as chief historian and later as guest minister.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Si wrote a letter opposing the expulsion of guests, citing historical examples.
details.label: included

details.point: The King of Qin abolished the expulsion order and promoted Li Si to Tingwei.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Si became prime minister after Qin unified the world.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Si proposed the burning of books and banning of private schools.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin Shihuang approved the proposal, leading to the burning of classics.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Si's sons married Qin princesses, and his daughters married Qin royalty.
details.label: included

details.point: After Qin Shihuang's death, Zhao Gao conspired with Li Si to forge an edict.
details.label: included

details.point: They made Hu Hai the crown prince and ordered Fusu to commit suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Hu Hai became Qin II, and Zhao Gao gained power.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Gao advised Qin II to implement harsh laws and kill princes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Si was arrested and tortured by Zhao Gao on false charges.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Si was executed by being cut in half in the Xianyang market.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Gao became prime minister and later forced Qin II to commit suicide.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Ziying killed Zhao Gao but later surrendered to Liu Bang; Qin fell.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Song, courtesy name Ziya, was born in Guangling and was a descendant of Liu Xu, King Li of Guangling in the Han Dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: He was recommended as a filial and incorrupt scholar but did not accept.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen called him to serve in the Prime Minister's Mansion and sent him as an envoy to Shu.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Song petitioned for relief in Shu without waiting for an answer, for which he was removed from office.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu of Jin appointed him Shangshu Sangonglang, responsible for laws and redressing injustices.
details.label: included

details.point: During Xianning, he inspected Jingyang and was transferred to Huangmenlang.
details.label: included

details.point: He acted as Tingwei and exonerated Shi Huyin, being compared to Zhang Shizhi.
details.label: included

details.point: After Wu was conquered, he judged that Wang Hun had the highest merit and Wang Jun middle merit, leading to his demotion.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as prefect of Hanoi and petitioned to demolish water dams that caused disasters.
details.label: included

details.point: As Prime Minister of Huainan, he reformed the construction of Shaopi, calculating labor value fairly.
details.label: included

details.point: He submitted a long memorial discussing enfeoffment, advocating for a feudal system to stabilize the state.
details.label: included

details.point: He argued that enfeoffment would prevent usurpation and ensure long-term stability, citing Zhou and Han examples.
details.label: included

details.point: He criticized the current nine-rank system and proposed reforms for official assessment and long tenure.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He opposed adding Jiuxi to Sima Lun, citing historical precedents.
details.label: included

details.point: He was posthumously granted the title of Marquis of Liangzo County for his service in killing Jia Mi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Chong, courtesy name Maozeng, was from Jiangxia and known for his learning and filial piety.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Chong argued against limiting slaves and land, stating it was impractical without a well-field system.
details.label: included

details.point: He opposed demoting Jie Deng for serving in a remote county, advocating consistent laws.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He promoted reclusive talents like Huo Yuan, emphasizing virtue over family background.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Chong served as prefect of Pingyang, promoting education and impeaching corrupt officials.
details.label: included

details.point: Fang Zhi, courtesy name Huixiang, baby name Fazhen, was the ninth son of Shizu.
details.label: included

details.point: He was granted Marquis of Xingliang in the third year of Taiqing.
details.label: included

details.point: He was granted King of Jin'an in the first year of Chengsheng.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as General Pingnan and Governor of Jiangzhou in the second year of Chengsheng.
details.label: included

details.point: In November of the third year of Chengsheng, Jiangling fell; Wang Sengbian and Chen Baxian agreed to welcome Emperor Jing back.
details.label: included

details.point: On February 2 of the fourth year of Chengsheng, he entered the imperial court from Xunyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Sengbian was appointed as Superintendent of Zhongshu and other high offices; Chen Baxian was appointed Sikong.
details.label: included

details.point: In March, Qi sent Xiao Yuanming to be Liang's successor; Pei Zhiheng was defeated and died.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Sengbian led his army and was stationed in Gushu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: On July 23, Wang Sengbian brought Xiao Yuanming across the river from Caishi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: On September 27, Chen Baxian raised troops, killed Wang Sengbian, and deposed Xiao Yuanming.
details.label: included

details.point: On September 29, Emperor Jing officially ascended the throne.
details.label: included

details.point: The reign name was changed to Shaotai; sentences were reduced and officials granted titles.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Baxian was appointed Shangshu Ling and governor of Yang and Nanxu prefectures.
details.label: included

details.point: Du Gong raised troops; Wei Zai responded; Chen Baxian attacked eastward.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Yue and Xu Sihui rebelled and occupied Stone City.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi reinforcements arrived; Chen Baxian defeated them at Jiangning.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In the first year of Taiping, sentences were reduced; Du Gong surrendered.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Baxian was promoted to prime minister and Duke of Yixing County.
details.label: included

details.point: In the second year of Taiping, Chen Baxian was made King of Chen; Emperor Jing abdicated to Chen.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu Wu's name was Yan, courtesy name Shuda, nickname Lian'er, descendant of Xiao He.
details.label: included

details.point: He was born in the eighth year of the Ming Dynasty (Jiachen year of Xiaowu in Song) in Moling County.
details.label: included

details.point: He had unusual physical features: two bones connected between his strands, protruding top of head, tattoo of 'Martial' on right hand.
details.label: included

details.point: He was knowledgeable, fond of strategy, talented in civil and military affairs, praised by celebrities.
details.label: included

details.point: He socialized with the Eight Friends including Xie Tiao, Wang Rong, Fan Yun, etc., at Jingling Prince's residence.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Rong predicted he would become ruler of the world.
details.label: included

details.point: In Jianwu 2nd year, he led reinforcements against Northern Wei at Yiyang, breaking the siege.
details.label: included

details.point: In Yongyuan 2nd year, after Xiao Yi's murder, he secretly planned rebellion and gathered troops in Xiangyang.
details.label: included

details.point: He sent Wang Tianhu with letters to Xiao Yingzhou, leading to Liu Shanyang's death and alliance with Jingzhou.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In February of Zhongxing 1st year, he set out from Xiangyang with over 10,000 soldiers, 1,000 horses, 3,000 ships.
details.label: included

details.point: He issued a manifesto denouncing Donghun's tyranny and listing his crimes.
details.label: included

details.point: He defeated Wu Ziyang at Jiahu, causing Yingcheng and Lushan to lose morale.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Chen Bozhi surrendered Jiangzhou after the defeat of Jiahu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In October, Zhu Sengyong surrendered Shitou; Donghun's forces collapsed at Zhuque.
details.label: not_included

details.point: On Bingyin in December, Donghun was beheaded by Zhang Dan and Wang Zhenguo.
details.label: included

details.point: Gaozu was appointed Grand Sima, Duke of Jian'an, and later Prime Minister, Duke of Liang, with nine bestowals.
details.label: included

details.point: He refused the nine bestowals initially but accepted after repeated requests.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to King of Liang with twenty counties.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Xuande issued an edict of abdication, handing the throne to King Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: Gaozu accepted the throne after persuasion from officials and auspicious omens.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Qian was a native of Shuyang, Linhuai, and his father Chen Jiao was a Situ of Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Qian was deep and resourceful; he advised his father during a false accusation by Liu Ye.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Qian served as Shangshu Lang, Grand Administrator of Zhongshan and Anping, and later as Sima, Changshi, and Yushi Zhongcheng.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to Shangshu and granted the title of Tinghou of Anguo.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Qian defeated Shu generals during the invasion of Longyou and later pacified the Zhuge Dan rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: He was appointed General Andong, Marquis of Guangling, and later General of Chariots and Cavalry, Duke of Gaoping County.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Qian captured Zhili city in Wu and defeated Tu Zhong's troops.
details.label: included

details.point: He warned Emperor Wu about Hu Lie and Qian Hong, who later failed in their posts.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Qian was magnanimous and resourceful, superior to colleagues like Maichong and Shi Bao.
details.label: included

details.point: He retired in Xianning third year and was honored with Gunmian and privileges.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Qian died at 81, posthumously named Wu, and was buried with honors.
details.label: included

details.point: Pei Xiu was from Wenxi, Hedong; his grandfather Pei Mao was a Han minister, father Pei Qian a Wei minister.
details.label: included

details.point: Pei Xiu was learned and well-mannered; he was recommended to Cao Shuang and served as Huangmen Shilang.
details.label: included

details.point: He participated in the campaign against Zhuge Dan and was granted Marquis of Luyang Township.
details.label: included

details.point: Pei Xiu proposed the fifth-class title system and was granted Marquis of Jichuan.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised Emperor Wen to establish Sima Yan as heir, saying Sima You had an imperial appearance.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Pei Xiu served as Shangshu Ling and Zuo Guanglu Daifu, later as Sikong.
details.label: included

details.point: He compiled the 'Yugong Regional Circle' map with six principles of cartography.
details.label: included

details.point: Pei Xiu died at 48; his posthumous name was Yuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Pei Xiu's son Pei Po was elegant and learned; he opposed Empress Jia and wrote the 'Chongyou Lun' against nihilism.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Kuai Tong lobbied Xu Gong, the magistrate of Fanyang, to surrender to Wu Chen, promising rewards.
details.label: included

details.point: Wu Chen followed Kuai Tong's advice and welcomed Xu Gong with honors, leading to the surrender of over thirty cities.
details.label: included

details.point: Kuai Tong persuaded Han Xin to attack Qi despite Li Shiqi's diplomatic mission, leading to Li Shiqi's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin conquered Qi and became its acting king, with Liu Bang later confirming him as King of Qi.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Kuai Tong urged Han Xin to rebel and create a tripartite balance, but Han Xin refused out of loyalty.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Xin was later demoted and executed, regretting not heeding Kuai Tong's advice.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Bang summoned Kuai Tong and pardoned him after Kuai Tong defended himself with the dog-barking analogy.
details.label: included

details.point: Kuai Tong recommended Shu Guo and Liang Shijun to Cao Shen, who treated them as honored guests.
details.label: included

details.point: Kuai Tong wrote a book on lobbying strategies titled 'Juan Yong'.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wu Bei advised King Huainan Liu An against rebellion, citing the stability of the Han dynasty.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wu Bei described the Han general as capable and loyal, warning that rebellion would fail.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Huainan ignored Wu Bei's advice and eventually rebelled, leading to his downfall.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wu Bei was executed despite his earlier praise of the Han, as he had initially planned rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Chong falsely accused Prince Liu Dan of incest, leading to the prince's deposition.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Chong gained Emperor Wu's trust by enforcing laws against nobles and investigating witchcraft.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Jiang Chong's witchcraft investigation led to the death of tens of thousands, including the crown prince.
details.label: included

details.point: The crown prince executed Jiang Chong but was later defeated and died.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Wu eventually learned the truth and annihilated Jiang Chong's clan.
details.label: included

details.point: Xifu Gong and Sun Chong fabricated a rebellion plot against King Shuping Liu Yun, leading to executions.
details.label: included

details.point: Xifu Gong was later disgraced, exiled, and died after being accused of cursing the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Jia Chong was from Xiangling, Pingyang, son of Jia Kui, governor of Yuzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: He succeeded his father as marquis and served as Shangshu Lang.
details.label: included

details.point: He participated in the campaign against Guanqiu Jian and Wen Qin under Emperor Jing.
details.label: included

details.point: He was sent to observe Zhuge Dan and reported that Zhuge Dan would rebel.
details.label: included

details.point: He advised digging deep moats and building high forts to defeat Zhuge Dan.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to Marquis of Xuanyang Township after the campaign.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Tingwei and was known for correcting wrongful cases.
details.label: included

details.point: During the attack on the Prime Minister's Mansion, he ordered Cheng Ji to kill the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: He was trusted by Emperor Wen and participated in revising the law.
details.label: included

details.point: He supported Emperor Wu as heir over Sima You.
details.label: included

details.point: He was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry and Shangshu Ling.
details.label: included

details.point: He was sent to guard Guanzhong but stayed due to the prince's marriage.
details.label: included

details.point: He was appointed commander-in-chief in the conquest of Wu, though he opposed it.
details.label: included

details.point: After Wu's surrender, he was rewarded with additional fiefs and honors.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He died at age 66 and was posthumously made Dazai with the posthumous name Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: His wife Guo Huai was jealous and caused the death of his sons, leaving no heir.
details.label: included

details.point: His grandson Han Mi was made heir by imperial decree.
details.label: included

details.point: His daughter Jia Wu had an affair with Han Shou and married him.
details.label: included

details.point: His grandson Jia Mi became powerful and was killed during Sima Lun's coup.
details.label: included

details.point: The historian criticized Jia Chong for flattery and causing harm to Wei and Jin.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Shu was born in Renchengfan, courtesy name Yangyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: His father died young and he was adopted by his maternal grandfather's Ning family.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Shu was eight feet two inches tall, handsome, and could drink more than a stone of wine.
details.label: included

details.point: He was slow and simple, not valued by villagers initially.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Yi of Taiyuan predicted he would become prime minister and helped him.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Shu passed the Xiaolian exam after studying a classic for a hundred days.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Chief of Mianchi, Jun Yi Ling, and Shangshu Lang.
details.label: included

details.point: He resigned from Shangshu Lang when incompetent colleagues were dismissed.
details.label: included

details.point: He impressed Zhong Yu with his archery skills.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen valued him, calling him the leader of everyone.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as governor of Yiyang and Rongyang with good reputation.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as governor of Jizhou for three years with a reputation for simplicity and benevolence.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu gave him silk for his honesty and simplicity.
details.label: included

details.point: He married three times, all wives died; he was given burial land and money.
details.label: included

details.point: He advocated for the Fengshan ceremony but the emperor disagreed.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Zuopushe and in charge of the official department.
details.label: included

details.point: He appointed Zhou Zhen, who was considered unlucky, without disaster.
details.label: included

details.point: He resigned due to old age and was allowed to return as Ju Yangzi with honors.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at 82, posthumously named Kang.
details.label: included

details.point: His son Wei Hun died young, and his great-nephew Wei Huang succeeded him.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Taizong's Jianwen was named Gang, courtesy name Shizuan, nickname Liutong.
details.label: included

details.point: He was the third son of Emperor Gaozu and half-brother of Prince Zhaoming.
details.label: included

details.point: Born on October 28, second year of Tianjian.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Granted title King of Jin'an in fifth year of Tianjian.
details.label: included

details.point: Held various military and civil posts including General Yunhui, Danyang Yin, and governor of multiple provinces.
details.label: included

details.point: Appointed crown prince on July 7, third year of Zhongdatong.
details.label: included

details.point: Became emperor on May 28, third year of Taiqing after Emperor Gaozu's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Issued edicts reducing sentences and releasing northern slaves.
details.label: included

details.point: Established crown prince and granted titles to princes in June of Taiqing third year.
details.label: included

details.point: Faced rebellion of Hou Jing, who forced Taizong to visit Xizhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Hou Jing proclaimed himself Prime Minister and King of Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Hou Jing killed Nankang successor king Huili in November of Dabao first year.
details.label: not_included

details.point: In Dabao second year, Hou Jing deposed Taizong as King of Jin'an and imprisoned him.
details.label: included

details.point: Hou Jing killed crown prince Daqi and other princes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Taizong died on October 2, Dabao second year, suffocated by a bag of soil.
details.label: included

details.point: Posthumously named Emperor Ming, temple name Gaozong, later changed to Emperor Jianwen, temple name Taizong.
details.label: included

details.point: Buried in Zhuangling on April 29, Dabao third year.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Taizong was intelligent, could compose at age six, read ten lines at a glance.
details.label: included

details.point: He was filial, mourned his mother excessively, and led Northern Expedition expanding territory.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He wrote many works including biographies, commentaries, and collections.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Er was a native of Daliang and a former retainer of Lord Xinling.
details.label: included

details.point: He married a wealthy woman and became magistrate of Waihuang.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Yu was from Daliang, loved Confucianism, and married a wealthy woman.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Er and Chen Yu became close friends, with Chen Yu treating Zhang Er like a father.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu (Liu Bang) had a relationship with Zhang Er when he was a commoner.
details.label: included

details.point: After Qin destroyed Wei, a reward was offered for Zhang Er and Chen Yu; they became gatekeepers in Chendi.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Er advised Chen Yu to endure a beating from a minor official.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen She rebelled; Zhang Er and Chen Yu joined him and advised against him proclaiming king too early.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen She ignored their advice and made himself king of Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Er and Chen Yu led a force to capture Zhao territory for Chen She.
details.label: included

details.point: They persuaded Wu Chen to declare himself King of Zhao, with Chen Yu as general and Zhang Er as prime minister.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen She reluctantly accepted Wu Chen's kingship and placed Wu Chen's family under house arrest.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wu Chen refused to send troops west and instead expanded Zhao territory.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wu Chen was captured by Yan but freed by a servant who convinced Yan that Zhang Er and Chen Yu wanted him dead.
details.label: included

details.point: Li Liang rebelled, killed Wu Chen, and razed Handan; Zhang Er and Chen Yu escaped.
details.label: included

details.point: They established Zhao Xie as King of Zhao and were besieged in Julu by Qin.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Yu refused to relieve the siege, causing a rift with Zhang Er.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu defeated Qin at Julu; Zhang Er blamed Chen Yu for not helping, leading to their split.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu enfeoffed Zhang Er as King of Changshan and Chen Yu as a marquis, causing Chen Yu's resentment.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Yu defeated Zhang Er, who then joined Liu Bang; later, Liu Bang killed Chen Yu and made Zhang Er King of Zhao.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Confucius compiled the 'Poems' and 'Books' and organized ritual music due to the decline of the Zhou royal way.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius traveled to over 70 states seeking office but was not employed.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius wrote the Spring and Autumn Annals based on Lu's historical records.
details.label: included

details.point: After Confucius's death, his disciples dispersed and taught in various states.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Warring States period, Confucianism was suppressed but persisted in Qi and Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: Qin Shihuang burned Confucian classics and killed scholars, causing the Six Arts to become incomplete.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen She rebelled, and Confucian scholars from Lu carried Confucius's ritual vessels to join him.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Han dynasty, Confucian scholars revived, and Shusun Tong established Han rituals.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen and Emperor Jing showed limited interest in Confucianism; Empress Dowager Dou favored Taoism.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Emperor Wu (current emperor) promoted Confucianism, appointing Zhao Wan, Wang Zang, and others.
details.label: included

details.point: After Empress Dowager Dou's death, Tian Fen became prime minister and promoted Confucian scholars.
details.label: included

details.point: Gongsun Hong, proficient in the Spring and Autumn Annals, rose to become prime minister.
details.label: included

details.point: Gongsun Hong petitioned to establish a system of academic officials and doctoral disciples.
details.label: included

details.point: The emperor approved the establishment of 50 doctoral disciples and a system of recommendation and examination.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Peigong taught the 'Poems' in Lu; his disciples included Zhao Wan and Wang Zang.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Gusheng debated Huang Sheng on whether Tang and Wu usurped the throne; he offended Empress Dowager Dou.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Sheng from Yan wrote 'Inner and Outer Commentaries' on the 'Poems'.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Sheng preserved the 'Shang Shu' by hiding it in a wall; he taught it to Chao Cuo.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Zhongshu, expert in the Spring and Autumn Annals, taught Gongyang studies and wrote on disasters.
details.label: included

details.point: Dong Zhongshu's disciples included Chu Da, Yin Zhong, and Lu Bushu; his teachings became influential.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wu of Zhou attacked King Zhou of Shang, destroyed the Shang Dynasty, and moved the Nine Tripods to Luoyi.
details.label: included

details.point: Boyi and Shuqi starved to death in Shouyang Mountain because they refused to eat Zhou millet.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius praised Boyi and Shuqi for their virtue.
details.label: included

details.point: Mencius said Boyi's demeanor made greedy people honest and cowardly people determined.
details.label: included

details.point: Four hermits (Yuan Gong, Qili Ji, Xia Huang Gong, Mr. Jiao Li) fled to Shangluo Mountain during Qin rule.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu of Han summoned the four hermits but they did not come.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Lu used Zhang Liang's strategy to have the crown prince welcome the four hermits, stabilizing his position.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Zizhen refused to serve under Wang Feng during Emperor Cheng's reign.
details.label: included

details.point: Yan Junping did divination in Chengdu, guiding people to good deeds, and taught Laozi.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang Xiong studied with Yan Junping and praised him.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Ji admonished the King of Changyi for excessive hunting and travel.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Ji warned the King of Changyi before he became emperor, advising him to respect Huo Guang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King Changyi was deposed after 20 days due to lewd behavior; Wang Ji was spared but sentenced to hard labor.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Ji criticized Emperor Xuan's policies and advocated for ritual and education over punishment.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Ji abandoned his wife for picking dates from a neighbor's tree without permission.
details.label: included

details.point: Gong Yu advised Emperor Yuan to reduce extravagance, including palace expenses and horses.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Gong Yu proposed abolishing coinage and returning to barter to encourage agriculture.
details.label: included

details.point: Gong Sheng refused to serve Wang Mang, starved himself to death, and was praised for his integrity.
details.label: included

details.point: Bao Xuan criticized Emperor Ai for favoring Dong Xian and relatives, and was imprisoned but later released.
details.label: included

details.point: The Wang family (Wang Ji, Wang Jun, Wang Chong) were known for honesty but increasing official rank.
details.label: not_included
