details.point: Ji Bu was from Chu, ambitious and chivalrous, famous in Chu.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiang Yu sent Ji Bu to lead the army, embarrassing Liu Bang many times.
details.label: included

details.point: After Xiang Yu's death, Emperor Gaozu offered a thousand gold for Ji Bu's capture and ordered punishment for those who harbored him.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji Bu hid at the Zhou family in Puyang.
details.label: included

details.point: The Zhou family shaved Ji Bu's head, put an iron hoop on his neck, dressed him in coarse cloth, and sold him as a slave to the Zhu family of Lu.
details.label: included

details.point: The Zhu family recognized Ji Bu, bought him, and put him to work in the fields, treating him equally with other slaves.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Jia went to Luoyang and visited Ruyin Marquis Teng Gong.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhu Jia argued that Ji Bu was acting in his duty for Xiang Yu and that pursuing him would drive him to the Huns or Yue, harming the Han.
details.label: included

details.point: Teng Gong agreed to speak to the emperor, and the emperor pardoned Ji Bu.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji Bu was summoned, pleaded guilty, and was appointed as a doctor.
details.label: included

details.point: During Emperor Hui's reign, Ji Bu served as Zhonglang General.
details.label: included

details.point: When the Xiongnu Chanyu insulted Empress Lu, Fan Kuai proposed a 100,000-man campaign; Ji Bu opposed, citing Emperor Gao's defeat at Pingcheng and the Qin's overextension.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Lu heeded Ji Bu's advice and dropped the campaign.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji Bu became governor of Hedong County.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wen summoned Ji Bu to appoint him as imperial censor but sent him back after hearing he was drunken and willful.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji Bu criticized Emperor Wen for being swayed by praise and slander, embarrassing the emperor.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Qiu, a Chu rhetorician, sought Ji Bu's favor; Ji Bu initially rejected him but later welcomed him after Cao Qiu cited the proverb 'a promise from Ji Bu is worth a hundred catties of gold'.
details.label: included

details.point: Cao Qiu promoted Ji Bu's reputation widely.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji Bu's younger brother Ji Xin was brave and chivalrous, famous in Guanzhong.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji Bu's uncle Ding Gong was executed by Emperor Gaozu for disloyalty to Xiang Yu.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu ascended the throne in the southern suburbs on Bingyin in the summer of the first year of Tianjian.
details.label: included

details.point: He performed a sacrifice to heaven, declaring that the Qi dynasty had lost its mandate and he was chosen to rule.
details.label: included

details.point: The edict justified the dynastic change by citing historical precedents like Yao, Shun, Han, and Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: The Qi dynasty was criticized for its cruel and corrupt rule, leading to chaos and suffering.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Yan claimed to have rescued the people by suppressing rebels and establishing a new ruler.
details.label: included

details.point: Auspicious signs from the sun, stars, and mountains indicated the mandate had shifted to him.
details.label: included

details.point: Officials and ministers urged Xiao Yan to accept the throne, which he reluctantly did.
details.label: included

details.point: After the ceremony, he entered Jiankang Palace and issued an amnesty for the empire.
details.label: included

details.point: The reign name was changed from Zhongxing to Tianjian, and the second year of Zhongxing became the first year of Tianjian.
details.label: included

details.point: Meritorious officials were granted titles, and widows and orphans received grain.
details.label: included

details.point: Arrears of taxes and old debts were canceled, and those convicted of corruption were pardoned.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The Qi emperor was demoted to King of Baling, and the Qi calendar and rituals were retained.
details.label: included

details.point: Posthumous titles were granted to Xiao Yan's father, mother, and concubine, and his brothers were named princes.
details.label: included

details.point: New princes and high officials were appointed, including Xiao Hong as governor of Yangzhou.
details.label: not_included

details.point: An edict condemned the luxury of the Song dynasty and ordered the release of palace women.
details.label: included

details.point: Foreign kings, including those of Goguryeo, Baekje, and Japan, were promoted in rank.
details.label: included

details.point: King Baling died and was given the posthumous title Emperor Qihe.
details.label: included

details.point: An edict ordered officials to observe customs, visit wise men, and report on local conditions.
details.label: included

details.point: A system of atonement by payment was established, following ancient Zhou laws.
details.label: not_included

details.point: The capital was moved to Jiankang, and the overseas Chinese registration system was reformed.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lord Shang, originally named Gongsun Yang, was a son of a concubine of the Kingdom of Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as a middle concubine under his uncle, the Prime Minister of Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: His uncle recommended him to King Wei Hui as a successor, but the king was silent.
details.label: included

details.point: His uncle advised the king to kill Gongsun Yang if not appointed, but Gongsun Yang did not flee.
details.label: included

details.point: King Wei Hui dismissed the advice, saying his uncle was confused.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After his uncle's death, Gongsun Yang went to Qin and gained an audience through Jing Jian.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Xiao of Qin initially rejected Gongsun Yang's advice on imperial methods.
details.label: included

details.point: Gongsun Yang later persuaded Duke Xiao with methods of enriching the state and strengthening the army.
details.label: included

details.point: Duke Xiao appointed Gongsun Yang to implement legal reforms.
details.label: included

details.point: The reforms included mutual surveillance, collective punishment, and rewards for reporting crimes.
details.label: included

details.point: Military merit was rewarded; private fighting was punished; agriculture was encouraged.
details.label: included

details.point: Nobles without military merit were stripped of privileges.
details.label: not_included

details.point: To build trust, Gongsun Yang erected a log and rewarded a man who moved it with 50 gold.
details.label: included

details.point: When the prince violated the new law, Gongsun Yang punished his tutors with tattooing.
details.label: included

details.point: After 10 years, the reforms made Qin prosperous and orderly.
details.label: included

details.point: Gongsun Yang led a campaign against Wei, capturing Prince Ang by deceit.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei ceded the Hexi region to Qin and moved its capital.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Duke Xiao granted Gongsun Yang the title Lord Shang and 15 cities.
details.label: included

details.point: After Duke Xiao's death, Lord Shang was accused of rebellion and executed by dismemberment.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian criticized Lord Shang as cruel and ungrateful, noting his eventual downfall.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou She was born in Runan'an, eighth grandson of Zhou Chan, son of Zhou Yi.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou She was intelligent, erudite, and eloquent.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Taixue doctor in Qi, later as chief administrator under Wang Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: In Liang, he was appointed Shangshu Temple Minister and contributed to ritual reforms.
details.label: included

details.point: He held various high offices including Zhongshu Shilang and Hongshanqing.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou She remained loyal to Wang Liang after his disgrace, arranging his funeral.
details.label: included

details.point: He served Emperor Gaozu for over 20 years, handling confidential affairs without leaking secrets.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou She was frugal, living simply with poor-quality items.
details.label: included

details.point: He was convicted for accepting a gift of noodles from Bai Guo and dismissed.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at age 56; emperor mourned and granted posthumous honors.
details.label: included

details.point: Xu Mian was born in Tan, East China Sea; grandfather Changzong, father Xu Rong.
details.label: included

details.point: Xu Mian was poor but diligent, praised by Wang Jian for prime ministerial qualities.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Zhongshu Minister and Shangshu Zuocheng, known for competence.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xu Mian worked tirelessly on military documents during northern campaigns.
details.label: included

details.point: He was Minister of Personnel, known for fairness and avoiding favoritism.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He served as Prince Zhan Shi, teaching Prince Zhaoming and managing palace affairs.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Xu Mian memorialized to enforce three-day burial rule, which was adopted.
details.label: included

details.point: He oversaw compilation of the Five Rites, completed in 1200+ volumes.
details.label: included

details.point: Xu Mian left no property to descendants, only integrity; wrote a letter to his son.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at age 70; emperor mourned, granted posthumous title Jian Sugong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Lao Tzu described an ideal state where people are content with their own customs and do not interact with neighbors.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Tai Shigong argues that modern conditions make Lao Tzu's ideal impractical.
details.label: not_included

details.point: People naturally desire pleasure, wealth, and power, and cannot be changed by preaching.
details.label: included

details.point: The best governance is to let nature take its course, then to follow the situation, then to educate, then to correct, and worst is to fight.
details.label: included

details.point: Different regions produce different goods: west of Mount Wei has wood, bamboo, jade; east has fish, salt, silk; south has gold, tin, cinnabar, ivory; north has horses, cattle, felt.
details.label: included

details.point: People rely on farmers, miners, fishermen, craftsmen, and merchants for necessities.
details.label: included

details.point: Economic activity is natural like water flowing; people work hard for their own desires without government orders.
details.label: included

details.point: The four occupations (agriculture, industry, commerce, natural resources) are sources of wealth; large sources make a country rich.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiang Taigang developed Qi by promoting textiles and trade, attracting people and wealth.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Guan Zhong continued Jiang's policies, making Qi prosperous and Duke Huan hegemon.
details.label: included

details.point: Wealth leads to etiquette and honor; poverty leads to their loss.
details.label: not_included

details.point: People everywhere pursue profit; even kings and officials fear poverty.
details.label: included

details.point: Ji Ran's strategies: observe cycles of good and bad years, prepare for floods during drought and vice versa, maintain stable grain prices between 30 and 80 qian per dou.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Goods should be sold when prices are high and bought when low; money should circulate like water.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Gou Jian used Ji Ran's strategies to enrich Yue and defeat Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Fan Li (Tao Zhugong) applied Ji Ran's methods to become wealthy three times, distributing wealth to the poor.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zigong became rich through trade and helped Confucius gain fame.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Bai Gui mastered timing in trade, buying when surplus and selling when scarce, and compared his methods to military strategy.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yidun, Guo Zong, Wu Shiluo, and Widow Qing became wealthy through iron, livestock, and cinnabar, gaining status.
details.label: included

details.point: The Han dynasty opened trade routes, moved wealthy families to the capital, and Guanzhong became the richest region, holding six-tenths of the world's wealth.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Dou Ying was the son of Queen Xiaowen's cousin and served as Zhan Shi under Emperor Xiaojing.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Ying opposed Emperor Xiaojing's plan to pass the throne to King Liang Xiao, angering Queen Mother Dou.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms, Dou Ying was appointed general and successfully suppressed the rebellion, earning the title Marquis of Weiqi.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Ying served as tutor to Crown Prince Li but failed to prevent his deposition, leading him to retire in protest.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Fen was the half-brother of Emperor Xiaojing and Queen Wang, later becoming Marquis of Wu'an.
details.label: included

details.point: After Emperor Wu ascended, Tian Fen became Taiwei and recommended Dou Ying as Prime Minister, while he became Taiwei.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Ying and Tian Fen promoted Confucianism, leading to conflict with Queen Mother Dou who favored Huang-Lao.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Mother Dou dismissed Dou Ying and Tian Fen from their posts in 135 BC after they attempted to limit her power.
details.label: not_included

details.point: After Queen Mother Dou's death, Tian Fen became Prime Minister and grew arrogant, dominating the court.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Fu was a brave officer who avenged his father's death during the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms, gaining fame.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Fu was known for his chivalry, disrespect toward nobles, and close friendship with Dou Ying.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Fen sought to seize land from Dou Ying, leading to a feud between them.
details.label: included

details.point: At Tian Fen's wedding feast, Guan Fu insulted guests, leading Tian Fen to imprison him on charges of disrespect.
details.label: included

details.point: Dou Ying tried to save Guan Fu by appealing to Emperor Wu, leading to a court debate between Dou Ying and Tian Fen.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Wu initially favored Dou Ying but later imprisoned him after discovering inconsistencies in his testimony.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Dou Ying was executed in 131 BC after being convicted of forging an imperial edict.
details.label: included

details.point: Guan Fu and his family were executed shortly after Dou Ying's death.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Tian Fen died in 130 BC, reportedly haunted by the ghosts of Dou Ying and Guan Fu.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Anguo was a skilled diplomat who resolved tensions between Emperor Jing and King Liang Xiao.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Han Anguo served as御史大夫 and opposed military campaigns against the Xiongnu, advocating for peace treaties.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Xiang was a descendant of Han official Wang Ji, born in Linyi, Langye.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Xiang was extremely filial, serving his stepmother despite her cruelty.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Xiang broke ice to catch fish for his stepmother in winter; ice cracked and two carps appeared.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Xiang guarded a red sand fruit tree for his stepmother, crying and hugging it during storms.
details.label: not_included

details.point: During the late Han wars, Wang Xiang fled with his mother and brother Wang Lan, living in seclusion for over 20 years.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Xiang served as an official under Lu Qian, defeating robbers and bringing peace to the state.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Xiang held various high offices including Da Sinong, Guang Luxun, Sili Xiaowei, Taichang, and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wansui Ting.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Xiang served as the third elder at the Imperial Academy, teaching the emperor political education.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Xiang refused to bow to Sima Zhao, stating he was a minister of Wei, not Jin.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Xiang was promoted to Taibao and Duke under Emperor Wu of Jin, but repeatedly requested retirement due to old age.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Xiang's will instructed simple burial, no valuables, and minimal mourning, emphasizing five principles of life.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Xiang died at 85; his funeral was attended only by wise ministers and relatives.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Lan, Wang Xiang's half-brother, protected Wang Xiang from their stepmother's poison attempts.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Lan held official positions including Qinghe prefect, Shaofu, and Zong Zhengqing, and died at 73.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zheng Chong was born poor, studied classics, and was appointed by Emperor Wen of Wei as literary minister.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Chong held high offices including Sikong, Situ, and Taibao, but did not interfere in world affairs.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Chong compiled the 'Collected Commentary of the Analects of Confucius' with others.
details.label: included

details.point: He Zeng was known for filial piety and strict adherence to ritual, but also for extreme extravagance in food and clothing.
details.label: included

details.point: He Zeng served as Sili Xiaowei, impeaching corrupt officials, and later as Taibao and Taifu under Emperor Wu of Jin.
details.label: included

details.point: Shi Bao rose from humble origins to become Grand Sima, but was falsely accused of rebellion and dismissed; later reinstated as Situ.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xuan had nine sons: Queen Mu Zhang gave birth to Emperor Jing, Emperor Wen, and Sima Wangqian of Pingyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Mrs. Fu gave birth to Sima Liang, Sima Nian, Sima Jing, and Sima Jun.
details.label: included

details.point: Mrs. Zhang gave birth to Sima Xu and Sima Lun.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian, King of Pingyuan, was granted the title in the Wei Dynasty and later became King of Pingyuan under Emperor Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian was known for his reclusive nature, not caring for government affairs, and letting his wealth rot.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian had unusual behavior, including leaving his concubines' coffins unsealed and viewing them.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian was appointed General Wei by Sima Lun and later Taibao after Emperor Hui was deposed and re-established.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian congratulated Sima Tong with a hundred coins after Sima Tong pacified Sima Lun.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian cried bitterly when Sima Tong was killed, lamenting the decline of the clan.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Sima Dian, King of Langye Wu, was talented and famous, served as General Ningshuo guarding Yecheng.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Dian was granted the title of King of Dongguan County and later King Langxie.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Dian played a key role in the pacification of Wu, receiving Sun Hao's surrender.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Dian was modest despite his achievements, and his staff were devoted to him.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Sima Dan, King of Wulingzhuang, was jealous and harmful, with no filial character.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Dan killed Guo Chu and Sima Chu's brother while drunk, giving their heads to Sima Lun.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Dan was exiled to Liaosai after his mother complained of his unfilial behavior.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Yao, King of Dong'an, was authoritative, learned, and filial, but was killed by Sima Ying.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Jun, King of Fufeng Wu, was clever and upright, with a good reputation in the clan.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Jun repelled Wu general Ding Feng and was known for his filial piety and literary works.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima You, King of Qi Xian, was wise, kind, and talented, and was favored by Emperor Wen as a potential heir.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Miao was a native of Kaifeng, Xingyang.
details.label: included

details.point: His father Zheng Tai was governor of Yangzhou and had a good reputation.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zheng Miao lost his father young and was insightful.
details.label: included

details.point: Xun You praised him, saying 'Zheng Gongye seems to be still alive.'
details.label: not_included

details.point: He fled to Jiangdong with his uncle Zheng Hun.
details.label: included

details.point: Hua Xin raised Zheng Miao as his own son.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zheng Miao returned to his hometown at age 17.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He warned Ren Lan to stay away from Wei Xie, who later caused disaster.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as Marquis of Linzi and Sili Gongcao under Emperor Wu of Wei.
details.label: included

details.point: He recommended Xu Yun, Lu Zhi, and Wang Ji to Wang Lang.
details.label: partially_included

details.point: As Li Yangling, he won the sincere conviction of subordinates and people.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was ranked first among county magistrates in prefect evaluation.
details.label: not_included

details.point: As prefect of Jiyin, he promoted filial piety and established schools.
details.label: not_included

details.point: As governor of Guangping, he prioritized education and was loved by the people.
details.label: included

details.point: He was promoted to Shaofu and granted title of Marquis of Ludantai.
details.label: not_included

details.point: During Guanqiu Jian's rebellion, he advised Emperor Jing to dig deep ditches and build high fortresses.
details.label: included

details.point: He recommended Liu Yi, Liu Shi, Cheng Xian, and Yu Jun for Mingtang Piyong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was granted title of Marquis of Ancheng Township and later Mi Lingbo.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He was appointed Sikong but repeatedly refused, eventually allowed to retire as marquis.
details.label: included

details.point: He died at age 85, posthumously named Mi Hao Yuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Can was the grandson of Wei Rui and son of Wei Gan.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Can served as an official under the King of Jin'an and later as infantry captain.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Can was a close friend of the crown prince and often served as a palace guard.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Can was appointed governor of Hengzhou in the 11th year of Datong.
details.label: included

details.point: In the 2nd year of Taiqing, Wei Can rushed to the capital with 5,000 elite soldiers to rescue it from Hou Jing's rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Can met with Liu Xiaoyi and then with Xiao Daxin to coordinate rescue efforts.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Can left his family behind and set off in a light boat.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Can proposed Liu Zhongli as commander-in-chief, but Pei Zhigao objected.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Can rebuked Pei Zhigao, and the generals agreed to Liu Zhongli's command.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wei Can was stationed at Qingtang and his camp fence was not completed.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Hou Jing attacked Wei Can's camp; Wei Can fought and was killed at age 54.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Can's son and three younger brothers were also killed in the battle.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Taizong mourned Wei Can and granted him posthumous honors.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiangzi was a seventh-generation descendant of Jiang Tong and served as magistrate of Suichang and Qu'a.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Jiangzi led naval troops to intercept Hou Jing but was betrayed by his deputy.
details.label: included

details.point: Jiangzi and his brothers Jiang Zisi and Jiang Ziwu attacked the rebels and were killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor granted posthumous honors to Jiangzi and his brothers.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Sheng was the son of Zhang Ji and served as governor of Wuxing.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Sheng refused to surrender to Hou Jing, fought, and was killed in the capital market.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Jun, as censor, confronted Hou Jing and was later killed by him.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jia, cousin of Liu Bang, was appointed general and pacified Sima Xin's territory.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jia led 20,000 troops to attack Chu, burned grain and supplies, and avoided direct battle.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jia recruited Zhou Yin to surrender, captured Jiujiang, and fought at Gaixia.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jia was made King of Jing after his military achievements.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jia was killed by Yingbu during Yingbu's rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ze, brother of Gaozu, was made Marquis of Yingling for defeating Chen Xi's general.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Sheng advised Zhang Qing to persuade ministers to make Lü Chan king, and suggested making Liu Ze king to stabilize Lü's power.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ze was made King of Langye, then later King of Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ze supported Liu Heng as Emperor Wen.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Ze's grandson Liu Dingguo committed incest and murder, leading to the abolition of the state.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bi, son of Liu Zhong, was made King of Wu after defeating Yingbu.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bi's son was killed by Crown Prince Liu Qi during a chess game, causing Liu Bi to resent the court.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bi exploited copper and salt resources to enrich Wu and avoid taxes.
details.label: included

details.point: Chao Cuo advocated reducing the territories of vassal kings to prevent rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bi rebelled in 154 BC, leading the Seven States Rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bi's letter to the princes justified rebellion by blaming Chao Cuo.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Jing executed Chao Cuo to appease the rebels, but the rebellion continued.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Yafu defeated Wu and Chu by cutting off their supply lines and avoiding direct battle.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Bi was killed by Dongyue after his defeat.
details.label: included

details.point: The rebellion was suppressed; Jiaoxi, Chu, Zhao kings committed suicide; others were killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Jiezi was from the North and promoted due to military service.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Jiezi blamed the kings of Loulan and Qiuci for killing Han envoys.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Jiezi killed a Xiongnu envoy while at Qiuci.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Fu Jiezi proposed to Huo Guang to assassinate the king of Loulan.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Jiezi tricked and assassinated the king of Loulan.
details.label: included

details.point: Fu Jiezi was made Marquis of Yiyang for killing the king of Loulan.
details.label: included

details.point: Chang Hui was detained by the Xiongnu for over ten years with Su Wu.
details.label: included

details.point: Chang Hui was sent as envoy to Wusun and coordinated Han-Wusun attack on Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: Chang Hui was made Marquis of Changluo for his mission.
details.label: included

details.point: Chang Hui punished Qiuci for killing Han captain Lai Dan.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Ji was appointed as the first Protector of the Western Regions.
details.label: included

details.point: Zheng Ji welcomed the Xiongnu prince Ri Zhu who surrendered.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zheng Ji was made Marquis of Anyuan.
details.label: included

details.point: Gan Yanshou and Chen Tang killed Zhizhi Chanyu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhizhi Chanyu had killed Han envoy Gu Ji and others.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Tang mobilized troops without authorization to attack Zhizhi.
details.label: included

details.point: The Han army besieged and killed Zhizhi Chanyu at his city.
details.label: included

details.point: Gan Yanshou was made Marquis of Yicheng, Chen Tang Marquis of Guan Nei.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Tang was later exiled for misconduct but eventually recalled.
details.label: included

details.point: Duan Huizong served as Protector and killed the Wusun prince Fanqiu.
details.label: included

details.point: Prince Zhaoming Xiao Tong was the eldest son of Emperor Wu of Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: His biological mother was Ding Guibi.
details.label: included

details.point: He was born in Xiangyang in September of the first year of Zhongxing in Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: He was made crown prince in November of the first year of Tianjian.
details.label: included

details.point: He started learning classics at age three and could recite the Five Classics by age five.
details.label: included

details.point: He moved into the East Palace on June 17 of the fifth year.
details.label: included

details.point: He was kind and filial, often missing his parents after leaving the palace.
details.label: included

details.point: He explained the Book of Filial Piety to Emperor Wu in September of the eighth year.
details.label: included

details.point: He was crowned in the Taiji Palace on the first day of the 14th year.
details.label: included

details.point: He was handsome, intelligent, and could compose poems quickly.
details.label: included

details.point: He believed in Buddhism, built Huiyi Hall, and wrote the Two Truths Dharmakaya Sutra.
details.label: included

details.point: Nectar fell on Huiyi Palace in April of the first year of the ordinary year.
details.label: not_included

details.point: He mourned his mother's death intensely, eating only one liter of rice porridge daily.
details.label: included

details.point: He participated in national affairs after crowning, handling memorials with care.
details.label: included

details.point: He was generous, recruited talented people, and built a library of over 30,000 volumes.
details.label: included

details.point: He enjoyed landscapes and refused female musicians, citing Zuo Si's poem.
details.label: included

details.point: He saved food during famine and helped the poor with money and clothes.
details.label: included

details.point: He opposed the canal project to avoid disturbing agricultural work.
details.label: included

details.point: He died on April 6 at age 31; people mourned greatly.
details.label: included

details.point: He compiled works including 20 volumes of collected works and 30 volumes of Selected Works.
details.label: included

details.point: Laozi was a native of Qurenli, Li Township, Kuxian County, Chu State, with surname Li, given name Er, courtesy name Dan.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as a historian in charge of the library in the Zhou Dynasty.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius visited Laozi to ask about etiquette; Laozi advised him to abandon arrogance and excessive desires.
details.label: included

details.point: Confucius compared Laozi to a dragon, saying he could not understand him.
details.label: included

details.point: Laozi wrote a book of over 5,000 words on morality at the request of Guanling Yinxi before leaving.
details.label: included

details.point: Laozi's whereabouts after leaving are unknown; some say he lived over 160 or 200 years.
details.label: included

details.point: There is confusion whether Taishi Dan (who prophesied to Duke Xiang of Qin) is the same as Laozi.
details.label: included

details.point: Laozi's son Li Zong was a general of Wei; his descendants are listed down to Li Jie.
details.label: included

details.point: Laozi advocated governing by doing nothing and quietness.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuangzi was from Mengyi, named Zhuangzhou, a minor official, contemporary of King Hui of Liang and King Xuan of Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuangzi's writings, over 100,000 words, used allegories to express Laozi's teachings and criticize Confucianism and Mohism.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhuangzi refused an offer to be prime minister of Chu, preferring to remain free.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Buhai studied Huang-Lao, served as prime minister of Han for 15 years, and wrote the book 'Shenzi'.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Fei was a Korean prince, studied under Xun Qing, wrote over 100,000 words including 'Shuo Nan'.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Fei's writings criticized Confucians and knights, and analyzed the difficulties of persuasion.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Fei's 'Shuo Nan' details the challenges of lobbying monarchs, including understanding their psychology.
details.label: included

details.point: King of Qin admired Han Fei's writings and attacked Han to get him; Han Fei was sent as envoy to Qin.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Li Si and Yao Jia slandered Han Fei, leading to his imprisonment and forced suicide by poison.
details.label: included

details.point: Shenzi and Hanzi's works were passed down; Sima Qian laments that Han Fei could not escape the disaster of lobbying.
details.label: included

details.point: Sima Qian concludes that Laozi's thought is profound, and the theories of Zhuangzi, Shen Buhai, and Han Fei all originated from it.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang was from Yangwu, Henan, and was fond of writing, music, and calendars.
details.label: included

details.point: In the Qin Dynasty, Zhang Cang served as censor in charge of household registration albums.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang fled home after breaking the law, then followed Pei Gong (Liu Bang) as a guest.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Ling saved Zhang Cang from execution because of his impressive physique.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang served as governor of Changshan, then as prime minister of Zhao and Dai.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang was granted the title Marquis of Beiping with 1,200 households.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang was familiar with world atlas, household registration, and calendar calculation.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang served as prime minister of Huainan and later as imperial censor.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Chang and his cousin Zhou Ke were from Pei and served Liu Bang from the start.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Ke was killed by Xiang Yu after refusing to surrender at Xingyang.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Chang was known for being strong and upright, and dared to speak bluntly.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Chang argued against deposing the crown prince, and Empress Lu thanked him.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhao Yao suggested appointing Zhou Chang as prime minister of Zhao to protect King Ruyi.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhou Chang was appointed prime minister of Zhao; Zhao Yao replaced him as censor.
details.label: included

details.point: After Gaozu's death, Empress Lu summoned King Zhao; Zhou Chang was summoned first, then King Zhao was killed.
details.label: included

details.point: Ren Ao served as censor and was granted title Marquis of Guang'a.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang became prime minister and corrected the calendar, adopting water virtue and black color.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang served Wang Ling's family like a father after Wang Ling saved his life.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Cang was dismissed after opposing Gongsun Chen's proposal for earth virtue.
details.label: included

details.point: Shen Tujia was a strong crossbowman who became prime minister and was known for uprightness.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen Qingzhi, courtesy name Ziyun, from Yixingguoshan, followed Emperor Gaozu from youth.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu loved chess; Chen Qingzhi stayed awake to play, earning appreciation.
details.label: included

details.point: He suppressed Jianye, served as chief secretary, and recruited soldiers with dispersed money.
details.label: included

details.point: In the ordinary years, he was appointed to receive Yuan Faseng of Wei who requested to attach Pengcheng.
details.label: included

details.point: He led 2,000 troops to guard Xuzhou with Xiao Zong.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei sent 20,000 troops under Prince Yanming and Prince Yuan; Chen defeated Qiu Dagan's fort in one battle.
details.label: included

details.point: After Xiao Zong fled, Chen cut bolts and retreated at night, saving his troops.
details.label: included

details.point: In the seventh year, he was sent to Shouchun; Li Xian surrendered after Chen attacked his forts.
details.label: included

details.point: In the first year of Datong, he attacked Guoyang; Wei sent 150,000 troops; Chen defeated their vanguard with 200 cavalry.
details.label: included

details.point: From spring to winter, hundreds of battles; Chen refused retreat, captured four of thirteen Wei forts, and took Woyang City.
details.label: included

details.point: He captured over 30,000 people in Guoyang and established West Xuzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Gaozu praised him in a letter, noting he was not from a general's family.
details.label: included

details.point: In early Datong, Chen was sent to support Yuan Hao of Wei; he defeated Qiu Dagan with 70,000 troops, capturing three forts.
details.label: included

details.point: He defeated Yuan Huiye, captured him, and seized 7,800 vehicles.
details.label: included

details.point: At Rongyang, with 7,000 troops against 300,000, he captured the city and defeated Yuan Tianmu's army.
details.label: included

details.point: He entered Hulao, and Yuan Hao entered Luoyang; Chen was made a servant and general.
details.label: included

details.point: Chen's troops wore white robes and were invincible; a nursery rhyme warned to avoid white robes.
details.label: included

details.point: In 140 days, he leveled 32 forts and fought 47 battles without defeat.
details.label: included

details.point: Yuan Hao became suspicious of Chen and refused reinforcements; Chen's deputy suggested usurpation but Chen refused.
details.label: included

details.point: When Erzhu Rong attacked, Chen defended Beizhonglang City, fought eleven times in three days, but was defeated; he became a monk and later returned to Liang.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor Xiaojing had fourteen sons.
details.label: included

details.point: Queen Wang gave birth to Emperor Xiaowu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Liu Rong, the Min king of Linjiang, was deposed as crown prince and later committed suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu De, the Xian king of Hejian, was granted the title in the second year of Emperor Jing's reign.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu De collected ancient books, including Zhou Guan, Shangshu, Rites, Mencius, and Laozi.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu De established doctors for Mao's Poetry and Zuo's Spring and Autumn Annals.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu De died after reigning for twenty-six years.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yuan, a later Hejian king, was deposed for cruelty and the kingdom was abolished.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yu, the Gong king of Lu, destroyed Confucius' old house and discovered ancient scriptures.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Fei, the Yi king of Jiangdu, attacked Wu during the rebellion and was awarded the emperor's flag.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Jian, son of Liu Fei, committed adultery, murder, and plotted rebellion, leading to his suicide.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Duan, the king of Jiaoxi, was cruel and physically weak, and his kingdom was abolished after his death.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Pengzu, the king of Zhao, was hypocritical and used coercion to control officials.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Sheng, the Jing king of Zhongshan, had over 120 children and was a drunkard.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Fa, the king of Changsha, was born to Tang Ji, a maid who impersonated Cheng Ji.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Yue, the Hui king of Guangchuan, died after thirteen years; his son Liu Qi was deposed.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Qu, son of Liu Qi, tortured and killed many concubines under Queen Zhaoxin's influence.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Qu was deposed and committed suicide; the kingdom was abolished.
details.label: included

details.point: Liu Shun, the Xian king of Changshan, was arrogant and his son Liu Bo was deposed.
details.label: included

details.point: The historian comments that most princes were arrogant and immoral, except Liu De of Hejian.
details.label: included

details.point: The Xiongnu ancestor was Chunwei, a descendant of the Xiahou family.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiongnu were nomadic, moving with livestock, no permanent cities or agriculture.
details.label: included

details.point: They had no writing, used oral agreements, and children learned archery early.
details.label: included

details.point: Men were all cavalry archers; customs favored attack when advantageous, retreat when not.
details.label: included

details.point: Social hierarchy: strong ate well, old ate leftovers; father's death son married stepmother.
details.label: included

details.point: Xia decline led to Zhou interactions with Rongdi; Zhou expelled Rongdi north of Jing and Luo rivers.
details.label: not_included

details.point: King You of Zhou killed by Quanrong with Shen; Zhou moved east, Qin became prince.
details.label: included

details.point: Qi Huan Gong attacked Shanrong; later Rongdi invaded Zhou, King Xiang fled.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Jin Wen Gong expelled Rongdi; Qin Mu Gong subdued eight Western Rong tribes.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhao, Wei, Yan built walls against Hu; Qin built Great Wall after conquering Yiqu.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Qin Shi Huang sent Meng Tian to attack Xiongnu, recovered land south of Yellow River.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiongnu Chanyu Touman failed against Qin; his son Maodun killed him and became Chanyu.
details.label: included

details.point: Maodun defeated Donghu, Yuezhi, Loufan, and Henan king, reuniting Xiongnu lands.
details.label: included

details.point: Maodun's Xiongnu had 300,000 archers; set up left/right kings, 24 officers, hereditary titles.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiongnu laws: death for murder, property confiscation for theft; no long imprisonment.
details.label: included

details.point: Maodun besieged Han Gaozu at Pingcheng; peace treaty with gifts and princess marriage.
details.label: included

details.point: After Gaozu's death, Maodun insulted Empress Lu; peace continued.
details.label: included

details.point: Laoshang Chanyu succeeded; Zhonghang Yue taught Xiongnu to resist Han culture.
details.label: included

details.point: Han Wudi launched campaigns: Wei Qing and Huo Qubing defeated Xiongnu, took Ordos.
details.label: included

details.point: After Huo Qubing's death, Xiongnu weakened; later Chanyu moved northwest, Han built cities.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Qian was a Han envoy sent to contact the Yuezhi against the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: He was captured by the Xiongnu and detained for over ten years.
details.label: included

details.point: He escaped and reached Dawan, then traveled to Kangju and Dayuezhi.
details.label: included

details.point: The Yuezhi had conquered Daxia and were not interested in attacking the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Qian spent over a year in Yuezhi and returned via the southern route, but was recaptured by the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: He escaped again and returned to Han after 13 years, with only one companion.
details.label: included

details.point: He reported on Dawan, Dayuezhi, Daxia, Kangju, and other states.
details.label: included

details.point: Dawan produced fine horses (sweating blood) and had walled cities.
details.label: included

details.point: The Han emperor was interested in expanding westward and contacting these states.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang Qian proposed a route through Shu to Daxia, avoiding Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: The Han reopened efforts to control the southwestern barbarians based on Zhang Qian's advice.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Qian was made Marquis of Bowang after accompanying Wei Qing.
details.label: included

details.point: He later lost his marquisate due to a military failure.
details.label: included

details.point: He proposed allying with Wusun to weaken the Xiongnu.
details.label: included

details.point: He led a second mission to Wusun with 300 men and many gifts.
details.label: included

details.point: Wusun was divided and did not agree to move east, but sent envoys to Han.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Zhang Qian sent deputies to Dawan, Kangju, Dayuezhi, Daxia, Anxi, Shendu, and others.
details.label: included

details.point: He died about a year after returning from Wusun.
details.label: included

details.point: His missions opened regular contacts between Han and the Western Regions.
details.label: included

details.point: Later Han envoys were often called 'Bowang Hou' to gain trust.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Hun, courtesy name Xuanchong, was from Jinyang, Taiyuan, son of Wei Sikong Wang Chang.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Hun inherited the title of Marquis of Jingling and served under Cao Shuang, but was dismissed after Cao Shuang's execution.
details.label: included

details.point: During the Xianxi period, Wang Hun became Yue Cavalry School Captain; after Emperor Wu's abdication, he was made General Yanglie and governor of Xuzhou.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Hun opened granaries to relieve famine and was later granted 1,800 additional households.
details.label: included

details.point: He served as General Dongzhonglang, guarding Zhuchang, and his governance strategies were often adopted.
details.label: included

details.point: As General of Conquering Captives and governor of Yuzhou, Wang Hun defeated Wu generals Xue Ying and Lu Shu.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Hun was appointed General Andong, Commander-in-Chief of Yangzhou military, guarding Shouchun.
details.label: included

details.point: He sent Ying Chuo to defeat Wu forces, burning grain, rice seedlings, and ships.
details.label: included

details.point: During the large-scale crusade against Wu, Wang Hun led troops from Hengjiang, capturing Wu generals and defeating enemy forces.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Hun's forces defeated Wu Prime Minister Zhang Ti, killing 7,800, leading to Sun Hao's surrender via He Zhi and Sun Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jun broke through Shitou and accepted Sun Hao's surrender, gaining greater fame.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Hun felt ashamed and jealous of Wang Jun, reporting his crimes; the emperor praised Wang Hun's role in pacifying Moling.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Hun was promoted to Duke, with additional households and titles for his sons and brother.
details.label: included

details.point: As General Zhengshu guarding Shouyang, Wang Hun comforted surrendered Wu people and was fair and decisive.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Hun advised against sending Sima You to a vassal state, citing historical precedents and family loyalty, but the emperor did not accept.
details.label: included

details.point: In early Taixi, Wang Hun became Situ; after Yang Jun's death, he was given military command but insisted on wearing civilian clothes.
details.label: included

details.point: During Sima Zhang's rebellion, Wang Hun feigned illness and resisted, later leading troops after Sima Zhang's execution.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Hun advised the emperor on conducting New Year's Day meetings to inquire about local conditions, which was accepted.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Hun died at age 75, posthumously named Yuan; his son Wang Ji succeeded him.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Ji, courtesy name Wuzi, was talented, married Princess Changshan, served as Zhongshu Lang and Sanqi Changshi, known for eloquence and extravagance.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Zhan was born in Linyi, Langye, grandson of Wang Hong.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Zhan studied diligently as a child, ignoring distractions.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Zhan was filial, mourning his father at age 12.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Zhan reformed from frivolous youth to disciplined adult.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Zhan served as Poyang Neishi and other official posts.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Zhan saved tens of thousands by advising against punishing rebels.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Zhan was known for three skills: shooting, chess, drinking.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Zhan died at 49, posthumously named Duzi.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jin married Princess Angu of Song.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jin resolved a land dispute by moral influence.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Jin released prisoners on winter solstice; one returned late due to wife's pregnancy.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Wang Jin refused to sign Donghunhou's head, earning Gaozu's praise.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jin was known for simple governance and charity during famine.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jin was a calligraphy sage, according to Xu Xixiu.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jin was tolerant, not prosecuting a thief who stole his curtains.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jun was calm during rebellion, keeping Guiyang stable.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Jun was indifferent to promotion, agreeing with Xie Yu to stop at Shizhong.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen was recommended as talented by Wang Gui.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Chen was a son of a famous official, cold to low-born people.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Xun was praised by Emperor as equal to Yan Hui, died at 26.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Xuanmu Zhang, named Chunhua, was from Pinggao, Hanoi, and married Sima Yi.
details.label: included

details.point: Zhang killed a maid to protect Sima Yi's secret feigned illness.
details.label: included

details.point: She gave birth to Sima Shi, Sima Zhao, Sima Gan, and Princess Nanyang.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Jinghuai Xiahou, named Yuanrong, was from Qiao, Pei, and married Sima Shi.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiahou was poisoned by Sima Shi in 237 for being a Wei relative.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Jingxian Yang, named Huiyu, from Mount Tai, married Sima Shi after Xiahou's death.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang was honored as Empress Dowager Hongxun after Sima Yan's ascension.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Queen of Civilization Wang, named Yuanyou, from Tan, married Sima Zhao.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang warned Sima Zhao about Zhong Hui's potential rebellion.
details.label: included

details.point: She gave birth to Sima Yan and other children.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Wu Yuan Yang, named Yan, from Huayin, married Sima Yan.
details.label: included

details.point: Yang was jealous and selected only fair-skinned women for the harem.
details.label: included

details.point: She opposed changing the crown prince despite his incompetence.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Empress Wu Dao Yang, named Zhi, was made queen in 274.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yang was deposed and starved to death after her father Yang Jun's execution.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Concubine Zuo Fen, named Fen, was a talented writer in the harem.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Hu Guifei, named Fang, was favored and once scratched Emperor Wu's finger.
details.label: included

details.point: Empress Hui Jia, named Nanfeng, married Crown Prince Sima Zhong.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Jia was jealous and cruel, killing pregnant concubines.
details.label: included

details.point: She was deposed and forced to commit suicide by Sima Lun in 300.
details.label: included

details.point: Mengchangjun's surname is Tian Mingwen, son of Jingguo Jun Tian Ying.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Ying was a younger son of King Qi Wei and brother of King Qi Xuan's concubine.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Ying served as prime minister of Qi for 11 years under King Xuan and King Min.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Ying granted Xue Yi to Tian Wen after King Min came to power.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Wen was born on May 5th and initially ordered not to be raised, but his mother secretly raised him.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Wen convinced his father Tian Ying to value him by arguing about fate and the portal.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Wen criticized his father for accumulating wealth without attracting worthy men.
details.label: included

details.point: Tian Ying changed his attitude and made Tian Wen head of household, attracting guests.
details.label: included

details.point: After Tian Ying's death, Tian Wen inherited Xue Yi and became Lord Mengchang.
details.label: included

details.point: Mengchangjun hosted thousands of diners, treating them equally and recording their relatives' residences.
details.label: included

details.point: A guest committed suicide after realizing Mengchangjun's food was the same as his own.
details.label: included

details.point: Mengchangjun was dissuaded from going to Qin by Su Dai's puppet analogy.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Mengchangjun went to Qin in King Min's 25th year and became prime minister, but was imprisoned.
details.label: included

details.point: A guest disguised as a dog stole the white fox fur to bribe King Zhao's concubine for his release.
details.label: included

details.point: A guest imitated a rooster's crow to escape Hangu Pass at midnight.
details.label: included

details.point: Mengchangjun passed through Zhao, where locals mocked his height; his guests killed hundreds.
details.label: included

details.point: Mengchangjun became Qi's prime minister after returning, and planned to attack Qin but was dissuaded by Su.
details.label: included

details.point: Mengchangjun dismissed Wei Zi for donating tax to a worthy man; later that man proved his innocence by suicide.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Mengchangjun fled to Wei after King Min planned to kill him, and later helped Yan defeat Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: Feng Xuan collected debts in Xue Yi, burned deeds for the poor, and later restored Mengchangjun's position by lobbying Qin and Qi.
details.label: included

details.point: First year of Putong: amnesty, tax exemptions for poor, aid for widows and orphans.
details.label: included

details.point: Solar eclipse on Bingzi day.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Hong appointed Taiwei and Yangzhou governor; Xiao Jing appointed Anxi general and Yingzhou governor.
details.label: included

details.point: Wang Feng succeeded Wang Lai as Shangshu Zuopushe after Wang Lai's mother died.
details.label: included

details.point: Funan and Goryeo sent tribute.
details.label: included

details.point: Canopus appeared in second month.
details.label: included

details.point: Gao Xi sent tribute in third month.
details.label: included

details.point: Henan king sent tribute in fourth month.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Tiao appointed chariot and cavalry general in sixth month.
details.label: not_included

details.point: Yangtze, Huai, and ocean floods in seventh month.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Lun appointed Jiangzhou governor in seventh month.
details.label: included

details.point: Wei Tiao died in eighth month.
details.label: included

details.point: Star appeared in east in ninth month.
details.label: included

details.point: Xiao Gang appointed Pingxi general and Yizhou governor in tenth month.
details.label: included

details.point: Second year: Xiao Zong appointed Zhenyou general; Xiao Gang moved to Xuzhou governor.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor sacrificed at southern suburbs in first month.
details.label: included

details.point: Edict: care for elderly and orphans, set up orphanage in capital.
details.label: included

details.point: Amnesty on Wuzi day.
details.label: included

details.point: Emperor sacrificed at Mingtang in second month.
details.label: included

details.point: Heavy snow in third month, three feet deep.
details.label: included
